Craig Bellamy suggested the new four-match international window had counted against Wales after Sunday's Nations League defeat against Denmark.

His side failed to build on Thursday's win over Norway as they were deservedly beaten thanks to a second-half Rasmus Hojlund penalty.

It was a third loss in four games played inside 10 days as part of the newly elongated international break.

Head coach Bellamy said his injury-hit squad paid the price for the heavy workload he feels benefits the bigger nations and "puts a real stress" on countries like Wales.

"Physically, I completely agree with the ones who don't like [the new window]. It makes no sense," he added.

"Four games at this type of levelâ¦ for the other nations, we know who they are because I was in the room when they all voted for it.

"I was one of the ones who wasn't [voting for it], because we know it's a complete disadvantage to us."

News.title: Courts backlog will fall despite scrapping of jury trial plan, minister says
News.content:
The courts backlog will still fall despite plans to curb jury trials being scrapped, the justice secretary has told the BBC.

Alex Norris said introducing legislation for judge-only trials "was always going to be the most complicated to implement" and would have slowed down reforms.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's decision abandons proposals introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government to allow judges in England and Wales to make the sole decision on cases that would lead to a sentence of less than three years.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said only complex fraud and financial offences would be judge-only - and it proposes thousands of medium-level crimes should stay with volunteer magistrates, who sit without a jury.

Norris told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the backlog would start falling "in this Parliament", but would not say by how much.

He said it would fall significantly over the next decade "as a result of the changes we're making".

The Conservatives said it was a "major victory" for those who fought to defend trial by jury, while criminal lawyers welcomed the decision but voiced concern about the implications of abolishing a defendant's right to ask for a jury trial.

The Criminal Bar Association (CBA) warned this would keep more middle-ranking cases before magistrates and shift 25,000 cases a year onto magistrates' courts.

Former justice secretary David Lammy first announced the plans to curb jury trials in December following a recommendation in a major review of the court system in England and Wales.

The series of radical reforms, including scaling back jury trials, were presented as the best way of turning around record backlogs which, in turn, were exacerbating the prison population crisis.

The backlog - which has led to record delays for defendants and victims - currently stands at nearly 81,000 cases, having rocketed largely thanks to cuts before the pandemic and court closures during national lockdowns.

News.title: Daughter of MP murdered five years ago tells BBC politicians still at risk
News.content:
Separately, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch confirmed to the BBC the man who pleaded guilty to sending her threatening messages also sent them to her family.

Kieran Kyle, 43, pleaded guilty to two counts of sending communication of an indecent or offensive nature to Badenoch and her family when he appeared in court in September. He will be sentenced on October 29.

"I just think that whether it's Nigel Farage, or even Keir Starmer who had his home fire bombed, that there is a threat to politicians that is increasing and we just need to crack down on this," she told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

Asked how Badenoch coped with threats to her safety, she replied: "it's really tough, but you just have to get on with it".

Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice, who told the BBC he also experienced threats to his safety, told the programme "this was far from where any of us want to be".

"We have to find the middle ground where we're accessible but we're protected and in the overall scheme of things if that requires a bit of extra taxpayers' money, I think hopefully voters would say 'yes'."

Amess said her father "loved meeting people", saying "he was one of the easier members of parliament to take a meeting with because that's what he lived for - to meet people, shake their hands, smile, help them with their problems. My dad wouldn't have wanted constituency surgeries to stop."

She added that he would have wanted to be alerted to someone being reported as a potential threat.

His killer, Ali Harbi Ali had been referred to the government's counter-terror programme Prevent in October 2014 but his case was closed in 2016.

A review published in February 2025 found Ali's Prevent case was closed too early after "problematic" assessments.

Anti-migrant protesters gathered in a seaside town as more than 100 migrants arrived in a dinghy after crossing the English Channel from France on Sunday.

French media reported there were around 120 migrants on board the vessel, which appeared to have set off from near the Utah Beach area of Normandy on Sunday morning. This marks the third such crossing from the area in the space of a month.

Around 100 anti-migrant demonstrators gathered near Haslar Marina in Gosport following reports that authorities were preparing for the arrival of the vessel. The dinghy was shadowed by French rescue vessels until it entered English waters, where it was met by RNLI boats, according to ship tracking data.

open image in gallery Anti-immigrant demonstrations have broken out across the coastal town of Gosport ( Getty )

Footage capturing scenes near Gosport’s Haslar Marina shows crowds gathered around police vans chanting “shame on you” and “deport the lot”.

The demonstration follows heightened scrutiny over migrant arrivals to the UK, where similar anti-immigration protests have flared up across coastal towns including Dover and Portsmouth.

Earlier today, the Reform leader of Hampshire council George Madgwick, said on X:“I hate to report that Gosport is the planned landing point for today’s migrant boat.

“This is an absolute shambles,” he said, “But there is hope. Last time they planned to dock there they changed course. Let’s hope they do the same today.

“If you’re heading there stay peaceful and calm.”

open image in gallery Demonstrators are hoping to deter the arrival of a vessel understood to be hosting immigrants ( PA Wire )

Similar scenes unfolded in Gosport last month when protesters gathered expecting a landing after coaches and ambulances were spotted nearby.

On that occasion, the passengers – 51 migrants who refused help from the French coastguard, arrived in Dover after being transferred to Border Security Command boats.

A government spokesperson said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border. It is vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival.”

The provisional total for Channel crossings this year is 19,451.

This is down 43 per cent on this time last year and 23% below the figure at this stage in 2024.

Authorities have since placed a dispersal order under Section 34 of the Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014 to cover the town of Gosport.

This order is in place until 7am on Tuesday, 6 October. Those who refuse to comply with the order are committing a criminal offence and are liable for arrest.

A sharp split in how male and female leaders perceive opportunities for career advancement at work has been highlighted in a new report.

A study conducted by the Chartered Management Institute (CMI) revealed that more than two in five male managers believed equal opportunities existed for men and women to progress into leadership or management roles, compared with just one in four female managers.

The survey, which questioned 600 UK managers, found that over four in five respondents could not rule out gender stereotypes or unconscious bias influencing young women's promotion prospects within their organisations.

Only one in six surveyed said unconscious bias or gender stereotyping never played a role in promotion decisions, while a quarter pointed to bias or a male-dominated culture as a key obstacle holding back young women from gaining their initial management or leadership position.

Just one in four managers strongly agreed that young women in their workplace received support to build leadership or management skills.

Ann Francke, chief executive of the CMI, said: "Men and women are looking at the same workplaces and seeing very different levels of opportunity.

"When male managers are almost twice as likely as female managers to believe the playing field is level, employers should be asking what they are missing.

"We spend a lot of time talking about the glass ceiling, but the problem starts much earlier.

"Young women want to lead, yet too many are not being seen, backed or given that crucial first opportunity to step up.

"Businesses cannot afford to let that talent go to waste. We need managers who actively spot potential, open doors and give the next generation the confidence and opportunity to lead."

The report concluded that a clear "deep divide" remains in how male and female managers evaluate career progression opportunities.

Restaurant chain Slim Chickens has set its sights on opening a raft of drive-throughs across the UK as part of expansion plans set to create up to around 1,000 jobs in the next year.

The brand, which opened its inaugural restaurant in the UK in 2018, is launching its first drive-through in Broughton Shopping Park, north Wales, on October 6, with the site to act as the blueprint for more nationwide.

Boparan Restaurant Group – which runs the master franchise for Slim Chickens in the UK and Europe – is looking to tap into booming demand for the convenience of drive-through fast-food and the ever-growing appetite for fried chicken.

Rich Pigott, managing director for Boparan Restaurants, told the Press Association the group is looking to open between 15 and 20 sites next year across the UK, with the majority set to be in the drive-through format.

With each site employing up to 50 workers, the expansion plans are set to see the firm create between 800 and 1,000 roles in the UK.

It sees the group accelerate its openings, after eight launches in 2026, which has already taken its UK estate to more than 80.

Mr Pigott said: “We’ve got ambitious plans for the drive-through format, and Broughton gives us the opportunity to take everything people love about Slim Chickens… and bring it to guests in a completely new way.”

He added it is “only the beginning for Slim Chickens drive-throughs in the UK”.

He said the drive-throughs will be focused on sites such as retail parks, adding to its current estate in high streets and shopping centres.

Founded in Fayetteville, Arkansas in the US, Slim Chickens’s American chain is largely focused on drive-throughs, and the format is becoming increasingly popular in the UK.

Mr Pigott said: “It’s convenient for people to go to a drive-through and take food home.”

He said it is a competitive market in the hospitality sector as consumers come under pressure amid soaring energy and fuel costs.

“People will reduce their spending habits to reduce their bills,” he said. “But they will still want to go out.

“People might cut back from going to a restaurant two or three times a week to once a week, so you’ve got to be the best in the market to make sure people come to you.”

Boparan Restaurant Group, which also runs brands such as Carluccio’s, Giraffe and Gourmet Burger Kitchen, is also planning expansion further across Europe through company-owned sites and franchise partnerships.

Tom Patrick, marketing director at Boparan Restaurants, said the drive-through launch in the UK is a “huge moment for the brand”.

He added: “We’re excited to be using our new app and new AI technology to make the guest journey in our drive-through as seamless as in-store.”

A public investigation probing fatalities among individuals receiving care from mental health services is evaluating whether to call an end to a contentious patient-monitoring camera technology.

The Lampard Inquiry, tasked with investigating the deaths of thousands of Essex mental health patients, is preparing to determine if emergency interim guidance should be issued regarding the placement of the Oxevision system on hospital wards.

Campaign groups have informed the panel that the technology presents safety risks, asserting that care staff have substituted direct human observations with digital monitoring, with fatal consequences for some patients.

Evidence submitted to the inquiry indicates that Oxevision has been adopted by 50 per cent of mental health trusts across England. The system operates by remotely tracking movement and abnormal behaviour, alongside calculating pulse and respiration rates.

Legal representatives from the firm Bindmans, acting on behalf of the Stop Oxevision campaign, have urged the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) to inspect whether the platform's collection, processing and storage of patient data complies with the law.

Nina Ali, a partner at Hodge Jones & Allen who represents 120 affected families in the proceedings, said: "People across the country are dying or being harmed while under mental health care as this inquiry continues to sit and hear evidence. We cannot stand by and let more people lose their lives and become part of these haunting statistics.

"The use of Oxevision has no place in mental health care. It is intrusive, clinically ineffective and potentially unlawful.”

A 24-hour invasive, non-consensual monitoring system must not and cannot ever replace quality human care, especially when, as seen in the devastating case of our client Elise Sebastian, staff muted alerts and left her alone for nearly 30 minutes before she was found unresponsive in her room and died.

"We have seen case after case where people have needlessly lost their lives because the system alerts were ignored, misunderstood or muted.

"Or where staff were, by default, heavily reliant on the system pitched as an ‘assistive tool’. This is a frightening show of neglect and patients deserve better."

She noted that her clients additionally want measures to address the "shambolic lack of CPR training for staff looking after the most vulnerable in our society".

Ms Ali added: "We are calling for all staff to undergo face-to-face CPR training delivered by an independent body, and any staff who fail to meet the requirements should be removed from patient care."

Among those monitored by Oxevision was Sophie Alderman, 27, who had a history of severe mental ill health and self-harm, and who died by suicide in August 2022 at Rochford hospital in Essex.

Her mother, Tammy Smith, informed the inquiry that the digital monitoring was unsafe and worsened her daughter’s paranoia.

Speaking ahead of Monday’s inquiry hearing, Ms Smith said: "Sophie was meant to be safe in hospital.

"Instead, a camera was placed in her bedroom without any clear record that she understood it, consented to it, or that anyone considered the impact it would have on a young woman whose illness contributed to a deep discomfort of cameras and a fear of being spied on.

"Oxevision invaded the only relatively private space Sophie had on an inpatient ward, it risked deepening her distress, and its alert function failed to protect her when it mattered most.

"No family should have to wonder whether their loved one died believing help was coming because a system had raised an alert that no-one answered.

"I will continue to add my voice to calls for the use of Oxevision to be halted, and hope that the coming hearings are a sign that Baroness Lampard is listening to those calls."

Lio, the business that created Oxevision, has been approached for comment.

In October 2025, Laura Cozens, head of patient safety at Lio, told the Lampard Inquiry "the platform may not be suitable for everyone – and we do recognise that".

As reported by the BBC, when asked by Nicholas Griffin KC: "Would you agree that filming a patient 24 hours a day constitutes a very significant invasion of privacy?" Ms Cozens said: "Possibly, yes".

Ms Cozens maintained that the technology played a crucial role in preventing severe incidents, including falls on a dementia ward.

She stated there were 1,774 instances where staff received support in responding to circumstances where patients could otherwise have suffered serious harm, adding that the platform assisted in freeing staff time from administrative paperwork, the BBC reported.

More than 160 offshore oil workers are considering strike action that their union claims could "severely disrupt" UK fuel supplies.

The Unite union said workers at oil and gas operator Apache had backed strike action over a pay dispute.

Unite said the action could begin this month and would include seven Apache assets associated with the Forties and Beryl oil fields.

It could lead to the entire pipeline system going down, it warned.

Average UK diesel prices have topped £2 a litre for the first time and have rocketed in recent months because of the disruption to global supplies caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine.

Higher fuel prices helped to drive inflation to a five-month high in August, ramping up the cost of living for householders.

Average UK diesel prices have topped £2 a litre for the first time ( AFP/Getty )

Last week, the UK and other leading G7 nations bowed to White House pressure and agreed to release 100 million barrels of fuel and oil from emergency stocks amid surging prices.

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said: "We will not tolerate unacceptable pay offers and threats to withhold back pay from Apache.

"The operator is raking in eye-watering profits. It’s treating its highly-skilled workers with contempt. Apache has been caught red-handed in embarking on shameful corporate greed."

Unite industrial officer Stevie Davies said: "Unite’s members are being left with no option but to take strike action. Any disruption to Apache’s platforms would have a direct hit on the Forties pipeline and potentially severely affecting the UK’s fuel supplies.

"The behaviour of Apache is reckless and it could have far reaching consequences for workers, operators and consumers."

Apache has been approached for comment.

A claim against Google seeking more than £1 billion in damages for millions of consumers over “hidden charges” on Play Store app sales is going to trial in the UK.

The class action is being brought on behalf of around 20 million UK consumers and businesses who purchased something on the Google Play Store or on an Android phone between October 1 2015 and July 31 2026.

The claim is being heard in the UK’s Competition Appeal Tribunal (CAT), with proceedings commencing on Tuesday.

It alleges that Google broke competition law by charging app developers a commission of up to 30% on purchases made through the Play Store, and that this cost was passed onto consumers in the prices they paid.

Paid-for apps, subscription payments like within dating, fitness, music and gaming apps, and upgrades to unlock ad-free versions or features are all included in the claim.

It also includes in-game extras like coins, gems, extra lives and power-ups that people paid money for.

For example, if a Candy Crush player spent £10 on gold bars for extra lives and power-ups then, for most of the claim period, Google kept £3 of that and passed £7 to the game’s maker.

The claim alleges that that £3 was passed onto players through higher prices.

Google says its Play Store offers some of the lowest fees in the market and that it would defend its services “vigorously”.

A spokesman said: “Android gives people more choice than any other mobile platform in deciding which apps and app stores they use, with Play offering some of the lowest fees in the market.

“This lawsuit ignores that choice as well as the competitive market in which we operate, and we will defend our services vigorously.”

The claim is being brought to court by Liz Coll, a consumer tech policy expert and former manager for charity Citizens Advice, and represented by law firm Hausfield.

Legal action was launched in 2021, but it has faced delays amid separate claims being settled, including Google’s owner Alphabet agreeing to pay £260 million in September to settle a class action on behalf of UK app developers.

A similar claim against Apple was won last year when the CAT found the company abused its dominant position in the market by charging about 30% commission on app sales and in-app purchases.

Liz Coll said: “Millions of us have paid for apps, games and subscriptions on our phones without knowing a hidden charge was built into the price.

“This trial is about getting that money back for people who use their phone and apps every day.”

Lesley Hannah, a partner at Hausfield, said: “Google has been able to use its position in the market to charge an excessive commission for well over a decade.

“And it’s the consumer that has paid the price.”

News.title: Jibulu emerges as England World Cup bolter in Sale defeat of Saracens
News.content:
Could Nathan Jibulu, the Sale Sharks hooker, emerge as a bolter for England’s World Cup squad? With Steve Borthwick, the England head coach, watching from the stands, the 23-year-old produced the kind of “wrecking-ball” performance in this surprise victory for the North West side that suggested he is on course to do so.

After their tame defeat by Bristol Bears in the opening round, few had predicted that Alex Sanderson’s side had much hope against Saracens, who were looking to back up their impressive win at Welford Road last weekend. But Jibulu’s powerhouse display on either side of the ball typified their stout and physical resistance, backed up by a masterly display by George Ford.

Given the age and injury profile of England hookers Jamie George and Luke Cowan-Dickie, who both missed this contest, and the fact that Theo Dan has yet to make a forceful challenge for the position in the national side, Sanderson is in no doubt that Jibulu has the X factor required to break into Borthwick’s squad this season.

“This is the player that any time you watch him play, he impacts – he takes metres either side of the ball – and we knew that he had that in him,” Sanderson said.

“It shows he’s of international class. He nailed his line-outs, on the back of that he was a wrecking-ball runner causing havoc around the field.

“This is the person that we knew, this is the player that we knew we had in him. It could be the year where he explodes onto the international scene. I hope it is, but it’s early days.

“He’s that quality, he’s that kind of an athlete. You can get away with being fast and skilful in the Prem, but it’s another level again in terms of the power that’s required at international level. And he’s got that ability, he’s immensely strong.”

Borthwick will have left the StoneX Stadium on Sunday evening with a full notebook. Ben Bamber, Sale’s 6ft 9ins lock, has also been attracting his interest and it was Bamber who crossed for the decisive try, Sale’s third, hitting a great line off Ford to finish like an outside centre.

News.title: Brilliant Hamilton storms to podium despite another Ferrari blunder
News.content:
One of the big talking points heading into the weekend has been the cooling vests drivers wear under their overalls (as opposed to the jacket-like ones they wear when they’re out of their cars). Russell told us in our Brits media session on Thursday that Mercedes had decided to forego the vests here, since the technology was not yet refined. The system works by pumping a coolant through thin tubes stitched into the vest.

Drivers have complained that the connecting valve to the pump, which was originally placed on the side of the vest, proved uncomfortable when combined with the high G-forces experienced in an F1 car. On some vests the connector has been moved to find a more comfortable position, but the thick material and tubing have also proved cumbersome under the driver’s fireproof overalls. There are also concerns over the reliability of some systems and the possibility that a failure will mean the vest will have the opposite effect and work as a heat insulator.preferring to spend that money instead on car upgrades. The money to develop the vests comes out of the budget cap.

But Russell added that the FIA should make the tech mandatory and develop it themselves, describing this race as like being in a “sauna”.The Briton’s comments prompted a sarcastic response from Verstappen - who doesn’t wear the vests either, out of choice - who said Russell “shouldn’t make a fuss”.

“I don’t need it,” Verstappen said. “Maybe I suffer a bit less from the heat.. I find a Finnish sauna at 85 degrees a lot hotter... You shouldn’t make a fuss. Yes, it is hot, but that’s part of it. You have to train for that.”

The Dutchman added: “When I was 18, I had a bit more trouble with these conditions. But after that, I started training more in the heat, such as in the sauna and a steam room, so that I can handle the sweating better and the fact that your head gets very hot. Maybe I should take him (Russell) to the sauna a few times.”

These two have history, of course. They’ve sniped at each other for years. In 2024, in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, it reached a peak when Verstappen described Russell as being “two-faced” and said he had lost all respect for him. Russell responded by saying Verstappen was “a bully”. Earlier this year, the Mercedes driver said Verstappen could always retire from the sport and drive sports cars if he didn’t like the regs.

News.title: Rees-Zammit taunts Pollock as Bristol outplay Northampton
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Bristol Bears vs Northampton Saints from the Gallagher Prem, with both teams looking to build on winning starts following the opening weekend of action.

Last season’s champions Northampton kicked off their title defence with an emphatic 59-26 victory over a new-look Newcastle Red Bulls outfit at Franklin’s Gardens.

While Henry Pollock’s new cornrow hairstyle was the centre of attention at kick-off, the limelight was soon stolen by Tommy Freeman and James Pater, who both notched hat-tricks for Phil Dowson’s side.

Of 19-year-old full-back Pater, who starts on the bench today, Dowson said afterwards: “He doesn’t let the occasion get to him. He has an incredible skill set, great speed and ability to manoeuvre away from defenders.”

Bristol, meanwhile, began their season with an impressive 34-24 victory away at Sale Sharks, with Pat Lam’s side ensuring Courtney Lawes’s return to the English game was a disappointing one.

Louis Rees-Zammit was operating in his favoured wing position and got Bristol off to a strong start with two tries in the opening 23 minutes, offering Lam hope of a fruitful campaign from the Welshman.

“When you look at our wingers in the past, they scored a lot of tries and Louis is a world-class finisher,” the Bristol director of rugby said. “You get the ball to him in space and you create the opportunity, there’s a good chance he’ll finish it.”

Northampton will be hoping for a repeat of the meeting between the sides at Franklin Gardens in May when they thumped Bristol 94-33, but they have not won at Ashton Gate since 2021.

Both teams have made a pair of changes following their opening-weekend victories, with England international Ellis Genge among the players to drop out after spraining his wrist against Sale.

News.title: Sublime England thrash Croatia in best performance for a decade
News.content:
We came out of the World Cup wondering if Tuchel really had an idea of how he can get England over the line. After last Saturday’s defeat by world and European champions Spain, followed by Tuesday’s win over the Czech Republic we still did not know.

But here the standard was set – it was an exhilarating example of the football England are capable of. On display we saw the speed, the movement, the passes under pressure, the ambition, the control and aggression. This was the full package. Bottle it. Bag it. Believe it.

Croatia have an ageing team and are in transition, but they were left looking callow. It looked as though it was men against boys. There were plenty of boys in the stands, with 6,200 children allowed in for what was supposed to be a behind-closed-doors fixture – Croatia’s punishment for crowd trouble.

Their new head coach Slaven Bilic would doubtless have been relieved that the match was not played in front of the usual, passionate, partisan crowd. Even then some of the kids booed and left early. Bilic looked shell-shocked. As well he might.

News.title: Russell must do something wacky now after disappointing Bahrain GP qualifying
News.content:
The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he says Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he said. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”

News.title: Bath complete revenge mission on Exeter despite imperious Feyi-Waboso
News.content:
Bath held off a furious comeback from Exeter, led by the irrepressible Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, to avenge their Gallagher Prem semi-final defeat here in June.

It felt as if lightning might strike Bath twice. Once again Exeter overturned a 26-10 half-time deficit, to manufacture a second-half lead thanks to a pair of blistering finishes by Feyi-Waboso. Four months ago, Bath failed to take a drop goal in the closing stages, but this time with the reassuring presence of Finn Russell at fly-half, they kept their cool.

The Scotland playmaker twice sent penalties deep into the Exeter 22 from where Stephen Varney conceded a yellow card and penalty try before Bath replacement Ted Hill powered through a thicket of Exeter tacklers.

“Finn is one of the best 10s in the world and I thought he had a very good game,” Johann van Graan, the Bath head of rugby, said. “His decision making is above most players in the world and I thought that came through tonight.”

Despite the appearance of yet another high-scoring shoot-out, both teams defended with real bite, although Bath struggled to lay a finger on Feyi-Waboso who ended up in a scrap with a fan in the stands here when he was a spectator in May. He exacted a measure of revenge beating eight defenders and carried for 132 metres.

“Manny still needs game time,” Rob Baxter, the Exeter director of rugby, said. “When he’s on the ball, you see something incredible, but it is his ability to get on the ball again. He is just getting his game minutes and match fitness up.”

News.title: FTSE 100 tumbles amid bond market sell-off
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. House prices fell unexpectedly last month as mortgage borrowers prepare for a jump in interest rates.

Typical property values declined by 0.2pc during September, reversing 0.2pc growth in August, according to the Nationwide house price index.

The figure was much worse than analysts had forecasts, with most expecting prices to remain steady.

Over the course of the year to September, the rate of house price growth halved from 1.6pc to 0.8pc, which was the weakest rate since December 2025.

The value of the average home has fallen to £274,251 over concerns the Bank of England is on the cusp of raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for mortgage holders.

Money markets indicate there is an 84pc chance policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4pc in November in an effort to bring down inflation caused by the Iran war energy shock.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:“Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop.

“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns.

“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank Rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Polanski urges Miliband to block Rosebank oil field over Israel links | Green leader claims North Sea project is a test of Foreign Secretary’s proposed sanctions regime

2) Netherlands ditches wealth tax over exodus fears | Dutch PM scraps plan to target paper profits, instead introducing a more convention capital gains levy

3) Diesel crisis deepens as UK’s biggest refinery shuts for 10 weeks | Fears of squeeze on supplies after fuel costs rise higher than £2 per litre

4) Debt-ridden France branded ‘the new sick man of Europe’ | Investors hope the European Central Bank sees the struggling country as ‘too big to fail’

5) Britain blocks foreign lawyers after surge in south Asian applicants | Bar Standards Board halts scheme unless candidates have already secured a position

What happened overnight

The cost of government borrowing edged higher in Asia as soaring energy costs sparked inflation fears.

Bond yields, a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money, surged in September as investors brace for a period where interest rates stay higher for ​longer.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year Treasury notes hit 5.31pc, the ‌highest level since mid-June 2007. The 10-year yield gained 87 basis points in the July-September quarter, the biggest quarterly rise since 1994.

Market focus has been on how long US Treasury yields stay above the psychologically important 5pc level, while some investors even contemplate the possibility of yields breaching 6pc.

Yields in Japan have climbed to multi-decade highs too, while those in Germany, France and Britain have all hit 17 to 19 year peaks.

On Thursday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government ​bond yield was at 3.11pc, not far from the 30-year high it hit last week.

Asian technology stocks rose after a boost from AI chipmaker Micron, ​although US bonds struggled ‌after their sharpest quarterly sell-off in more than three decades as inflation risks from elevated energy prices linger.

Stalling peace talks between the US and Iran to end the seven-month-long war in the Middle East have kept crude prices aloft.Brent futures surged 42pc in the July-September quarter.

The high-stakes earnings from Micron, a key supplier to AI bellwether Nvidia, signalled strong demand for AI memory chips, with financial commitments under long-term supply agreements at $32 billion, up from $22 billion in June.

That helped push tech-heavy stock markets in Asia higher. Japan’s Nikkei jumped over 3pc, and South Korea’s Kospi reversed earlier losses to gain 1.7pc. Taiwan’s stock benchmark was 0.8pc higher.

News.title: Chewing tobacco killed 250,000 people in one year, study shows
News.content:
Chewing tobacco killed around a quarter of a million people in 2023, with use of the product remaining stubbornly high, according to research.

The smokeless tobacco, which is placed between the cheek and lower gum, is particularly popular in south Asia. It is flavoured and sometimes sweetened, and users often spit out unwanted juices while chewing. It is often viewed as safer than smoking but it is a major cause of stroke, as well as head and neck cancer.

Chewing tobacco is different to white snus or nicotine pouches, which contain no tobacco. These white pouches are also made up of flavourings and sometimes sweeteners, and deliver a hit of nicotine through the lining of the mouth.

Despite a successful fight against smoking over the last few decades, rates of chewing tobacco use have fallen little and it has often been overlooked in tobacco control efforts, researchers point out. In a study published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation in the US estimate that 241 million people aged 15 years and older used chewing tobacco in 2023.

Researchers looked at data on use in 204 countries between 1990 and 2023 and found that there was no significant decrease in the number of users of chewing tobacco over that period. And in 24 countries there was a significant uptick in the number of people using the product. Researchers estimate that about one in five men and one in 10 women in south Asia chewed tobacco in 2023.

Bangladesh has seen the biggest increase in the number of people using the product with 15 million new users between 1990 and 2023. Nepal, Madagascar and Yemen also saw increases in the number of users.

In India 105 million people chew tobacco regularly, accounting for just over two thirds of users globally. Historically, Indians would chew paan, tobacco in its raw form which was mixed with betel leaf and areca nut, a mild stimulant. But the use of chewing tobacco exploded in the 1980s when manufacturers began grinding these into a powder and selling them in packets known as gutkha. This was banned in 2012 but is still widely available. Chewing tobacco is also popular in Pakistan, China and Vietnam.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Mardle: Humphries can do it against anyone from any position
Sports.content:
Sky Sports Darts pundit Wayne Mardle reflects on Luke Humphries becoming a two-time World Grand Prix champion after 'Cool Hand' rallied from 3-0 down against Gerwyn Price in the final to triumph 6-4 at the double-start event…

I may be wrong but, a few years ago, I don't think Luke would have hung in a game like that to win it.

That was sheer belief: guts and determination knowing that you can do it - and he can do it against anyone from any position.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Wayne Mardle looks at how Humphries' win sets him up for the rest of the darting year

When you have won before, and Luke has done many, many times and in many, many ways, there is that belief of, 'I'm under pressure but let's just see as I know if I settle down my game can win', rather than 'oh no, I am going to get beat or get embarrassed 6-0'.

He played his game and he won. I am not saying it's that simple but sometimes you have to simplify it.

When he won the fourth set he relaxed and Price tightened up.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Humphries' 105 checkout to deny Price a 4-0 lead in the final proved crucial in Leicester

Humphries was in trouble, then a bit more and then a bit more - so to get out of it was an incredible effort.

The last two sets were his best.

He was under the cosh for more than an hour but didn't succumb. He stood up to everything Gezzy threw at him, which was a lot.

Luke can now go into the World Championship thinking, 'someone stop me'. To do it in set-play registers and sticks with you.

If Humphries and Price meet in a World final, something could crop up. This is all about one-upmanship.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Humphries explains why his World Gran Prix victory - his first major crown in over a year - means so much to him

On to Price, and he says things in the spur of the moment but the way he competes, he wants it. You can't be as focused as he was in the final if you don't care.

It is disheartening and disappointing when you are 3-0 up and don't win but he has lost enough finals to know nothing is a given.

He is still a young man and will get many more opportunities. He knows he is good enough.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gerwyn Price was left to rue 'missed opportunities' as he surrendered a big lead against Humphries and remained without a major win since 2022

But let's get it right, the way Humphries played in the last two sets - a 106 average and a 107 average - is unplayable.

Gezzy can't beat himself up too much.

What's next?

Sports.title: Sale defy Vermeulen's first-half red card to beat Saracens
Sports.content:
Sale Sharks won a real battle against Saracens in the Gallagher Prem

Sale defied Jacques Vermeulen's first-half red card to dispatch Saracens 21-17 with Tom O'Flaherty emerging as the star of a slugfest at StoneX Stadium.

Vermeulen was shown a 20-minute red for a dangerous tackle on Tomos Williams at a point in the first half when Alex Lozowski was in the sin bin because of the same offence.

Saracens then took control but it was only temporary and in the 41st minute O'Flaherty produced the match's pivotal moment by racing over for a dynamic solo try.

It was part of a dominant second half from Sale, who capitalised on the hosts' lifeless performance to bounce back after losing to Bristol on the opening weekend with their hooker Nathan Jibulu also outstanding.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

Referee Joe James and TMO Hamish Smales experienced a busy opening half an hour, issuing two cards and disallowing a Saracens try.

It had started so well for Sale when Jibulu finished a driving maul but soon after centre Lozowski was sent to the sin bin for a high tackle on Alfie Barbeary, who was forced off for an HIA.

Worse was to come when Vermeulen was given his marching orders for a dangerous challenge on Williams as the Sharks looked to press home an attack down the right touchline.

It meant Saracens were given the opportunity to play against 13 for three minutes and Sale's situation would have deteriorated further had Courtney Lawes not seen an attempted deliberate knock go backwards.

Almost immediately the hosts appeared to have taken advantage but a Nick Tompkins try was ruled out because of obstruction by Nick Isiekwe and it was not until Eroni Mawi bundled over in the 34th minute that they were off the mark.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

For all Saracens' sustained pressure they still trailed 7-5 and a minute into the second half that became 14-5 after O'Flaherty caught a George Ford up and under that went sideways and then slipped through the home defence before sprinting over.

Sale ran out of tacklers to enable Sione Va'enuku to strike back almost immediately but they resumed on the front foot and were frustrated to be penalised just short of the whitewash on two occasions.

They continued knocking on the door and suddenly changed pace with a series of runs gaining yards until Ford sent Ben Bamber galloping over.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

Sale now led 21-10 and Saracens' dismal afternoon continued when Theo Dan limped off while his fellow hooker Jamie George watched from the stands, sidelined by injury.

Charlie Bracken combined with brother Jack to race over with eight minutes to go and the Sharks then let another commanding position slip away because of a penalty close to the line, but they had already done enough to see off Saracens.

Sports.title: Taylor stars as Colts cruise past Commanders in NFL's return to London
Sports.content:
Jonathan Taylor scored twice as Indianapolis Colts overcame Washington Commanders 30-13 at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium to open this year's triple-header of NFL International Series games in London.

The Commanders initially had the better of things, limiting the Colts offense to 20 total yards in the first quarter as they claimed a 6-0 lead.

But an injury to QB Marcus Mariota when sacked on the play prior to Washington's second field goal proved a turning point, with third-stringer Athan Kaliakmanis - a seventh-round draft pick - unable to lead the Commanders to victory despite a couple of eye-catching plays, including a 47-yard deep-ball TD for his first in the NFL.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Washington Commanders rookie quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis finds Treylon Burks for his first NFL touchdown

Colts quarterback Daniel Jones, who had two turnovers in the first half, ran in Indianapolis' third touchdown of the game early in the fourth quarter to stretch their lead to two scores - and there was to be no way back for Washington.

Image: Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones dives in for the game-clinching touchdown in the fourth quarter

The NFL returns to Tottenham next Sunday for a clash between the Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars, who are back in action facing the Houston Texans at Wembley a week later, on Sunday October 18.

Stats leaders:

Indianapolis Colts

Passing: Daniel Jones, 19/34, 143 yards, 1 rushing TD, 1 INT

Daniel Jones, 19/34, 143 yards, 1 rushing TD, 1 INT Rushing: Jonathan Taylor, 20 carries, 95 yards, 2 TDs

Jonathan Taylor, 20 carries, 95 yards, 2 TDs Receiving: Laquon Treadwell, 9 catches, 42 yards

Image: Jonathan Taylor scored two rushing touchdowns for Indianapolis Colts

Washington Commanders

Passing: Athan Kaliakmanis, 15/33, 186 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT

Athan Kaliakmanis, 15/33, 186 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT Rushing: Marcus Mariota, 1 carry, 35 yards

Marcus Mariota, 1 carry, 35 yards Receiving: Dyami Brown, 3 catches, 65 yards

The Colts fell behind early when Jones lost the football after he was accidentally tripped by his own team-mate, with the Commanders scoring a field goal after Odafe Oweh recovered the ball at the 20-yard line.

Mariota, filling in for injured starting QB Jayden Daniels, left the game with a knee injury when sacked on the play prior to Washington's second field goal.

Kaliakmanis came in, the 223rd overall pick from the seventh round of the 2026 NFL Draft, and though he found the going tough early on his NFL debut, Colts veteran Jones was similarly struggling and was picked off by Rasul Douglas.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jonathan Taylor runs into the end zone for the Indianapolis Colts' first touchdown in their NFL clash with Washington Commanders in London

But the Colts soon took over again on downs after the Commanders' call to go for it on fourth down from their own 46-yard line. It would prove a poor decision, helping set up Taylor's opening TD for Indianapolis to see them into a lead that they stretched to four by the half with the first of Spencer Shrader's three field goals. Taylor celebrated his score by pantomiming drinking tea in the end zone.

Kaliakmanis threw a costly interception early in the third quarter, with Taylor's second five-yard scoring run of the game then making it 17-6.

Kaliakmanis bounced back on the next drive, though, hitting Treylon Burks on a stunning, 47-yard touchdown pass deep down the left sideline that closed the gap as Burks got past star cornerback Sauce Gardner.

But the Colts (2-2) answered back with further Shrader field goals either side of Jones' touchdown run from four yards out early in the fourth quarter.

Sports.title: Labuschagne hits timely ton as Australia warm up for South Africa Tests
Sports.content:
Marnus Labuschagne scored a speedy, and timely, century in Australia's sole warm-up match before the three-Test series in South Africa from Friday, live on Sky Sports Cricket.

Labuschagne struck 111 from 89 balls, reaching three figures from 76 deliveries and hitting 19 fours, before retiring out against a Cricket South Africa Invitation XI in Potchefstroom.

The 32-year-old will hope to carry that form into the Test arena, starting in Durban this week, having gone 43 innings and over three years without a hundred in the format.

After Labuschagne - who is averaging 25.43 since the 2023 Ashes - made scores of one, 31 and four in the recent 1-1 series draw at home to Bangladesh, ex-Australia captain Ricky Ponting told Sky Sports that the batter's spot in the XI had become "untenable".

However, the Baggy Greens have kept faith with the South Africa-born player and he seems set to line up in his usual No 3 berth at Kingsmead as Australia begin their first Test series in the country since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

Image: Steve Smith will play Test cricket in South Africa for the first time since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal

Smith scores half-century in Test tune-up

Steve Smith - who along with David Warner and Cameron Bancroft received a ban for the role he played in using sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball - Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Matt Renshaw are the survivors from that contest eight years ago.

Smith, who followed Labuschagne in retiring out, and Renshaw scored 61 and 32 respectively on the second and final day of the tune-up for this month's Tests, while Alex Carey made 57 as Australia replied to the hosts' 318-7 with 368-6.

On day one, Australia used 11 bowlers in order to manage workload with seven taking a wicket apiece and none of the seamers getting through more than 10 overs.

Image: Josh Hazlewood was one of a plethora of bowlers used by Australia on day one of the tune-up fixture

All-rounder Cameron Green did not feature after picking up an abdominal injury in the final ODI against South Africa last week and appears a doubt for the first Test.

After the series opener in Durban, the teams will meet in Gqeberha from October 18 and then Cape Town from October 27.

South Africa also host Bangladesh and England in Test cricket this winter, with the series against Joe Root's men starting at Wanderers in Johannesburg on December 17.

Sports.title: Let’s stop doubting Thomas Tuchel: England are impressive and Euro 2028 is the target
Sports.content:
Move fast and fix things. It has been a fine week so far for Thomas Tuchel as he attempts the cyclical task of soldering together not just an England team, but a way of looking like one, all the while being battered by the to-and-fro conflicting winds of England managerdom.

There is nothing new here. This is a job that involves not just picking the right players and making high-stakes calculations over your second-half substitutions, but carrying out these basic duties while wrestling with aggrieved members of the Thuggee cult on a collapsing rope bridge outside the Temple of Doom, and simultaneously having your heart ripped out.

No other nation makes quite the same twin-track demands. Manage the games. Yeah, do that obviously. But also tell us who we are and how we should play. This is why the job will always take its pound of mince meat, why these people end up drained and hollowed out, an empty tracksuit resigning in the Wembley toilets, Roy Hodgson in Nice looking like a desiccated vampire, saying “I don’t know why I’m here”.

It is also why it was heartening in Rijeka to see Tuchel gripped with the familiar energies, still whirling about on the touchline in penitent black shoes and black trousers, looking as ever like a famine-ridden earl out taking the hounds for a walk, while simultaneously cracking the Enigma code in his hunting shed.

It feels absurd to say that Tuchel is now safe in the job, if only because the idea he wouldn’t be is so hysterical. Tuchel was never realistically in any trouble. But such is the nature of a role where you’re only ever a few rapid-fire defeats away from the incredible twin feat of a greatest-ever overseas World Cup and a near-instant heaving from the job.

We should of course keep a sense of scale over a couple of Nations League wins against underpowered opponents. The 7-0 steamrollering of Croatia was always a strange affair. From the moment the doors opened the whole occasion felt like a youth club association sports day, where everyone gets a medal at the end and the teachers do a disco dance routine.

It was an atmosphere that seemed to communicate itself to the Croatia players even as they were warming up in a notably fun and jokey way, cheered by shrill groups of junior ultras, and blasted by the Croatian version of We Didn’t Start the Fire through the ear-shredding speaker system.

Croatia played from the first minute like a team recovering from a dose of herbal sleeping tablets. Luka Modric’s every touch was met with the kind of noise more usually associated with an appearance by a Korean boyband at an Apple Store launch event, but one of the great players of the age was simply run over by England’s youthful and hungry midfield.

View image in fullscreen Jude Bellingham was superb in the win over Croatia, as he was during the World Cup. Photograph: Igor Soban/Pixsell/MB Media/Getty Images

These are also the teams you play, however. Croatia were decent enough at the World Cup. Mainly, though this came at an absolutely vital moment in the age of Tuchelism. The next 20 months are basically it, the engine room, the space where Tuchel gets to decide how good his team can be, leading in to a tournament England will never have a better chance of winning.

The only questions that really matter right now are: is there vision of a team and a way to play? And do we have forward progress? The answers to both of which are yes.

England were good in an interesting way in Croatia. We’re used to England teams that seem powerful but also flawed. In Rijeka they looked like a World Cup semi-finalist that has used that experience to improve, strong in every area, physically, technically and in its basic balance.

At times in the current era England have brought to mind the Gareth Southgate team of 2019 into 2020, when some key new players entered a blooming environment, and suddenly they were blowing away mid-range opponents. The Covid break would complicate that arc. An unprovable counter-factual: nudge those first Southgate Euros forward a year and England might have had the momentum to overpower Italy in the final.

There are two aspects to Tuchel’s England this time around. First, the reckoning up with the mistakes of the recent past. Why, oh why didn’t he take Cole Palmer? Well, maybe for the same reason Palmer’s not here now. Well, why of why, then, didn’t he take Phil Foden? This has also answered itself. The same goes for not selecting the back-up striker who is now, it turns out, playing in Saudi Arabia. It is entirely legitimate to still disagree with all these things. But it feels clearer that there was logic and reasoning here.

The past can re-litigate itself. The second key element is the sense of progress. This was always likely to be the case. It takes time to get to know your players. Tuchel had never been to an international tournament before. He was never the knockout specialist some seemed to assume. Just take a look at his record. He’s a process guy. And we are now right in the middle of that process.

View image in fullscreen Lewis Hall has enjoyed a fine international break and looks to be first choice for England at left-back. Photograph: Darko Bandić/AP

So what has changed? Most obviously making Jude Bellingham the hub of this team is an excellent idea, and not just because of his astonishing talent. Rallying around Bellingham is Tuchel’s version of Southgate’s inflatable unicorns, the talk about Spitfires, the away-days with the SAS crawling through an assault course made entirely from Cheddar cheese and Eccles cakes.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

How do you make players want to play for England? Here’s a short cut. Give them aura, brand power, magnetism. Put the big guy right at the centre. Everyone’s turning up if Jude is loving it, and you have a chance for two weeks to exist in his forcefield.

Then there’s the way England have played. There is always talk about “a Premier League style”, which has never been a single thing. But these players are definitely best suited to high-intensity, hard-running, duel-winning football. This wasn’t only there in successfully outmuscling an ageing Mateo Kovacic, who even in his pomp had the air of a frail Victorian child masquerading as an elite modern midfielder, shorts hiked up, skinny legs gamely covering the turf.

England also played like this for half an hour against the world champions, and narrowly lost a game where they went 1-0 down after a minute and missed a late penalty. This felt like an evolved version of the “packet-ball” intensity that blew Croatia away at the World Cup for 20 minutes then could never quite click into gear again. The next Euros are in England. Cancel the heatwave, and they can play like this for longer.

Then there is the issue of balance. Lewis Hall: yes, a proper left-back with a left foot. Jarell Quansah makes lots of sense now, offering something of the Kyle Walker-style recovery athleticism. Alex Scott looked really good in Rijeka, a genuinely smart, head-up, surging midfield presence.

Tuchel is right. He can’t roll into a tournament with two first-choice midfielders. Scott offered something different in the exact area England lose these high-stakes, high-intensity games. He even knows who his back-up centre-forward is now, and it is of course Jude. Ask any question right now. The answer is likely to be the same.

Here is another unprovable counter-factual. England would have beaten that Argentina team in Atlanta with this team in Rijeka. This should not be a source of why-oh-why frustration. It’s forward momentum, learning new patterns, adding new tricks. Stick Bellingham up front in the second half, pack Scott into a three-man midfield, and they’ve got a far better chance of seeing that game out.

The process is also far from done. England need competition on the right wing. Bukayo Saka is an excellent footballer. But he’s not a weapon other teams will fear. Add an England-issue Michael Olise, for example, and this team looks entirely different in its threat levels. Max Dowman is still just a very nice idea at this point. But there’s time. And he doesn’t need to be perfect.

Finally, and back to the key figure in this cycle, there is the total weaponising of Bellingham, whose role in the team is now beautifully clarified. Station him in forward areas and he will still press and harry and add a defensive function. But turning, running, breaking in transitions, making risky creative passes, he is just a supreme footballer. Not to mention a one-man mission statement of the way this team wants to play.

Tournaments aren’t won with a 7-0 win on the Adriatic coast in front of 6,000 over-caffeinated schoolchildren. But there is progress here. And that time will pass in a wink.

Sports.title: Denmark sink Wales as Rasmus Højlund makes Danny Ward pay for blunder
Sports.content:
Wales crave momentum but, a few days after surely the sweetest high of Craig Bellamy’s two-year reign, a sapping international window ended on a bum note. At least until Bellamy was informed Portugal’s comeback victory over Norway means Wales will spend the next six weeks in third, and not bottom of Nations League A4 owing to their superior head-to-record. “That’s actually quite nice,” the Wales head coach said, slowly digesting the silver lining about half an hour after the final whistle. “That’s brightened up a real rubbish moment.”

Bellamy suggested last Thursday’s victory over Norway blew the group wide open with a hand grenade but Danny Ward detonated one to give Denmark a second-half penalty and Rasmus Højlund’s flawless spot-kick ultimately proved the difference. The galling thing for Ward was that until his moment of madness, he had kept his country in the game, his best stop a sublime right-hand save to deny Gustav Isaksen. A first clean sheet since beating Liechtenstein last November also went out of the window for Wales. The life of a goalkeeper, eh?

The difficulty for Wales was always going to be trying to replicate the all-action performance from their triumph over Norway, the obvious caveat that their opponents played almost all of the second half with 10 men. The emotions felt after that game were always going to be hard to match but despite the awkward 7.45pm kick-off on a Sunday night, the Barry Horns, the brass brand who enthusiastically soundtrack Wales matches, made a racket and contributed to a fine atmosphere. Even without a full house, the anthem was stirring if not spine-tingling.

Bellamy said it was impossible to keep the same XI owing to the toll of four matches across 11 days but in the end Daniel James was the only player to make way, Brennan Johnson taking his place on the wing. Ben Davies, whose only minutes for Tottenham came against a Charlton Athletic B team in the Carabao Cup, started a fourth successive game this window, together with Neco Williams and Ethan Ampadu, whose Leeds team visit Arsenal in Saturday’s early kick-off when the Premier League resumes. Ward also made it four in a row and in doing so has played four times as many games for his country as he has this season for his club, Wrexham.

It is a familiar problem for Wales and Bellamy, who is hopeful Joe Rodon will return from a hamstring injury in time for next month’s trip to Oslo and home date with Portugal. “We started well and then as the game unfolded, the intensity started to drop for us,” said the 47-year-old. “We couldn’t sustain the intensity, we couldn’t get the energy up enough to be able to have a bigger say in the game. I felt it in the first half: we’re not moving enough now. We tried to make one or two substitutions to freshen it up. We shouldn’t really have played Ben – I’m just hoping he’s not injured but he’s a warrior. We don’t have enough players playing week in, week out, certainly not at the top level. When you don’t do this week in, week out, it’s a shock to the system. It was a touch of reality.”

View image in fullscreen Rasmus Højlund celebrates his second-half winner for Denmark. Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Ward’s first real save, to deny Højlund at the start of the second half, was smart but his second was phenomenal. Joakim Mæhle raced down the left and before reaching the byline flung into the box a feathery, hanging cross. Isaksen, of Lazio, tracked the ball all the way and cleverly adjusted his body position to pick his spot, the target the bottom right-hand corner of Ward’s goal. Isaksen appeared to have executed the perfect header but Ward got a brilliant right hand to the ball and pushed it on to his right post. At that point, Ward was Wales’s hero.

But then, out of nothing, Ward conceded a clumsy penalty. Ben Cabango shifted the ball to his goalkeeper, from right to left, but Ward, looking to move the ball on again, inadvertently shovelled a miskicked pass straight to Isaksen. A panicked Ward tried to make amends but his desperation got the better of him and he clattered into Isaksen and the damage was done. Højlund waited for Ward to dive to his left and slotted the ball into the opposite corner.
