Search for 6 aboard medical jet enters second day after crash near Nantucket

The Coast Guard continues to search for six people aboard a medical transport aircraft after search crews located a debris field off Nantucket, Mass., on Saturday. U.S. Coast Guard

Authorities declined to speculate on what caused a medical evacuation jet to crash off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts, on Saturday morning, as crews continue to search for the six missing passengers.

The U.S. Coast Guard found a debris field approximately 20 miles off the coast of Nantucket. Crews have searched roughly 2,840 square miles over more than 53 hours, said Rear Adm. Matt Lake, commander of the Coast Guard’s Northeast District.

“This is a large and demanding search area. Our crews are employing fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, boats and cutters to search the area,” Lake said. He added that authorities hope to use sonar to search the seabed.

The six people on board were four Canadians and two Bermudians. A source familiar with the matter told NBC News the Bermudians were a patient and the patient’s son.

Governor says Tennessee’s prisons chief is resigning after failed execution of Christa Pike

Christa Pike in court in 2001. Knoxville News Sentinel via Reuters

The head of Tennessee’s prison system is resigning after the failed execution of Christa Pike, Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday.

In response to the resignation news, Pike’s attorneys told NBC News that Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada’s departure was “justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now.”

“What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” they said. Pike remained unconscious in a hospital as of Friday.

Pike has remained unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital in the four days since her failed execution in Tennessee, and her prognosis might not be known for days more, one of her lawyers said Sunday.

World.title: Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson exits game vs. Titans with ankle injury
World.content:
Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson missed the second half of the Ravens’ 24-18 win against the Tennessee Titans on Sunday because of an ankle injury.

Jackson was on the sideline without a helmet during Baltimore’s first possession of the third quarter, with the Ravens holding a 24-7 lead at the time. The team announced that he was questionable to return, but Jackson did not play another snap.

He was also seen wearing a boot on his left ankle after the game, according to ESPN.

Jackson was off to a hot start before leaving. He completed 15 of 20 passes for 222 yards and two touchdowns in the first half. He also carried the ball twice for 20 yards.

He was tackled on the second-to-last play of the half and appeared to be favoring his ankle after going to the sideline. He was replaced by backup Tyler Huntley to start the third quarter.

Huntley finished the game completing 8 of 9 passes for 63 yards, and Baltimore did not score again.

Injuries have been an issue at times for Jackson, a two-time MVP. He missed four games last year, and the Ravens went only 2-2 in his absence. Baltimore finished the 2025 season 8-9 and missed the playoffs.

In 2021, Jackson missed five games, and the Ravens went 1-4 without him, missing the playoffs. The following season, he again missed five games and didn’t play in Baltimore’s first-round playoff loss.

The Ravens entered this season with high expectations despite parting ways with previous head coach John Harbaugh. He was replaced by former Los Angeles Chargers defensive coordinator Jesse Minter, who was a defensive coach under Harbaugh in Baltimore from 2017 to 2020.

The Ravens entered Sunday with a 2-1 record, defeating the Indianapolis Colts and Dallas Cowboys, with their only loss coming against the New Orleans Saints. Baltimore is now tied with the Cleveland Browns at the top of the AFC North after Sunday’s win.

Jackson, 29, is in his ninth season with Baltimore, which selected him with the final pick of the first round in the 2018 NFL draft. Entering Sunday, he had thrown for 745 yards and four touchdowns this season and run for one more score.

Jackson is in the second to last year of a five-year, $260 million contract he signed in March 2023. He and the Ravens reportedly did not seriously discuss a long-term extension before this season.

World.title: Florida GOP governor candidate Byron Donalds courts skeptic Black voters
World.content:
MIAMI — For most of his nine years in Congress, Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, of Florida, rarely made his race part of his political pitch. This past weekend, in a string of Black voter outreach events across the Miami area, he did — carefully, and on his own terms.

In an interview with CBS News, the Republican nominee for Florida governor said he's now targeting "north of 20%" of the Black vote.

"I think there's a lot of Black voters who are looking at my campaign because they're just trying to figure out who's going to be the best person to lead Florida into the future," Donalds said. "I think the other thing with Black voters: they're starting to not be as monolithically tied to the Democrat Party."

For comparison, around 13% of Black voters backed Gov. Ron DeSantis's reelection bid in 2022, according to CBS News exit polls. President Trump won around 15% of Black votes in Florida during his 2024 presidential bid.

In 2024, Donalds was one of Mr. Trump's most visible surrogates to Black voters nationally, co-headlining a multi-city tour with Rep. Wesley Hunt of Texas billed as "Congress, Cigars & Cognac" — informal, sit-down conversations meant to make the case for Mr. Trump in rooms that weren't always receptive. Now he's running that same playbook for himself, as the principal rather than the surrogate.

A potential win for Donalds would put him in an exclusive club of Black state executives. Only three elected governors have been Black in U.S. history. Donalds is among three nominees this year who would be the first Black Republican governors ever elected.

Asked what it would mean to him to make history, Donalds paused, smiled to himself, and let his guard down for a moment. "It's wild, honestly," he told CBS News — a rare admission from a candidate who has spent his campaign avoiding identity-based appeals.

"I don't talk about my race in this campaign," Donalds told a crowd at the Black Professionals Summit's Legacy Con on Saturday, one of several stops targeting the key voting bloc. "Florida is a meritocracy. Here in Florida, we have people who have come from so many different parts of the country. What they really care about now is: Can you get the job done?"

Republican Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds speaks at the Black Professionals Summit's Legacy Con on Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. Seiji Yamashita/CBS News

Legacy Con's organizers told CBS News they also invited Democratic nominee David Jolly to address the summit, but he didn't attend, citing a scheduling conflict.

With less than a month of campaigning left, Donalds also pushed back on criticism that his minority outreach was new or narrow. "We're actually targeting every voter," he said, pointing to his team's door-knocking aimed at Black voters in North Miami and Broward County, Hispanic voters in Doral and Hialeah, and more.

But some voters he met during his South Florida swing say his loyalty to the president is clouding their opinion of him. At a retail stop at the Black-owned Lorna's Caribbean Restaurant in Miami Gardens, Jermaine Woodside, 54, said he came in skeptical but left more open to the congressman after an hour-long dinner conversation, even as he said bluntly that Donalds should not associate himself with Mr. Trump. "That's going to hurt him, and that's the reason why I was reluctant to be a part of his campaign," Woodside told CBS News.

Donalds told CBS News voters shouldn't judge him solely on his history with Mr. Trump.

"Look at the issues I'm pushing forward. Look at the ideas that I talk about. Yes, the president's endorsed me. Yes, a couple years ago I endorsed him to be president. But I'm running to be governor of Florida," he said.

Not everyone was swayed. Miami resident Kalyn James came alone to a meet-and-greet Donalds hosted at an outdoor event space in the predominantly Black Overtown neighborhood. James quietly protested the event by holding a sign that read "Vote Blue" with Donalds' name crossed out while he worked the room, talking to other attendees.

"I just don't think that he has a buy-in that he thinks he has," James told CBS News. "And honestly, [his win] would make history, but I think he'd be on the wrong side of history."

Jasmine Burney-Clark, founder of the nonpartisan voting rights group Equal Ground, had sharper criticism. She noted Donalds declined to sign her organization's candidate pledge, affirming an intent to sign into law a Democratic-backed state voting rights bill — which Jolly did sign — and argued his weekend events were not genuine.

"Byron Donalds has been Black at the start of this election, and he will be Black at the end of this election," Burney-Clark told CBS News. "Black voters are not going to be fooled by his targeting and his manipulation tactics to pander to get their vote."

The outreach comes as recent polling shows a surprisingly tight race for an office a Democrat hasn't won since the 1990s. For Donalds, the math is clear even if the politics are complicated: close the gap with Black voters, and Democrats' path back to the governor's mansion gets much harder.

World.title: FBI arrests woman accused of surveilling Taiwanese president's son for China
World.content:
The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News.

Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.

Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.

It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney.

Wanying "Heather" Zhang. FBI

A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.

Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.

Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.

"If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint.

Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades. It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured.

CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment.

The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home.

Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening.

CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu.

Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.

The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account.

"Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote.

FBI agents arrested Wanying "Heather" Zhang at Los Angeles International Airport on Oct. 4, 2026. U.S. Department of Justice

The complaint claims Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security.

Holt's affidavit claims Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission.

She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint.

On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said.

Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties.

Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications.

Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA, Taiwan's national news agency.

Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S.

Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang, 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent.

Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents.

The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime.

New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China.

In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China.

World.title: Experts are training AI how to do their jobs
World.content:
Music producer Robbie Hiser is confident there will always be a place for creatives like him even though he taught artificial intelligence some of the tricks of his trade.

Hiser trained AI for Mercor, a company that works to make AI models like ChatGPT or Claude better in a wide variety of subjects from finance to poetry. The multibillion-dollar company has assembled more than 100,000 freelancers in a wide range of industries, available to teach AI what they know about their fields.

But Hiser and other trainers said they don't believe they're training themselves out of a job. Hiser thinks creative work like great songwriting, for example, will always require a human touch.

"AI doesn't have any life experience to pull from," he said. "An AI never had a girlfriend break up with it."

Still, nearly three-fourths of Americans now fear AI is coming for our jobs, according to a Pew Research study. And a September report from McKinsey Global Institute found AI could force 11 million U.S. workers into new careers by 2035.

Robbie Hiser. CBS News

A natural evolution?

Mercor CEO Brendan Foody sees the changes prompted by AI as a natural evolution. He believes with the use of AI, people will be freed from the dull, repetitive parts of their job, leaving them with more time to do other more meaningful and engaging work.

The evolution is happening across the country. Columbus, Ohio, law firm Vorys, Sater, Seymour and Pease, for instance, worked with Stanford University's Liftlab to build AI personas trained on the experience and philosophy of some of its senior lawyers. These AI personas can offer feedback from the unique perspective of individual Vorys partners on documents, trial lawyer and partner Kim Herlihy said.

"AI is never going to walk into the courtroom and give an opening statement to the jury," she said. "But it helps us have additional tools to use as we prepare that opening statement."

Kim Herlihy. CBS News

The AI may have Herlihy's expertise, but she said it's designed for optimization, not replacement.

"AI cannot take the place of what's a fundamentally human business," she said. "You call your lawyer because you want to look in their eye and say, 'What should I do about this issue?'"

AI training is currently America's fourth-fastest-growing job category on LinkedIn. At the moment, the gig work training AI at Mercor can pay $20 or even $200 an hour. To Foody, it's the career of the future.

What a top economist says

Foody's sunny picture is at odds with what Nobel Prize-winning economist Daron Acemoglu fears could be coming for American workers. On its current trajectory, many areas are set to become more automated, leading to worker displacement.

"What we are living through with AI is unprecedented," said Acemoglu. "The first phase of the Industrial Revolution took 80 years. Today it's taking place in one or two years and it's taking place across many different sectors at the same time."

In a worst-case scenario, unemployment could triple in the next decade, if nothing is done and the U.S. continues on its current course, Acemoglu said.

And while Acemoglu acknowledged there will be employment for people training AI, he said, "The number of people they're employing in these positions is small relative to the number of people who will be replaced."

"I mean, that's the whole point of automation," Acemoglu said.

Who will be impacted as AI advances?

While unemployment is generally steady at the moment, research from Stanford shows hiring is down for young people in the most AI-exposed jobs — like software developers. Research from the U.S. Census, found hiring and wages among recent college grads in AI-exposed majors have declined due to AI.

Clara Shih, who oversaw major AI divisions at Salesforce and then Meta, said at her workplace there used to be dozens of people involved in conceiving a product, creating a prototype and ultimately delivering it to customers. Now, she said, the same task can be done with just a few people using AI agents.

Clara Shih. CBS News

Shih was so alarmed by what this meant for the future of work that she quit her tech job in January and started a nonprofit helping young workers, who've been among the hardest hit, navigate the new economy.

"Traditionally, the tasks that you might assign to a young person, maybe doing some market research or creating the first draft of a memo, AI is just really good at doing those now," Shih said.

Shih believes AI could ultimately affect workers across every profession, impacting more than just workers' livelihoods.

"It's never just about the jobs. It's people's sense of self-worth. It's the fracturing of communities," Shih said.

What can be done?

Shih witnessed the decline of factory work when her family moved from Hong Kong to Ohio. She sees clear parallels between the impacts of globalization and automation and what AI could mean for the white-collar workforce

"I think what we can learn is that first we have to be honest with people about what the risks are," Shih said. "I think, you know, sugarcoating that this AI utopia, maybe we'll get there, but there's a lot of hurt that could happen between now and there."

For Acemoglu, it's not about saying no to technology.

"Absolutely not. But in every technological revolution there is pushback, and that pushback takes many different forms," he said.

Acemoglu said there is a lot that can be done to ensure AI doesn't lead to mass unemployment — companies could intentionally design AI to make humans better, not expendable, or the government could implement a tax code that incentivizes companies to hire real people.

But the window to act is closing.

"It should move us into thinking about what we can do because there is a lot we can do," Acemoglu said. "Because the future is so uncertain, because the future is so much subject to our choice and agency, it is all the more important that we have this discussion."

World.title: 60 Minutes Transcript: Artificial intelligence and the future of work
World.content:
AI Jon:

This past week in Washington, America's tech titans met with President Trump to talk about, well, the future of humanity … specifically, will AI, artificial intelligence, mark the end of civilization as we know it? Only slightly less grave and only slightly less depressing, there's a related, more immediate question: Will AI take our jobs?

Real Jon walks out:

That right there? Not me … That was AI. So it is, we don't exempt ourselves in wondering: is any line of work safe? So far this year, U.S. companies have cited AI as the No. 1 reason for layoffs. AI, after all, doesn't sleep, or take sick days. Is this technology simply going to transform how and where we work, much the same way other workplace revolutions did? Or is this one different? Is the great job apocalypse upon us?

Tape:

Here in this nondescript office in downtown San Francisco, these 20-somethings are designing the future of your workplace.

You may not have heard of Mercor, but it's quickly become a leader in a booming new industry built around supercharging the already supercharged rise of artificial intelligence.

BRENDAN FOODY: We were, in January last year, about 20 people.

JON WERTHEIM: How many now?

BRENDAN FOODY: Now it's 400 people in San Francisco, yeah.

Brendan Foody. 60 Minutes

Brendan Foody is Mercor's CEO. It's now a multibillion-dollar company, and he's now a 23-year-old billionaire. Backstory: four years ago, ChatGPT came out and Foody and his two co-founders — high school buddies — saw where the technology was heading. To get better, AI needed more information than what was widely available on the internet.

JON WERTHEIM: AI went from this high-powered search engine to all of a sudden we're in astrophysics. We've gone from cutesy to holy moly in a very short amount of time.

BRENDAN FOODY: I think that's spot on. And the core thing powering that huge transformation and the capabilities is human intelligence.

JON WERTHEIM: It seems like overarching goal, anything we humans can do, we want AI to be able to do.

BRENDAN FOODY: I think a significant portion of things. Everything that humans want AI to be able to do — we wanna teach it how to do that.

So what does Mercor do? Well, when the big AI companies want, say, ChatGPT or Claude to improve in a particular field, they hire Mercor to make their models smarter. Pick a subject, any subject: finance, architecture, poetry. Mercor has assembled an army of more than 100,000 freelancers — humans! — ready to use their hard-earned expertise to train the AI.

Shawna Miller: I work late in the evening …

We met three such experts: Shawna Miller, a winemaker; Robbie Hiser, a music producer; and Melania Poonacha, a physician.

JON WERTHEIM: When you're assigned a task, what are you actually doing? How are you training AI?

DR. MELANIA POONACHA: On one project we were training the AI to be able to accurately interpret laboratory results.

ROBBIE HISER: For a songwriting project, you might get two different versions of the same lyric. And then you go through and give feedback on it.

All three have full-time jobs. AI training is just a side gig. Long-term, by spending hours teaching a computer the tricks of their trade, are they not training themselves out of a career? No, they insist. Hiser believes that great songwriting, for instance, will always require the human touch.

ROBBIE HISER: AI doesn't have any life experience to pull from you know, an AI never had a girlfriend break up with it.

JON WERTHEIM: Real-life inputs that impact songwriting in a way that–

ROBBIE HISER: Absolutely.

JON WERTHEIM: –the robots– yeah–

JON WERTHEIM: There's no way to write that in?

ROBBIE HISER: I don't think so.

Ultimately, Brendan Foody foresees a utopia: advanced AI helping us cure cancer and tackle climate change. And the untold millions of workers? Liberated from the dullest parts of their jobs, they'll be more productive than ever.

JON WERTHEIM: People still have this fundamental question, is my job safe from AI? How do you answer that?

BRENDAN FOODY: I think the key thing to look at is if you become more productive, is there more demand for your expertise in the economy?

JON WERTHEIM: If you're training AI to do what people have spent years and years perfecting in their careers, aren't you necessarily endangering human work?

BRENDAN FOODY: Well, I think that you're changing human work. It might not necessarily be that repetitive task that people have done in the past, but there's still so many other things that people could be able to do. And so I think that evolution is natural.

Whether workers asked for it or not, that evolution is already happening, and not just in the tech hotbeds.

Kim Herlihy speaks with Jon Wertheim. 60 Minutes

In places like, Columbus, Ohio, where the law firm Vorys, Sater, Seymour and Pease has been serving clients' needs since 1909, Kim Herlihy, a trial lawyer, is a partner at the firm.

JON WERTHEIM: You're going into courtrooms and facing a judge and jury. How is AI gonna help with that?

KIM HERLIHY: AI is never gonna walk into the courtroom and give an opening statement to the jury. But it helps us have additional tools to use as we prepare that opening statement.

A year ago, Vorys worked with Stanford University to build an internal tool for the firm: individual AI personas trained on its senior lawyers. How do they think? What kind of advice do they give? Presto: an AI version of a Vorys partner. Herlihy has her own, which she consulted for us.

KIM HERLIHY: So, what you have on your screen here is a draft opening statement.

JON WERTHEIM: This is. "Ladies and gentlemen of the jury."

Now Herlihy asks her AI double to give notes.

KIM HERLIHY: can see it's an AI comment from my persona, is saying, "The legal phrasing is too stiff for an opening statement."

JON WERTHEIM: I'm just struck that people who aren't familiar with AI, they might think, you know, it's robots, and avatars, it's just a Word doc.

KIM HERLIHY: Yeah, it is. You're not seeing a picture of me, I'm not talking out loud.

Not yet anyway. Still, we wondered: Is today's worker optimizer not tomorrow's worker replacement?

JON WERTHEIM: So we built this model with partner Kim Herlihy's expertise baked into it. It's not hard to see a future in which the client just goes right to the model, is it?

KIM HERLIHY: That's hard for me to see. AI cannot take the place of what's a fundamentally human business. You call your lawyer because you want to look in their eye and say, "What should I do about this issue?"

This sunny picture, it's at odds with the bleak labor predictions many AI executives have been issuing.

It's early and overall unemployment remains generally steady, but mounting research shows that, for the most AI-exposed jobs — take software developers — hiring has slowed and wages have declined. The impact focused on one group in particular: 20-somethings.

CLARA SHIH: Traditionally, the tasks that you might assign to a young person, maybe doing some market research or creating the first draft of a memo. AI is just really good at doing those now.

Until January, Clara Shih was overseeing major AI divisions at Salesforce and then Meta.

Clara Shih.

JON WERTHEIM: You've seen how powerful this can be.

CLARA SHIH: Oh yeah. I've seen us go from previously requiring dozens of people to conceive of a product, prototype it, build it, to now being able to do that with one or two or three people using AI agents.

Shih was so alarmed by what this meant for the workforce, she quit her plum tech job and founded a nonprofit helping young people navigate this new economy — and she has emerged as an AI Cassandra.

CLARA SHIH: I think AI's gonna have a profound impact on every profession. There are a lot of people whose jobs it is today within companies to prepare information, research, analyze data for other individuals in that company. And increasingly, although it's starting with the entry level, it could result in a lot of people losing their jobs.

JON WERTHEIM: And job loss means what as you see it?

CLARA SHIH: It's never just about the jobs. It's people's sense of self-worth. It's the fracturing of communities.

Shih knows this cycle firsthand. Her family came to the U.S. from Hong Kong in the 1980s and landed in Ohio, where globalization was hollowing out — factories, then neighborhoods. She sees clear parallels.

CLARA SHIH: I think what we can learn is that first we have to be honest with people about what the risks are. I think, you know, sugarcoating that this AI utopia, maybe we'll get there, but there's a lot of hurt that could happen between now and there.

The public is beginning to revolt. Nearly three-fourths of Americans now fear AI is coming for our jobs and amid this growing backlash, the big tech firms have been massaging their message. Here's OpenAI's Sam Altman in June:

Sam Altman: But I think our industry underestimated how much we're going to be able to keep people at the center of everything in an economy that is and a world that is based on people.

JON WERTHEIM: For a time, the AI companies were trumpeting that this product is gonna make work obsolete. And now there seems to be a pivot and a change of tune. What do you make of this shift?

CLARA SHIH: I think that they ha– the AI labs have every incentive to sell what they're doing to the public now, and I don't think that they actually believe that AI won't hurt jobs.

Back at Mercor, typical trainers can be paid anywhere from $20 to $200 an hour. Not bad. We spoke with more than a dozen Mercor trainers — past and current. Some were happy. Many more said that the gig work comes unpredictably, or not at all. No substitute for a full-time job with benefits.

JON WERTHEIM: I mean sometimes you have experts that are twice and three times your age, and they've spent a lot of time in their field, and one thing they've gotten is a level of predictability and stability in their job. And then it seems like the hours are much more erratic here.

BRENDAN FOODY: Yeah, the hours are more erratic. But it's also something that we're very transparent with them about.

JON WERTHEIM: I mean, it does not sound like stable work.

BRENDAN FOODY: Right now, it generally is more part-time work is what experts 

Today, AI training is America's fourth-fastest-growing job category on LinkedIn. And just as machinists once replaced artisans, Brendan Foody insists he's creating a career of the future. Out of work? Fear not. Come train AI.

BRENDAN FOODY: Literally, all of the top 20 economists in America, they would say the exact same thing, which is that there's gonna be more jobs in 10 years than there are today.

JON WERTHEIM: You're a top economist in America. What say you?

DARON ACEMOGLU: No. No, not on our current trajectory. I don't see how that could happen. What we are living through with AI is unprecedented. The first phase of the Industrial Revolution lasted for 80 years. Today, it's taking place in one or two years, and it's taking place across many sectors at the same time.

Daron Acemoglu, is a Nobel Prize-winning professor at MIT, who studies technology's impact on labor.

JON WERTHEIM: We were told by a lawyer and also a music producer there are some things that humans– that are so fundamental, humans do them, robots can't. Do you buy that?

DARON ACEMOGLU: Today, absolutely. 100%.

JON WERTHEIM: You said today?

DARON ACEMOGLU: Today. In 15 years' time, what it's going to be capable of doing, I don't know.

JON WERTHEIM: But there's gonna be this huge sector of work training these AI models. So if you're a law student, you have a hard time finding a job, you can still use your expertise.

DARON ACEMOGLU: Here is one thing I'm not uncertain about. What you just described is B.S.

JON WERTHEIM: Why do you say that?

DARON ACEMOGLU: Because the number of people they're employing in these positions is small relative to the number of people who will be replaced. I mean, that's the whole point of automation.

Acemoglu says we could see unemployment triple in the next decade if we do nothing and continue on our current course.

DARRON ACEMOGLU: I am very, very, very cautious in saying we should say no to technology. Absolutely not. But in every technological revolution there is pushback, and that pushback takes many different forms.

He comes with suggestions: designing AI that makes humans better, not expendable, a tax code that incentivizes hiring real people. But the window is closing. And Acemoglu fears for the stability of society itself.

JON WERTHEIM: That shouldn't scare the hell out of us?

DARON ACEMOGLU: It should. And it should move us into thinking about what we can do because there is a lot we can do. Because the future is so uncertain, because the future is so much subject to our choice and agency, it is all the more important that we have this discussion.

Produced by David M. Levine and Meghan Lisson. Associate producer, Mimi Lamarre. News associate, Eric Frank. Edited by Mike Levine.

World.title: 60 Minutes Transcript: Sen. Thom Tillis
World.content:
Is it possible to be an effective Republican senator in the age of Donald Trump? Someone who makes deals and checks the White House – without becoming a political martyr or an ex-Republican? This is the tightrope that Thom Tillis, the senior senator from North Carolina, has been walking for the last two years. He votes like a reliable Republican while talking and maneuvering like a maverick. He's a caustic critic of many administration officials, all while insisting he just wants to help the president succeed. It's been a fascinating performance. But now Tillis is heading for the exits, at the sprightly-for-a senator age of 66, after crossing the White House one too many times. As his party faces a potential midterm wipeout, we talked to him about his high wire act, his relationship with President Trump, and whether it's possible to make the Senate great again.

Sen. Thom Tillis: Around here, if you're in motion, you're generally ahead. And if you're not, then you're behind.

Keeping up with Thom Tillis on Capitol Hill is not for the faint of heart. He knows the U.S. Capitol inside out: the passageways, staircases, the Capitol subway system, and miles of underground corridors that connect Senators' offices to the Capitol itself. When reporters manage to interpose themselves, they know they can rely on Tillis for a soundbite:

Reporter: Do you think that Senators even understand A.I.?

Sen. Thom Tillis: No. A lot of them can't spell it. They just don't have the experience.

Sen. Thom Tillis and Ross Douthat 60 Minutes

Sometimes those soundbites reflect his beefs with the White House, an escalating series of fights that culminated when Tillis announced he was voting "no" on the One Big Beautiful Bill, arguing it would push too many low income North Carolinians off Medicaid. In response, the president called Tillis "a talker and complainer, not a doer."

Sen. Thom Tillis: I respect the president. I still feel like we have an odd relationship, where I've clearly made him angry. But it took years before he even made the first negative comment about me. But I react to anybody on this earth the same way. If you come at me with what I think is unfair or incorrect data I'm going to come back after you.

The president threatened to find a primary challenger to run against Tillis. The senator announced that he would be retiring. Instead of fighting for his seat, Tillis has written an unfiltered, profanity-laced book. The title sounds like it's taking aim at President Trump.

Sen. Thom Tillis: It's a little take on Dale Carnegie, but it's "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents."

Ross Douthat: Any presidents in particular?

Sen. Thom Tillis: Well, I mean, the more recent one. But I did a good job of antagonizing Biden and a little bit with Obama back in the day.

But the cover doesn't feature President Trump. Instead, it features unflattering photos of some of Tillis' least favorite administration officials. It should be noted that he voted to confirm all of Trump's Cabinet nominees – including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, a vote he now calls his "biggest regret."

Ross Douthat: Do you hold him responsible for the struggle in the Iran War? Because you've said that you supported the initial decision to go to war.

Sen. Thom Tillis: I'm glad the president went in. You know, I think that they got so caught up after the immense success of the first strike that Hegseth probably didn't listen to his best military advice and say, "Now we should probably move to a different posture."

He's calling for Hegseth to resign. It is not the first time he's gone after big game in Trump's Cabinet. Earlier this year, he helped speed Kristi Noem's departure, when the deportation campaign in Minneapolis led to the deaths of two American citizens — Renee Good and Alex Peretti — at the hands of federal agents.

Sen. Tillis (during Noem hearing): The fact that you can't admit to a mistake which looks like under investigation is going to prove that Miss Good and Mr. Pretti probably should not have been shot in the face, and in the back!

Sen. Thom Tillis: I'm not very often that angry. But when I'm angry, I believe there's a reason behind it, and people should listen.

Ross Douthat: What were you thinking then? What had gone wrong with her tenure?

Sen. Thom Tillis: I was thinking about the $200 million that the Department of Homeland Security was spending on an ad campaign with her riding a horse. I was thinking about her calling people that were shot, potentially domestic terrorists. That's proven not to be true.

Ross Douthat: Why do you think the president picked her?

Sen. Thom Tillis: I think there are some people that are in the Cabinet because, to use the president's term, "they're right out of Central Casting." I think Noem and Hegseth are probably the poster children for men and women who should never have the authority they've been granted.

Sen. Thom Tillis 60 Minutes

This is the Tillis tightrope walk: talk about how much you want President Trump to succeed, while heaping blame on his advisers and subordinates.

Sen. Thom Tillis: The problem I have with some of the people on the front page of that book and a few others is that they're not looking around corners for him. Most of the issues that we're dealing with here have less to do with what he wanted to accomplish but how he went about it.

The president and the senator were reared in very different circumstances. Born in 1960 in Jacksonville, Florida, Tillis was one of six kids. He grew up all over the South, moving nearly every year. His father's itinerant life kept the family — in his words — "on the economic bubble."

Sen. Thom Tillis: Depending upon the circumstances, we were, either in a house that we rented, sometimes we owned it, and when things got really spicy we were in a trailer park.

Ross Douthat: Do you think that your background, I don't know, does it make you different from your colleagues?

Sen. Thom Tillis: Well, you know what? I tell ya what, it's why I probably react so quickly to this concept of, "We don't have an affordability problem." You always have an affordability problem. There's some segment of our society that always does. But denying it by definition means that you don't recognize the problem and if you don't recognize it you're not solving it.

It's those bread and butter issues that now threaten Republicans with, in his words, an "electoral bloodbath" in the midterms. But many of his colleagues are still afraid to break with the White House.

Ross Douthat: You say in the book that at least 30 of your Republican colleagues in the Senate expressed reservations, about many of the president's actions in private.Why can't, in cases like Hegseth, those 30 turn into five votes against confirmation that gets you a different secretary of defense?

Sen. Thom Tillis: Okay, there are some that just really do not want to bear–

Ross Douthat: They don't want to put their head out?

Sen. Thom Tillis: They don't want to bear the weight of the president. I get that. You're up for reelection? He'll target you in a primary. And so look, you know what all martyrs have in common? They're dead. There were probably a few instances where if kind of ripped the bandaid off early then I think we'd have had a lot better midterm environment than we're confronted with now.

Tillis was first elected to the senate in the 2014 midterms, just before Trump and MAGA took over the GOP.

Ross Douthat: What kinda conservative were you at that moment?

Sen. Thom Tillis: The same conservative I am today, pro-Second Amendment, pro-life, limited government, fiscal restraint. The only difference between me and a lotta people that call themselves true conservatives is I got a long list of things that were ratified and they don't.

Tillis' mentor in the Senate was Mitch McConnell. He even named his dog Little Mitch. He was a quick study of parliamentary procedure, vote counting and calculated risk taking. At 66, he seems as fit as anyone on the hill — and as competitive, as we found out waiting by the Senate subway tracks.

Sen. Thom Tillis: Do you, do you think you can jump and clear it?

Ross Douthat: I think so. I think I could.

Sen. Thom Tillis: You want to do it?

Ross Douthat: I'm not in your kind of shape. I mean look …

Sen. Thom Tillis: If you could make it …

Ross Douthat: All right.

Sen. Thom Tillis: If you can't…

Female voice: Oh my gosh!

There was no way he could resist.

Sen. Thom Tillis: 66!

Sen. Tillis on the subway 60 Minutes

In the second Trump administration, though, there's been too little legislative work for an energetic senator. Every recent White House, Tillis complains, has been eager to govern by executive order — but Trump 2.0 has been especially imperial.

Ross Douthat: What don't they understand about the Senate and Congress

Sen. Thom Tillis: That we're a co-equal branch. And they're at our best when they treat us like a peer.

Ross Douthat: But this runs both ways, right? That they're more likely to treat you as a coequal branch if you act like a coequal branch. Do you think the Republican Senate in Trump 2.0 has acted like a coequal branch?

Sen. Thom Tillis: I think in some cases yes. In most cases no. And I would say the same thing for Democratic-controlled Senate under Biden and Obama. Look, we always make the mistake when our guy's in office of conveying power to the White House. And I've had a real problem with that because it almost always comes back to bite you.

Another thing that's come back to bite Republican senators, repeatedly, is the president's own words. As much as Tillis trains his fire on Trump's advisers, he also acknowledges what he calls Trump's "W-T-F moments" ... threatening to seize Greenland … casting himself as Jesus … or Easter day musings about annihilating Iran.

Sen. Thom Tillis: I think he said, "Open the f***ing strait"

Ross Douthat: Were you worried that we were going to start carpet bombing Iranian civilians?

Sen. Thom Tillis: No. And I've told the president this before. "I think you really need to understand the weight of your words and how literally people take you."

Ross Douthat: But how do you tell the difference between what people are supposed to take literally and what they aren't?

Sen. Thom Tillis: You know, I'd like to think that most of the time the president would be surrounded with people who would finally say, "Mr. President, if you do that, I'm walking out this door."

Ross Douthat: There's a Russian expression. "If only the tsar knew." Which means people don't want to blame the tsar when bad things happen. They want to blame his advisors. But in this case, with Trump, it's on him, right, in the end. Whoever he has around him — he's the czar.

Sen. Thom Tillis: Truman famously said that, "The buck stops here." I get that–

Ross Douthat: It's a good line.

Sen. Thom Tillis: I get that. But Truman had great advisers.

The Tillis balancing act extends to the events of Jan. 6, 2021. He's still angry in a way that stands out among his Republican colleagues.

Sen. Thom Tillis: Look, this was the first time in the history of this country that we had not had a completely peaceful transfer of power on that day. And that was despicable. The people that led the charge, the people that assaulted police officers, I wish they were still in prison and serving a very long sentence.

Ross Douthat: But they were there for the president.

Sen. Thom Tillis: Yeah, I think so. I found it disgusting.

But he wasn't disgusted enough to convict Trump in the impeachment trial. He says it was because the process was rushed and unsenatorial.

Ross Douthat: I read your book and one of your themes was that senators need leverage. This was a moment when you, as a Republican senator, and your colleagues you had all the leverage over him. You had the power to make sure he wasn't president again.

Sen. Thom Tillis: Yeah but what you're doin' is a means justifies the end rationalization. So cheapening the impeachment process to prevent somebody from running in the future, I just don't buy it.

Ross Douthat: We're about to have a midterm election. Do you have any concerns about how this same president, who you've been condemning for Jan. 6 will react if Republicans have a bad night in the midterms?

Sen. Thom Tillis: I think there's a risk. I really do. It would be another political unforced error if we do that.

Sen. Thom Tillis shows Ross Douthat a Jan. 6, 2021 plaque honoring the Capitol police. 60 Minutes

Earlier this year, Tillis used his parliamentary skills to circumvent the speaker of the House and get a long-promised plaque installed honoring the Capitol police and other officers for protecting Congress that day. It's mounted by the door that presidents take to deliver their inaugural addresses — and hand over power. As we made our way out onto that terrace, Tillis told us he hopes the plaque will be a reminder, and a warning — even if the current president seems unchastened.

Ross Douthat: You talk a lot in your book about the risks of authoritarianism. What are you worried about?

Sen. Thom Tillis: The executive branch, with its outsized influence, threatening people in primaries, basically degrading their independence or eliminating it all together, then we become a one-institution country, which is exactly what we fought a Revolutionary War over. I mean, we will have a sort of dictator king if we're not careful.

Ross Douthat: It seems like there's a step change where presidents just ignore Congress or don't even try and get things passed.

Sen. Thom Tillis: Oh, I agree. And all we've seen over the last four administrations is a constant escalation. I want checks and balances. I want all three branches to have their individual role and continue to check power as they have for 250 years. And I think because we've been such a successful democracy for so long, it's hard for the American people to understand how quickly we can lose it all.

Produced by Graham Messick. Associate producer, Alex Ortiz. Broadcast associates, Paloma Vigil and Novi Zhukovsky. Edited by Michael Mongulla. Assistant editor, Aisha Crespo

World.title: Sen. Tillis worries about the "outsized influence" of the executive branch
World.content:
As Sen. Thom Tillis exits the Senate, he's blasting many of the advisers President Trump has surrounded himself with as "sycophants, and calling on his colleagues to stand up to executive power like the co-equal branch of government they are."

The 66-year-old senior senator from North Carolina unloads on what he calls the "WTF moments" of the second Trump Administration in a new book, "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents." Having served in the Senate during the Barack Obama, Joe Biden and both Trump presidencies, Tillis said he's increasingly worried about how the nation's system of checks and balances is being tested by the outsized influence of the executive branch.

"We will have a sort of dictator king if we're not careful," he said.

Make the Senate great again?

Every recent White House has been eager to govern by executive order, something that's been especially true during the current Trump administration, Tillis said. Presidents, he said, fail to understand that Congress is a coequal branch that should be treated as a peer, and that Congress needs to act as such.

"I would say the same thing for Democratic-controlled Senate under Biden and Obama," he said. "We always make the mistake when our guy's in office of conveying power to the White House. And I've had a real problem with that because it almost always comes back to bite you."

Sen. Thom Tillis 60 Minutes

He writes in his book of the risks of authoritarianism. Tillis said there's been "constant escalation" across four administrations of presidents ignoring Congress.

"I want checks and balances. I want all three branches to have their individual role and continue to check power as they have for 250 years," he said. "I think because we've been such a successful democracy for so long, it's hard for the American people to understand how quickly we can lose it all."

The Tillis tightrope act

Tillis was first elected to the Senate in the 2014 midterm elections, just before the rise of Mr. Trump and his Make America Great Again populist movement took over the Republican Party. He said he's the same kind of conservative now that he was back then: "pro-Second Amendment, pro-life, limited government, fiscal restraint."

"The only difference between me and a lotta people that call themselves true conservatives is I got a long list of things that were ratified and they don't," he said.

The senator is now exiting Washington after a series of fights with the White House. The breaking point, he says, came in June 2025, after Tillis announced he would vote against Mr. Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, arguing that it would push too many low-income North Carolinians off Medicaid.

Mr. Trump responded by calling Tillis "a talker and complainer, not a doer," and threatening to back a primary challenger against Tillis. The senator decided he would retire instead of fighting for his seat.

Sen. Thom Tillis shows Ross Douthat a Jan. 6, 2021, plaque honoring the Capitol police. 60 Minutes

"I respect the president. I still feel like we have an odd relationship, where I've clearly made him angry," Tillis said recently. That was before details of his profanity-laced private texts with Trump about what prompted his retirement leaked, because Tillis included them as part of his upcoming book.

Tillis said he is not done fighting, recently calling for Trump to fire Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

It should be noted that Tillis voted to confirm all of Mr. Trump's Cabinet nominees, including Hegseth. But he now calls that vote at the start of the second Trump Administration his "biggest regret."

While Tillis said he is glad "the president went in" to Iran, he thinks "they got so caught up after the immense success of the first strike that Hegseth probably didn't listen to his best military advice and say, 'Now we should probably move to a different posture.'"

It's not the first time Tillis has gone after a member of Trump's cabinet. Last March at a senate hearing, he leveled a blistering critique of Department of Homeland Security Advisor Kristi Noem, calling out, among other things, the way she handled the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis. that went viral, Tillis ripped into Noem. "I was thinking about her calling people that were shot, potentially domestic terrorists," he said. "That's proven not to be true."

Two days later, the president fired her.

"I think Noem and Hegseth are probably the poster children for men and women who should never have the authority they've been granted," Tillis said.

It's one example of the tightrope that Tillis has walked in the second Trump administration: saying how much he wants the president to succeed, while heaping blame on his advisers and subordinates. Besides Noem and Hegseth, Tillis s also highly critical of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, for "not looking around corners for" Mr. Trump.

Tillis' balancing act in Washington also extends to the events of Jan. 6, 2021. The senator is still angry about the attack on the Capitol, and threat to the peaceful transfer of power, calling what happened that day "despicable." Still, Tillis elected not to convict Mr. Trump after he left office during his second impeachment trial, criticizing the process as rushed and politicized.

"Cheapening the impeachment process to prevent somebody from running in the future, I just don't buy it," he said.

Sen. Thom Tillis sits in his office. 60 Minutes

An "electoral bloodbath" in the midterms

Asked if he fears a Jan. 6-like reaction if Trump-supported candidates lose their elections during the midterms, Tillis was somber.

"I think there's a risk. I really do," he said, adding, "It would be another unforced error if we do that."

Tillis predicts Republicans are about to suffer an "electoral bloodbath" in the upcoming midterm elections, with bread-and-butter affordability issues a main concern. Still, he said many of his colleagues are afraid to break with the White House.

In his book, Tillis writes that at least 30 Republican senators have expressed reservations about many of Mr. Trump's actions, but usually are only willing to speak up privately, fearing that if the president decides to target them, their days will be numbered.

"They don't want to bear the weight of the president. I get that. You're up for reelection? He'll target you in a primary. And so look, you know what all martyrs have in common? They're dead," Tillis said. "There were probably a few instances where if [you] kind of ripped the bandaid off early, then I think we'd have had a lot better midterm environment than we're confronted with now."

World.title: Friars turn to modern technology to repair 13th century basilica
World.content:
Sergio Fusetti went as far as humanly possible after a pair of powerful earthquakes cratered part of the roof of the Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi. Yet, almost three decades have passed, and Fusetti has been unable to figure out where more than 80,000 fragments of the 13th century church belong.

"This is impossible," he said in Italian. "Only artificial intelligence can help us here."

And that's exactly what's happening. A team of art historians and software engineers has joined forces with the Franciscan friars to try to finish the restoration — this time with the help of digital wizardry and AI.

Earthquakes and the Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi

The Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi, constructed in the hills of Umbria in central Italy, is the resting place of one of Christianity's most beloved saints. Francis, sometimes called the original hippie, rejected his family's wealth for a life of poverty. Medieval masters, including Cimabue, Pietro Lorenzetti, Simone Martini and Giotto, lined up at the basilica to paint beautiful scenes of Francis' life.

The basilica has endured more than 20 earthquakes in the years since it was constructed, according to Fusetti, who has worked to restore art at the church since the 1970s. Two of the quakes hit one after the other in 1997.

Four people were killed by falling rubble, and Fusetti was hospitalized with injuries he suffered during the second quake.

Friar Guiulio Cesareo, who was a student at the church at the time, is still scared of earthquakes. He remembers seeing a stone archway in the church shaking during the 1997 quakes.

Friar Guiulio Cesareo 60 Minutes

"I am always terrified," he said. "If I have the impression that there is something shaking, maybe it's just the wind, immediately I feel, you know, sort of cold coming from inside. The damage was a shock for the Italian country."

Using 21st century technology to restore a 13th century home

Restorers painstakingly repaired frescos and art treasures at the basilica. Yet some frescos are still pockmarked, some walls still bare.

Friars are now working with Haltadefinizione, a technology company specializing in ultra-high-definition photography. Chief Technology Officer Giovanni Borelli is leading the project to create a digital twin of the basilica. The camera he and his team use is no ordinary piece of equipment; it can capture details the human eye cannot.

"You can see all the smallest details of the work of art, the strokes of the painting, of the brush. You can see everything in great detail," he said.

Borelli's team is using cameras, drones and lasers to take hundreds of thousands of photos. They'll stitch them together to make the highest-resolution 3D blueprint of a building ever made.

Basilica of Saint Francis 60 Minutes

With it, restorers will have an exact reconstruction road map if the area is struck by an earthquake again.

The basilica's digital twin will be complete next year and will be available to the public.

Borelli's team of computer experts is also planning to use AI to fit together some of the missing pieces in the church and to tackle other problems.

"Like cracks in the paintings, discoloration — layers of paint, lifting. That kind of analysis done by hand and with the eyes of a physical person would require years to just do one round of the whole building," he said. "With AI, minutes."

Expanding access while preserving history

Borelli also wants to make the art more accessible. The technology he's using at the basilica has also been used to capture the remains of a thermal bath built by a Roman emperor. A laser scanner captured details of rooms with 30-foot ceilings and delicate mosaics. The cameras revealed hidden chambers and passageways that had been forgotten by history.

Virtual reality technology is also being used to allow users to step inside Italy's past.

"When I founded one of the companies that built this kind of technologies, I was a software engineer – pretty new to the art world," Borelli said. "The main question that I was focused on is a kind of philosophical one: How good can the digital representation of a physical object be? What is missing?"

Bill Whitaker and Giovanni Borelli 60 Minutes

While Borelli acknowledges that virtual reality technology can't duplicate the emotional impact of standing in front of a piece of history or work of art, he sees it as a valuable tool.

"You can run, let your fantasy run wild," Borelli said.

Friar Cesareo sees all the technology as a tool toward a specific goal: sharing the "treasure of faith and beauty."

"Technology helps us to go farther away, to reach more people than we could before," he said. "And in a more efficient way."

World.title: Brazil's presidential race heads to Lula–Bolsonaro run-off as right gains ground
World.content:
Brazil's presidential race heads to Lula–Bolsonaro run-off as right gains ground

toggle caption i Mauro Pimentel, Sergio Lima/

AFP via Getty Images





RIO DE JANEIRO —Brazil's presidential race is heading to a runoff between left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro after neither candidate secured the more than 50% of valid votes needed to win outright.

The race was tight, with Bolsonaro finishing ahead of Lula in Sunday's first-round election. With over 98% vote counted, Flavio Bolsonaro leads with over 47% of the vote and Lula holds second place with 44% of the vote.

If that sounds like déjà -vú, it's because in many ways, this election is a rerun: Lula narrowly defeated Bolsonaro's father, former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro, in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro is now serving a 27-year prison sentence under house arrest after being convicted of plotting to overturn that election and prevent Lula from taking office.

Sponsor Message

Flávio has pledged to carry on his father's legacy. But Sunday's results also pointed to a broader rightward shift in Brazilian politics, with the Bolsonaro camp performing strongly across the country.

Lula supporters gathered in a downtown Rio de Janeiro plaza cheered as the results came in, but also voiced apprehension about the runoff.

The presidential candidates who came in third, fourth, and fifth place are all right-wing, suggesting that Bolsonaro could have a natural pool of voters to draw from in the runoff. That could set the stage for another extremely tight contest on October 25.

Brazilians also chose governors and state and federal lawmakers Sunday, with early results showing that the right also made significant gains in Congress, particularly in the Senate. That could give Bolsonaro a stronger political base if he wins the presidency.

Lula, 80, is aiming for his fourth nonconsecutive term and has pledged to continue broad social spending and to stand up to Trump's aggressive policies toward Latin America.

Bolsonaro, 45, pledges to slash the deficit and realign the country's foreign policy with Washington. The result suggests Lula will now have to do more than defend his record: he will need to rebuild the broad coalition that returned him to power in 2022, including among younger voters who have shown less enthusiasm for his campaign.

Sponsor Message

This year's presidential campaign featured smaller rallies compared to past years, perhaps because both of the candidates felt like known quantities to voters.

"I think the campaign feels more muted because people are tired of fighting," said 38-year-old nutritionist Raysa Tavares after she voted Sunday afternoon in the Rio de Janeiro favela of Vidigal.

Businessman Caio Farias, 37, who voted in Rio's upscale neighborhood of Leblon, said that he preferred other right-wing candidates to Bolsonaro, but voted for Bolsonaro in an effort to try to get the election over in one round.

Now, Brazilians are gearing up for another three weeks of campaigning. In the 2022 election, the second round of the election saw a sharp uptick in political violence, with dozens of people physically attacking each other for political reasons, Brazilian news site Pública reported.

Beyond the fact that this year's contest features a younger Bolsonaro, there's something else setting it apart from the last one: Trump is in the White House, with big ambitions for drawing politics in Latin America to the right. Lula has accused the United States of trying to meddle in Brazil's election, which the U.S. State Department has denied.

Bolsonaro rallies have featured American flags and a giant inflatable doll of Trump holding a jailed Lula, while Lula has campaigned on the idea of protecting Brazilian sovereignty from foreign interference—a rarely-heard watchword in 2022. In Rio on election day, voters could be seen on the streets both with Trump T-shirts and "out with Trump" stickers.

The topic of Brazil's relationship with the United States is sure to feature in second-round campaigning, as are domestic themes of security policy, corruption, and the economy, which polls say are top of voters' minds.

But the first-round results have added another defining issue to the runoff: whether Brazil wants to continue with Lula or embrace the broader rightward shift that emerged from Sunday's vote.

World.title: Brazil votes, with Lula facing Bolsonaro's son
World.content:
Brazil votes, with Lula facing Bolsonaro's son

In Brazil, President Lula da Silva faces Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former president, in a tight race. If neither wins more than half the votes they'll face each other again on Oct. 25.
