World.title: Colombia’s top corporate lobbyist resigns over reported tensions with president
World.content:
The director of one of Colombia’s most powerful business associations, Bruce Mac Master of the ANDI, resigned amid tensions with President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a letter to the ANDI, Mac Master said that “it is time for me to step down from my role as head of the National Association of Entrepreneurs of Colombia.”

According to the former ANDI boss, “unexpected and troubling circumstances” made working for the association “particularly complex” and ‘multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously.”

In recent weeks, unexpected and troubling circumstances have arisen that have made the Association’s operating environment particularly complex, with potential adverse effects on its members and staff. Multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously. In the face of these challenges, I have sought to act with firmness and prudence, always prioritizing institutional channels and placing the interests of the ANDI above any personal considerations, in an effort to resolve this situation. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master’s resignation followed news suggesting that De la Espriella instructed his cabinet of boycotting the ANDI chief.

According to political news magazine La Silla Vacia, the rift between the ANDI and the government was because De la Espriella’s law firm was never allowed to join the ANDI and the association’s donations in response to the august 10 earthquake bypassed the First Lady’s newly founded and very controversial foundation.

“The General Board of Directors, its Executive Committee, and I did everything in our power to facilitate a solution and create conditions that would allow the Association to fully fulfill its role, seeking to keep channels of dialogue open and to continue contributing,” but “all of those attempts were unsuccessful.”

I deeply regret this, because I have always believed in collective intelligence and in the need for the government, the private sector, and institutions to work together—even in the face of differences—with respect, independence, and a sense of national responsibility. We tried, but we were unsuccessful. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master said that he hoped that his resignation would restore “collaboration between the national government and the business community—as represented by the General Board of Directors, the members, and the various divisions of the Association.”

The former ANDI chief had been trying to represent the business interests of its approximately 1,600 members since 2013.

World.title: Colombia seeks to tighten checks on public protests
World.content:
Colombia’s government published a draft decree that seeks to tighten regulations on public protests.

The draft was published weeks before labor unions and social organizations plan regional anti-government protests ahead of a national strike that is set for November.

The draft seeks to update the Decree #3 of 2021, which was issued months before a national strike that was violently repressed by the police and the military.

In an attempt to prevent another bloodbath, the decree seeks to regulate authorities’ response to protests and the coordinated use of force in response to acts of vandalism and violence.

The decree regulates dialogue between the protesters and law enforcement authorities to promote the peaceful nature of protests.

The decree additionally limits the use of police intelligence against those organizing and participating in the protests.

Last but not least, the decree seeks the effective prosecution of those arrested during protests through increased surveillance and a permanent police presence.

The decree comes amid social tensions that surged after the far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August and announced counterrevolutionary measures that seek to undo reforms by his leftist predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro.

Swelling student protests have been publicly accused of being fueled by insurgencies and De la Espriella has warned that police may enter universities if they find evidence they are used to prepare acts of vandalism or terrorism.

World.title: Colombia breaks diplomatic ties with Iran
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had broken diplomatic ties with Iran and designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.

The foreign ministry made the announcements in two separate statements that were published in its website.

In the first statement, the government claimed that the decision claimed to defend “national and hemispheric security, and the fight against transnational crime.”

According to the foreign ministry, the Iranian government has “alleged ties to international terrorist groups and other narco-terrorist groups that threaten [Colombia’s] security.”

Colombia also took into account the documented human rights violations committed by the Iranian government on its territory, the verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities’ obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran’s nuclear program. Foreign Ministry

In regards to the IRGC, the foreign ministry claimed that the Iranian armed force “poses a serious threat to international peace and security” through “covert operations beyond Iran’s borders.”

“Colombia will strengthen its control and security measures to prevent individuals associated with the IRGC from entering its territory,” said the foreign ministry in a second statement.

In his 2017 book “Watch Your Backyard,” Foreign Minister Omar Bula claimed that “Iran and Islamic extremist groups such a Hezbollah and Al Qaeda have profusely penetrated Latin America.”

As part of his foreign policy, President Abelardo de la Espriella has renewed ties with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

In a response, the Iranian government said that the accusations of the De la Espriella government go “against the principles of mutual respect” and damage both countries’ “interests and benefits.”

“It is clear that none of the arguments put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical, and that this measure was adopted solely under the influence of the Zionist regime and the United States,” said Iran’s foreign ministry.

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Colombia withdraws support for ICJ genocide case against Israel
World.content:
Colombia has withdrawn its participation in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Tuesday.

In a statement, the court in The Hague said that Colombia’s government “decided to withdraw the Declaration of intervention that it had filed… on 5 April 2024 in the case concerning Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip.”

The decision of the administration of President Abelardo De la Espriella is part of a wider attempt to restore ties with Israel and its main sponsor, the United States, and appease its Evangelical Christian support base.

In response to the ongoing genocide in Palestine, former President Gustavo Petro took a leading role in diplomatic efforts that sought to isolate Israel and seek justice for Israel’s victims through the world court.

In a response, the US Government put Petro on a blacklist and actively campaigned for the election of De la Espriella to prevent another leftist victory in elections earlier this year.

The new president, who took office in August, immediately restored diplomatic ties to Israel and lifted a ban on coal exports to the country in West Asia.

World.title: ACSN crime group shuts down parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast
World.content:
Santa Marta-based crime group ACSN shut down parts of the city and the surrounding region after Colombia’s armed forces killed one of their commanders.

Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” and six of his comrades were killed during an offensive on Monday.

The son of Fredy Castillo, a.k.a. “Pinocho,” who is one of the alleged bosses of the crime group, was reportedly among those killed during the operation.

Shortly after, a pamphlet that was signed by the ACSN ordered an “armed strike” of 48 hours because of the “the fierce attacks that the government has been launching against our organization in the Sierra Nevada since this afternoon.”

Multiple buses were incinerated in the region around Santa Marta.

We hereby declare a 48-hour armed strike throughout the province of Magdalena, particularly along the Troncal del Caribe highway, in the city of Santa Marta, and in the banana-growing region. We do not want any businesses to remain open for a period of 48 hours. ACSN

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who traveled to the city, “they are trying to intimidate the public by promoting an armed strike.”

“I will not allow any criminal organization to subjugate citizens through threats and terror,” the president added.

Notwithstanding, multiple shop owners in Santa Marta and along the highway kept their shops closed on Tuesday, afraid to challenge the authority of the local crime bosses.

The district government closed public schools in neighborhoods where the ACSN is believed to have a strong presence. Public transport was suspended as videos of armed men opening fire on shops that failed to close voluntarily were posted on social media.

The ACSN control much of drug trafficking to the port of Santa Marta and to the coastline of the neighboring La Guajira province.

De la Espriella ended attempts to negotiate the group’s surrender and ordered a military approach after taking office in August.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: US withdraws all its bombers from Britain's RAF Fairford base
World.content:
US withdraws all its bombers from Britain's RAF Fairford base

4th Sunday, October 2026 - 21:35 UTC Full article

The base, in Gloucestershire, is a forward operating location for the US Air Force's Global Strike Command

The United States has withdrawn all the bombers it had deployed at RAF Fairford, in western England, a week after the incident near the base that British counter-terrorism police are investigating. Washington gave no reason for the decision.

“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Defense Department official said on Sunday. The aircraft were B-1B Lancer bombers, around a dozen according to CNN; six B-52s had already returned in late September.

The base, in Gloucestershire, is a forward operating location for the US Air Force's Global Strike Command. Since March, bombers had flown from there in the war against Iran, after the British government approved its use for what it called defensive strikes.

On September 27, five men were arrested near the base after reports of three suspicious vehicles, and on Thursday police arrested a sixth man, a dual British-Iranian national, in London. All six are on bail and none has been charged. Washington publicly criticised the suspects' release, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham defended, citing the strict conditions imposed.

Burnham has said there are “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident, without giving details. Tehran denies any involvement. The British government had not commented on the bombers' withdrawal at the time of writing.

World.title: Falklands Chamber of Commerce backs the Punta Arenas route despite Argentine warnings
World.content:
Falklands Chamber of Commerce backs the Punta Arenas route despite Argentine warnings

4th Sunday, October 2026 - 21:19 UTC Full article

“Now we need to see this continue and see the ship at sea heading to the islands, and then we can start to talk about it being a success. Success comes when the goods arrive,” Summers said

The president of the Falkland Islands Chamber of Commerce, Mike Summers, has defended reopening trade with Chile's Magallanes region despite Argentina's campaign against economic activity linked to the archipelago, and warned that this week's business meeting in Punta Arenas will only be a success once cargo starts crossing the sea.

“Now we need to see this continue and see the ship at sea heading to the islands, and then we can start to talk about it being a success. Success comes when the goods arrive,” Summers said in an interview with the Chilean newspaper La Prensa Austral. He said the interest shown by Magallanes companies had exceeded the delegation's expectations, with opportunities concentrated in construction, agricultural fodder, hospitality and tourism. For the sea link to be viable, he added, there will need to be “an adequate supply of business in both directions”.

Asked about the arbitration announced by Argentine President Javier Milei and about warnings from Tierra del Fuego to those trading with the islands, Summers avoided confrontation. “We have heard this for many, many years,” he said. “We will keep talking about the opportunities and trading with southern Chile as long as it is possible to do so. If it is no longer possible, we will have to find other ways.” He noted that supply lines from northern Europe are currently “very long” and that “it makes sense” to trade with “our friendly neighbours”. If Chilean companies had concerns, he said, “they will say so and decline”, though his experience this week had been the opposite.

Summers, born in Stanley in 1952, headed the Falkland Islands Development Corporation from 1989 to 1996 and spent two decades as a member of the Legislative Assembly, leaving in 2017.

The meeting, held on September 28 and 29, brought together some 60 Magallanes companies and 32 companies and organisations from the archipelago, with 822 business meetings. Chilean shipping company Easter Island Naviera plans to launch a direct route between Punta Arenas and Stanley with a Chilean-flagged vessel between November and the end of the year. The Chilean government has called the initiative “a business between private parties”.

World.title: Trump declines to back Lula or Flávio Bolsonaro as Brazil votes
World.content:
Trump declines to back Lula or Flávio Bolsonaro as Brazil votes

4th Sunday, October 2026 - 08:57 UTC Full article

Trump gave vague answers. “I'm following it very closely. It's a very important country. The people of Brazil are fantastic. It's a very important election”

US President Donald Trump has not endorsed either of the two leading candidates in Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, unlike in recent elections in Honduras, Colombia, Chile, Argentina and Costa Rica.

Asked twice this week by reporters before boarding the presidential helicopter, Trump gave vague answers. “I'm following it very closely. It's a very important country. The people of Brazil are fantastic. It's a very important election,” he said on Thursday. “We're looking at the whole thing and following it very closely,” he repeated on Friday.

Over the past year, Trump publicly backed candidates including Nasry Asfura in Honduras, Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia ahead of the runoff, Javier Milei in Argentina, José Antonio Kast in Chile and Laura Fernández in Costa Rica. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, met him in the Oval Office in May, leaving with a joint photograph but no statement of support.

Trump's caution contrasts with his administration's tensions with Brasília. In July, Washington imposed new tariffs on Brazilian goods and sanctioned two Brazilian citizens and three companies over alleged links to the First Capital Command, which it designated a terrorist organisation along with Comando Vermelho. In 2025 it had sanctioned ministers and judges involved in the trial of Jair Bolsonaro, sentenced to 27 years for attempting a coup, a process Trump called a “witch hunt”.

The Brazilian Intelligence Agency raised the risk of US interference to “critical level” in a classified report sent in late August to the presidency, the Superior Electoral Court and the Justice Ministry. The assessment is preventive and does not claim that actual interference has occurred. According to Reuters, agency officials told a French and German delegation in September that there was interference from both the United States and Russia. In Washington, some thirty Democratic lawmakers, including Senator Bernie Sanders, accused Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a letter of acting “as an agent of interference and destabilisation” in Brazil.

Polls show Lula and Bolsonaro tied in a possible runoff, which would take place on October 25 if no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes today. Voting is electronic and results are usually known within hours of polls closing.

World.title: Scientific workshop on Illex Squid in Vigo with the participation of Falkland Islands
World.content:
Scientific workshop on Illex Squid in Vigo with the participation of Falkland Islands

3rd Saturday, October 2026 - 17:11 UTC Full article

The workshop forms part of an international scientific cooperation process that began with meetings held in Chile and Panama and continued with a scientific gathering in Bangkok

Argentine unions linked to the fishing, maritime and port industries have complained bitterly to the International Transport Workers Federation against a workshop on the Shortfin Squid (Illex Argentinus) organized by OPPC3, in Vigo with the suppot of the Sustaianble Fisheries Partnership, and to which Argentina allegedly has not been invited, but it does include the Falkland Islands.

OPPC3 stands for Organization of Producers of Freezer Trawlers for Hake, Cephalopods and Other Species. OPPC3 is based in Vigo, was started in 1986 when Spain joined the EU and represents approximately 60% of the European Union's freezer vessel fleet specializing in species like hake and squid.

The workshop with scientists from Brazil, Uruguay, the Falkland Islands, Spain, China and South Korea participating, aims to build a regional database and update scientific knowledge in order to assess the abundance and exploitation status of Argentine shortfin squid (Illex argentinus), which supports the largest fishery by landed volume in the South Atlantic Ocean.

Under the name of 4th International Scientific Workshop on Argentine shortfin squid (Illex argentinus) the event brought together scientists specializing in fisheries biology, population dynamics and stock assessment from the above mentioned countires.

The workshop aim was to continue advancing the development of a shared regional database and improve scientific knowledge of the abundance, productivity and exploitation status of this species.

The initiative is organized and funded by the Organization of Producers of Freezer Trawlers for Hake, Cephalopods and Other Species (OPPC3), with facilitation support from Sustainable Fisheries Partnership (SFP).

The workshop forms part of an international scientific cooperation process that began with meetings held in Chile and Panama and continued with a scientific gathering in Bangkok. The Vigo meeting represented a new step forward in strengthening collaboration between scientists and representatives of the fleets harvesting Illex argentinus throughout the Southwest Atlantic.

The fishery operates across waters shared by multiple nations and fishing fleets, in a context where no fully operational regional governance framework currently exists to coordinate stock assessment and resource management. Against this backdrop, the workshop seeks to foster greater cooperation among stakeholders by encouraging the exchange of scientific and fisheries information that can help reduce uncertainty regarding the status of the stock.

According to Edelmiro Ulloa, Managing Director of OPPC3, collaboration is essential to ensuring the long-term sustainability of the fishery: “The sustainability of a shared fishery requires the fleets operating on the resource to work together to improve the information available. Reducing uncertainty benefits companies, workers, administrations and scientists alike, while contributing to more responsible, predictable and sustainable management of the resource.”

OPPC3 believes that scientific cooperation and information exchange should be viewed as an opportunity to strengthen the health of the fishery and safeguard the economic activity and employment that depend upon it.

The workshop was scientifically chaired by Rubén Roa-Ureta, an independent expert in statistical modelling and fisheries stock assessment who has supported the initiative since its earliest stages.

According to Roa-Ureta, Illex argentinus is a species of enormous ecological, economic and social importance for the countries, industries and communities that depend on it. As a result, obtaining the best possible scientific assessment of its status and dynamics is a shared priority.

The work carried out in Vigo is expected to help consolidate a common technical foundation for future assessments, improve understanding of population dynamics and identify the key uncertainties that still need to be addressed.

World.title: Argentina to sell citizenship to foreigners for US$350,000 to raise dollars
World.content:
Argentina to sell citizenship to foreigners for US$350,000 to raise dollars

3rd Saturday, October 2026 - 09:52 UTC Full article

The legal basis is a May 2025 decree that tightened naturalisation requirements — with two years of continuous residence — and created an investment route, with a dedicated agency

Argentina's government has unveiled a citizenship-by-investment programme that will allow foreigners to obtain an Argentine passport in exchange for a non-refundable US$350,000 contribution to the Treasury or the purchase of US$800,000 in a seven-year government bond. Applications would open before the end of the year.

Economy Minister Luis Caputo and Cabinet Chief Diego Santilli announced the programme on Friday at the Argentine embassy in Paris, during Argentina Week, the investor gathering led this week by President Javier Milei. Amounts rise with family size: an extra US$100,000 for a spouse and for each unmarried, childless son or daughter aged 18 to 25, and US$25,000 for each child under 18. A family with two minor children would pay US$500,000.

The stated aim is to attract foreign currency. The Treasury faces substantial foreign-currency debt payments in 2027, and the government has postponed its return to international bond markets in a week when country risk hit its highest level of the year. According to estimates by a consortium of firms advising the government, cited by the Associated Press, the programme could raise up to around US$2.5 billion if it reaches the expected number of applicants.

“The Argentine passport is highly valued, accepted in more than 140 countries,” Caputo said, referring to destinations that do not require Argentine citizens to obtain a visa in advance, including the Schengen area. According to the minister, the idea emerged in July 2024, when US technology executives expressed interest in Argentine citizenship during a visit by Milei to Sun Valley, Idaho.

The legal basis is a May 2025 decree that tightened naturalisation requirements — with two years of continuous residence — and created an investment route, with a dedicated agency. The international tender to run the programme was cancelled in April this year.

Argentina would be the first South American country with such a programme. Only about a dozen states, several of them Caribbean islands, offer citizenship by investment, while some 60 grant residence. “It's not just about the advantages you get inside Argentina; you also get global benefits in terms of where you can go,” said Kristin Surak, a professor at the London School of Economics.

Such programmes have been criticised for their vulnerability to corruption. The Financial Action Task Force has warned they can be used to conceal identities, launder money and evade justice, and the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled Malta's programme unlawful in April 2025. Caputo said intelligence services and financial oversight bodies would vet applicants' identities, criminal records and sources of funds, to protect “the international standing of Argentine citizenship”.

World.title: Uruguay ranks third in Latin America for international air passengers per capita
World.content:
Uruguay ranks third in Latin America for international air passengers per capita

3rd Saturday, October 2026 - 09:40 UTC Full article

Uruguay ranked third in Latin America and the Caribbean in 2025 for international air passengers per inhabitant, according to Airports Council International figures presented in Lima this week, despite its small share of the region's total traffic.

The country recorded 0.67 international passengers per inhabitant, behind only the Dominican Republic, at 1.71, and Costa Rica, at 1.62. As an outside reference, the United States recorded 0.77. Argentina, by contrast, stood at 0.34.

Absolute volume tells a different story. Uruguay's airports handled some 2.3 million passengers in 2025, compared with 235 million in Brazil, 191 million in Mexico, 100 million in Colombia and 50 million in Argentina. In total passengers per inhabitant, Uruguay recorded 0.68, below most of the region's large markets and above Paraguay, Ecuador, Guatemala and Honduras, among others.

The director general of the organisation's Latin American branch, ACI-LAC, Rafael Echevarne, attributed Uruguay's position to the development of Carrasco International Airport and its integration with logistics activity. “Uruguay is one of the star countries, not only in the region but almost worldwide,” he told the newspaper El País. He highlighted the Latin America Cargo City logistics centre at Carrasco, which he said has become a regional hub for the pharmaceutical industry serving Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay, as well as the integration between the airport and the port of Montevideo. The airport and its logistics centre are operated by the Corporación América group.

The figures come against a regional market growing at a more moderate pace. In the first half of 2026, passenger traffic in Latin America and the Caribbean rose 1.9% and cargo 3.6%. ACI-LAC projects long-term growth of 3.1% a year, taking the region from some 809 million passengers this year to around 1.5 billion in 2045, with required investment estimated at US$178 billion over thirty years.

The post-pandemic recovery has been uneven: according to the organisation, 133 airports in the region remain below their 2019 passenger traffic and 161 have not recovered their cargo levels.

World.title: Alternative media and Trump are influencing Brazilian voters
World.content:
Alternative media and Trump are influencing Brazilian voters

3rd Saturday, October 2026 - 07:36 UTC Full article

Bolsonaro Junior, the new face of the hard right, and Lula, in his eighties and with half the voters believing the accusations that he is a ‘thief’

By Gwynne Dyer - “Flávio Bolsonaro is Trump’s candidate and what Trump wants is to colonize Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust,” claims the latest video released by President Luiz Inácio ‘Lula’ da Silva’s re-election campaign.

The weird thing is about half of Brazil’s voters would be OK with Trump running the country (through Bolsonaro). However nobody in Brazil thinks that Flávio Bolsonaro is his own man.

He is the son of Jair Bolsonaro, the hard right ex-soldier and former president who tried a coup after he lost the 2022 election. It was even clumsier and more half-hearted than Trump’s brief excursion in sedition after he lost the US 2020 election – but Jair Bolsonaro went to jail for his attempt.

In a strange way, Trump even recognizes the parallel, showing special sympathy for his imprisoned fellow traveler. He claimed that the senior Bolsonaro was the victim of a “witch-hunt” by the Brazilian Supreme Court and slapped 50% tariffs on the country.

And next Sunday, Oct. 4, the junior Bolsonaro faces Lula in another presidential election.

We already know that there will be a second round of voting on Oct. 25, when the other three candidates have dropped out and it’s a straight race between Lula and Junior.

It is difficult to anticipate what that outcome will be, because the two men have been only one or two points apart (i.e. ‘within the margin of error’) in every opinion poll for months.

We know where that extraordinary stability comes from, because it is the same in the United States and in many other democracies. Most Brazilians have abandoned ‘legacy media’ and get all their information from a vast network of alternative news sites, YouTube channels, social media influencers, Facebook pages, WhatsApp groups and legions of bots.

Or rather, from two vast and mutually exclusive networks of the same approach. Whatever your opinion is now, it will likely be the same next year, because little else is getting through. Moreover, in the Brazilian case, there’s not really much to get excited about.

Inflation is low, unemployment is low, and the economy is growing faster in Brazil than in most other G20 countries. A big bank failed last year, causing a long-running corruption scandal, and the murder rate is preposterously high, but relatively speaking, Brazilians should not have much to complain about, so in the end it will probably come down to ‘sovereignty’.

Lula recently warned on ‘X’ that Flávio Bolsonaro will “hand our natural resources over to the United States…If it’s up to him, Brazil will become a colony again.”

The president portrays that as a threat, and traditionally the vast majority of Brazilians would have agreed, but both Flávio and his imprisoned father Jair would see it almost as a happy ending.

Neither of them puts it exactly like that in public, but both men see the long military dictatorship of 1964-1985 as a lost golden age. Jair served it as an active-service officer and has praised its torturers (“The dictatorship’s mistake was to torture but not kill”).

His son says “there was security, there was quality health and education, there was respect.”

Actually there was terror, lies and legalized looting, but we need not re-litigate that here. The problem is how quickly people forget, and a softer, gentler version of those brutal regimes is taking over all across Latin America.

Keiko Fujimori, the old dictator’s daughter, is the new president of Peru. The father of Chile’s new president José Antonio Kast was a Nazi who fought for Hitler, and he himself had links to the bloody dictator Pinochet. President Javier Milei of Argentina is a chainsaw-wielding ‘anarcho-capitalist paleo-libertarian’.

Abelardo de la Espriella, Colombia’s new president, restarted the war with insurgents on his first day in office. Delcy Rodriguez, once vice-president of Venezuela under Maduro, has switched to being leach president under Trump and signed over the country’s oil. There’s Daniel Noboa in Ecuador and Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, and Cuba awaits its fate at Trump’s hands.

A shady lot, you might say, and they are all selling the same deal: prosperity and security in return for obedience. That’s not a terrible deal if the autocrats keep their end of bargain, but generally they can’t or at least won’t. There will be tears before bedtime.

There are only two big hold-outs to the populist wave in Latin America. Mexico in the north seems all right for the moment, but Brazil in the south is teetering on the brink. All that really stands between it and failure is one 80-year-old man – but he is a very tough old man, and if his health holds he may be able to pull it off.

World.title: Brazil votes with Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro tied and a small group of undecided voters holding the key
World.content:
Brazil votes with Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro tied and a small group of undecided voters holding the key

3rd Saturday, October 2026 - 07:06 UTC Full article

Brazil holds the first round of its presidential election on Sunday, with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro tied in a prospective runoff and a narrow band of undecided voters, along with abstention, able to tip the result.

The latest polls show an electorate that has barely moved. Quaest's survey, published on Monday, gave Lula 39% and Bolsonaro 34% in the first round, and a 42% tie in the second, due on October 25. According to that poll, 5% of voters have yet to decide and 10% say they will vote blank, spoil their ballot or abstain. Datafolha, in last week's survey, put the undecided at 2%. The other candidates — Augusto Cury, Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema — total around 12% between them.

“The vote is already crystallised in at least 80% of the Brazilian population; the question is what the remaining 15 or 20% will do,” political scientist Leonardo Paz of the Getúlio Vargas Foundation told the newspaper El País, comparing the dynamics to US elections, where the contest is fought over specific niches of the electorate. The candidates focused their final events on the outskirts of São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais, the three states with the most voters.

In the last week, both reached out to voters wary of polarisation. “You don't need to dress in red, just think that Brazil can go further,” Lula said. “If you also want change, you don't have to like me,” Bolsonaro said. The only debate planned with both, on Thursday on TV Globo, was cancelled after both stayed away and a series of court rulings.

“I'll decide right there, in front of the ballot box,” Elza Mendes, a cleaner in Rio de Janeiro, told the same newspaper, torn between Bolsonaro's security pledges and her fear of cuts to social programmes.

Turnout will be another factor. Although voting is compulsory, abstention in the first round in 2022 reached about 21% of the electorate, the highest since 1998. Analysts warn it could be higher this year and would hurt Lula most, as his support is concentrated among lower-income groups, who abstain the most.

Besides the president, Brazilians will elect all 27 state governors, the entire Chamber of Deputies and two thirds of the Senate.

World.title: Know your Mexico City neighborhood: Historic center of Coyoacán
World.content:
Borough: Coyoacán

Established: 1521, as Villa Coyoacán

Location: 10 km south of the Angel de la Independencia



Pre-Columbian inhabitants: Colhuas, Tepanecs and Mexica

Who lives here

The Historic Center of Coyoacán comprises several smaller neighborhoods, including Villa Coyoacán, Del Carmen, Santa Catarina and La Concepción. Its bohemian lifestyle attracts young families and artists, while its proximity to UNAM makes it a hub for students. According to government data, 23% of the borough’s inhabitants are between the ages of 25 and 49. There is a notable mix of newcomers and families that have lived here for generations, adding to the area’s eclectic feel.

A litany of colorful characters have lived in Coyoacán’s Historic Center, notably Frida Kahlo, León Trotsky, Octavio Paz and Rufino Tamayo — as well as at least three Mexico News Daily staff members.

A brief history of Coyoacán

The Colhuas of Culhuacan transformed the future Coyoacán into an urban center, settling here in the 7th century. In the 15th century the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco arrived, displacing the Colhuas and establishing the area as a center of trade, agriculture and commerce. At some point, the settlement acquired its current Nahuatl name, which is most often translated as “place of coyotes.”

Coyoacán’s strategic position on Lake Texcoco caught the attention of the Mexica, who soon seized the area from the Tepanecs. Plazas, residential zones and temples were constructed to the chagrin of the conquered Tepanecs, the majority of whom detested the Mexica. In 1521, Hernán Córtes and his allies launched their campaign against the Mexica Empire, they chose Coyoacán as their headquarters, establishing the town of Villa Coyoacán. A strategic location, abundant agricultural resources and local support made the cultural hub an ideal place to become the first capital of New Spain.

Coyocán remained its own municipality until 1857, when it was officially incorporated into the Federal District. It retained its small-town and semi-rural character until sometime in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when it was swallowed up by the urban sprawl of what is now Mexico City. The borough of Coyoacán, taking its name from the ancient town, was designated in 1928, and is still the physical heart of Mexico City, sitting dead in the center of the metropolis.

A guide to Coyoacán today

Today, the quaint Barrio Mágico is known for its cobblestone streets, colonial architecture and vibrant cultural scene. The weekends are especially lively. Expect streets lined with food carts selling everything from churros to esquites, live music in Plaza de La Conchita and various amusement park-style rides for the little ones. Don’t miss the neighborhood dance party on Sunday evenings at the Jardin del Arte Allende.

The Saturday art market in Plaza Allende is smaller than its more famous cousin in San Ángel, but still worth checking out if you find yourself in the area.

Coyoacán is great if: You love Spanish colonial architecture, colorful facades, traditional festivals and an authentically Mexican community.

What to do in Coyoacán

Frida Kahlo Museum: Also known as the Casa Azul, this is the former home of Mexico’s most iconic female artist. Reservations must be made in advance.

Church of San Juan Bautista: This 16th-century church is the spiritual center of Coyoacán

Leon Trotsky Museum: The house where the exiled Russian revolutionary lived and met his unfortunate demise by way of ice pick.

Plaza Hidalgo and Plaza de la Conchita: Two lively squares surrounded by cafes, restaurants, street performers and food carts. The church in the center of the square is said by some to be Mexico’s oldest. The two are linked by Calle Higuera, believed to be the first street laid down by the Spanish during the early days of the conquest. Visit weekend mornings for a chance to jam with unofficial resident band KoolBananas, while enjoying coffee and cake from one of the coffee shops that dot the square.

Jardín Centenario: Home of the famous Coyote Fountain.

Avenida Francisco Sosa: A charming, tree-lined street with colonial-era architecture and art galleries. Attractions include the Casa Alvarado — the last residence of Nobel prize winner Octavio Paz, now home to the National Sound Archive — and some of the best coffee and wine stores in the city.

National Watercolor Museum: Tucked down a side street a stone’s throw from the Casa Alvarado, the museum hosts an array of works from across the country.

Viveros de Coyoacán: A 39-hectare park and tree nursery with trails and — you guessed it — trees. Thousands of them. Keep in mind that food is not allowed in the park, and security searches bags at the gate.

Honorable mentions: Though not in the Historic Center proper, any visitor to the borough of Coyoacán should see the Anahuacalli Museum, which houses Diego Rivera’s personal collection of pre-Columbian art, and the central campus of the National Autonomous University of Mexico, a Unesco World Heritage Site since 2007. The surrounding area is also home to major sports teams, notably soccer giants Club América and rugby titans Coyotes.

Where to eat in Coyoacán

Tostadas de Coyoacán: A stall in the Coyoacán Market known for crispy tortillas topped with ceviche or cochinita pibil.

Mercado de Comida de Coyoacán: Located at the tip of Calle Higuera, on the corner with the main square, visitors can make the most of a genuinely authentic street food market.

Tacos Chupacabras: A legendary taco stand known for its special “Chupa Cabra tacos,” which are a mix of chorizo and carnitas, garnished with various toppings.

Mi Compa Chava: The second branch of chef Salvador Orozco’s Sinaloan-style restaurant is never not packed with seafood lovers. The ambience alone is worth the wait for a table.

Los Danzantes: The sister restaurant to Oaxaca’s legendary Michelin star winner is located opposite the Coyote fountain.

Coyoacán hidden gem

The Callejón del Aguacate, or Avocado Alley. Legend has it that in the 1930s, a uniformed soldier was sauntering down this tiny alley when a young boy, captivated by the soldier’s appearance, asked to play with him. The boy was so insistent that the soldier lost his head and killed the boy.

His regret mounted so much that he did what any repentant murderer would do: supervise the construction of a Virgin Mary statue at the site of the child’s death. In this way, all future visitors to the alley could be given the opportunity to clean their sinful slates by offering prayers to the statue. Some say, if you tune in, you can feel the boy’s spirit wandering the alley.

Have we missed any must-see sights in out Coyoacán guide? Let us know down below!

Bethany Platanella is a travel planner and lifestyle writer based in Mexico City. She lives for the dopamine hit that comes directly after booking a plane ticket, exploring local markets, practicing yoga and munching on fresh tortillas. Sign up to receive her Sunday Love Letters to your inbox, peruse her blog, or follow her on Instagram.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Guanajuato residents mistake arrival of French acrobats for third ‘French Intervention’
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

GUANAJUATO, Guanajuato — Civic vigilance reached a 160-year high in the historic capital of Guanajuato on Saturday evening after local residents, observing a group of French performers scaling public buildings and suspending high-tension ropes across historic plazas, mistakenly believed the French Republic had launched a third military intervention in Mexico.

Members of the Paris-based Chaillot National Theater, who arrived in the city to perform a collaborative aerial circus piece titled “Vértigo” for the 54th International Cervantino Festival, were met with suspicious glances and immediate defensive maneuvering from municipal historians, local shopkeepers, and neighborhood watch organizers who recalled that previous French arrivals had resulted in imposed monarchies and six-year occupations.

“We saw men in fitted performance gear deploying cables across Plaza Allende and securing anchor points near the Cervantes Theater,” said local historian and retired educator Don Héctor Morales, who admitted to briefly scouring his cellar for period-appropriate artillery. “Naturally, given the diplomatic history of 1838 and 1862, we assumed the French government was once again attempting to collect unpaid bakery debts or institute an unconstitutional monarchy. It turned out they were just balancing on a wire to live ambient jazz.”

The diplomatic confusion mounted when highliner Jean-Claude Moreau walked across a slackline suspended decades above the cobbled streets, an act interpreted by several onlookers as an attempt to establish aerial dominance over the state’s historic center. Public concern was only eased when municipal officers confirmed that France was merely participating as the festival’s invited guest nation to celebrate 200 years of mostly peaceful diplomatic relations.

The production, which combines contemporary dance, live music, and aerial arts, required local authorities to release a clarification confirming that highliners hanging mid-air were engaged in artistic expression rather than strategic reconnaissance. Organizers assured the public that despite the visible presence of French acrobats hovering near historic architecture, no foreign princes would be installed in Chapultepec Castle as a result of the performance.

World.title: USA defeats error-prone Mexico, hands Márquez first loss as boss
World.content:
This one is going to hurt for a while.

El Tri face-planted in the first real test of the Rafa Márquez era, producing a handful of blunders that a grateful U.S. team converted into a 3-0 rout on Saturday night in Arizona.

TRES A CERO IN THE DESERT! 🇺🇸 https://t.co/CI3plLNTrD — U.S. Soccer Men’s National Team (@USMNT) October 4, 2026

Worse than the self-inflicted wounds that left Márquez screaming in frustration, the bloopers by key players might produce significant line-up juggling for Tuesday’s game against Chile.

Multiple errors by goalie Raúl Rangel, fullback Mateo Chávez and defender Diego Campillo might not cost them roster spots for next month’s Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals, but a loss of confidence is surely a possibility.

Mexico pressed forward during the opening 25 minutes, creating three scoring opportunities though failing to get a shot on target.

Then, against the run of play, El Tri was caught napping.

With two Mexico defenders hard against the sideline, U.S. midfielder Gio Reyna charged into the vacated space well ahead of his marker, Orbelín Pineda.

Reyna got deep into the box before sending a low cross that Rangel should have handled. Instead of corralling the ball, the Chivas goalie watched it clank off his right foot and bounce into the path of Julian Hall who, left unmarked by Campillo, simply poked the ball into the net.

Fifteen minutes later, Santi Giménez had a chance to equalize, but was unable to redirect a deflected pass on net from the back side.

Though Mexico enjoyed 60% possession, El Tri went to the locker room trailing 1-0.

Chávez came on to start the second half, but was off-tune from the outset. He turned the ball over the first two times he touched it and was out of position on two other occasions.

In minute 62, Rangel committed a howler. Looking to pass out of the back while outside the goalie box, he passed it straight to Cavan Sullivan and the 17-year-old forward calmly chipped the embarrassed Rangel for a 2-0 lead.

Before Mexico could regain equilibrium, Chávez lost his cool, unnecessarily fouling Yunus Musah before lashing out at Sebastian Berhalter and earning a red card.

Sebastian Berhalter got right in Mateo Chávez’s face after the foul on Musah, refused to back down, and ate a two handed slap that earned Mexico the red. Some will say he lost control and left his teammates exposed in a rivalry scrap, but that sending-off left El Tri with 10 men and the USMNT closed it out 3-0. Mateo Chávez should have controlled himself and better still fall to the immediately he was pushed https://t.co/wme6irdsN1 — @DailyFootyTakes (@DailyFootyTakes) October 4, 2026

El Tri spent the remaining 23 minutes chasing shadows, but was unable to prevent further damage.

In minute 84, Campillo allowed a back pass to roll into the box while trying to shield the ball from Malik Tillman, but the U.S. midfielder circled him and blasted a left-footer into the net past a helpless Rangel.

After this latest gaffe, cameras caught an exasperated Márquez turning toward the El Tri bench, venting his incredulity that the culprits were players expected to be stalwarts in the run-up to the 2030 World Cup.

Rangel, 26, starred for Mexico during the just-completed World Cup, posting four shutouts, while Chávez, 22, appeared to be the heir apparent at left back, scoring a goal in his only World Cup start (against Czechia). Campillo, 24, is bidding to stake claim to a spot in the defensive rotation.

World.title: 6 Mexican comfort foods to warm you up this autumn
World.content:
As cold weather sets in across most of the Northern Hemisphere, bringing heavy coats and low temperatures, the seasonal change in Mexico is a subtle shift marked by increasingly chilly mornings and nights alongside mild days.

It might not be cold enough to break out winter coats, but it is chilly enough to whet the appetite for steaming broths, warm tortillas fresh off the comal, and other comforting flavors.

From north to south, here are six dishes from across Mexico to whet your autumn appetite.

Apapacho de mamá – cheese soup

El Mejor Caldo de Queso Estilo Sonora

Watch this video on YouTube

Hailing from the northern cattle-ranching state of Sonora — characterized by freezing winters in its highlands — this cheese soup is a simple yet comforting dish that feels like an apapacho de mamá (“warm hug from mom”).

The broth features tomato, onion, garlic and chiles, into which cubes of queso fresco or regional cheese are added. Unlike other cheese soups around the world, these cheese cubes do not melt — rather, they soften without completely losing their shape. Depending on the specific recipe, the soup may also include potato, zucchini, corn, cilantro and fried tortilla strips for added texture.

A nourishing dish – milpa soup

Milpa is a pre-Hispanic crop-growing system in which several plants were cultivated together, with maize as the central element.

Farmers in present-day Puebla, Tlaxcala, Mexico City, Hidalgo and central Mexico overall would prepare a broth incorporating all ingredients of the milpa, primarily corn kernels, onion, squash blossom and chilies.

Following the Spanish conquest, crops grown in the milpa diversified, and chicken broth became the base of the soup.

Today, milpa soup represents an accessible, balanced and nourishing meal that will keep you going through the colder months.

The Mexican paella – morisqueta

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Michoacán (@visitmichoacan)

Think of paella, but make it Mexican — that is morisqueta, one of the most cherished dishes of Michoacán’s Tierra Caliente region.

This humble yet classic dish is full of flavor, featuring cooked white rice served with pot-style beans and topped with a red sauce made from tomatoes, chili peppers, onion and garlic. In some households, it is garnished with queso fresco and may also include pork, dried meat and eggs.

Some scholars suggest that its name reflects the cultural syncretism that occurred after the Spanish conquest. It is derived from the Spanish words Moros (Moors) and Cristianos (Christians), referencing the combination of rice — introduced to Spain by the Moors — and beans, which were grown in present-day Mexico.

A hearty soup, not a taco – birria

View this post on Instagram A post shared by @sabor_casero29

Birria has taken the world by storm, with many restaurants abroad featuring birria tacos on their menus. However, few people know that authentic birria is mostly consumed as a soup rather than a taco.

Originally from the western state of Jalisco, birria is a traditional slow-cooked stew served in a deep bowl with its hot broth or consommé, making it more akin to a hearty soup than a taco filling.

The classic version is prepared with goat meat marinated in adobo made from dried chiles, garlic, onion, vinegar, tomato and spices such as cumin, oregano, cloves, pepper and cinnamon.

It is served with warm tortillas and garnished with cilantro, onion and a few drops of lime.

A comforting breakfast – huevos motuleños

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Tasos Mitselis (@tasos_mitselis)

Huevos motuleños is an iconic breakfast dish originally from Motul, Yucatán, a town located in the north-central region of the state.

This heartwarming dish features a fried corn tortilla topped with refried black beans and fried eggs, covered by a warm tomato sauce made from onion, diced ham and peas. It is often garnished with queso fresco and fried plantain.

The combination of ingredients encapsulates Yucatecan cuisine, which is characterized by Caribbean flavors (plantain), pre-Hispanic ingredients (corn) and Spanish elements (eggs and pork).

Sopa de lentejas

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Karina Valladares (@kari.receta)

Although lentils are typically associated with Middle Eastern dishes, this ancient crop found a place of its own in Mexican cuisine following its introduction during the viceregal era.

In southern Mexico, including the states of Chiapas, Tabasco and Oaxaca, lentils are cooked in a base of tomato, onion and garlic, and may include ingredients such as carrot, potato, chili pepper, epazote or cilantro. It can also be enriched with bacon, smoked pork chop and chorizo, infusing the warm dish with deeper flavors and protein.

In Oaxaca specifically, the soup is garnished with fruit, including southern staples such as plantain and pineapple.

Gabriela Solís is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: From jungle to wildflowers: How Mexico made me a botanical artist
World.content:
It all started with a twisted scarlet seedpod … such a beautiful, unexpected thing lying at my feet. Then curiosity set in, and I began to notice the plants around me.

Mexico’s amazing plants eventually inspired not just curiosity, but creativity. Thus, for the first time in 30 years, I picked up a sketchbook again. That was two and a half years ago. Today, my third sketchbook is almost complete.

1 of 6

Pages are filled with huge leaves, wildflowers and edible treasures like tejocote, mamey and nance; plus, seedpods of all shapes and sizes. Native plants, edible plants, healing plants … I’ve sketched them all, plus the pollinating creatures they attract: butterflies, metallic green bees and beetles.

Now, I am an artist. Bel the Batty Botanist. I deeply thank Mexico for this.

A passion for natural beauty

The medicinal healing properties of native plants have become a passion, as have edible plants. Enjoying edible treasures like Jamaican cherries that taste like cotton candy. Or the crunchy delights of pepino kat, a long, ribbed cucumber-like fruit.

It seems every time I step outside, something delights me. The cheery yellow of Mexican prickly poppies, the plant of resilience and endurance, waving in the sunshine. The smell of vanilla from beach spider lilies after a swim.

These botanical beauties inspire my art. I sketch in black ballpoint pen or fine-line markers, with watercolor pencils and paints and on different-colored papers. Which, I must say, really makes a white subject shine.

Inspired by seeing a chicalote, a native white poppy in the Central Highlands, I looked for ways to capture its brilliance. Soft gray paper for a dreamy, romantic feel seemed right. Because, to me, poppies are dreamy.

1 of 6

Sometimes it’s nice to sit quietly. As seen on my passionflower page. Within 20 minutes, while sketching, I witnessed a Gulf fritillary butterfly lay eggs. I saw its spiky orange caterpillars varying from tiny to huge, ready to form their chrysalis … mature butterflies pollinating the flowers. An entire life cycle was revealed to me on a single vine.

Other times, a collection of found treasures inspires something new. Hurricane Beryl two years ago, for example, brought down a bounty of botanical treasures for me to paint.

So, who knows what I’ll find tomorrow. Something as beautiful as that twisted scarlet seedpod, I hope. But I bet it will be magical.

Mexico Correspondent for International Living, Bel Woodhouse is an experienced writer, author, photographer and videographer with 500+ articles published both in print and across digital platforms. Living in the Mexican Caribbean for over seven years now, she’s in love with Mexico and has no plans to go anywhere anytime soon.

World.title: Remembering the Tlatelolco student massacre of 1968
World.content:
The Tlatelolco student massacre of 1968 — one of the most pivotal events in modern Mexican history, one that the renowned National Security Archive organization has called “Mexico’s Tiananmen Square” — all began with a fracas between two rival public vocational high schools that erupted into an out-and-out brawl in a Mexico City marketplace built for the upcoming 1968 Olympics.

The next day, riot police arrived at the two schools, wielding clubs and beating anyone within reach, attacking students and faculty with equal brutality. The following day, students took to the streets in protest of the previous day’s beating, which then, in turn, drew the police out for more violent confrontations.

How protests escalated into the 1968 Tlatelolco Massacre

“Those protests provoked more repression, which provoked more protests,” journalists Julia Preston and Samuel Dillon explained in their 2005 book, “Opening Mexico: The Making of a Democracy.”

By the fourth day of protests, tensions escalated. To express solidarity with their fellow teenage protesters, the students of the prestigious high school, San Ildefonso Preparatory — officially known as the National Preparatory School — declared a strike. When Mexican President Gustavo Díaz Ordaz learned that the students at the prestigious government-run school were on strike, he ordered the Mexican army to take the campus.

Soldiers in Jeeps and small tanks moved across the city, aiming to confront the students of San Ildefonso. When they arrived at the campus, they found the entrance locked, so soldiers blew the school’s ornate 18th-century wooden door, hand-carved by Indigenous craftsmen, to bits.

The soldiers rampaged through the school, beating anyone they could find. They then turned on other high schools, and even attacked unsuspecting pedestrians they encountered on surrounding streets.

“By the end of the day, 400 people had been hospitalized and 1,000 arrested,” Preston and Dillon noted.



“Through the military occupation of the San Ildefonso School, the government elevated the situation from a local, primarily police matter to an issue of national security,” wrote Mexican historian Enrique Krauze, author of the seminal book “Mexico: Biography of Power.”

A history of government repression

For most Mexicans, government repression was nothing new. In 1959, railroad workers who went on strike, asking for better working conditions and a modest pay increase, were viciously put down, a pattern well-established with striking miners, doctors, nurses and even teachers. Strikers were routinely either beaten into submission or cajoled into joining a newly created government-run union. But this episode — the government violently attacking a high school — stunned most Mexicans.

In response, on July 31, Javier Barros Sierra, the politically moderate rector of the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) — which was in charge of San Ildefonso Preparatory and is the largest and most prestigious university in Latin America — led a dignified, peaceful march of 50,000 faculty and students through Mexico City’s leafy suburbs.

That Barros had the temerity to lead such a protest earned him the enmity of Díaz Ordaz; later that summer, it cost him his job. That march, however, moved the center of protests against the government from Mexico’s high schools to its universities.

Taking inspiration from the U.S. civil rights movement and the earlier 1968 student protest movements in Paris, West Germany, Czechoslovakia, Poland and Japan, the Mexican university student activists had happened upon an issue that already deeply resonated with the general Mexican public: government brutality.

Students stand up in dissent

Raúl Álvarez Garín, a 27-year-old physics student from Mexico’s National Polytechnic Institute, emerged as one of the student leaders. Álvarez came from a family steeped in a tradition of protest and of standing up for its beliefs. His grandfather was an aide to Mexican Revolutionary General Álvaro Obregón. His parents were communists. His wife was the daughter of one of the leaders of the aforementioned railroad workers’ strike of 1959.

Álvarez helped draw up a modest list of demands: The government should release the recently jailed students, as well as the railroad union leaders still imprisoned since 1959. They should also compensate the families of injured protesters, disband the riot police and repeal vague laws used to jail anyone who dissented with the government.

Álvarez and his fellow activists weren’t advocating regime change or overthrowing the government. They were advocating that the political process in Mexico become more tolerant, open and democratic. But, for Díaz Ordaz, this was beyond the pale. The government never responded to the demands.

In the face of government silence, the student activists decided to hold a march from the southern suburbs to the Zócalo. They set the date for August 13, hoping to attract a few followers. On that day, by the time they reached the Zócalo, there were 200,000 people in tow. While many were students and families of students, there were also nurses, teachers, and every kind of worker in the city in the crowd. Speeches were delivered, and the event was entirely peaceful. As Preston and Dillon pointed out, “The unexpected size of the crowd proved that the students were voicing frustrations felt by Mexicans of all ages in a modernizing Mexico.”

A warning to protesters

The students then planned another march to the Zócalo for August 27, and this time, 400,000 people showed up. On this occasion, though, some students congregated under the balcony of the National Palace, the building from which Mexican presidents traditionally preside over annual Independence Day celebrations, standing on a balcony. Those students then started chanting, “Sal al balcón, chango hocicón” (“Come out to the balcony, you big-snouted monkey”) — referring to Díaz Ordaz’s pronounced buckteeth and frequent comparisons to a monkey.

As nighttime fell, most protesters left, but at the approach of midnight, a few thousand stragglers continued to mill around. At that point, a dozen armored personnel carriers rolled into the Zócalo; the army mercilessly beat any remaining protesters.

Then on September 1, Díaz Ordaz delivered his annual State of the Union address, essentially offering a warning.

“We can’t allow our legal order to continue to be ruptured so inexcusably,” the president declared in his speech. “We wouldn’t like to find ourselves in a situation where we would have to take measures we don’t want to. But we’ll take them if we must. We’ll go as far as we have to.”

Unfortunately, the students did not recognize the warning.

Politician and ex-education minister of Mexico City Salvador Martínez della Roca, one of the student leaders from UNAM at the time, told U.S. journalist Mark Kurlansky, “It was a threat, but we didn’t really listen.”

By September 24, “Mexico City was living under a barely camouflaged state of siege,” Krauze explains.

Mexican military mobilizes against campuses

On that day, the army seized the National Polytechnic Institute (IPN), known colloquially as the Politécnico; government forces had already occupied the UNAM campus. IPN students fought the army for hours, but there was only so much that unarmed civilians could do against tanks.

Although the army withdrew from both campuses on September 30, the message had been sent. Unfortunately, students failed to recognize that, for Díaz Ordaz’s government, a hard-and-fast deadline was quickly approaching: the 1968 Olympic Games, scheduled to begin in Mexico City on Oct. 12.

The Olympics were seen by many in the nation as Mexico’s moment to shine: The world no longer saw it as a chaotic, strife-ridden backwater nation but as the “Mexico Miracle” — with a powerful economy and a newly minted middle class. From the 1950s through the 1960s, Mexico’s economy had grown at 6% per annum (8% in 1968). In 1968, Mexico had the strongest economy in all of Latin America, with an inflation rate lower than the United States.

Díaz Ordaz was not about to let a bunch of long-haired students, whom he viewed as spoiled, ruin the opening of the Olympic Games and Mexico’s moment of glory.

President Díaz Ordaz sees conspiracies everywhere

Much like former U.S. president Richard Nixon, Díaz Ordaz was a tremendously insecure man, about his appearance and when interacting with others. “Ever since he was a little boy, the sense of being ugly had tortured him,” Krauze explained. “His mother would freely say to anyone, ‘But what an ugly son I have!’ It would take its toll on his life.”

And much like Nixon, Díaz Ordaz saw conspiracies everywhere. If students were protesting, it must be at the behest of French communists or Cuban agitators. In reality, this seems unlikely; even the CIA station chief in Mexico City, Winston Scott, doubted it.

“Although the [Mexican] government claims to have solid evidence that the Communist Party engineered the fracas of 26 July, and reportedly had indications of Soviet Embassy complicity, it is unlikely that the Soviets would so undermine their carefully nurtured good relations with the Mexicans,” Scott told CIA headquarters at the time.

It never occurred to Díaz Ordaz that it was, in fact, his policies — or his overreaction to a minor skirmish — that spurred the student protests.

After a few more protests, at which some buses were set on fire, the student leaders scheduled a rally to be held on October 2 at the Plaza de las Tres Culturas. This plaza sits in the Tlatelolco neighborhood on the north side of Mexico City. Perhaps more than any other site, it best represents Mexican history: Aztec ruins there are flanked by a Franciscan church.

In the 1960s, the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) government built a housing project there, one building of which was Edificio Chihuahua. The third floor of the Edificio Chihuahua had an open-air hallway with a three-foot wall overlooking the plaza. It was from this third-floor balcony that the speakers decided to address the crowd on October 2.

The day of the Tlatelolco Massacre

By 8:30 a.m. that morning, the army had taken up positions in each corner of the plaza — not necessarily unusual — as the army often posted soldiers at protest rallies. But something about this day seemed off: Witnesses later mentioned seeing men with short haircuts in civilian clothes, all wearing a white glove on one hand.

Myrthokleia Gonzáles Gallardo, a 22-year-old Politécnico student, had been chosen to introduce the speakers that day, even though her parents warned her not to go, fearing something might happen with the increased military presence.

Myrthokleia described her entry into the Plaza:

“As I approached the Tlatelolco with the four speakers, I was introduced, and we were warned to be careful, as the army had been seen nearby. But I wasn’t afraid, though we decided to make it a short meeting. There were workers, students, and families coming into the plaza, filling it up. We didn’t see any [soldiers] in the plaza.

“We took our place on the third floor and started our speeches. Suddenly, off to the left, over the church, were helicopters with a green light. Suddenly, everyone down in the plaza started falling. And then men with white gloves and weapons appeared, maybe from the elevator. They ordered us down to the ground floor, where they began beating us.”

Gunfire erupts and continues for hours

Raúl Álvarez Garín was also whisked down to the ground floor and made to stand facing a wall as government forces beat him relentlessly. Álvarez remembered the sound of automatic gunfire continuing for a full two hours. Other witnesses remember sporadic gunfire until 11 p.m.

The next morning, journalist Elena Poniatowska arrived at Tlatelolco at dawn. There were tanks and soldiers everywhere, yet no one tried to impede her strolling around the plaza. She had heard from a friend that bodies covered the plaza, but by morning, they all had been taken away.

In the newspaper Excelsior, Poniatowska learned that Italian journalist Oriana Fallaci was in Mexico to cover the Olympics and had been wounded while attending the rally. Poniatowska tracked down Fallaci in a hospital and interviewed her.

“What savagery!” Fallaci told her. “Police dragging students away by the hair. I saw many people get hit — until I was hit too. I lay in a pool of my own blood for 45 minutes.”

Shocked by what she heard, Poniatowska wrote an article detailing the events. Her editor immediately rejected it.

“There’s an order,” the editor announced, according to Preston and Dillon. “We’re going to concentrate on the Olympic Games. We’re not printing anything more about Tlatelolco.”

The legacy of the Tlatelolco Massacre

The Tlatelolco student massacre was a tragic and immensely consequential event in Mexican history. The Olympic Games may have gone off without a hitch, but at what cost? Over 400 people were murdered in cold blood by government troops. Hundreds more simply disappeared, never heard from again. Hundreds more were imprisoned for years. Hundreds, if not thousands, went into hiding, fearing retaliation for simply expressing their ideas about the nature of their society.

Before 1968, most Mexicans felt proud of their nation’s economic achievements. During the Mexican Revolution, one leader after another had been brutally assassinated. In the wake of the Revolution, the PRI provided stability and economic growth, and Mexico had become a modern nation. In 1959, American academics conducted a poll and found that while most Mexicans were tired of their country’s endemic corruption, they were generally proud of their political system and its achievements and felt their presidents were, for the most part, benign. After 1968, however, most middle-class Mexicans felt disillusioned, resentful and utterly distrustful of their government.

Perhaps the students’ National Strike Council (CNH) final statement, issued in December 1968 upon its dissolution, summed it up best:

“Democracy in Mexico is just a concept, another formalism,” it announced. “Politics is carried out behind the backs of the popular majorities and of their aspirations, interests and demands.”

While the student movement of 1968 was neutralized, the Tlatelolco massacre has had a long-lasting impact on Mexican politics and history: More than 50 years later, October 2 is commemorated every year across Mexico with civilian demonstrations. Films and documentaries and countless books have been written about it — in Mexico and around the world.

Groundwork laid in 1968 also spawned a generation of the nation’s activists and political leaders, who were involved in Mexico’s electoral reform in the 1980s, which ultimately led to the end of the PRI’s uninterrupted rule over Mexico for 70 years in 2000, with Vicente Fox’s election as president.

Kurlansky, in his book “1968: The Year that Rocked the World,” commented: “But very much in the same way that the invasion of Czechoslovakia was the (beginning of the) end of the Soviet Union, Tlatelolco was the unseen beginning of the end of the end of the PRI.”

Robert McLaughlin, Ph.D. is a historian specializing in Cold War Latin American history.

World.title: African Union Leaders Meet in Egypt on Trade and Water
World.content:
Key Facts — What happened African leaders opened the Eighth Mid-Year Coordination Meeting of the African Union (AU) on Sunday 4 October 2026 in El-Alamein, Egypt.

— Who hosts President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi hosts, with AU chair Évariste Ndayishimiye of Burundi and AU Commission chair Mahmoud Ali Youssouf.

— Why it matters The talks cover the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and which institutions deliver it on the ground.

— The theme Water and sanitation is the AU’s theme for 2026, and Egypt used its opening speech to link shared rivers to integration.

— What comes next A draft declaration is on the agenda for adoption. Its final text and any dated commitments are not yet public.

Egypt is hosting the African Union and the continent’s regional blocs on the Mediterranean coast. The agenda is trade, water and who turns Agenda 2063 into projects.

The African Union (AU) opened its Eighth Mid-Year Coordination Meeting on Sunday 4 October 2026 in El-Alamein, on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast. Egyptian outlets also call the venue New Alamein. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi is the host. The meeting brings the AU together with the Regional Economic Communities (RECs) and Regional Mechanisms (RMs), the blocs that carry out much of its programme.

For readers in the United States, the practical question is trade. The AU’s free trade project, the AfCFTA, only works if regional blocs align customs rules, standards and corridors. That is the subject of this forum, and it shapes where American exporters and investors can expect one rulebook rather than many.

What the coordination meeting is for

The meeting is the AU’s main yearly forum for working with the RECs and RMs. The AU says the 2026 edition aims to advance continental integration and the priorities of Agenda 2063, its long-term development plan, known as “The Africa We Want”.

The programme, as published by the AU, runs through several items. They include the state of continental integration, the role of the development agency AUDA-NEPAD, AfCFTA implementation, coordination between the AfCFTA and the RECs, and policy harmonisation between the AU and the blocs. It also covers water, sanitation and sustainable infrastructure, and the adoption of a draft declaration.

Presenters include Angola’s President João Lourenço on AUDA-NEPAD and Kenya’s President William Ruto on the AfCFTA, according to the AU. Water and sanitation is the AU’s theme of the year: “Assuring Sustainable Water Availability and Safe Sanitation Systems to Achieve the Goals of Agenda 2063”.

The Suez Canal at Port Said, northern Egypt. File photo, not from the meeting.
