What Sisi told the delegates

In his opening speech, published by the Egyptian State Information Service, Sisi called coordination “not an end” but a way to move from fragmented efforts to integrated ones. He said shared pressures, from conflict and terrorism to higher energy, food and financing costs, exceed what any single country can face alone.

He also said Egypt rejects external interference in the domestic affairs of African states. He urged that natural resources and transboundary rivers be managed “in accordance with international law”.

On water, Sisi called the management of shared resources “a true test” of Africa’s capacity for integration. He welcomed the adoption of the Africa Water Vision 2063 and Policy 2063 document and asked for a swift first implementation plan. Egypt depends heavily on the Nile, so the water language is also a signal on regional disputes.

Why El-Alamein matters to Cairo

Sisi presented the host city as a symbol. He described El-Alamein as a site of fierce fighting in the Second World War and of landmines, now turned into what he called a platform for investment and construction. His message was that African states can turn the aftermath of conflict into development.

Egypt also signed a host country agreement with the AU Commission for the meeting. A business forum ran in El-Alamein from 2 to 4 October, and the AUDA-NEPAD Founders Summit took place on 3 October. Hosting gives Cairo visibility in continental diplomacy at a time when it sits at the centre of several regional questions, including the Horn of Africa. See our earlier reports on tensions among Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt.

Who is in the room

Heads of state and government, the AU Commission and the chairs of the RECs and RMs attend. Youssouf opened with a call for Africa’s integration agenda to move “decisively from aspiration to implementation”. Ndayishimiye, who chairs the AU, said Africa “must produce in Africa, transform in Africa and add value to resources in Africa”.

South Africa’s President Cyril Ramaphosa arrived on Saturday 3 October to lead participation as chair of the Southern African Development Community (SADC). He is accompanied by International Relations Minister Ronald Lamola and Trade Minister Parks Tau. Development partners, including the UN Economic Commission for Africa and the African Development Bank, are also listed as participants.

Trade is the test

The AfCFTA aims to create a single African market, but the RECs run much of the customs and corridor work. If they do not align, traders face overlapping rules. That is why the AU lists cross-border trade facilitation, industrial development, regional value chains and macroeconomic convergence among its focus areas.

The AU also lists peace and security coordination and conflict prevention. Investors treat these as part of trade risk, because insecurity closes corridors. For background on where the trade deal stands, see our AfCFTA status report.

What it means for you

If you invest in or sell to Africa from the US, this meeting does not move markets on its own. It signals whether the AU and the regional blocs can agree who does what. A clear division of labour would make tariff and customs rules more predictable across borders. A vague declaration would leave exporters negotiating bloc by bloc.

What is not known

The text of the declaration is not public. We do not know whether it sets deadlines, funding or named responsibilities. Any outcome on water or on the Horn of Africa tensions will be clear only when the closing documents appear.

The next step is the declaration itself. If it assigns tasks to the RECs with dates, that is the first real test of the coordination Sisi and Youssouf called for. If it repeats earlier language, the forum will have been mainly a showcase for Egypt as host.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is the Eighth Mid-Year Coordination Meeting? It opened on Sunday 4 October 2026 in El-Alamein, Egypt. Egyptian outlets also call the venue New Alamein. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi hosts it. What is the purpose of the meeting? It coordinates the African Union with the Regional Economic Communities and Regional Mechanisms. The aim is to advance continental integration and Agenda 2063, including the AfCFTA. Who is chairing and attending? AU chair Évariste Ndayishimiye of Burundi and AU Commission chair Mahmoud Ali Youssouf attend, with heads of state and government and the chairs of the regional blocs. South Africa’s Cyril Ramaphosa attends as SADC chair. What is the 2026 AU theme? The AU theme for 2026 is “Assuring Sustainable Water Availability and Safe Sanitation Systems to Achieve the Goals of Agenda 2063”. Water is on the meeting agenda. Has the final declaration been published? A declaration was on the agenda for adoption. Its text was not public when this article was updated on 4 October 2026.

World.title: ATLS Plans Djibouti Fuel Rail Link to Ethiopia
World.content:
Key Facts — Who African Terminal & Logistics Services (ATLS), a subsidiary of the privately owned Hayel Saeed Anam Group, is building the terminal at Djibouti’s Doraleh port.

— What Phase one offers 288,000 cubic metres of fuel storage, with loading arms for the Ethiopia-Djibouti railway and for tanker trucks.

— When First operations are scheduled for June 2027, according to Ethiopian media reports on 27 September 2026.

— Why it matters Ethiopia, a country of more than 100 million people with no coastline, depends on Djibouti for much of its fuel. Today about 350 tanker trucks a day carry it over the road.

— Why US readers care The route runs beside the Bab el-Mandeb strait, a Red Sea shipping lane that also hosts a US naval base. A second, US$660 million pipeline project was announced on 24 September 2026.

A privately owned Djibouti terminal plans to load fuel straight onto trains bound for Ethiopia from June 2027. If it works, it would take pressure off one of Africa’s busiest tanker-truck corridors.

African Terminal & Logistics Services, known as ATLS, is developing a petroleum hub at the Doraleh Multipurpose Port in Djibouti. Its aim is to move imported fuel into landlocked Ethiopia by rail as well as by road. Capital, an Ethiopian newspaper, reported the plan on 27 September 2026.

For a reader in the United States, the story matters for two reasons. Ethiopia is a country of more than 100 million people whose fuel supply runs through a single foreign port. That port sits at the southern gate of the Red Sea, a route that matters for global oil and container shipping.

What ATLS is building at Doraleh

Phase one of the terminal is planned at 288,000 cubic metres of storage. Ecofin Agency reports that capacity is expected to rise to about 500,000 cubic metres and eventually to about 750,000 cubic metres.

The design combines marine unloading, storage and onward distribution. Train-loading arms would connect the site directly to the Ethiopia-Djibouti Railway, while several truck-loading bays would let tankers fill in parallel.

The mix is deliberate. Rail would serve high-volume destinations, and trucks would reach places the railway does not.

ATLS is a subsidiary of the privately owned Hayel Saeed Anam Group. The terminal is separate from the existing Horizon Djibouti Terminal, which is the departure point for much of today’s fuel traffic.

Archive photo: a US Navy patrol boat guards the oiler USNS Big Horn off the Port of Doraleh in 2018 (Photo: US Naval Forces Europe-Africa, public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why the current system is under strain

About 350 tanker trucks a day carry fuel from the Horizon terminal toward Ethiopia, according to Capital. The route depends heavily on road transport.

Congestion, border procedures, truck availability and shipping delays all slow supply. Because Ethiopia has no direct sea access, every hold-up at the port or the border reaches filling stations in the highlands.

In February 2026, the Ethio-Djibouti Joint Railway Commission agreed to speed up railway links to Doraleh and to the Horizon terminal. That decision signalled official support for moving more fuel onto the tracks.

A second project: the Dangote pipeline

A separate plan targets the same bottleneck. On 24 September 2026, a Thursday, Ethiopia, Djibouti and Nigeria’s Dangote Group marked the start of a reported US$660 million, 120-kilometre pipeline from Damerjog in Djibouti to Dewele in Ethiopia, as covered in our earlier report on the pipeline.

Reports on the announcement give storage of about 375,000 cubic metres at Damerjog and about 800,000 cubic metres at Dewele. The line would carry refined products such as diesel, petrol and jet fuel. The partners have not disclosed financing terms or each side’s share, and the timetable is unproven.

The two projects are different in ownership and design. Together they point to a broader effort to give Ethiopia rail, road and pipeline options for its fuel imports.

The wider contest around Djibouti

The country is also home to military bases of several foreign powers, including the United States and China. Its position at the Bab el-Mandeb makes the logistics around its ports a strategic question as well as a commercial one. Our Djibouti explainer covers the bases, ports and politics, and Africa: The New Scramble places them in the wider competition for influence.

What it means for you

For investors, the projects signal that Djibouti wants to earn more from Ethiopian trade than simple transshipment fees. Storage, rail loading and pipelines capture value that used to pass straight through.

For travellers and expats in Djibouti, the changes could bring construction and logistics work. If rail takes a larger share, they could also mean fewer tankers on the corridor.

For fuel buyers in Ethiopia, any gain would show up first in reliability. Price effects are not yet known.

What is not known

ATLS has not published an investment figure in the reports reviewed. It is also unclear how much fuel the terminal will move by rail in its first year.

The June 2027 date is a schedule, not a commitment. Construction progress and railway connection agreements will show whether it holds.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the ATLS fuel hub in Djibouti? It is a petroleum storage terminal under development at Doraleh Multipurpose Port by African Terminal and Logistics Services, with 288,000 cubic metres of planned capacity in phase one. When will the Djibouti fuel route to Ethiopia open? First operations are scheduled for June 2027, according to Ethiopian media reports published on 27 September 2026. Train-loading facilities are planned for the Ethio-Djibouti Railway. How is fuel moved from Djibouti to Ethiopia today? Mostly by road. About 350 tanker trucks a day reportedly leave the Horizon terminal in Djibouti for Ethiopia, facing congestion and border delays. How does the ATLS terminal differ from the Dangote pipeline? ATLS is a storage hub with rail and truck loading. The US$660 million Dangote project is a 120-kilometre pipeline from Damerjog to Dewele, announced on 24 September 2026. Why does the Djibouti fuel route matter to the United States? The corridor sits beside the Bab el-Mandeb, a Red Sea shipping lane, and Djibouti hosts a US military base. Ethiopia, with more than 100 million people, depends on it for fuel.

World.title: Chile Police Seize 3 Kilos of Gold, About US$298,000
World.content:
Central Santiago, where police carried out the raid (file photo of the Plaza de Armas; not the premises searched).

CHILE · SECURITY

Key Facts — Who Chile’s civilian investigative police, the PDI, working with the FBI.

— What Detectives seized 3 kilograms 276 grams of gold, plus jewellery and metal ingots, at a commercial premises in Santiago. One man was arrested.

— Why it matters Police say Chilean gangs steal jewellery in US and European cities and sell it in Chile. The gold alone was valued at about US$298,000.

— What it means for you Anyone buying gold or jewellery in Chile should expect closer checks on where it came from.

— Still open Which thefts the gold comes from, who the buyers were and what charges the arrested man faces.

Chilean police announced on Sunday 4 October 2026 that they had seized more than three kilograms of gold in central Santiago. Police valued the gold at CLP 294,917,400 (about US$298,000 at the RT rate of 989.60 pesos per US dollar). Detectives say it is linked to jewellery stolen in the United States and Europe.

The operation, called Operation Pantera, was run by the PDI, Chile’s civilian investigative police, with help from the FBI. For American readers, the case matters because the alleged thefts took place in US cities and the loot appears to have been sold in Chile.

What police found in Santiago

Officers from the PDI’s Centro Norte robbery unit (BIRO) raided a commercial premises in the commune of Santiago. They found 3 kilograms 276 grams of gold, along with other jewellery and ingots of yellow and white metal. Police gave the estimated commercial value of the gold as CLP 294,917,400, which they described as almost CLP 300 million (about US$298,000).

The raid was backed by SINAPRO, the PDI section that checks the paperwork showing where goods come from. The jewellery and ingots are now with experts for examination. Police have not said what share of the metal is pure gold.

A 33-year-old Chilean man with a police record was arrested at the premises. Police have not named him. The reports seen by The Rio Times do not say what charges he faces.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on chile crime Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How the alleged route works

According to police, the investigation targets groups of Chileans who operate abroad. They allegedly steal jewellery in homes and in non-residential buildings in several cities in the United States and Europe.

Commissioner Jennipher Ramírez of BIRO Centro Norte said part of the loot is brought into Chile illegally. Once here, she said, the pieces are “commercialised and reduced” in different local businesses. In Spanish police usage, “reducir” means to resell stolen goods through a fence, a middleman who buys stolen property.

Co-operation with the FBI helped investigators identify targets of interest and places where the goods were distributed. That led them to the shop in Santiago. The reports do not say which US or European cities were hit, or how much was stolen in total.

Why this matters beyond Chile

Residential burglary rings that target jewellery are a familiar problem for US police. The Chilean case suggests that some of the proceeds may leave the country where the crime took place and reach a legal market abroad. Gold is easy to melt down and carry, which makes it hard to trace once it has been reduced to ingots.

The case also shows Chilean investigators working with a US federal agency on a property-crime case, not only on drug or organised-crime investigations. Chile has been pressing a wider security agenda under President José Antonio Kast; see our report on Kast’s security reform and our earlier story on police dismantling a synthetic drug lab in Ñuñoa.

Gold seizures also carry a reminder about due diligence. A buyer of jewellery or bullion in any country can be caught up in a case like this one if the seller cannot show where the metal came from. SINAPRO’s role, checking provenance papers, is aimed at exactly that gap.

File photo of a gold bar from a Swiss money museum. It is not the gold seized in Santiago. Photo: Ank Kumar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

What it means for you

If you live in or visit Chile, this is not a safety warning. Police described a targeted operation against a single premises, and no tourist or resident is mentioned as a victim.

If you buy gold or jewellery in Chile, ask for a receipt and the origin of the piece. Reputable dealers should be able to supply both. For US investors with Chilean exposure, the story is a small data point on law enforcement co-operation, not a market event. The latest peso level is in our Chile market report, and more national coverage sits in our Chile section.

What is not known

Police have not said which thefts the gold is tied to, or whether any of it can be matched to victims in the United States or Europe. The reports do not name the shop, its owner or the arrested man, and they give no court date.

It is also unclear how the CLP 294,917,400 valuation was reached. Police said the figure was an estimated commercial value, so the final worth could change once the experts finish their examination.

What stabilises the picture is that police, the FBI and the provenance unit are all involved, which gives prosecutors several routes to prove where the goods came from. What could weaken it is the same gap seen in many fencing cases: stolen jewellery is often melted down before it can be matched to a victim.

How much gold did Chilean police seize?

Police seized 3 kilograms 276 grams of gold in Santiago, announced on 4 October 2026. They valued it at CLP 294,917,400 (about US$298,000 at 989.60 pesos per US dollar).

What is Operation Pantera?

Operation Pantera is a PDI investigation into groups of Chileans who allegedly steal jewellery in the United States and Europe and sell it in Chile. The FBI helped identify targets and distribution points.

Who was arrested?

A 33-year-old Chilean man with a police record was arrested. Police did not name him, and the reports do not state the charges.

Has the gold been linked to specific thefts?

Not yet in public reporting. The jewellery and metal ingots are being examined by experts, and police have not said which thefts they match.

Is this a risk for tourists or foreign buyers in Chile?

Police described a targeted operation at one premises. Buyers of gold or jewellery should still ask for a receipt and proof of origin.

Sources: Meganoticias, Operación Pantera, La Tercera, Puranoticia. USD conversion at RT USD/CLP 989.60 (4 October 2026). Retrieved 4 October 2026.

World.title: Stellantis Pauses Two Saltillo Truck Plants for a Week
World.content:
Key Facts — Who Stellantis, the carmaker behind Ram, Jeep and Chrysler, through its Mexican unit Stellantis México.

— What Two truck plants in Saltillo, Coahuila, will each stop for one week for line changes, maintenance and staff training.

— Why it matters The Light Duty plant builds the Ram 1500 pickup, and the pause comes while tariffs and USMCA talks shape where Ram trucks are built.

— Pay and jobs Stellantis says wages will be paid in full. No layoffs or closure have been announced.

— Still open The company has not given start or restart dates, or any output figures.

Stellantis will halt two truck plants in Saltillo, in Mexico’s northern state of Coahuila, for one week each. The company says the pause is for line changes, maintenance and employee training. Miguel Ceballos, communications director at Stellantis México, confirmed the plan to the Saltillo-region daily Vanguardia on Sunday, 4 October 2026.

The two sites are the Saltillo Truck Light Duty plant, where the Ram 1500 pickup is built, and the Saltillo Heavy-Duty Truck plant. Workers will keep their full pay during the stoppage. For US readers, the news matters because the Ram 1500 is sold in the United States and Mexico-built vehicles sit at the centre of the tariff debate.

What the stoppage involves

Stellantis describes the break as planned.

Wages are the key point for local households. Stellantis says the full salaries of affected workers will be paid without change. No layoffs have been announced, and the plants are not closing.

The company has not published start or restart dates. It has also not said how many workers are affected, how many vehicles will not be built, or which models the line changes will touch. Those gaps leave the cost to Stellantis and to local parts suppliers unquantified for now.

Traffic on the Bridge of the Americas between Ciudad Juárez and El Paso, a major USMCA freight link. File photo. (Photo: U.S. Customs and Border Protection, public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Stellantis (Mexico) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Saltillo in the Stellantis network

Its Truck Light Duty plant builds the Ram 1500, according to Vanguardia. The second site is the Heavy-Duty Truck plant.

For investors and supply-chain analysts, the rhythm of these plants is a useful read on how Stellantis sees North American demand. A one-week maintenance break is routine in the industry. It arrives, however, at a time when trade policy has made production planning harder.

The USMCA is the trade pact linking Mexico, the United States and Canada. Our explainer on Mexico nearshoring and the USMCA review sets out why that pact matters to carmakers.

A different pause from April 2025

Stellantis has stopped Mexican lines before. In April 2025 it suspended its Saltillo Van plant, which builds the Ram ProMaster, from 31 March to 13 April. It also paused its Toluca plant in April and May. El Universal reported at the time that Stellantis linked those halts to the 25% US tariff on vehicles that do not meet USMCA rules.

President Claudia Sheinbaum said on 4 April 2025 that the suspension at Toluca was temporary and did not imply job cuts.

This week’s announcement is different in two ways. It covers the two truck plants rather than the van and Toluca sites. And the company gives operational reasons, not tariffs.

Tariffs and the Michigan question

On 15 September 2026, Automotive News reported, citing supplier managers, that Stellantis was asking suppliers to assess the business case for moving heavy-duty Ram pickup production from Mexico to Michigan. The aim would be to avoid tariffs amid shifting US trade rules and USMCA talks. The plan would move that production to Warren Truck Assembly.

That is an evaluation, not a decision. No official announcement of a transfer of production or of job reductions has been found. Stellantis’s public comments on Saltillo this week speak only of maintenance, line changes and training.

The timing invites questions, but nothing published links the two. Readers should treat any connection between the pause and the Michigan study as unconfirmed. The wider trade picture is in our report on Mexico’s tariff talks with Washington and on Trump’s stance on the USMCA.

What it means for you

If you follow Stellantis shares or buy Ram trucks, a one-week pause at two plants is unlikely to change the picture on its own. Watch for the company’s next production and delivery updates, which would show whether Ram output from Mexico shifts in the coming months.

If you work with Saltillo suppliers or have staff there, expect a quiet week on the shop floor, with pay unchanged. The bigger variable is where Ram heavy-duty production is built over the next few years, and that rests on tariff policy rather than on this maintenance break.

What is not known

Stellantis has not said when each plant will stop or restart, whether the two weeks run together or one after the other, or how many workers are involved. It has not said which models will change on the lines, nor given an output impact. Until it does, the stoppage is best read as a short, scheduled break.

Which Stellantis plants in Saltillo will stop?

The Saltillo Truck Light Duty plant, which builds the Ram 1500, and the Saltillo Heavy-Duty Truck plant. Each will stop for one week, according to Stellantis México.

Will workers be paid during the stoppage?

Yes. Stellantis says the full salaries of workers will be paid without change during the one-week pause.

Why is Stellantis pausing the plants?

The company cites line changes, maintenance and employee training. It has not linked the pause to tariffs or to weak demand.

When will production restart?

Stellantis has not given start or restart dates. The pause is described as lasting one week at each plant.

Is Stellantis moving Ram production to Michigan?

Not by any announced decision. Automotive News reported on 15 September 2026 that Stellantis asked suppliers to study moving heavy-duty Ram pickup output from Mexico to Warren, Michigan. No transfer has been confirmed.

World.title: Brazil Candidate Zema Took Phone Into Voting Booth
World.content:
Photo: Mateus S. Figueiredo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

BRAZIL · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Brazil is voting in the first round of its presidential election on Sunday 4 October 2026, with a runoff set for 25 October if no candidate wins outright.

— What happened Presidential candidate Romeu Zema, of the Novo party, voted in Araxá, Minas Gerais, with a cellphone in the booth at Escola Estadual Delfim Moreira.

— Who is who Carlos Henrique Perpétuo Braga, president of the Regional Electoral Court of Minas Gerais (TRE-MG), said the court will look into the episode.

— Why now Brazilian electoral law bars phones from the voting booth, and the Electoral Code sets up to two years’ detention for violating or attempting to violate ballot secrecy.

— What it means for you The case shows how Brazil guards ballot secrecy even when the person in the booth is a presidential candidate. No charge has been announced.

— Still open The local electoral judge must establish the facts and pass the case to TRE-MG. Any criminal case would need action by the Electoral Prosecutor’s Office.

Presidential candidate Romeu Zema took a cellphone into the voting booth while casting his ballot in Araxá, Minas Gerais, on Sunday morning, 4 October 2026. The Regional Electoral Court of Minas Gerais (TRE-MG) says it will investigate whether the act broke electoral law.

The episode matters beyond Minas Gerais. Brazil is voting in the first round of a presidential election, and ballot secrecy is the rule that keeps votes free from pressure. A candidate breaking that rule, even by accident, draws attention to how it is applied.

Zema voted at Escola Estadual Delfim Moreira in Araxá, according to reports by Estado de Minas and other Brazilian outlets. Braga, the TRE-MG president, said the court would examine the facts. He described the use of a phone in the booth as irregular.

“First of all, the rules apply,” Braga said, according to Brazilian media reports, adding that the rules do not allow a phone in the voting booth. He called what happened “a succession of errors” and said polling-station workers are meant to prevent phones from entering the booth.

What the law says about phones in the booth

Brazil’s Electoral Law, Law No. 9,504 of 1997, Article 91-A, bars voters from carrying a mobile phone, camera or filming equipment into the voting booth. The rule targets photographs or recordings that could prove how someone voted.

That proof is what makes vote-buying and coercion possible. A voter who can show a photo of the ballot screen can be paid or pressured to vote a certain way. The phone ban is one of the safeguards against that.

The Electoral Code, Law No. 4,737 of 1965, Article 312, sets detention of up to two years for violating or attempting to violate the secrecy of the vote. Braga said the conduct can constitute a crime that carries detention. However, carrying a phone into the booth does not by itself prove that crime.

Archive photo: a voter uses a Brazilian electronic voting machine. The image is illustrative and does not show the Araxá polling station.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Zema says habit, court sees possible failure

Zema said he carries his phone all day and called it “almost like a finger”. He said nobody reminded him to leave it outside, so he went to vote normally. He denied photographing his ballot.

Braga did not treat the matter as only the candidate’s responsibility. He pointed to a “succession of errors” and said polling-station workers are meant to keep phones out of the booth. He also said that responsibility for any crime would need deeper investigation.

Reports differ slightly on how Zema described it. Some outlets wrote that he forgot the phone, while others quoted him on carrying it constantly. This article uses only his words as reported by Agência Brasil.

What happens next

The local electoral judge will establish the facts and send the findings to TRE-MG for a final decision. Any criminal prosecution would require action by the Electoral Prosecutor’s Office, known as the Ministério Público Eleitoral.

No sanction or charge had been announced in the reports reviewed. The court has not said when the review will finish. Whether the case ends as an administrative irregularity or becomes a criminal matter is not yet known.

What it means for you

For readers in the United States, the case is a small window into how Brazil runs its vote. The country uses electronic machines nationwide, and secrecy rules are enforced at each polling station. Investors and observers following the first round will see this as a procedural story, not one that changes the count.

The outcome could still shape the debate over polling-station discipline ahead of the possible 25 October runoff. For live results and the wider picture, see our coverage of election day voting, the detentions over vote-buying and the first-round count. Our Brazil hub carries the full file.

What is not known

It is not yet clear whether the phone was used for anything, whether any photograph exists, or whether polling-station staff will face scrutiny. The court has not said whether it will refer the case to prosecutors, and no deadline has been given.

What did Romeu Zema do in the voting booth?

He voted at Escola Estadual Delfim Moreira in Araxá, Minas Gerais, on 4 October 2026 with a cellphone in the booth. He said he did not photograph or record his vote.

Is carrying a phone into a voting booth a crime in Brazil?

Electoral law bars phones from the booth, and the Electoral Code sets up to two years’ detention for violating or attempting to violate ballot secrecy. Authorities must still decide whether secrecy was put at risk.

What did Zema say about the incident?

Zema said he carries his phone all day, “almost like a finger”, and that nobody reminded him to leave it outside. He denied photographing his vote.

Who is investigating the case?

The Regional Electoral Court of Minas Gerais, led by president Carlos Henrique Perpétuo Braga, will investigate through the local electoral judge. Any criminal case would need the Electoral Prosecutor’s Office.

Does this affect the election result?

No report reviewed suggests the episode changes the count. The investigation is a separate procedure from the election itself.

Sources: Agência Brasil, Estado de Minas, Metrópoles, Terra, Law No. 9,504/1997 and Law No. 4,737/1965 (Planalto). Retrieved 4 October 2026.

World.title: Venezuela Stays Outside OPEC+ Quotas as Targets Hold
World.content:
File photo: the eastern shore of Lake Maracaibo, Venezuela. Photo: Breddyjgalvis, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

VENEZUELA · ENERGY

Key Facts — Who Seven OPEC+ producers: Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman. Venezuela is not one of them.

— What On Sunday 4 October 2026 they kept November output targets at September levels, about 31 million barrels per day (bpd) combined.

— Why Venezuela matters It is exempt from OPEC+ quotas but sells into the price the group defends. Brent was about US$102 a barrel on Friday 2 October.

— Why US readers care Venezuelan crude shipped to the United States averaged 553,000 bpd in August, so the oil price and the Venezuelan supply story reach US refiners and drivers.

— Still open The seven meet online again on 1 November 2026. A ministerial meeting is due on 29 November 2026.

OPEC+ kept its November oil output targets unchanged on Sunday 4 October 2026. It is the second month in a row without a change. Venezuela is not among the seven countries that decided, but the price they are defending is the one Venezuela sells into.

Brent crude was about US$102 a barrel on Friday 2 October (RT spot series; The National reported a settlement of US$102.25). For readers in the United States, steady targets mean no extra official barrels are coming, at a time when Gulf exports are disrupted.

What the seven decided

The seven core members met online and decided to “maintain September 2026 required production for November 2026”, according to The National. They are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman.

TASS published the November required-production levels. They are 10.478 million bpd for Saudi Arabia, 9.949 million for Russia, 4.431 million for Iraq, 2.676 million for Kuwait, 1.628 million for Kazakhstan, 1.007 million for Algeria and 841,000 for Oman. Together that is about 31 million bpd.

The group raised its targets each month from April to September. In September it finished unwinding 1.65 million bpd of voluntary cuts from 2023, then paused the increases in October. A further 2 million bpd of cuts agreed in 2022 stays in place until the end of the year, The National reported.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Venezuela Transformation Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Targets are not barrels

A quota is a ceiling on paper, not a measure of what reaches ships. The Moscow Times reported that the seven pumped about 25 million bpd in August. That was 630,000 bpd more than in July, but roughly 5 million bpd below February, before the war involving Iran began on 28 February.

Gulf producers are pumping well below their targets because exports have been disrupted. The National reported that the Strait of Hormuz, which carries about one-fifth of global crude and liquefied natural gas, has been effectively closed since fighting began.

OPEC+ also warned that actions undermining energy supply security can increase market volatility. The Moscow Times noted that output increases this year have been “largely on paper”. In plain terms, the group can freeze targets, but the war is what is holding barrels back.

Why Venezuela is outside the decision

Venezuela is a founding OPEC member, but it does not have a production target to hold. Under the Declaration of Cooperation, the framework that links OPEC and its partners, Venezuela, Iran and Libya are exempt from quotas (US Energy Information Administration; Semafor). The exemption reflects sanctions or conflict that disrupted their output. Semafor wrote in September that there is an understanding quotas will not apply until production has sufficiently recovered.

So this decision does not change a Venezuelan allowance. It changes the market Venezuela sells into. Reuters shipping data, published by the BOE Report, showed Venezuelan exports of 1.17 million bpd in August, almost unchanged from July.

The destinations shifted. Shipments to the United States fell to 553,000 bpd from a record 786,000 bpd in July. Exports to India rose 66% to 297,000 bpd, and deliveries to Europe almost tripled to about 260,000 bpd.

The same data pointed to operating strain. Tanker queues and waiting times at Venezuelan terminals grew in August because of terminal deterioration, crude quality problems and a late-July blackout at facilities of the state company PDVSA. Venezuela also imported about 166,000 bpd of fuel, mostly US naphtha used to dilute its heavy crude.

For earlier context, see our fact-check on what Venezuela actually produces for the US and our report on output returning above one million barrels a day.

File photo: an oil tanker passes under the General Rafael Urdaneta Bridge over Lake Maracaibo, in the heart of Venezuela’s oil region. Photo: Wilfredor, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What it means for you

If you buy fuel or hold energy shares in the United States, the message is that official supply is not growing. With Brent near US$102, a pause in quota increases removes one possible source of relief, although the quotas were never the binding constraint.

Venezuela is one of the few suppliers whose heavy crude suits US Gulf Coast refineries, which is why the August drop in US-bound cargoes to 553,000 bpd is worth watching. If those flows recover, they would add supply outside OPEC+ quota discipline.

The picture cuts both ways. Firm prices help Caracas, which needs revenue. Higher prices also hurt importing economies, and a ceasefire or a reopened Hormuz could ease them quickly.

What is not known

The seven have not said whether the pause will last beyond November. The Moscow Times reported that output adjustments are unlikely before 2027, pending a review of members’ production capacity that has been delayed by the uncertainty in the Middle East.

We have not found a published Venezuelan production figure for September, so this article does not give one. Reported export levels and official production measures can differ, because sources count condensates and natural gas liquids differently.

What comes next

The seven will meet online again on Sunday 1 November 2026 to review the market. World Oil reported that a full ministerial meeting and the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee are set for Sunday 29 November 2026.

Watch three things before then: whether Hormuz traffic recovers, whether Venezuelan loadings to the United States rebuild from August’s low, and whether Brent holds above US$100. A steadier Gulf would let quota decisions matter again.

Is Venezuela part of the OPEC+ group that kept November targets?

No. The decision was taken by seven countries: Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman. Venezuela is an OPEC member but is exempt from production quotas, together with Iran and Libya.

What exactly did OPEC+ decide on 4 October 2026?

The seven countries agreed to maintain September 2026 required production for November 2026. That is the second month in a row without an increase, and the combined target is about 31 million barrels per day.

When is the next OPEC+ meeting?

The seven countries meet online on 1 November 2026. World Oil reported that a full ministerial meeting and the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee are scheduled for 29 November 2026.

Why are actual barrels below the targets?

Gulf producers have been pumping well below their targets because exports have been disrupted by the war involving Iran. The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed since fighting began on 28 February, according to The National.

How much oil does Venezuela export to the United States?

Reuters shipping data published by the BOE Report put August shipments to the US at about 553,000 barrels per day, down from a record 786,000 in July. Total exports were about 1.17 million barrels per day.

Sources: TASS, The National, The Moscow Times, World Oil, BOE Report (Reuters data), Semafor, US Energy Information Administration, RT (Brent spot, 2 October 2026). Retrieved 4 October 2026.

World.title: Argentina Wool Exports Jump 28% in 2025/26
World.content:
ARGENTINA · TRADE

Key Facts — The country Argentina is one of South America’s largest agricultural exporters, with a wool sector centred on Patagonia and the Pampas.

— What happened Wool exports rose 28% by volume and 66% by value in the 2025/26 commercial season, which ran from July 2025 through June 2026.

— Who is who Argentina’s Secretariat of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries published the figures; El Litoral and Agrositio reported them on 3 October 2026.

— The numbers Shipments reached 39,730 tonnes on a greasy-wool basis, generating US$189.6 million, up from 31,088 tonnes and US$114.3 million in 2024/25.

— What it means for you US-based buyers of wool and textile inputs face a supplier that is regaining ground, and Argentina earns more hard currency from a small but fast-moving export line.

— Still open The official release does not say how much of the value gain came from prices, product mix or exchange rates.

Argentina’s wool exports grew 28% by volume and 66% by value in the 2025/26 commercial season, which ran from July 2025 to June 2026. Shipments reached 39,730 tonnes (greasy-wool basis) and earned US$189.6 million, according to the Secretariat of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries. For a small export line, that is a sharp rebound in one year.

Wool is a niche product next to Argentina’s soy and beef. Still, it matters for Patagonia’s sheep farms and for foreign buyers in China and the European Union. It is also an early sign of how much Argentine producers can earn in dollars when global demand firms.

What the full-season figures show

The 2024/25 season had delivered 31,088 tonnes and US$114.3 million. The new season therefore added 8,642 tonnes and US$75.3 million. El Litoral, an Argentine regional newspaper, published the full-season figures on 3 October 2026, citing the Secretariat.

Value grew more than twice as fast as volume. An RT calculation from the official totals puts the average export value at about US$4,770 per tonne in 2025/26, against about US$3,680 a year earlier, a rise of roughly 30%. That is a blended figure for several wool products, so it is a guide and not a price quote.

Against 2023/24, the picture is stronger. Volume rose 69% and foreign-currency earnings rose 101.4%, according to the Secretariat. Put simply, the sector has roughly doubled its dollar income in two seasons.

One data note helps anyone tracking the series. A June 2026 release covered July to April only, with 31,825 tonnes and US$149.5 million, up 23.5% and 57%. The full-season totals above include two more months and replace those partial figures.

File photo: the Rio Manso in Argentine Patagonia, where much of the country’s wool sector is based.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Patagonia (Argentina) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

China and the EU lead demand

China and the European Union are the main buyers. China leads in greasy (unwashed) wool, while the EU leads in combed wool, known in the trade as tops, which is processed further.

In the July to April data, China’s share of export value rose from 23% to 33%. The Secretariat linked April’s 70% yearly increase to demand for Argentine wool that filled a gap left by lower production, mainly in Australia, a much larger wool exporter.

The official release does not give a destination table for the full season. How much of the gain came from China, and how much from the EU, is therefore not yet public in detail.

Momentum carries into 2026/27

The new season started strongly. In July and August 2026, Argentina exported 6,901 tonnes of wool (greasy basis), up 39% on a year earlier, worth US$37.4 million, up 103%.

The same RT arithmetic implies roughly US$5,400 per tonne for those two months, up from about US$3,700 a year earlier. Two months is a short window, and one strong quarter does not make a trend.

What it means for you

For US investors, the story is mostly about Argentina’s dollar earnings. Wool brings in far less than grains or beef, but more export revenue helps the country’s hard-currency position at a time when foreign exchange is closely watched. For US importers of textile inputs, a supplier regaining ground adds one more source outside Australia. For travellers and expats in Patagonia, wool towns and estancias are where the gains show up first.

Readers following the wider farm-export story can compare it with Argentina’s beef exports in the first half of the year and with the jump in beef shipments linked to the US quota. More coverage is on the Argentina hub.

What is not known

The official data do not separate price gains from changes in product mix or currency effects. They also do not say how long Australian supply will stay tight, which helped Argentine sellers earlier this year.

Critics say the sector’s long decline is not reversed by one good season. Later monthly export figures will show whether the jump holds.

How much did Argentina’s wool exports grow in 2025/26?

Exports rose 28% by volume and 66% by value, reaching 39,730 tonnes and US$189.6 million, according to the Secretariat of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries.

Which countries buy the most Argentine wool?

China and the European Union are the main destinations. China leads in greasy wool and the EU in combed wool.

Is the recovery continuing into the new season?

So far, yes. Exports in July and August 2026 rose 39% by volume and 103% by value against the same months a year earlier, to 6,901 tonnes and US$37.4 million.

Why did China buy more Argentine wool?

The Secretariat tied strong demand to lower production mainly in Australia. China’s share of Argentine wool export value rose from 23% to 33% in the July to April period.

How does this compare with two seasons ago?

Against 2023/24, volume is up 69% and dollar earnings are up 101.4%.

Sources: El Litoral, Agrositio, Argentine Secretariat of Agriculture (July to April release, 16 June 2026). Per-tonne values are RT calculations from the official totals. Retrieved 4 October 2026.

World.title: Flávio 49.6% in Brazil Count, 65% Counted
World.content:
Live tonight Follow Brazil’s vote count live The official TSE count with every candidate’s share, the state map and what a runoff would mean, updated through the night. Open the live results →

Brazil’s presidential election goes to a runoff. With 99.52% of polling stations counted, Flávio Bolsonaro has 47.13% of valid votes and Lula 45.04%, and neither can now reach 50%. The two meet again on Sunday 25 October.

Key Facts The count: 99.52% of polling stations counted (496,856 of 499,248) as of 21:39 Brasília time on 4 October (20:39 US Eastern, 01:39 Lisbon on 5 October), according to the electoral court (TSE).

Flávio Bolsonaro: 47.13% of valid votes (55,960,302 votes). He is a senator for the conservative Liberal Party (PL).

Lula: 45.04% of valid votes (53,484,316 votes). He is the leftist president, from the Workers’ Party (PT).

The rest: Augusto Cury 2.90%, Renan Santos 2.25%, Ronaldo Caiado 2.19%, Romeu Zema 0.27%. Six other candidates are each below 0.2%.

Why it matters: A candidate needs more than 50% of valid votes to win outright. No candidate has it, and the 0.48% of polling stations still to report cannot change that. The top two meet in a runoff on Sunday 25 October.

What it means for you: Brazil’s stock market reopens later today, Monday 5 October. The first round is settled in outline, but the winner is not.

Where the Count Stands

Brazil’s electoral court, the TSE, showed Flávio Bolsonaro ahead with 47.13% of valid votes at 21:39 Brasília time (20:39 US Eastern, 01:39 Lisbon). Lula had 45.04%. The gap was about 2.5 million votes, or 2.09 percentage points. Neither is above 50%.

The TSE had counted 99.52% of polling stations, which is 496,856 of 499,248 sections. Only 2,392 sections, or 0.48%, were still to report. The TSE has not yet declared the final result, but the arithmetic is clear: the remaining sections have fewer than 770,000 registered voters, while Flávio Bolsonaro would need more than 6.8 million additional valid votes, all for him, to reach 50%. A first-round win is no longer possible for either candidate.

The lead has narrowed all night. At 19:14 Brasília time, with 64.81% counted, Flávio Bolsonaro had 49.58% and Lula 42.25%, a gap of 7.3 points. By 20:40 it was 3.65 points, and it is now 2.09.

The rule is simple. A candidate wins in the first round with more than half of the valid votes. Blank and null ballots are not valid. When nobody passes the line, the top two go to a second round.

Behind the two leaders, Augusto Cury has 2.90%, Renan Santos 2.25%, Ronaldo Caiado 2.19% and Romeu Zema 0.27%.

Why the Gap Narrowed

States report at different speeds, and the late ones favoured Lula. In the TSE’s state tables, pulled at 01:35 Lisbon (20:35 US Eastern), Paraná and the Federal District were complete. Flávio Bolsonaro led both, with 60% and 51%.

Bahia (98% counted), Ceará (98%) and Pernambuco (99.7%) had nearly finished. Lula led them with 66%, 63% and 63%. São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, two of the biggest electorates, were above 99.9% counted. Flávio Bolsonaro led São Paulo with 52% and Rio de Janeiro with 53%. In Minas Gerais (99% counted) he led with 48% to Lula’s 43%.

The final polls had pointed to a different order. Datafolha, in a poll published on 3 October, had Lula at 45% and Flávio Bolsonaro at 42% of valid votes. A poll is not a result. Read more in our final polls report.

Who Is Who

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) is a senator for Rio de Janeiro and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. His Liberal Party sits on the political right.

Lula (PT) is Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the president since 2023. He also governed from 2003 to 2010. His Workers’ Party is on the left, and his running mate is Vice President Geraldo Alckmin.

Augusto Cury (Avante) is an author and psychiatrist. Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) is a former governor of Goiás. Renan Santos (Missão) represents the newer Missão party. Romeu Zema (Novo) represents the Novo party.

Why It Matters for the US

Brazil is the largest economy in Latin America, and US investors hold it through stocks, bonds and funds. The B3 exchange in São Paulo is closed on Sundays. The first market test comes later today, Monday 5 October.

US-listed shares of Petrobras and Vale, and the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ), trade during US hours on Monday. The real, Brazil’s currency, will also react. A runoff keeps the uncertainty alive until 25 October.

The winner will also set the tone of Brazil’s relations with Washington, including trade. Our guide on what the election means for US investors covers the market angle, and our election explainer covers the rules.

What Happens Next

The TSE will finish the count and declare the first-round result. The top two, Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula, then meet in a runoff on Sunday 25 October 2026. Polling stations close at 17:00 Brasília time, which is 16:00 US Eastern.

Campaigning for the second round starts at once. The other candidates will be courted for their voters, who total about 7.6% of the valid vote between Cury, Santos, Caiado and Zema. Our live results page carries the state map.

What Is Not Known

We do not know whether Cury, Santos, Caiado and Zema will endorse either finalist, or how their voters will split. We also do not know the final margin, which depends on the last 0.48% of polling stations. The TSE count answers that.
