World.title: Who Pays Tax on Rent in Costa Rica? The Numbers Don’t Add Up
World.content:
Costa Rica has more than 360,000 rented homes, but just over 32,000 people and companies are registered to pay tax on income from renting property. Former Finance Ministry officials say the gap between the size of the rental market and the size of the tax base does not add up.

At the end of 2025, the Finance Ministry counted 32,373 active taxpayers under the tax on real estate capital income, which is the levy that applies to rent. Of those, 14,441 were individuals and 17,932 were legal entities such as corporations. The housing figure comes from the National Household Survey run by the National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (INEC). It counts homes only. Offices, retail space, warehouses and land leased across the country are not included.

The registered base has barely moved since the tax took effect. In 2020, the first year it was applied after the 2018 fiscal reform, the ministry counted 32,291 active filers. Five years later the total had grown by 82, or 0.3%, and between 2021 and 2024 it stayed below 30,000.

The rental market grew over the same period as the household survey counted about 360,000 rented homes in 2025, up 25% from five years earlier. It also found 120,500 people who reported receiving some kind of rental income, an increase of 28%, though that figure includes rentals of movable property such as vehicles.

Revenue tracked the taxpayer count rather than the market. Adjusted for inflation, collection from the tax stayed between ₡72.5 billion and ₡77.5 billion (about $157 million to $168 million) each year from 2021 to 2025. The ₡76.5 billion (about $166 million) collected in 2025 represented 3.1% of total income tax revenue.

The numbers do not mean that more than 300,000 property owners are evading taxes. A single owner can rent out several homes. The household survey and the tax registry measure different populations, and some rental income is legally declared under other tax categories.

Fernando Rodríguez, a researcher at the National University (UNA) and a former vice minister of revenue, said the registered number does not appear reasonable given the size of the market. He said part of the gap likely reflects how difficult rentals are to monitor, because landlords can stay invisible to the tax system when tenants have no need for an invoice to deduct the expense.

Rodríguez said the problem is sharper for residential leases than for commercial ones, since businesses usually need a receipt to claim value-added tax credits or deduct costs. He added that under certain conditions individuals and companies can report rental income under the corporate profits tax instead, such as when the property is tied to their main business activity.

Former Finance Minister Elian Villegas described the rental market as opaque and said the tax administration should carry out a significant review of it. Villegas said that review should extend to capital gains from property sales, where he believes considerable revenue is being lost.

Rodríguez cautioned that closer enforcement is costly for an administration with limited resources. Tracking tourist rentals, for example, can require monitoring booking platforms and intelligence work to identify hosts missing from tax records. That effort competes with audits likely to recover larger sums.

The system also places the first burden on taxpayers. Mario Ramos, director general of the Tax Administration, has said Costa Rica’s tax system runs on self-assessment. Taxpayers register, calculate what they owe and file on their own, and the ministry checks afterward.

Under current rules, anyone who receives rent from property in Costa Rica must register and declare it, whether the owner is an individual or a company. The tax is 15% of the rent after a standard 15% deduction for expenses, which works out to roughly 12.75% of gross rent. Returns are filed monthly through the ministry’s TRIBU-CR platform, by the 15th day of the month after the rent is collected.

The obligation applies even to modest rents. Law 9635 exempts home rents of up to 1.5 base salaries, currently ₡693,300 (about $1,500) a month, from value-added tax, but that exemption does not cover income tax. Above that threshold, tenants pay 13% VAT on the full rent, which the landlord collects and passes on to the ministry.

The gap fits a broader concern raised by international organizations, though none has singled out rentals. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) found in its 2025 economic survey of Costa Rica that about 43% of taxpayers required to issue invoices do not do so. The International Monetary Fund has described Costa Rica’s tax base as relatively small and eroded by exemptions and compliance gaps.

How much of the difference between the rental market and the tax rolls comes from legal structure, and how much from unpaid taxes, remains an open question. For now, the number of registered filers stands almost exactly where it did when the tax began.

World.title: Costa Rica Plans to Spread El Niño Power Costs Over Three Years of Bills
World.content:
Costa Rica wants the extra cost of generating electricity during El Niño to reach consumers gradually, spread over three years of power bills rather than arriving as a sudden rate jump. A directive from the Ministry of Environment and Energy (Minae), published Friday in the official gazette La Gaceta, proposes recovering through electricity tariffs, over the next 36 months, the extraordinary generation costs that the Costa Rican Electricity Institute (ICE) will incur because of El Niño.

The ministry expects the phenomenon to bring less rain, greater water stress and lower flows into hydroelectric reservoirs through 2026 and 2027. To keep the grid reliable, ICE will need to burn more fuel, buy more energy and take other measures, which the directive describes as an extraordinary and temporary increase in generation costs.

Recovering those costs over a short period could cause abrupt swings in electricity rates, according to the directive, which is why it proposes diluting them over a longer horizon. The text states that tariff stability does not mean leaving rates unchanged, but ensuring that any adjustment reflects costs that are necessary, efficient and properly demonstrated.

Minae instructed ICE to provide the Public Services Regulatory Authority (Aresep), which sets electricity rates, with the information needed to analyze a gradual recovery of the extra costs. No estimate of the effect on household or business bills had been made public as of Friday afternoon.

The proposal shows how exposed Costa Rica’s electricity system is to drought. Hydroelectric plants produce roughly 70% of our power and when reservoirs drop, ICE turns to thermal plants running on imported fuel and to energy bought on the regional market. The last strong El Niño showed what that shift can cost. Aresep reported that in the first half of 2023 Costa Rica generated more thermal power than in 2017 through 2022 combined.

Its quarterly update of the Variable Generation Cost, the component of ICE’s rates that covers fuel and energy imports, meant an increase of 14.43% that year, and the regulator later identified El Niño as the main cause of the higher electricity rates approved for 2024.Earlier this year, Regulator General Eric Bogantes said Aresep anticipated a possible increase in 2027 because of fuel spending, which enters rates through that same variable cost. For 2026, by contrast, the regulator had calculated the component as negative, reflecting lower thermal generation and higher electricity exports.

ICE executive president Marco Acuña has warned that El Niño deepens the system’s dependence on thermal generation just as fuel prices have begun to rise. The institute has been arranging the rental of thermal plants valued at about $415 million to cover the gap. The directive does not set new rates on its own. Any adjustment would come through Aresep’s review of the figures ICE submits, and until then the size of the impact and when it would first appear on monthly bills remain unknown.

World.title: Your smart meter can reveal what’s driving up your BEL bill
World.content:
Your smart meter can reveal what’s driving up your BEL bill

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Wondering which appliance is eating up your electricity? Belize Electricity Limited says the answer may be right outside your home.

At a media session last week, BEL demonstrated how customers can use the Smart AMI meters installed at their homes to keep an eye on their own power usage.

AMI stands for Advanced Metering Infrastructure. Unlike older meters, these devices record consumption electronically and send the readings back to BEL remotely, without the need for a meter reader to visit.

BEL Energy Audit Officer Ezar Pol walked the media through how customers can read the meters and follow their consumption in real time. That means homeowners can watch how their usage changes when they switch on an air conditioner, a water heater or other high demand appliances.

For customers trying to understand a high bill, that kind of visibility can make it easier to spot the culprits and adjust habits to save money.

BEL says the meters also give customers a way to verify their own consumption, adding a layer of transparency between the company and the people it serves.

Customers who have questions about reading their meters can contact BEL for assistance.

World.title: Guyana strengthens its passport. Is Belize next?
World.content:
Guyana strengthens its passport. Is Belize next?

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Guyana has just made its passport more powerful, and it raises a question many Belizeans are asking: when will our Government do the same?

This week, Guyana announced that its citizens can now enter Saudi Arabia with a visa on arrival or an electronic visa, without needing a US, UK or Schengen visa first. Guyana says it is the only South American country with that privilege.

The breakthrough came through focused diplomacy. Guyana’s foreign ministry says it grew out of stronger bilateral relations and shared interests in trade, investment and tourism with Saudi Arabia. Guyana has also committed to improving its passports to meet international standards.

For ordinary Guyanese, the benefit is real. No agents. No embassy visits. Just a passport and a fee.

Belizeans know the frustration of visa applications, costly fees and long waits to travel to many countries. A stronger passport means easier travel for work, study, business, religious pilgrimage and family visits.

So the question stands. What is the Government of Belize doing to expand visa free and visa on arrival access for Belizeans? Which new agreements are being pursued, and how is the Ministry of Foreign Affairs working to raise the value of the Belizean passport?

Guyana has shown what targeted diplomacy can achieve. Belizeans deserve to know what our plan is.

BBN invites the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to share what steps are being taken to strengthen the Belizean passport.

World.title: French Guiana thrashes Belize 2 to 0 in Belmopan
World.content:
French Guiana thrashes Belize 2 to 0 in Belmopan

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Jaguars had the home crowd. French Guiana had the goals.

Belize went down 2 to 0 to French Guiana on Saturday night at the FFB Stadium in Belmopan in Concacaf Nations League B action.

The Jaguars could not find the back of the net, while French Guiana struck twice to walk away with all three points.

“Not the result we wanted,” the Football Federation of Belize admitted after the final whistle.

It is a tough setback for a Belize side that opened its campaign with a 1 to 0 away win over Sint Maarten.

But there is no time to dwell. The two teams meet again on Tuesday.

World.title: Belizeans compare prices as potatoes and onions rise in Mexico too
World.content:
Belizeans compare prices as potatoes and onions rise in Mexico too

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belizeans love a Chetumal run, especially when the belief is that everything across the border is cheaper. But when it comes to potatoes and onions right now, the numbers tell a different story.

The debate over vegetable prices in Belize has intensified on social media, with some users arguing that basic produce is significantly cheaper in Mexico.

However, recent prices observed at Chedraui in Chetumal suggest the difference may not be as dramatic as some online posts make it seem.

According to prices recorded on October 2, potatoes were selling for 54 Mexican pesos per kilogram, while white onions were priced at 64 pesos per kilogram.

Using the exchange rate cited in the comparison, that works out to approximately BZ$3.20 per pound for potatoes and BZ$3.50 per pound for onions.

For comparison, potatoes in Belize were reported to be selling for around BZ$3.50 per pound, while onions were around BZ$4.00 per pound.

That means the savings on these two staples may amount to only a few cents per pound, before Belizean shoppers even factor in fuel, transportation and the time required to travel across the border.

The figures also show that high vegetable prices are not only a Belize problem.

Consumers in neighboring Mexico are also paying more for basic food items as inflation and supply pressures continue to affect household budgets.

The Belize Marketing and Development Corporation has defended its pricing, saying it operates with as low a profit margin as possible while avoiding losses and continuing to invest in local operations and the Belizean economy.

The comparison does not mean every grocery item costs the same in Belize and Mexico. Prices can vary significantly depending on the store, location, season and product.

But for potatoes and onions, at least, the latest Chetumal prices challenge the popular social media claim that crossing the border automatically means dramatically cheaper vegetables.

For Belizean families already watching every dollar at the supermarket, the real story may be simpler: food is expensive on both sides of the border.

World.title: Have you seen 15 year old Angelique Castillo?
World.content:
Have you seen 15 year old Angelique Castillo?

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Belize City teenager is missing, and her family needs your help.

Angelique Castillo, 15, was last seen on Saturday, October 3. Crime Stoppers Belize has issued an alert asking the public to keep an eye out.

She is described as a Hispanic girl with a clear complexion, about 4 feet in height.

If you have seen Angelique or know where she may be, call Crime Stoppers anonymously at 922. Tips can also be sent through the P3 app at P3tips.com or reported at any police station.

Please share this post and help bring Angelique home.

World.title: Waitress charged after slapping and pulling co-worker’s hair
World.content:
Waitress charged after slapping and pulling co-worker’s hair

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 23 year old waitress of Ketz Lagoon Street, Orange Walk Town, has been charged with harm.

She is Arleny Lailanie Coye.

Police say a 25 year old waitress of San Jose Village reported that around 10:00pm on Sunday, September 27, she was leaving work at a restaurant in Trial Farm Village when a co-worker suddenly slapped her on the left side of her face.

When she tried to defend herself, the co-worker allegedly pulled her hair, causing pain.

A doctor later certified her injuries as harm.

Coye was formally arrested and charged on Saturday, October 3. She chose to remain silent when cautioned.

World.title: Guinea Grass man charged with stealing truck battery
World.content:
Guinea Grass man charged with stealing truck battery

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 30 year old laborer of Guinea Grass Village, Orange Walk District, has been charged with theft.

He is Jorge Jimenez.

Police say a 59 year old truck driver reported that he parked and locked his company truck, a 1997 Ford F700, in front of his home around 9:30pm on Tuesday, September 29.

When he checked the truck the next morning, the battery was gone. Someone had removed the protective cover, opened both locks and taken it.

The battery, a Black Atlas 1000CCA, was valued at $551.25.

It was later recovered, and Jimenez was formally charged with theft on Friday, October 2.

World.title: Over 1 kilo of suspected cannabis found at Orange Walk dump site
World.content:
Over 1 kilo of suspected cannabis found at Orange Walk dump site

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Orange Walk police have recovered more than a kilogram of suspected cannabis at a dump site in Orange Walk Town.

Police say that around 5:30pm on Thursday, October 1, Special Branch received information about a man carrying a black bag toward the end of Smith Sonia Street, near the dump site, where he approached an old green pickup cabin.

Orange Walk GI3 officers went to the area and searched. Inside the old pickup cabin, they found a black plastic bag.

It contained a large sealed package, a smaller sealed package and a green plastic bag holding 11 small zip lock bags, all filled with suspected cannabis.

The drugs weighed a total of 1,104 grams. No one was in the area at the time, and the cannabis was recorded as found property.

World.title: Buyers now in control of Kingston and St Andrew property market, says Matalon
World.content:
Gary Matalon

After some 15 years of sellers holding the upper hand, the Corporate Area property market is reportedly shifting in the buyers’ favour.

That’s according to Deputy CEO of Kingston-based real estate dealer different Capital, Gary Matalon, who says the company’s data shows that buyers have more room than ever to negotiate.

“For most of the last decade and a half, sellers in Kingston and St Andrew set the terms. That has changed,” he told Observer Online on Sunday.

“Over the past two years, roughly one in five properties listed for sale has cut its asking price, and fewer than half have sold,” he continued. “When that many sellers are adjusting and that much stock is sitting, the negotiating power has moved to the buyer.”

According to Matalon, the trend is being driven by buyers having relatively more options than years past and sellers competing for the same pool of qualified purchasers.

He also noted that “uncertainty” has sidelined diaspora buyers.

“They traditionally supported the upper end of the market but with inflation and so much global uncertainty…some are in a holding pattern,” he said.

Different Capital tracks listings, price changes and sales across Jamaica. Matalon emphasised that the trend does not mean the market has crashed.

“It’s not a crash and not every property is a bargain,” Matalon said. “Well priced real estate in good locations still sell strong.”

How long will it last? Matalon said that depends on interest rates and how quickly new supply is absorbed by the market.

The Bank of Jamaica last week raised its policy rate by half a percentage point to 6.0 per cent. The increase was the central bank’s first since November 2022.

The policy rate is what the BOJ pays deposit-taking institutions on balances held at the central bank. It does not automatically change the rate on an individual mortgage or business loan, although it can influence the rates lenders offer over time.

World.title: SEAWATER SOLUTION
World.content:
A seawater desalination plant transforming salty ocean water into fresh, drinkable water.

AS Jamaicans confront the recurrent threat of drought, worsened by the El Niño weather phenomenon, a renewed proposal to convert seawater into potable supplies has received mixed reactions from specialists who see potential in desalination but question whether it is a practical solution at scale, given its operating cost and heavy reliance on energy.

The issue was raised during a webinar hosted by the Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR) last Wednesday. Duane Rowe, the OUR’s director of regulation, policy, monitoring and enforcement, argued that desalination could be an option to settle some of the island’s water challenges.

Rowe noted that, having lived and worked in the Middle East for 15 years, he saw how that region — which lacks significant ground and surface water reserves — depends on desalination for much of its domestic and industrial water usage.

However, he reasoned that due to the energy-intensive nature of the process, Jamaica must first lower its electricity costs to make it a viable and economically sound option. “You need a lot of energy to extract the salt from the seawater. And, of course, the Middle Eastern countries, they have a lot of energy, so it only makes sense. For Jamaica, we would need to significantly reduce the cost of energy going forward, and maybe at that point we’ll be able to access that technology,” Rowe said.

Calling for umbrella legislation to facilitate better coordination among water sector agencies, Rowe argued that it could address gaps in the current framework that require coordination, including information sharing and joint planning. In that case, he pointed out that greater collaboration between energy and finance stakeholders could bring the country closer to finding a path towards desalination.

“[A country’s] energy costs and environmental impacts must be tested against alternatives, including loss reduction and improved existing supplies… Regulations should seek the least-cost path to dependable water and evidence that proves spending benefits consumers. Stakeholders can help shape these decisions,” said Rowe.

For her part, National Water Commission (NWC) Acting Vice-President of Operations Dr Phillipa Campbell-Francis said that desalination is not currently an economically sound solution. She explained that the NWC’s primary concern revolves around economic, financial, and environmental barriers. “It would be extremely expensive because of how energy-intensive it is. In addition to that, there is also a concern as it relates to brine.

The brine that is produced usually goes back to the sea. When it goes back to the sea it doesn’t mix with the regular seawater, it goes to the bottom, and then you have issues with oxygen availability and so on,” Campbell-Francis said, adding that the deoxygenation issue could be remedied, but would also be costly. She posited that a more practical way to strengthen the island’s water resilience is to lessen the NWC’s consistently high non-revenue water (NRW) levels.

Campbell-Francis noted that NRW — treated water that is produced and pumped but lost to leaks or theft before reaching billed customers — accounts for roughly 70 per cent of the utility’s water supply. “If we are able to manage NRW with the loss rate that we have, we do not even have to go too far into looking at desalination if it is that we can stem the losses and make more water available to our customers,” she argued. Despite this, Campbell-Francis said the possibility of desalination in Jamaica is not completely off the table.

“We have not thrown it through the window, because ministers have started some discussions around that, like [for] some areas in St Thomas and so on. There are studies going on to look at the possibility for those areas, but it would be small, separated facilities as opposed to an islandwide plan,” she explained. In August, Water, Environment, and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda announced that feasibility studies are underway in St Thomas and Clarendon to assess the viability of potential desalination projects.

Speaking during a ministerial interview with Jamaica Information Service’s (JIS) Chief Executive Officer Giovanni Dennis, Samuda said the studies relate to a proposed integrated, pumped, hydro storage system that would use solar-powered infrastructure to extract seawater and pump it into a reservoir for storage and later use. “We would generate energy by releasing water from that reservoir to a lower reservoir and, in that process, you would extract the salt from the water… [the process is] called reverse osmosis.

The energy generated would allow us to afford the extraction,” the minister explained. However, Samuda said desalination is not being considered nationwide because high operating costs and potential environmental harm are major deterrents. “Desalination, if it were done at a national level, would significantly change the average tariff that you pay at the household and commercial level for water,” he reasoned.

While Samuda did not elaborate on the price, industry information is that a desalination system can cost up to $10.49 million annually, depending on the size, energy source and local conditions. Still, the water minister shared that feasibility testing will continue in named water-stressed areas, followed by an engineering phase expected to commence by 2027, with a proposed procurement aspect in 2028.

Last Tuesday, principal director of the Meteorological Service, Evan Thompson offered his thoughts on the issue, saying that desalination must be among water resilience options considered by the Government as the country continues to experience recurrent water shortages. Speaking on Nationwide News Network’s OPM on Air during Cliff Hughes Online, Thompson urged the Government to give the extraction process earnest thought. “It’s time for serious consideration of it.

I know that the minister has already started to look at that, and has been looking at it for a long time, because we have had some talks about that… and, of course, we have to weigh the costs versus benefits of all these things that we are looking at… Whatever we need to do, we need to do that now,” Thompson said. Last December, Jamaicans in Falmouth, Trelawny, benefited from a desalination project courtesy of the Bahamian Government which responded to the need for potable water in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa’s rampage across the island’s south- and north-western ends.

The project, set up at the Falmouth pier, was connected to 10 standpipes on the grounds of the nearby Church of the Assemblies of God. At the time, Alveta Knight, The Bahamas’ consul general to Jamaica, explained that the seawater, accessed through pipes planted in the sea, was pushed through a reverse osmosis plant and distributed to 10 spigots in the church parking lot. “So people can come at their leisure throughout the day and collect potable water,” Knight told the Jamaica Observer.

“We are churning out 1,000 gallons an hour, so we are inviting everybody. If you have a truck we can actually connect the truck directly to our system.” In 2024 the JIS reported that the island received a $61-million technical assistance grant from the United States Trade and Development Agency to undertake a study on the impact of reverse osmosis technology on the environment.

The study, JIS said, was to be undertaken at 13 National Environment and Planning Agency-approved reverse osmosis sites across the island. It would also examine reverse osmosis systems being utilised in at least four international jurisdictions to determine whether best practices in those territories can be adopted in Jamaica at the industrial or municipal scale and inform the permit process.

World.title: Dark October
World.content:
Executive director of the Jamaica Cancer Society, Roshane Reid-Koomson, stands next to the organisation’s mammogram machine, which is no longer operational. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

OCTOBER is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time when women are urged to prioritise their breast health, get screened, and act early. But the Jamaica Cancer Society (JCS) has started the month without a functioning mammogram machine, forcing hundreds of women to seek screening elsewhere.

A mammogram is a specialised, low-dose, X-ray image of the breast used to detect early signs of breast cancer, tumours, or cysts before they can be felt by hand. The non-government organisation, which prides itself on providing affordable screenings for women, said its only machine went out of service on August 29, 2026.

Prior fund-raising efforts to replace it before it stopped working have fallen short of the more than $35 million needed to purchase a new machine. Executive director of the JCS, Roshane Reid-Koomson, said the organisation is down but not out, appealing to Jamaicans both locally and internationally to help with replacing the equipment. “I feel very sad to see the mammogram department in darkness and closed, knowing that we are unable to provide the test that we so strongly encourage women to do,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

“We can’t do any mammograms up here. It’s disheartening. Some of the customers, when we tell them, you can hear when their voices drop because some of them depend on us because we are the most affordable, in terms of cost. Because we are a charity, so we ensure that we keep our costs at a minimum so that the ordinary person can afford it,” said Reid-Koomson.

She said thousands of women come in for mammograms annually, with the numbers ranging from a high of 15,000 to a low of 3,000. She noted that while most women are from Kingston, St Andrew, and St Catherine, some travel from as far as Clarendon, St Thomas, Portland, and even Montego Bay, St James, to take advantage of the affordable service.

“The impact is severe because we are in October, which is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, and the interest and awareness are heightened at this time, as you can imagine. People started to call us from September to book their appointments, but we cannot accept those appointments because the machine is not working,” said the executive director.

“It doesn’t make sense for us to fix the machine because the cost to fix it is so high that it only makes sense for us to direct those funds towards a new machine. What the supplier has advised us is that the parts to supply this machine [that is broken] are obsolete, so we can’t even find the parts that we require for the machine,” she explained.

Reid-Koomson said the organisation has been redirecting women to other private facilities to get screened, but the inconvenience and added cost have led some to delay acting. “There are some customers that we have that we realise want to wait ,but we have to advise them that this is not a waiting thing. We will not advise any individual who wants to get a mammogram done, or any individual who is due a mammogram, to wait until we get a machine, so we have been redirecting our customers to other entities and will continue to do so,” she told the Sunday Observer.

The executive director noted that the organisation did apply for a grant through the Ministry of Health and Wellness to purchase a new machine, which is under consideration, but they have not received anything in writing that has been concretised. “I would just like to appeal to Jamaica to assist us in any way possible. We have been on this fund-raising drive for a while, because we knew that the machine would reach the end-of-life stage based on how it has been operating. We started the fund-raising drive a few years ago — and especially last year, we heightened that drive — but we weren’t able to yield much from it,” said the executive director.

“We are at the stage now where we are inoperable in terms of offering mammograms and so we are appealing to Jamaicans here and abroad to assist us, contribute whatever you can. Every mickle makes a muckle. Please donate whatever you can so the Jamaica Cancer Society can get a new mammogram machine,” she pleaded. Individuals who wish to donate can visit the JCS website at https://jcs.live/donate/ Meanwhile, the foundation said it continues to offer its many other services to individuals seeking to get cancer screenings.

“We continue to offer pap smears, we continue to offer prostate screening, and we continue to advocate and do our educational sessions at corporate entities, churches, and facilities,” she said. Reid-Koomson further urged individuals to get screened. “Check it, catch it, beat it. It’s important for you to be aware of your body. It’s important for you to check your body. It’s important for you to get your annual screening done, and it’s also important to follow up if your results are abnormal,” she stressed.

World.title: Life without children
World.content:
An AI-generated image of a farmer. The 65-year-old farmer has found joy as a father figure to his nieces and nephews.

WHILE the figures behind Jamaica’s birth rate crisis paint a daunting picture — women are having an average of 1.3 children in their lifetime, among the lowest in the world — the stories of some of those behind the statistics offer a more intimate perspective.

Five middle-aged and elderly Jamaicans shared with the Jamaica Observer their experiences without children, from feelings of anguish and regret to satisfaction and even hope.

The respondents, three women and two men ranging from ages 50 to 78, included an entrepreneur in her 50s who never wanted children, a 78-year-old teacher who was unable to conceive, a 56-year-old accountant who never found the right time, a commuter who never found the right woman, and a 65- year-old farmer who was concerned about finances.

Several of the interviewees said their feelings on children were shaped by their relationships with their own parents. “I recall clearly having goals around not being a mother,” said the entrepreneur.

“My parents were both in their late teens when I was born, so my first goal was not to be a teenage mom; my second goal was not to have the indignity of scrambling to get a taxi while pregnant.”

Similarly, the 56-year-old accountant, whose parents passed away within two years of each other before she hit 16, said their deaths were a major reason she shied away from having children early. As a Christian, she did not consider having a child out of wedlock, and years went by without a suitable partner.

When she finally found a partner that she wanted to have a child with, she was unable to get pregnant. “I mean, the amount of pregnancy tests that I have used…one of the times I got so stressed…it just would not happen,” she explained.

For the 78-year-old teacher, she was simply unable to get pregnant. She spoke to the Sunday Observer from the senior living facility at which she is now well cared for. “That was one of my regrets, not having children. But I have accepted it,” she said gently.

The teacher, who had a picture of her late husband propped up beside a photo of her younger self in her room, shared that her joy came in the form of caring for her sister who now, in turn, cares for her.

“She was far younger than me, [20 years], so through the years we were extremely close. People used to think she was my daughter… Everywhere I go, she was right behind me,” the elderly woman reflected with a laugh.

Other respondents shared similar experiences, including the accountant who delighted in taking care of her nieces, two of whom lived with her for some time. The 65-year-old farmer also found joy as a father figure to his nieces and nephews. For him, though, being that figure sometimes served as a painful reminder.

“They were fun to be around…but you know that sometimes made me wish I had my own,” he shared. In youth, he had been deeply concerned with the financial aspect of parenthood, expressing that he did not want to have a child and not be able to care for him or her.

“I have regrets, because I might not have worked a lot of money but I’ve seen people who were in much worse condition than I was, have even three or four and they turn out to be good children, and I know that the Lord would provide just the same for me,” he said.

As he grew older the desire also grew, the farmer said. However, not so for the commuter in his 50s who spoke to the Sunday Observer, on condition of anonymity, as he was travelling. He shared that he had not found a woman to marry and as a result, children had never entered the equation.

“I grew up in a Christian family,” he said, which for him meant marriage before children. And now, as he ages, it’s not something that bothers him at all; in fact, he shared: “The way the economy is, education and all that, it would be a horrible burden on me financially.”

Noting that he helps financially with his godchildren, who are particularly dear to him and contributes to him having a fulfilling life, he expressed that he is genuinely at peace with his decision, unburdened by societal pressure to produce children. For the entrepreneur, this pressure was something she also easily brushed aside. “Anyone who tried that with me was firmly put in her place — and yes, it’s usually other women.

I recall telling one mom who kept urging me to join the club, ‘You can have more if it’s so important to you. I’m good!’ ” Reflecting on her life, the entrepreneur expressed appreciation for the freedom being child-free has afforded her. “Being child-free has saved me from back-to-school drama, PEP [Primary Exit Profile] stress, my kids being bullied at school, having to cook vs cooking when I feel like it, etc,” she said, adding, “But seriously, I view parenthood as a huge responsibility.

No matter how old the person [is] that you brought into the world, that is your child. “I would always be wondering if my child is okay; ‘Did my child eat today?’ ‘Who do I need to hurt because he/she hurt my child or me?’ Nope, too much pressure. I’m not built for that, and I’m glad I recognised that from early on,” she said. Similarly, the accountant said being child-free has allowed her to contribute to building two homes and travel extensively.

“The first time I travelled [was] a FAME road party…to Antigua…and I mean, I went by myself and I said, ‘Look here, I don’t have a chick nor a child so I can spend the money and go and enjoy myself,’ ” she laughed. In reflecting on their decisions, the respondents had varying feelings.

The farmer indicated he would have acted differently in youth. “You know, I, as I say, I have regrets; I never was too far away from home so, in terms of my freedom, it would not have mattered…My child would not have been a liability. I think it would be an asset to my life,” he said. The teacher, despite her own regrets, urged young people, especially women, to consider parenthood carefully.

“We just take it lightly… but it is something that you should think deeply about, bringing this little one into the world. I would advise you to ask the Lord to give you a husband because you know the men nowadays…they are terrible, to be honest, so don’t just go have a baby for having a baby’s sake,” she cautioned. Similar words were shared by the farmer who said: “I think one of the basic things is that you have to have a love for children to want to have a child.” The entrepreneur reflected with peace and satisfaction.

“I’m still building my legacy and working towards my greatest achievements but I love my life, and I am proud of all I have done. I am sure that if I had children my life would have been totally different,” she said, emphasising that it was the right choice for her. The accountant, for her part, said, “Sometimes I would say, ‘God, you know why I’m not having it?

Because I don’t want the headache, I don’t want the stress.’ ” In the same breath, she shared an article that she had seen of a woman over 50 who got pregnant and delivered her baby safely. “I am looking at it, and sometimes I really think about it and say, ‘God, would that really be possible?’ I really think about it…if it does happen, it happens; I will embrace it with joy and love and everything. But if not, I am still here,” she said.

World.title: Minister Blessed launching third EP
World.content:
Minister Blessed

GOSPEL recording artiste Minister Blessed is gearing up to launch his third EP titled I Can Do All Things.

It is the follow up to the Sterling Gospel Music Awards-nominated EP I Did it Anyway, which was released in 2024. To date, Minister Blessed has released four full length studio albums. On I Can Do All Things, Minister Blessed said the focus is slightly shifted to dancehall-based songs, compared to the multiple genres that were explored on his previous EP.

“My previously nominated body of work I Did It Anyway delved into exploring multiple genres within gospel such as dancehall, reggae, and traditional worship sounds. The approach to this latest body of work is completely different, as my focus here is strictly dancehall-based, so the songs are harder-hitting and highly energetic.

From a growth point of view, I am much more fearless and bold in delivering hard-hitting Bible-based lyrics while also making way for my comical side to come to the forefront so it’s an interesting balance. There is one song where I act as the voice of God seriously calling sinners to repentance and for everyone to Respect the Name (Jesus).

On the other hand, I have a song called Laughter, which explores different scenarios whereas God’s people we can just sit and laugh at certain situations from in the Bible as well as current events,” he said.

The project, according to Minister Blessed, took 18 months to complete, beginning with the first song that was recorded in February 2025 and the last song recorded in June of this year. “Admittedly, I didn’t set out to work on a project from the start, but rather just focused on doing singles and to keep recording.

However, once I had voiced three or four songs it felt natural to evolve into an EP, which I envisioned could be completed with another few songs,” Minister Blessed told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday. Minister Blessed spoke about the themes that he explored on I Can Do All Things.

“There is a plethora of topics covered on this EP, including holiness, reverence, spiritual warfare, confidence, self-esteem, motivation, loyalty, laughter, fun, fellowship, and praise. The first single, Fun Inna Di Son, was released in the summer of 2025. The response to this song was really positive and it helped to pave the way for me to make my debut performance at an event dubbed Gospel Heatwave held in London, England.,” she shared.

He continued: “This year I released another single Operation Consecration in the Easter season, which felt like the perfect time to make a clarion call for believers to return to the altar and surrender fully to God.” The artiste noted that he held off releasing another single until the release of the EP.

“There was an initial plan to either release another single or the full project during the summer, but based on varying factors and following God’s leading, I decided to wait for my birthday for the next release which will be the full project,” he said.

The launch of the EP will take place on Friday, October 23, at Prayz House at Sunshine Plaza Balcony at 137 Maxfield Avenue in Half-Way-Tree. The debut will also coincide with Minister Blessed’s birthday celebration.

It promises to be an unforgettable night of games, fun, fellowship, music, and live performances Gospel artiste Goddy Goddy, Mighty Mic, Nadine Marie, and Minister Blessed himself are among the acts scheduled to perform, with music by DJ Marshy Redz.

Said Minister Blessed: “Up to the end of August the plan was to simply release the project online, but I have partnered with Marshy Redz and the Prayz House team to do a physical event.

The main goal is to help raise funds for members of my family who have been experiencing significant health challenges.

Outside of that, as the EP release coincides with my birthday, it felt like a good opportunity to have a celebratory type of event with fans, f riends, and well-wishers. The event also marks the return of Prayz House, which was on pause for a little while.”

Among the producers who contributed to the EP are Newlyfe Records from the United Kingdom, DaJourney who is based in Canada, Yagga Muzik Production, Lazaraus Productions, and Gospelix Records. Minister Blessed, who migrated from Jamaica nine years ago, currently resides in Manchester, England.

He worships on Sundays at the Lighthouse Church with his wife and three children.

World.title: Dervan Malcolm hailed as humble man
World.content:
Dervan Malcom’s father Eric and sister Mitsie mourn during the thanksgiving service for the late broadcaster at Boulevard Baptist Church on Saturday. (Photos: Joseph Wellington)

VETERAN broadcaster Dervan Malcolm was on Saturday eulogised as a man of deep humility, humanity, and sincerity who served as a bridge between people of varying views while making giant contributions to his family, Jamaica, and his alma mater Calabar High School.

Malcolm, whose voice was a familiar presence on Power 106 FM for more than three decades, died in August following a period of illness.

He was 50 years old. Award-winning journalist Earl Moxam remembered Malcolm as “a hybrid broadcaster, possessed of an old soul, but groomed to meet the demands of a new age”.

He told family, friends and colleagues of the late broadcaster at Boulevard Baptist Church in St Andrew that within months after the establishment of Power 106 in late 1992, under the leadership of Newton James, “in walked the young Dervan Malcolm, wet behind the ears but blessed with a multilingual tongue and an engaging smile”.

“Alongside him there was the almost-as-young Althea McKenzie and several other aspirants, anxious to carve their place in broadcast history. They joined a small cast of experienced hands and off they went on that history-making trek.”

Moxam said that Malclom’s multifaceted approach and tireless work ethic were soon bearing fruit in his roles as producer, announcer, news reporter, sports reporter, and commentator.

“Like many of his predecessors of decades past, he had the smooth diction, the articulate delivery, and the technical skills of the solo operator. Those qualities were matched by his humility… his humanity… and his sincerity,” Moxam said. “Thus, he made that seamless connection with his audience, in studio and on the road in diverse parts of our enchanting island.

Then, in the fulness of time, he embarked on the road less travelled and entered into the homes and hearts of our Jamaican communities… yearning for the comfort of an anchoring voice from the land of their birth,” Moxam added. “Ultimately, that connection might be considered his most clearly defined broadcast legacy, for which he will long be remembered and revered.”

Malcolm was described by the members of the Diaspora as “a bridge between Jamaica and Jamaicans across the world”. He was, “A bridge between generations, between ideas, between people who did not always see eye to eye,” said Florida Diaspora representative Rose Marie Adamson Lewis.

“He understood the truth many forgot. You do not have to agree with someone to give them dignity and pay them some respect. He made the Diaspora feel seen, he made us feel heard, and most importantly, he made us feel connected. The Diaspora has lost a wonderful friend. Jamaica has lost a beloved son and a wonderful broadcaster,” Adamson Lewis said.

Dr Jermaine McCalpin, who delivered the Calabar Old Boys’ Association (COBA) tribute, said the late broadcaster was lionised by the association. “I want to remind you as to why he has been lionised. Dervan was short in height, but a giant in his contribu tion to his family, Calabar, Jamaica, and the world.

This remembrance is personal, but it also carries the sentiments of Calabar lions across Jamaica and the Diaspora,” McCalpin said. “His gift as a broadcaster was making every person feel as though he was speaking to an audience of one. Perhaps no testimony captures Dervan’s relationship more fully to Calabar than the sentiments of COBA. They remember Taura Campbell (centre) is comforted by two family members as she grieves for her brother, Dervan Malcolm. him as a mentor’s mentor.

He was always there to listen and to advise. He sought the middle ground necessary to accomplish the task, and he never trumpeted his good deeds. His life is a living tes tament,” added McCalpin. Over the course of his career Malcolm took on several roles in broadcasting, including news presenter, editor, sportscaster, talk-show producer and execu tive producer of programmes.

In March 2007 he became the host and producer of Both Sides of the Story on Power 106 FM, a current affairs pro gramme that became closely associated with his commit ment to public education, em powerment, and advocacy.

His contribution to media and community development earned him several recogni tions, including the Diaspora Ambassador in Media Award from the Union of Jamaican Alumni Associations in New York. He was also honoured with the Bickle Award from Team Jamaica Bickle for his work highlighting issues affect ing Jamaicans overseas, and received further recognition from the City of Los Angeles and the Jamaica Awareness Association of California for his contributions to the Jamaican community.

World.title: REBUILD IN MOTION
World.content:
Interim Jamaica Head Coach Rudolph Speid issues instructions to his players on the touchline during their Concacaf Nations League A Group B football match against hosts El Salvador at Estadio Cuscatlan in San Salvador on Friday night. (Photo: AFP)

INTERIM Reggae Boyz Head Coach Rudolph Speid says the team has entered a dedicated rebuilding phase, after Jamaica’s 2-0 win over El Salvador in their Group B Concacaf Nations League A football match at the Estadio Cuscatlán on Friday night.

Striker Javon East scored goals in both halves to secure the victory and pick up three points for the visitors. However, Speid’s post-match comments focused heavily on the technical team’s deliberate strategy to trust a young group of players during a high-stakes away fixture.

After Jamaica’s failed World Cup-qualifying campaign earlier this year, Speid and his coaching staff decided to build for future campaigns by giving immediate international exposure to young talent.

In San Salvador, Jamaica fielded its youngest-ever senior international player, Jahmarie Nolan, at 16 years old, while also handing a start to a 17-year-old player, Jamone Lyle. By the end of the match, nine of the players who took the pitch for Jamaica were under the age of 23.

“It was a result that we needed,” Speid said after the match. “It was a good performance for a number of reasons.

Jamaica played its youngest-ever player to play on the senior national team, at 16 years and some days old today. We also played a 17-year-old today.

We’re in a rebuilding phase, and we’ve never beaten El Salvador since 2015, so there are a lot of good things happening to us and we’re grateful.”

Speid says giving younger players early exposure in tough environments like the Estadio Cuscatlán is now the primary objective of the coaching staff.

“Well, I know that by the end of the game we actually had nine players that we fielded who were under 23 years old,” Speid said. “It was good for us in our rebuilding efforts. After our failed World Cup-qualifying campaign this is a rebuilding effort, and we’re just happy that we’re giving a lot of these players opportunities.”

The match changed early in the first half when El Salvador defender Rudy Clavel was shown a red card in the 20th minute for a bad foul on East.

The red card forced El Salvador to play almost 70 minutes with 10 men.

Speid says his squad had to manage their emotions directly after the incident, as some of the younger players showed too much aggression in their challenges immediately following the dismissal.

“It’s a part of the game, and when it happened we really had to make adjustments so I thought the team was a little bit too enthusiastic with some of the tackles,” Speid said. “So that was the result of it tonight.”

Jamaica found the opening goal in the 39th minute when defender Miguel Freckleton sent a cross into the box for East who controlled the ball and finished in the bottom corner.

In the second half, Jamaica doubled their advantage in the 64th minute. Substitute Nolan set up East inside the penalty area, and the striker lifted a left-footed shot into the top corner of the net for his second goal of the night.

The victory ended an 11-year winless run against La Selecta.

The result moves Jamaica into second place in Group B with six points from three matches, trailing leaders Suriname by one point.

Friday’s victory puts Jamaica in a strong position to advance to the next round of the tournament without needing help from other results in the group.

“It means a lot to us,” Speid said. “We’ve put ourselves in a position where qualifying from this round is in our hands.

Basically, we don’t really have to depend on anyone. Once we get a good result in Honduras, that would be good for us.”

Jamaica will now travel to face Honduras on Monday night in their final match of this window, where a win or a draw will secure their spot in the quarter-finals.

World.title: Island Challenge participants plant 300 trees in Hurricane Melissa recovery push
World.content:
Participants in the Sandals Foundation Island Challenge are all smiles.

OCHO RIOS, St Ann — Participants in the Sandals Foundation Island Challenge traded running shoes and kayaks for rugged trails and seedlings on Saturday, as day two of the four-day endurance event combined physical exertion with efforts to help restore Jamaica’s forests following the devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa last year.

The day began with participants climbing the world-famous Dunn’s River Falls here before heading to the Bogue Forest Reserve, also in the parish, for a rainforest trek and tree-planting exercise. According to Sandals Foundation Public Relations Manager Patrice Gilpin, the demanding activities are ultimately tied to a greater purpose.

“They are doing it all for a good cause. There is no better way to connect tourism, health, doing good, and philanthropy,” Gilpin said. The Sandals Foundation Island Challenge, being held in Jamaica for the first time, aims to raise £100,000 to strengthen neonatal and paediatric health-care services at Falmouth Public General Hospital in Trelawny.

The approximately 30 participants are from the United Kingdom and include athletes, travel industry figures, and other supporters. Friday’s opening day saw the participants completing a 10-kilometre run from Rio Nuevo Fishing Beach in St Mary to Sandals Ochi Beach Club in St Ann, followed by a five-kilometre kayak journey along the White River Fish Sanctuary.

Following Saturday morning’s climb at Dunn’s River Falls, attention shifted to the Bogue Forest Reserve where participants were tasked with hiking through the forest and contributing to reforestation efforts by planting trees.

The exercise builds on an established relationship between Sandals Foundation and the forest reserve. The philanthropic organisation has previously carried out conservation activities at the site, including the planting of 300 trees in 2023 as part of its Earth Day activities.

Saturday’s initiative carried added significance in the wake of Hurricane Melissa, the record-breaking Category 5 system which pummelled sections of Jamaica on October 28, 2025.

Described as the strongest hurricane to strike Jamaica in recorded history, the Forestry Department estimated that approximately 51 per cent of the country’s forests, more than 270,000 hectares, were damaged. Ian Wallace, group acting operations manager of Island Routes, briefed participants ahead of the hike and tree-planting exercise, explaining why restoring vegetation has become particularly important since the hurricane. “Many of the trees were uprooted.

We lost a lot of our vegetation and, as part of their hike today, they will be planting a tree along the way,” Wallace said. Sandals Foundation Executive Director Heidi Clarke said Saturday’s activity allowed participants to contribute directly to that recovery.

“We have joined relief efforts to reforest. It will always be a commitment of ours, as we realise how important trees are,” Clarke said.

“Today we are letting our Island Challenge guests leave their legacy in this forest.” Georgia Crawford, environmental manager at Sandals Foundation, also highlighted the foundation’s long-standing relationship with the Bogue Forest Reserve and the importance of continuing the efforts after Melissa.

“Each year, especially on Earth Day, we take our volunteers as well as other groups like the Jamaica Fire Brigade, into this space to plant trees,” Crawford said. “This year was very important because it was on the heels of Hurricane Melissa, which caused damage to a lot of the island.

We are going to plant 300 West Indian cedar trees. These are very important because they are native trees and you don’t need a lot to take care of them.” For participant Nick Svoronos, completing the trek and putting a tree into Jamaican soil provided another reminder that the Island Challenge extends beyond testing endurance.

“We did some tree planting to help revitalise the trees from last year’s hurricane. Overall, it was a fantastic experience,” Svoronos told the Jamaica Observer. “I have planted trees before, and all for good causes, but coming here and contributing to planting and reviving the vegetation of the island is of big significance,” he said.

The challenge intensifies Sunday as participants are expected to travel west to Trelawny for a 21-kilometre half-marathon through the historic town of Falmouth, where they will be joined by local runners. The route will take them past Falmouth Public General Hospital, the beneficiary of this year’s fund-raising effort, before continuing towards Good Hope.

The Sandals Foundation Island Challenge concludes on Monday in St Andrew, when participants are scheduled to tackle a military endurance challenge in Newcastle before taking on a partial hike of the Blue Mountains, approximately 4,500 feet above sea level.

World.title: Former Belgian PM Verhofstadt investigated in EU Parliament intern probe
World.content:
“OLAF has merely requested information from our client regarding the supervision of a number of interns … in which he, as group chair, was not personally involved,” lawyers Christine Mussche and Quinten De Keersmaecker, who are representing Verhofstadt in the case, told Knack.

“Verhofstadt himself has not yet been interviewed, and there are currently no specific allegations against him. He is cooperating fully with OLAF and has provided the requested explanations with complete transparency,” the lawyers added.

Reached by POLITICO, Verhofstadt declined to comment further.

In a written reply Sunday, EPPO spokesperson Tine Hollevoet said: “As a general rule, the EPPO does not comment on ongoing investigations, nor do we publicly confirm which cases we are working on, in order not to endanger the possible ongoing procedures and their outcome.”

The Belgian Federal Prosecutor’s Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Verhofstadt, who was Belgium’s prime minister from 1999 to 2008 and served as an MEP from 2009 to 2024, is a prominent pro-EU figure who represented the European Parliament in the Brexit negotiations following the U.K.’s 2016 referendum on EU membership.

He left the Parliament in 2024 and is currently president of the board of the European Movement International, a pro-Europe lobby.

World.title: Le calendrier chargé d’Emmanuel Macron complique sa venue à la COP31
World.content:
Reste que pour le moment, l’intérêt d’Emmanuel Macron pour le grand raout des discussions climatiques demeure timide : invité à prendre part à la pré-COP, qui se tiendra du lundi 3 au jeudi 8 octobre aux Fidji, il a laissé la priorité à sa ministre de la Transition écologique, Monique Barbut.

De “Make our planet great again” au détricotage

Cette attitude tranche avec les débuts au pouvoir de celui qui se plaçait alors en héritier de l’Accord de Paris, dont l’objectif est de contenir le réchauffement climatique “bien en dessous” de 2 °C. A peine un mois après son élection, en juin 2017, le président de la République avait ainsi trouvé un écho international en prononçant le discours “Make our planet great again”, en réponse à Donald Trump qui venait d’annoncer le (premier) retrait des Etats-Unis du traité.

Dix ans plus tard, les avancées écologiques du premier quinquennat ont pour partie été détricotées lors du second, sur la rénovation thermique des bâtiments ou la lutte contre l’artificialisation des sols, entre autres. Ces reculs ont eu des conséquences sur l’influence de la France sur la scène internationale, analysait auprès de POLITICO, en juin 2025, Arnaud Gilles, ancien porte-parole du WWF et spécialiste des questions environnementales.

Le risque d’une image ternie à l’international

Ce n’est pas la première fois qu’Emmanuel Macron laisse planer le doute sur sa venue au sommet mondial sur le climat. L’an dernier, il avait officialisé son intention de s’y rendre un peu plus d’une semaine avant l’événement. Il n’était finalement resté que quelques heures sur place, à Belém, le temps d’une escale entre deux visites d’Etat au Brésil et au Mexique. Il s’était également montré discret lors des célébrations du 10e anniversaire des Accords de Paris.

Une impasse sur le dernier sommet mondial sur le climat de son mandat viendrait écorner un peu plus l’image de champion de l’écologie qu’Emmanuel Macron cherche à renvoyer à l’international. D’autres n’ont pas traîné pour officialiser leur participation. Le Premier ministre britannique, le travailliste Andy Burnham, l’a annoncée dès sa première allocution parlementaire, début septembre, après son accession au pouvoir.

Nicolas Cossic a contribué à cet article.

World.title: Moscow says it will step up strikes on Ukraine after Kyiv vows to hit Russian oil refineries
World.content:
“The people of Ukraine should blame only the head of the Kyiv regime for this,” the Russian Defense Ministry stated, referring to the Ukrainian president. “It is Zelenskyy who bears full personal and political responsibility for this.”

In an interview with Reuters, Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukrainian forces “have to respond in any way we can” to Russian attacks, which are increasingly targeting bridges across the Dnipro River in the capital.

“With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” he added, while saying Ukraine would not retaliate by deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure.

The Russian government also accused Kyiv of attempts “to disrupt voting in the elections … through terrorist strikes on civilian targets on Russian territory.” President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party largely dominated the results of Russia’s legislative elections, held from Sept. 18 to 20.

Russia’s threat to intensify strikes on Ukraine came on the same day as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a surprise one-day visit to Kyiv in a show of support to Ukraine.

During Merz’s visit, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that Russia had struck the roadway of the North Bridge in the city. On Saturday, Russia’s foreign ministry issued a warning against foreign visitors and diplomats and urged them to leave Kyiv.

Merz is expected to renew Germany’s support for Ukraine with a new military aid package worth around €1 billion, in addition to generators, substations and repair kits worth €350 million to strengthen the Ukrainian power grid under attack.

Zelenskyy and Merz visited Kyiv’s National Academy of Sciences, which was recently hit by Russian drones in an attack that killed two people and injured seven others and “was deliberate,” the Ukrainian president said on social media.

World.title: Latvian PM’s election win boosts chances for pro-Ukraine coalition
World.content:
Despite the decisive victory — far stronger than pre-election polling suggested — Kulbergs will still need to negotiate with other parties to form a majority government.

Two partners in his outgoing coalition, the conservative National Alliance and center-right New Unity, cleared the 5% threshold and are set to return to parliament. They appear to have enough seats for a majority without the Union of Greens and Farmers, which fell below the threshold.

That gives Kulbergs a solid path to another pro-Ukraine coalition without having to seek support from Šlesers’ Latvia First, an option that had loomed over the election campaign, which was marked by high inflation, uncertainty around the troubled national airline airBaltic and instrumentalized migration orchestrated by Russia and Belarus.

Kulbergs became prime minister in late May after his predecessor, Evika Siliņa, stood down following a backlash over stray Ukrainian drone strikes.

The final stretch of Latvia’s election campaign also spilled into Brussels last week, where Kulbergs initially opposed an EU deal to remove Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the bloc’s sanctions list.

Latvia ultimately abstained, allowing the broader sanctions regime to be extended after a compromise among EU countries.

World.title: Germany’s Merz visits Kyiv amid fears of ‘hardest’ winter in war
World.content:
Germany will furthermore provide Ukraine with financial assistance for the mass-production of new drones to intercept Russia's particularly dangerous high-speed jet drones. Berlin will also provide generators, substations, and repair kits worth €350 million to make the Ukrainian grid more resilient against Russian attacks.

Kyiv warned this week that it's running out of funds to buy weapons to defend itself, highlighting a €24 billion defense funding gap, to which the European Union reacted by accelerating the disbursement of a €45 billion loan. Germany is the biggest contributor to the financial and military support for Ukraine.

Ukraine is facing harsh Russian drone and missile attacks on its infrastructure, power and heating plants as well as other civilian targets, which are feared to further intensify this winter.

In contrast to previous visits from Western leaders, during which Moscow had largely refrained from attacks on the Ukrainian capital, air raid sirens could be heard in Kyiv during Merz's visit. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that Russia had struck the roadway of the North Bridge in the city. On Saturday, Russia's foreign ministry issued a warning against foreign visitors and diplomats and urged them to leave Kyiv.

This is Merz's first bilateral visit to Kyiv and his second trip as chancellor, after travelling there in May 2025 visit alongside leaders from France, the U.K. and Poland.

“If we fail to stop Moscow, sooner or later the Russian war machine will turn against us", Merz said upon arrival in the Ukrainian capital, adding: “I will tell President Zelenskyy today, 'You can continue to count on our help.'”

World.title: EU neighbors shun Kyiv’s plea to free trapped grain
World.content:
"It's very, very critical," Vysotskyi told POLITICO during his visit.

The answer: Sorry, but no. Two of the countries with the most vital infrastructure for boosting shipping and storage capacity, Poland and Romania, said there is nothing more they can or will do to help.

“The interest for our own farmers remains a priority,” Barna Tánczos, Romania’s agriculture minister, told POLITICO. Excess Ukrainian grain, combined with low water levels on the Danube, is already overloading his country’s ports, preventing Romanian farmers from selling their own goods.

The rebuff illustrates a persistent gap between the EU’s ambitions to support Ukraine and domestic political realities. As one of the world’s breadbaskets, Ukraine poses a real threat to the livelihoods of European farmers, a powerful constituency in many member countries. Even before the latest eruption in Black Sea fighting, Poland, Slovakia and Hungary barred imports of Ukrainian grain.

Currently, less than half of the exports are able to get out through the European rail, road and river shipping routes, Vysotskyi said. Up to 35 million tons could end up being stuck in Ukraine this year if the blockade persists.

Romania is trying to optimize its logistics, Tánczos stressed. Last month, Bucharest even signed a memorandum of understanding to ease border crossings with Kyiv and boost rail links.

World.title: Tory conference 2026: What POLITICO reporters are watching for
World.content:
U.K. Political Editor Dan Bloom

My biggest question for Badenoch’s speech at 11 a.m. Wednesday will be: can she end Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s honeymoon?

Since July, Labour has jumped to 26% in the polls while the Tories lag behind Reform on 19%. There will simply be fewer lobbyists and hangers-on than at Labour’s jamboree.

Badenoch will spend this week arguing that Burnham, with his crusade against “40 years of neoliberalism,” has ushered in the kind of classic left-right ideological fight that she relishes. Expect her to bang on about cutting welfare to fund defense — two weak points for Labour. And the self-described “badass Kemi” plans to be more abrasive than Burnham, who went out of his way not to attack anyone in his speech.

I reckon two things will decide if she can cut through: her personal brand, and how far she can differentiate the Tories from Labour and Reform (plus, well, her own party from 2024). She will try to paint the Tories as the party of fiscal responsibility but that’s a crowded marketplace. It’s worked for the Conservatives in the past but we aren’t in two-party politics anymore — though admittedly, the five-party split has become less dramatic since the summer.

There will be economic policy announcements but perhaps not on the scale of last year’s pledge to scrap stamp duty. Badenoch has talked about getting rid of inheritance tax but aides appear to be suggesting an announcement isn’t ready.

I can’t wait to see the peacocking by would-be candidates for a general election. Tory aides are shouting from the hills that they are on a “war footing” and candidate selection is ramping up. Some of the high-profile Tories who were rejected for being too centrist are swerving this year’s conference, but former West Midlands Mayor Andy Street will be prominent on the fringe. Critics complain that Badenoch has bulldozed the transepts off her party’s ideological church.

World.title: 2 Iranians charged with alleged bomb plot against Britain’s Jewish community
World.content:
Police said the two men received instructions and materials to make a homemade bomb for possible use on Jewish targets.

Two Iranian men have been charged with terror offenses over an alleged plot to bomb Manchester’s Jewish community.

Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, appeared in a British court on Saturday on charges of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism.

Police said the two men, who were arrested last month on the eve of the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, had received material and instructions on how to make a bomb, identified targets and carried out reconnaissance ahead of an attack on Jewish targets.

World.title: Judo 2026 World Championships: Koga and Yusifov Strike Gold on Opening Day in Baku
World.content:
Welcome to Baku, Azerbaijan, where new legends will rise to claim their red back patches at the Baku World Judo Championships 2026.

 

At -48kg, Italy’s Assunta SCUTTO claimed her place in the final for the third time in a row with impressive judo all morning. Her third time in a World final, but could she take the gold for a second time?

Meeting her there was Japan’s KOGA Wakana. The Japanese judoka was in fantastic form, with high quality judo throughout the day. KOGA already has a World bronze and silver, would this be the year to claim the missing gold? With every contest, she looked increasingly assured, carrying real momentum into the final.

In the final the two experienced judoka clashed. It was a tightly fought contest, with neither judoka giving much away, before KOGA seized her opportunity on the ground. Calm under pressure, she converted the opportunity decisively to bring the contest to an emphatic close. It was KOGA who walked away crowned the World Champion. A breakthrough moment for the Japanese star.

The great spirit from the fans, the energy that was coming in came into me and I managed to achieve better because of the support from the fans in the arena. Interview KOGA Wakana (JPN)

Azerbaijan National Olympic Committee Secretary General Mr Azer ALIYEV awarded the medals.

In the -60kg, Ahmad YUSIFOV secured his first time in a World final here in his home nation. An impressive feat for the local favourite who was looking to claim his red backpatch. With the Baku crowd firmly behind him, the stage was set for a huge home final.

Facing him was Kazakhstan’s Sherzod DAVLATOV, also in his first World final. Would DAVLATOV secure himself a place in history? The Kazakh had looked composed and dangerous throughout the day.

YUSIFOV rose to the occasion in front of a passionate home crowd to claim victory. With the pressure at its highest, YUSIFOV came from a score down, sparking huge celebrations and creating what is sure to be one of the standout moments of this World Championships.

International Judo Federation Executive Committee Member Mr Timur KEMELL awarded the medals.

There are always good things in my mind, I wouldn’t have lost a contest in front of the audience here and now I’m feeling great. Ahmad YUSIFOV (AZE)

What an incredible first day here in Baku. Join us tomorrow in the land of fire.

World.title: Sánchez in talks with coalition partners on reflection day: will he call elections in Spain?
World.content:
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez held talks with ministers and PSOE leaders on Sunday as he weighs whether to call an early general election, after Congress rejected two housing measures put forward by the government.

 

According to government sources quoted by RTVE, Sánchez began this period of reflection after Friday’s defeat in Parliament and is seeking the views of ministers and senior figures within the PSOE. His deliberations are also taking into account the demonstrations and housing protest camps held in various parts of Spain.

No decision has yet been taken. Some socialist figures have openly backed going to the polls. The secretary general of the PSE-EE, Eneko Andueza, has said it could be "a good moment for society to decide", while the leader of the PSOE in Castile and León, Carlos Martínez, has spoken of a "window of opportunity".

The situation arose after Congress rejected two decrees on Friday that had been approved earlier that week by the Council of Ministers. The first received 172 votes in favour and 178 against; the second, 166 in favour and 184 against. PP, Vox and Junts were decisive in preventing the texts from going through.

The government’s proposals included extending protections against eviction for vulnerable people, introducing new rules for temporary and room rentals, changing tax arrangements and providing greater stability for certain primary-residence tenancy agreements, according to official information from Moncloa.

29 November, first possible date

If Sánchez were to call an election immediately, Sunday 29 November would be the earliest possible date. To meet that timetable, he would need to announce his decision on Monday, with the decree dissolving Parliament and calling the election published in Tuesday’s edition of the Official State Gazette.

Electoral law stipulates that, in the event of an early dissolution, an election must be held 54 days after it is called. For now, Sánchez still has the opening of the National Congress of Family Business in Madrid in his diary on Monday, and is due to travel to Split, Croatia, on Wednesday to attend the MED9 summit.

The alternative would be to allow the parliamentary term to continue and try to revive the rejected housing measures, which would require the government to rebuild its support in Congress.

Thousands of people took to the streets in cities across Spain to demand action in response to the housing access crisis, while the groups behind the protests are considering stepping up their campaign towards a general strike.

The potential electoral impact of this discontent, however, remains unclear. Ignacio Urquizu, a sociologist, professor at the Complutense University of Madrid and chief executive of Metroscopia, said on Friday on Onda Cero's "La Brújula" that the latest data from his institute showed Vox gaining ground, the PP holding steady and left-wing parties losing support.

According to Urquizu, the housing protests had not, at least up to that point, translated into increased support for the left.

In the PP, the party's secretary general, Miguel Tellado, has directly urged Sánchez to call an election this Monday, claiming that the head of government "is still lying on the Moncloa psychiatrist's couch".

The prospect of an election has also prompted activity among the other parties. Sumar brought together its ministers and representatives of the parties within its alliance on Sunday to assess the situation and prepare for a possible election call. The second deputy prime minister, Yolanda Díaz, stressed that the decision rests solely with Sánchez.

Podemos, meanwhile, is calling on the government to continue bringing forward housing measures. Its secretary general, Ione Belarra, has argued that citizens want "solutions, not elections".
