We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of over 100 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending the city of Lviv – which is now in Ukraine but was then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of World War Two. The work continues recent moves towards reconciliation over the issue of exhuming victims of the war, which has long been a point of contention between the two countries. ℹ Komunikat o zakończeniu prac ekshumacyjnych na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie ⚠️ Zakończyły się prace ekshumacyjne na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie, znajdującej się obecnie w granicach administracyjnych Lwowa. Działania… pic.twitter.com/w9rSHuLeua — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) September 28, 2026 During the work on a 260-square-metre area at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv, which began in August, experts found 133 burials. They were identified as 115 soldiers from the Polish army and 18 from the German Wehrmacht. They died during the Battle of Lwów in September 1939, when Poland sought to defend the city from Nazi Germany, which had invaded from the west on 1 September, and the Soviet Union, which invaded from the east on 17 September. On 22 September, the Polish forces surrendered and the city came under Soviet control, as Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union had decided when secretly agreeing to divide up Poland in the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact earlier that year. Efforts are now focused on identifying the remains. Experts have taken bone samples for DNA testing, which will be compared with samples from possible relatives. Another part of the puzzle will be the roughly 2,900 objects – including identification tags, bayonets, helmets and religious items – discovered at the site alongside the remains. “For us, the identification of the remains is the most important stage of the work, because it is important to return these people their names,” said Dominika Siemińska, a researcher from Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), in a statement published by Lviv city council. “Currently we have a list of 76 [potential] names,” she added. However, because “so many years have passed, it will be difficult to find their relatives”. Siemińska also expressed her gratitude to the authorities in Lviv “for providing us with protection, support and the opportunity to work peacefully”. She said that “cooperation with the Ukrainian side is going very well”. The final stage of the work will be the burial of the recovered remains of Polish soldiers at the Polish cemetery in the Ukrainian city of Mostyska. The date of the ceremony has not yet been announced. The German remains are being handed over to the Volksbund organisation, which specialises in searching for and reburying German soldiers, said the IPN. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 Last year, Ukraine also granted permission for the exhumation of Polish soldiers in Lviv. Researchers subsequently found the remains of 31 people, as well as possible remains of dozens more that were difficult to identify due to them having been reburied and the manner of their death in artillery fire. They were also reburied in Mostyska, at a ceremony attended by prominent officials from both Poland and Ukraine. Previously, from 2017 to 2024, Ukraine had banned searches for Polish victims of World War Two on its territory in response to the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist partisan formation that fought against the Soviets but also led the massacre of ethnic Poles. However, in a major diplomatic breakthrough last year, Ukraine allowed exhumations to resume, including both the Polish soldiers in Lviv as well as victims of the UPA-led massacres, tens of thousands of whom are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Researchers have subsequently uncovered the remains of dozens of victims of the massacres, who have also been reburied in ceremonies attended by both Polish and Ukrainian officials. However, such steps towards reconciliation have been hindered this year by a dispute sparked by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision to name a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest state honour. Since then, both sides have moved to calm tensions, with Zelensky setting out a five-point plan to resolve the dispute, including issuing “a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. World.title: Polish coal mining giant JSW to shed 4,200 jobs – 21% of its workforce – this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish state-owned mining firm Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa (JSW), which is the EU’s largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland’s biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year. The plans come as JSW seeks to turn around its finances after years of large losses, as well as a broader shift in Poland away from reliance on coal. Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa do końca 2026 r. zwolni ponad 4,2 tys. osób. – Musimy kierować się interesem spółki – mówił na konferencji prasowej prezes JSW. Więcej: https://t.co/7Sxrhuuaja pic.twitter.com/evJoQal0c3 — Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) October 1, 2026 On Wednesday, JSW’s management board announced that it expected the size of its workforce to decline by 4,248 by the end of this year, bringing it below 16,000, down from 20,135 at the end of March. “We anticipate that approximately 2,200 people will leave in the third quarter, and about 1,400 in the fourth quarter,” adding to those who have already left, said the firm’s CEO, Bogusław Oleksy, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Last year, Poland introduced a new law making it easier for coal companies to close mines and reduce their workforce. It provides for large severance payments and other measures intended to soften the blow for those who lose their jobs. News service Strefa Inwestorów says that, on this basis, more than 3,000 JSW employees have the option to take so-called mining or mineral-processing leave while just under 1,200 can opt for one-off severance payments. President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill that makes it easier to close down coal mines and provides severance pay of 170,000 zloty to miners. The measures are seen as a key part of Poland’s transition towards cleaner forms of energy https://t.co/vH6MU4nBsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 The workforce reduction is part of JSW’s recovery plan for 2026-2035, announced this week. Other key objectives include cutting costs and investment without decreasing production while increasing the share of coking coal in output. When asked how the workforce reduction would affect production, Oleksy said the company would optimise its operations to make more efficient use of employees and equipment. He noted that most of the losses would be administrative positions rather than staff directly involved in production. In February this year, the company reached an agreement with unions to reduce labour costs in order to help stabilise the company’s financial position. JSW employees almost unanimously supported the agreement, reported broadcaster TVN. The initial results of the cost-cutting measures are beginning to show. In the first half of 2026, the cost of extraction per tonne fell to 609 zloty (€139) from 778 zloty a year earlier. JSW’s long-term goal is to bring the cost down to around 560 zloty per tonne. The company is still posting heavy losses, though those have also fallen this year. JSW posted a net loss of just over 1.0 billion zloty in the first half of 2026, around half the 2.1 billion zloty figure from the same period a year earlier. For the full year 2025, the company recorded a loss of 6.3 billion zloty, which was down from a record figure of 7.3 billion zloty in 2024. Polish state-owned mining giant JSW, the EU's largest producer of coking coal, has reported a record annual loss of 7.3bn zloty. It attributed the results to falling coal prices, lower production volumes, and the impact of a one-off write-off https://t.co/vrSgRu630b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 11, 2025 JSW’s announcement comes just as some officials and industry representatives are warning that the energy crisis caused by conflict in the Middle East could increase demand in Poland for coal, which is still used to generate around half of electricity and to heat almost a fifth of homes. Polish coal is among the most expensive in the world to extract, and the industry survives largely due to heavy public subsidies. In 2026, the state is expected to spend 5.5 billion zloty propping up the sector, after an outlay of 9 billion zloty last year. Successive governments have been seeking to move away from coal, which went from producing 87% of Poland’s electricity in 2015 to 52.2% in 2025. Meanwhile, between 2015 and 2024, the proportion of households using hard coal for heating fell from 40% to 17%, while those using natural gas doubled from 10% to 21%. However, the energy crisis prompted by US and Israeli attacks on Iran this year has resulted in natural gas prices soaring. As a result, Poland’s state assets minister, Wojciech Balczun, said last month that the geopolitical situation meant coal’s role this year would be “larger than we anticipated”. “We are currently increasing output at coal companies and are aware of the energy sector’s demand for coal as a stabilising factor,” he said, quoted by news service Money.pl. World.title: Polish president backs down and approves government’s windfall tax on fuel companies
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has reversed course and signed into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits that he had previously blocked. The government had been pushing the president to approve the measures amid soaring fuel prices. In announcing his decision on Thursday, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, insisted that he now expected the government to move to lower fuel prices for consumers. A few hours later, the government confirmed that it would do so, and on Friday morning it announced cuts in VAT and excise duty on fuels. Nie pozwolę rządowi dłużej odsuwać od siebie odpowiedzialności za tę trudną sytuację. Podpisałem ustawę dotyczącą nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych i zakończę proces ustawiania Polaków w roli politycznych zakładników. To rząd ponosi pełną odpowiedzialność za ceny paliw -… pic.twitter.com/7AX8v4a9Q0 — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) October 1, 2026 The windfall tax will levy a one-off charge of 60% of excess profits from liquid fuel sales, calculated as the amount that would have been generated using a company’s average 2025 fuel sales margin, increased by 20%. It is expected to raise around 4 billion zloty (€914 million). When announcing the plans, the finance ministry said the levy was justified by this year’s “exceptional economic and geopolitical conditions that have led to above-average financial results in a specific segment of the fuel sector, not resulting from improved operational efficiency…but from a supply shock”. The tax was intended to offset some of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by cutting VAT and excise duty and introducing a maximum daily price. Those measures were initially in place from March to June. However, in July, Nawrocki announced that he would not sign the windfall tax into law. He instead sent it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) for assessment. That process can take years, effectively killing off the bill. The president argued that the proposed measures “raised serious constitutional concerns”. In particular, he criticised the fact that the tax would be retroactive, applying to revenue earned from the beginning of March. Since then, he and the government have been locked in a dispute over the issue, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk arguing that measures to reduce fuel prices, which were briefly reintroduced in the last two weeks of August, can only be restored if Nawrocki signs the windfall tax. Nawrocki’s office, however, has argued that fuel companies would pass the costs of the tax onto consumers, therefore actually increasing prices. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 In September, the government’s majority in parliament passed the windfall tax bill a second time. And Nawrocki has now backed down, announcing in a recorded speech on Thursday evening that he would sign the bill into law. However, he has still asked the TK to assess its constitutionality. Nawrocki declared that he was seeking to call the government’s bluff. He claimed that they were actually hoping the windfall tax would fail so that the treasury could continue obtaining normal tax revenue from high fuel prices, as well as dividends from state oil giant Orlen. By signing the bill, the president said he was “ending the process of holding Poles hostage”. He now expected the government to “immediately” reintroduce measures to bring down prices at petrol stations, as well as the cost of fuel for farmers. To nie ja wygrałem. Wygrali Polacy, którzy już w weekend zapłacą mniej za paliwa. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 1, 2026 In response, government spokesman Adam Szłapka told broadcaster TVN that they were ready to make the necessary decisions to reduced prices on Friday and that the measures could be in force already by the weekend. “It’s good that the president has stopped blocking this,” he said. On Friday morning, the government announced that it would reduce VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and cut excise duty – both measures it also used earlier this year. The new policies will be in place until 31 December. Energy minister Miłosz Motyka told Polskie Radio that maximum daily prices would also be reintroduced. Earlier, on Thursday evening, finance minister Andrzej Domański announced on social media that he estimated fuel costs would be reduced by 1.2-1.3 zloty per litre once the subsidies were reintroduced. According to price monitoring service ePetrol, diesel prices are currently averaging around 9.14 zloty per litre while PB95 petrol is at 8.19 zloty. Those are both record highs. Ustawa o podatku od nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych właśnie wpłynęła do RCL. Jeszcze dziś będzie ogłoszona. Oznacza to, że już w weekend ceny na stacjach paliwowych będą niższe. Szacunkowo o około 1,2-1,3 zł na litrze. I po co były te gierki, Panie Prezydencie? — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) October 1, 2026 The dispute over financing fuel price cuts comes at a time of growing concern over Poland’s public finances, something Nawrocki referred to in his address on Thursday. Poland has been running one of the EU’s highest deficits, despite the government committing to bringing it down after being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. Public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time this year. Last month, Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The last time the country was at A3 level was in 2002. World.title: Leading Polish business owners invest in small nuclear reactor venture
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A group of prominent Polish businesspeople have announced that they are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by the country’s richest man, Michał Sołowow. Among them are Rafał Brzoska, founder of delivery giant InPost, and Mati Staniszewski, CEO of ElevenLabs, a leading artificial intelligence firm. The group is investing 500 million zloty (€114 million) in Sołowow’s Synthos Green Energy (SGE), which, together with 1.35 billion zloty from foreign investors, will secure the company’s financing for the next two years as it seeks to roll out BWRX-300 reactors in Poland, Central and Eastern Europe and the UK. As a European SMR development platform headquartered in Warsaw, Poland’s energy security is of special importance to us. We are proud to announce that today our founder, Michał Sołowow, unveiled a PLN 500 million investment by a group of leading Polish entrepreneurs in SGE’s… pic.twitter.com/J2SerVjIlG — SGE (@SGE_Nuclear) September 30, 2026 The investment, which was formally announced at a business conference in Warsaw on Wednesday, comes as Sołowow seeks to expand his nuclear project beyond SGE’s troubled partnership with Polish state energy giant Orlen, where disagreements have delayed plans to build SMRs in Poland. Alongside Brzoska and Staniszewski, the other new investors are Dariusz Gałęzewski, co-founder of drinks maker Oshee; Krzysztof Pawiński, CEO of food company Maspex; Michał Brański of media group Wirtualna Polska; and Michał Wypychewicz of ZPUE, the largest manufacturer of transformer stations in Europe. “They invested their own private funds because they understood the problem and then believed in the concept and the solution,” Sołowow told Business Insider Polska. SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed on site, are seen by their proponents as a fast and cost-effective way of installing nuclear capacity. In July, SGE announced plans to build 14 BWRX-300 reactors with a combined capacity of 4.2 gigawatts (GW) across three sites in the UK, which it said would generate enough electricity to meet 11% of the country’s demand. The company also hopes to deploy up to 26 reactors across six locations in Poland. The BWRX-300 is a 300-megawatt water-cooled small modular reactor. Construction of the first ever unit began in Canada in 2025, with completion planned for 2029 and commercial operation expected in 2030. Synthos Green Energy, a firm owned by Polish billionaire Michał Sołowow, has announced plans to build 14 small modular nuclear reactors in the UK. It says that the £35 billion project could deliver enough power to meet 11% of the UK’s demand https://t.co/YTMIzYERuJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 Brzoska said that developing SMR technology “is an investment in Poland’s future”, because without “reliable, predictable and competitively priced energy…it is difficult to talk seriously about further growth in industry, data centres, artificial intelligence, automation or modern logistics”. Staniszewski, whose company recently received an $11 million investment from Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) to establish an AI development centre in Poland, said lower electricity prices were important for the sector. SGE notes that demand for electricity is set to rise 40% in Poland over the next 14 years, according to grid operator PSE. Electricity prices have risen rapidly in recent years and are now the second most expensive in the European Union in relation to the cost of living. Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Poland remains the EU’s most coal-dependent country, with more than half of its electricity generated from coal. Over the past decade, however, the country has diversified its energy mix, with the share of renewable energy sources tripling to nearly 30% in 2025. Poland plans to reduce its reliance on coal further, including through the construction of its first nuclear power plant (of the traditional type, not an SMR). The 3.75-gigawatt project is scheduled to be commissioned in 2036. Sołowow has also been pursuing the deployment of SMRs in Poland through Orlen Synthos Green Energy (OSGE), a joint venture between SGE and state energy giant Orlen, Poland’s largest company, to develop BWRX-300 reactors in Poland. OSGE is seeking a so-called contract for difference (CfD) framework, an agreement with a state that guarantees a fixed price for electricity and helps shield developers from market swings, covering 14 reactors at three sites. Polish state energy firm Orlen has announced an agreement to build the country’s first small modular nuclear reactor (SMR). It says Poland will be the first country in Europe to deploy an SMR developed by US-based firm GE Hitachi Nuclear Energy https://t.co/MPWXS3qZ1d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2025 The project, however, has been delayed by disagreements between the two shareholders. Sołowow told Business Insider Polska that they reached an agreement last month that would allow construction of two reactors to move forward, but said he regretted entering into the partnership with Orlen. “I find it deeply regrettable, because it is precisely due to Orlen’s unnecessary involvement that we are discussing this project in political terms, even though it is not a political project,” he said. Sołowow has argued that a private-sector model can shorten construction times and improve cost control compared with traditional state-led nuclear projects. At the same time, he has highlighted the importance of the state’s role in implementing the project, saying its success depends on coordination between private investors and state policy. This includes contracts for difference, administrative procedures and the preparedness of the nuclear regulator. World.title: Activists launch world’s first abortion pill delivery locker in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Activists in Poland have launched what they say is the world’s first delivery locker that provides women with abortion pills, access to which is normally tightly restricted. They have placed the device opposite parliament in Warsaw, a location intended to send a message to the politicians who have made Poland’s abortion laws among the strictest in the world. The locker (called an “abortomat” in Polish, combining the words aborcja, meaning abortion, and automat, meaning an automatic machine) has been launched by Women Help Women (WHW), a global organisation that provides “self-managed abortion”, and Abortion Dream Team (ADT), a Polish activist group. They emphasise that the installation “is completely real [and] not an artistic performance”. It consists of 22 numbered lockers and a numeric keypad. Women who have contacted WHM seeking an abortion are given a six-digit PIN code that opens one of the doors, inside which is a package containing the pills. Recipients can either take the pills at home or do so in a specially prepared space opened last year by ADT and where the locker is located. The activists emphasise that such delivery mechanisms for abortion pills are particularly important in Poland because of the country’s highly restrictive laws. Abortions are only allowed in two circumstances: if pregnancy is the result of a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. As a result, only 851 legal terminations took place in Poland last year. However, activist groups such as WHW, ADT and Women on Web (WOW) say that they help tens of thousands of women in Poland obtain abortions each year through other means, in particular by providing pills. But they face legal risks for doing so: assisting someone in obtaining an unlawful abortion is a crime punishable by up to three years in prison. In 2023, ABW activist Justyna Wydrzyńska was convicted of that offence. Two years later, the sentence was annulled on a technicality and a new trial was ordered. Polish activist Justyna Wydrzyńska, who was convicted for providing abortion pills to a pregnant woman, has succeeded in having the conviction overturned on appeal. However, the case will now return to the lower court, where it will be heard again https://t.co/U3J5FmXdMw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 14, 2025 “The abortomat transforms a closely guarded, criminalised procedure into something as simple as picking up a package,” wrote ADT. “A door that opens when all others have slammed shut.” They say that the machine is intended for women who have an urgent medical need that means they cannot wait for the several days it takes to deliver pills by post, or who are in abusive, controlling relationships that make postal delivery unsafe. Wydrzyńska’s conviction came after the husband of a woman she helped obtain abortion pills found them and reported the case to the police. However, although assisting a woman in obtaining an unlawful abortion is an offence, the woman who had the abortion is not criminally liable. “The abortomat is not a human being, and the person collecting the pills, in accordance with the regulations, is not breaking the law,” said Wydrzyńska, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. WHW and ADT do not collect any personal information from women using the service. The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that Poland violated the rights of a pregnant woman who had to travel abroad to obtain an abortion after her foetus was diagnosed with a birth defect https://t.co/TgckusMxmJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 13, 2025 Under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, the abortion law was tightened and was strictly enforced. In December 2023, a new, more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk came to power, promising to liberalise the abortion law. However, it has so far failed to pass any such legislation. In 2024, a move to decriminalise abortion assistance up to the 12th week of pregnancy was rejected by parliament, after the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition joined the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Tusk subsequently admitted that it would be impossible during the current parliament to soften abortion laws. Instead, his government issued guidelines on when and how abortions can be carried out, with the aim of ensuring that doctors and prosecutors “take the women’s side” when making decisions on the issue. World.title: Fugitive opposition politician granted safe passage to return to Poland against prosecutors’ wishes
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Warsaw court has approved a request from Marcin Romanowski, a fugitive former government minister who has been on the run for almost two years, to receive safe passage back to Poland. Romanowski is believed to currently be in the pro-Russian Moldovan breakaway region of Transnistria. Although Polish prosecutors have long been seeking Romanowski’s return, they opposed his request for safe conduct, arguing that he cannot be trusted to comply with its terms given that he has repeatedly sought to evade the law. Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, has already announced that prosecutors will appeal the court’s decision, which he claims was issued by an illegitimately appointed judge and in violation of regulations. Nie ma i nie będzie bezkarności dla ludzi Zbigniewa Ziobry. Prokuratura złoży ZAŻALENIE na decyzję o wydaniu listu żelaznego dla Marcina Romanowskiego. Spójrzmy prawdzie w oczy: kto jednoosobowo próbuje zapewnić nietykalność człowiekowi podejrzanemu o gigantyczne nadużycia w… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 30, 2026 Romanowski served as deputy justice minister in the former Law and Justice (PiS) government between 2019 and 2023. After PiS lost power, prosecutors sought to bring charges against him for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served in government, including participating in an organised criminal group. However, Romanowski fled Poland in December 2024 and was granted asylum by Hungary, which was then ruled by Viktor Orbán, a conservative ally of PiS. When Orbán lost power earlier this year, Romanowski went on the run, and for months his location was unknown. In August, it emerged that Romanowski had sent a letter to Poland requesting safe passage to return. The document indicated that he was in Tiraspol, the capital of Transnistria, a region that sought to break away from Moldova in the 1990s and is now effectively under Russian control. Prime Minister @donaldtusk says that, based on intelligence sources, Poland is now “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia https://t.co/mdvmJpkFf7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 18, 2026 At the time, the spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, Przemysław Nowak, said that there were “no grounds whatsoever” to approve Romanowski’s request for safe passage to Poland. He noted that “the suspect has evaded legal proceedings, questioned the legality of the authorities’ actions, left Poland and then Hungary to avoid arrest, and publicly declared his lack of intention to return to the country due to the ongoing criminal proceedings against him”. However, on Wednesday, Warsaw’s district court approved Romanowski’s request. A spokeswoman for the court said that the decision had been made as “previous methods used [to secure Romanowski’s return] were ineffective” and safe passage would “allow the case to be clarified”. World.title: Prague’s Oldest Nightclub Lávka is Closing After 36 years
World.content:
One of Prague’s best-known nightlife venues is closing after more than three decades beside the Charles Bridge.

Lávka, which opened in 1990 on the banks of the Vltava, held its final farewell party on September 30. The club will leave its historic premises by October 8 as the City of Prague prepares to renovate the building.



For 36 years, Lávka was more than a nightclub. Its programme included concerts, theater, exhibitions, fashion shows and other cultural events. Its visitors included former president Václav Havel, politician Karel Schwarzenberg and singer Karel Gott.

The venue also hosted Czech acts including Lucie and Lunetic, as well as international performers such as Supertramp and R.E.M.

The first version of the venue was modest. It began as a theater bar in the Bedřich Smetana Museum, replacing the building’s cloakroom. With little money available, co-founder Boris Gaydečka and his partners constructed the bar themselves using scaffolding and wooden boards found on the site.

Advertising on the newly launched Radio Evropa 2 helped attract customers, and the business soon outgrew its original space.

Over the years, Lávka became a regular stop for performers from very different parts of Prague’s cultural scene. Its stage hosted the avant-garde Opera Mozart, the Semafor theater and the Spejbl and Hurvínek Theatre.

During the catastrophic floods of 2002, water eventually reached the ceiling despite efforts to protect the premises.

The damage was extensive. Seating was destroyed, a piano borrowed from the museum was swept away and doors were torn from their hinges.

The building is now being cleared

The end of Lávka’s original premises is linked to a wider renovation of the historic building.

The former Old Town Waterworks building belongs to the City of Prague and has been associated with the Bedřich Smetana Museum since 1936. The museum will also leave the building as part of the planned renovation.

Lávka will continue operating a canteen and café in the neighboring building owned by the Czech Association of Scientific and Technical Societies.

World.title: Only 29 Percent of Czechs Have a Higher Education Degree, OECD Finds
World.content:
Only 29 percent of people aged 25 to 64 in Czechia have completed higher education, according to the latest data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

The figures highlight a persistent difference in the country’s education profile compared with other developed economies. While university-level education remains less common in Czechia, upper secondary education is far more widespread.

Around two-thirds of Czech adults have completed upper secondary education, compared with an OECD average of 39 percent. Vocational secondary education remains particularly common, although its share is gradually declining, as younger generations attain higher levels of education.



The change is most visible when comparing age groups. Vocational secondary education is the highest level of education for around 70 percent of Czech residents aged 55 to 64. Among people aged 25 to 34, the figure has fallen to 52 percent.

Across the OECD, the proportion of younger adults completing higher education has continued to increase. Czechia, however, is also facing a less positive trend at the lower end of the education scale.

Among 25- to 34-year-olds, the share of people who have not completed upper secondary education increased from 6 percent in 2015 to 7 percent in 2025. The trend is moving in the opposite direction across the OECD as a whole, where the average fell to 12 percent last year.

Young Czechs have relatively low unemployment

Despite the country’s comparatively low share of university graduates, Czechia performs well on several employment indicators.

In 2025, just 7 percent of people aged 18 to 24 were neither in education nor employment. The OECD average was twice as high, at 14 percent.

The unemployment rate among recent graduates has also declined over the past decade. In Czechia, it fell from 3 percent in 2015 to 2 percent in 2025. The corresponding OECD average was 5 percent.

Education is reflected in Czech wages

The OECD data also show a clear relationship between educational attainment and earnings in Czechia.

People whose highest qualification is general secondary education, including graduates of gymnasiums, earn an average of 8 percent less than the national average wage.

The difference is larger for people with vocational secondary education, whose earnings are 16 percent below the national average. Those who have not completed secondary education earn 33 percent less on average.

Higher education is also associated with greater access to remote work. Around 31 percent of Czech employees with a university education work remotely at least occasionally. Among workers with secondary education, the proportion is approximately 10 percent.

Czech education spending remains below OECD average

The OECD report also points to differences in public investment.

In 2023, public expenditure on education from primary schools through universities amounted to 3.6 percent of GDP in Czechia. The average across OECD countries was 4 percent.

Czechia also spent less per student than the OECD average. Annual expenditure stood at $11,861 per student, compared with $13,601 across OECD countries.

The figures are included in the OECD’s latest assessment of education systems in member countries, covering education levels, employment outcomes, earnings and public spending.

World.title: Rising Number of Czech Families Struggle to Afford School Lunches
World.content:
A growing number of Czech parents are unable to cover the cost of school lunches for their children.

The non-profit initiative Lunches for Children (Obědy pro děti), run by Women for Women, cites divorce, job loss, or serious illness as the primary causes driving families to apply for help. Even state food subsidies are proving insufficient.



At the start of this school year, demand for support is especially steep. Between January and September, the program aided nearly 16,000 pupils through cooperation with more than 1,150 schools and cafeterias nationwide.

Participation rose by about 15 percent compared with the same period last year, with sharp increases in Prague and the Ústí nad Labem region. A typical lunch costs 30–50 crowns, but for older students, monthly totals can exceed 1,000 crowns.

Under Women for Women’s rules, schools help identify children in need. Class teachers, principals, and canteen managers evaluate applications based on factors such as low income, single-parent status, or sudden financial crisis. Schools apply on behalf of families; funding is granted under donation agreements and routed directly to the schools (not to parents).

The heaviest wave of applications arrives each September, when the new school year begins. In more strained regions, quota limits have already been reached. The Ministry of Education endorses the project as a model of effective public–nonprofit partnership.

Marta Hekl, the organization’s director, emphasizes that the school lunch is more than nourishment: “Children feel part of a community, gain confidence, and receive the energy they need for learning.” Nejedlá adds that even in Prague, the country’s wealthiest region, applications have risen by 20 percent, as living costs outpace wages.

Historically, need is greatest in regions burdened by high unemployment and social difficulties—especially Ústí nad Labem and Karlovy Vary.

Some corporate donors also back the program. For instance, ADM Olomouc offered a significant grant to the Lunches for Children project, helping nearly 100 children eat lunch with their peers all year.

World.title: Lego to Open New Prague Store on Na Příkopě Street on October 22
World.content:
Lego will open its second Czech store on Na Příkopě Street in central Prague on October 22.

The Lego Store Prague City Center will open to the public at 10 a.m. The 496-square-meter shop will carry the full Lego range, including sets available exclusively through Lego stores.



The interior will incorporate references to Prague and Czech history.

Among the models on display will be Lego versions of the Prague Astronomical Clock, Charles Bridge, Charles IV and the Czech double-tailed lion. A model of a Prague tram will also be part of the store’s design.

Visitors will have access to several interactive features, including a station where they can create their own minifigures and a Pick & Build area.

Prague-wide Lego Game

The opening campaign will begin earlier in October with a series of Saturday challenges. During the first three Saturdays of the month, families will be able to follow clues published on social media and search different parts of Prague for project ambassadors.

The ambassadors will be carrying Lego models representing Prague landmarks, including a tram, the Astronomical Clock and Charles IV. Participants who find the correct location will have to give the ambassador a specific password revealed through the published clues.

The campaign will involve content creators and public figures including Bára and Ondřej Havel, Janek Rubeš and Honza Mikulka, known for their Kluci z Prahy project, as well as influencer Karel “Kovy” Kovář.

Three families will win the opportunity to attend the new store’s opening ceremony. As part of the event, they will assemble a large golden key from Lego bricks outside the store, which will be used to symbolically open the new shop.

The store will also host a special activity in November. On November 4 and 5, visitors will be able to build their own Lego model of a Prague tram and take it home.

World.title: Petr Pavel to Miss Local Elections After Trip Planning Error
World.content:
Czech President Petr Pavel will not vote in next week’s local elections in Černouček, the village in the Litoměřice region where he lives, because he will be abroad on a private trip.

The Presidential Office confirmed on Friday that Pavel had left the Czech Republic and would not be able to participate in the municipal elections. The Castle said the president regrets the planning mistake.



Pavel is expected to return to his official schedule on October 19, when he will receive newly appointed ambassadors. During his absence, he will remain in contact with the Presidential Office in case a situation requiring his attention arises.

A post by Czech rally driver Martin Prokop has linked Pavel to the Rallye du Maroc. Prokop shared a photograph with the president and wrote that Pavel had visited the event.

The rally is taking place in Morocco from September 28 to October 3.

According to Czech media reports, Pavel’s private trip is a motorcycle holiday. The Presidential Office itself has not confirmed the location of the trip.

The timing of the trip is notable because Pavel himself formally set the dates for this year’s elections in June.

Under recently amended electoral rules, local and regional elections are held on the Friday and Saturday of the first full week of October.

World.title: VIDEO: Hollywood Actress Zendaya Takes Over Prague for New Sportswear Campaign
World.content:
Zendaya recently came to Prague to film a promotional campaign for Swiss sportswear and footwear brand On, with several recognizable locations across the city serving as the backdrop.

The actress filmed at the Strahov ventilation towers, the building used by Prague’s Technical Road Administration for tunnel management, and the roof of the National Museum’s New Building.



The two-minute campaign video follows Zendaya as she runs through Prague while being pursued by a group of women. The opening scenes were filmed around the Strahov ventilation towers before the action moves to the brutalist TSK tunnel administration building.

A fight takes place outside the building and continues underneath it, before Zendaya escapes and heads toward the National Museum’s New Building.

The final part of the video was filmed inside the museum building, including its staircase and corridors, and on the roof. The campaign ends with Zendaya jumping from the rooftop.

The video was directed by Pantera, an Argentine directing trio. On selected Prague for the launch of its new collection, using the city as the setting for both still photography and the campaign film.

Zendaya is the latest major international star to film in Prague, which has become an increasingly popular location for international productions.

Several recent projects have used Prague neighborhoods and buildings as filming locations. The horror film Resident Evil was shot at locations including Karlín and Holešovice late last year.

Holešovice has also attracted international television productions.

Apple TV selected a tax office building in Prague 7 as a filming location for Birdwatcher, with production taking place there for two weeks. Wyatt Russell, the son of actors Goldie Hawn and Kurt Russell, is among the series’ lead actors.

World.title: Prague Passengers Can Now Request Czech or English Speaking Bolt Drivers
World.content:
Bolt has introduced two new ride categories in Prague that allow passengers to request drivers who speak either Czech or English.

The new options are available at the same price as a standard Bolt ride.



They are open to drivers of any nationality who can communicate in the relevant language at a level suitable for everyday conversation.

Czech-speaking passengers who are less comfortable communicating in English can request a Czech-speaking driver, while foreign residents, tourists and business travellers can choose a driver who speaks English.

Bolt already provides automatic translation for communication between passengers and drivers within its app. Booking information, addresses and messages can therefore be translated automatically. The new categories are designed to cover situations in which communication takes place outside the app, particularly during the journey itself.

The company said the new options are already available in Prague, where it has enough partner drivers who meet the language requirements.

Drivers can choose whether to participate in the new categories. They may offer rides in Czech, English, both languages or continue driving exclusively in the standard category.

Participation is voluntary.

Passengers will see the two new options directly in the Bolt app. The Czech-speaking category is identified by an icon featuring the Czech flag, while the English-speaking option uses an English flag icon.

World.title: Pegasus Airlines Completes Acquisition of Czech Airlines and Smartwings
World.content:
Pegasus Airlines has completed its acquisition of Czech Airlines and the Smartwings Group, marking a major change in the ownership of one of the Czech Republic’s most established aviation businesses.

The Turkish low-cost carrier announced the completion of the transaction on Thursday, October 1, following the approval of the relevant regulatory authorities and the fulfilment of the required closing conditions.



The deal brings together Pegasus Airlines and the Czech-based Smartwings Group, creating an aviation group with a combined fleet of more than 175 aircraft.

The two airlines also have firm orders for a further 140 aircraft.

For passengers in Prague and across the Czech Republic, Smartwings will continue to operate under its existing brand. Its day-to-day operations, customer relationships and service are expected to remain in place, while the company will gain access to new opportunities for expansion and development through its new ownership.

Pegasus expands further into Central Europe

Founded in 1990, Pegasus Airlines has operated as a low-cost carrier since 2005. The airline currently serves 161 destinations in 57 countries from its main hub at Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen Airport and other bases in Türkiye.

Its network covers Europe, the Middle East, North Africa and Asia, making the acquisition an opportunity to strengthen Pegasus’ presence in Central and Eastern Europe.

Smartwings, meanwhile, operates a network of around 80 destinations across 20 countries. The group has a particularly strong position in the Czech leisure travel market, with scheduled and charter services as well as private flights and special flights for international companies and organisations.

The Czech airline has been operating under the Smartwings name since 1998, while the Czech Airlines (ČSA) brand is one of the oldest names in European aviation.

The combined business is expected to benefit from the complementary networks of the two airlines. Pegasus brings a large international network and experience with the low-cost model, while Smartwings has an established customer base and strong relationships with tour operators in the Czech Republic and wider Central European market.

Pegasus said that Smartwings will continue operating under its established brand following the completion of the acquisition.

Pegasus carried a record 43.3 million passengers in 2025 and operates one of Europe’s younger aircraft fleets.

World.title: What the UAE aviation FZ1073 incident can teach Hungary about resilient critical systems
World.content:
The security incident aboard flydubai flight FZ1073 on 30 September is still under investigation, and that fact should discipline every serious discussion of it. UAE authorities have confirmed that the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv experienced a security incident, was diverted and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia. The UAE Attorney-General has formed a specialised investigation team to establish the circumstances and motives, while officials have warned against speculation. I agree with that caution. We do not need to guess the motive to recognise the security question the incident has placed in front of us. FZ1073 incident raises security lessons for Hungary:

Written by Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi, Author and Researcher specializing in Security, Heritage, Risk Management, and Control Room Operations.

Hungary’s manufacturing, logistics and transport networks make this question relevant far beyond aviation. The UAE and Hungary have both attracted investment that depends on reliable infrastructure and increasingly automated operations. As those systems become more connected, organisations will spend heavily to keep unauthorised users out. They should devote equal attention to what legitimate users can do after they are in.

For decades, security has become very good at asking who is allowed through the door. We verify identity, role, clearance and permission. I have spent years in security environments where those controls matter every day. Yet authorisation answers only the first question. The harder question begins after entry: if circumstances or behaviour change, can the system recognise that change and intervene without waiting for the consequences to prove that trust should have been reconsidered?

This is not an argument for treating trusted professionals as suspects. Complex systems cannot function without trust. Pilots, engineers, controllers, operators and administrators need real authority to do their jobs. My concern is different: organisations sometimes confuse justified trust with permanent trust. A badge, clearance or professional title can explain why someone was admitted yesterday; it cannot guarantee the safety of every action tomorrow.

That is why I distinguish between access control and authority control. Access control decides who may enter. Authority control asks what an authorised person can do after entry, how critical power is distributed, what abnormal conditions trigger challenge, and how quickly others can limit or redirect authority if the risk picture changes. The second problem is harder because it sits inside the trusted system rather than outside it.

For Hungary, this is also a competitiveness issue. Investors do not only ask whether a facility is protected; they care whether disruption can be contained and operations restored. Authority that is too concentrated can turn one internal failure into a business-continuity event. A resilient institution therefore gives trusted people enough power to work while ensuring that critical actions remain visible, challengeable and reversible.

The response should not be another layer of suspicion for its own sake. Better design is more useful: clear escalation routes, meaningful redundancy around critical actions, a culture in which questioning an abnormal action is not treated as disloyalty, and emergency procedures that are designed before the emergency. Human courage will always matter, but a mature security system should not make last-minute heroism its final control.

If you missed it: Pro-Palestinian and pro-Israel demonstrations held simultaneously in Central Budapest

FZ1073 also reminds us that resilience crosses borders. What began aboard a UAE-registered aircraft required a safe operational response in Saudi Arabia, and the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs later expressed appreciation to the Saudi authorities for their cooperation and handling of the incident. A crisis rarely respects the organisational or national boundary where it begins. The next system in the chain may suddenly become part of the solution.

The investigation should determine the specific lessons for aviation. The broader lesson is already worth asking in every high-consequence sector: are we protecting only the boundary, or are we also protecting what happens after legitimate access has been granted? The door still matters. So do the clearance and the background check. But modern security must be equally prepared for the question that begins one second later: now that the person is inside, how does the system remain safe?

Sources: UAE GCAA / Emirates News Agency, 30 September 2026; UAE Attorney-General and Ministry of Foreign Affairs / Emirates News Agency, 1 October 2026; flydubai official update.

World.title: Budapest to get more police officers as public safety moves up the agenda
World.content:
Budapest could soon see a visibly stronger police presence, with the government promising a significant increase in officers as public safety becomes a bigger focus in the capital.

The plan was discussed at the first meeting of the re-established Budapest Development Council, where Prime Minister Péter Magyar told participants that the government intends to significantly increase police numbers in Budapest.

According to Budapest City Hall, one way of achieving this would be to replace police officers currently performing security duties at government ministries with other forms of guarding and security. Those officers could then be reassigned to policing duties elsewhere in the capital.

Police have already stepped up targeted checks

The announcement comes after Budapest police launched a broader public-order operation during the summer, carrying out targeted checks at several locations across the capital.

In the first 30 days of the operation, officers checked 11,167 people, arrested 252 and took another 195 to police stations, according to the Budapest Police Headquarters.

The BRFK said the locations and priorities of the checks were determined using public-safety data, police experience and reports from residents and local authorities. Officers took action in cases involving robbery, drug-related offences, disorderly conduct, theft and various traffic violations.

The operation involved district police departments, central BRFK units, the Rapid Response and Special Police Services, municipal law-enforcement bodies and other partners. Also, the the capital already relies on reinforced patrols in busy nightlife districts, while Budapest police logged around 1.4 million hours of public-space duty in 2025.

High-profile incidents have drawn attention to safety in Budapest

Public safety has also received increased attention following several widely reported incidents in the capital in recent months. One of the most striking cases occurred in September, when a 21-year-old British tourist was suspected of attacking a 43-year-old pedestrian on Szent István körút in central Budapest.

Video footage showed the victim being knocked to the ground and repeatedly struck. He lost consciousness and was taken to hospital with head injuries. The suspect later told investigators that he could not remember what had happened because he had been heavily intoxicated.

The incident attracted significant attention because it appeared to be an unprovoked attack in a busy central area and was captured on video.

This attack was one of several violent incidents in Budapest that attracted attention in September. Earlier that month, a 33-year-old man was stabbed several times on tram 4 near Wesselényi Street, prompting a police investigation and renewed concern over safety on public transport.

Later, on 18 September, a 36-year-old man was fatally stabbed near Akácfa Street and Dob Street in the city’s busy nightlife district. Police later arrested two suspects in connection with the killing.

While these cases do not in themselves prove a broader rise in violent crime across the capital, their high-profile nature has helped keep public safety in the spotlight.

If you missed it: British tourist says he remembers nothing of brutal Budapest assault – VIDEO

More officers do not necessarily mean crime is rising

The recent cases and the government’s decision to increase police numbers do not by themselves show that Budapest is experiencing a citywide rise in violent crime.

The government and City Hall have not presented new comparative crime statistics alongside the announcement that would demonstrate a general increase in offences across the capital.

What is clear, however, is that public safety has moved higher on the agenda, with both targeted police operations and plans to increase the number of officers serving in Budapest. The Budapest Development Council is expected to meet again in the coming weeks, when further details of the government-city agreement may emerge.

World.title: Hungarian payment technology powers transactions at Malaysia’s Sepang Circuit
World.content:
The F1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia got underway today, with Festipay technology once again providing fast and secure cashless payment at the Bahrain International Circuit (BIC) event.

The partnership between Festipay and Bahrain International Circuit began in 2024, when the Bahrain Formula 1 circuit selected BIC PAY, a system developed by the Hungarian company, to introduce cashless payment. Since then, the system has continued to evolve, and today the event operates with a hybrid payment solution: visitors can pay both by bank card and with RFID-enabled BIC cards manufactured by Festipay.

The system is designed to provide more than one hundred thousand visitors with a fast, simple and secure payment option, while also providing merchants with an efficient and integrated sales solution.

Hungarian payment technology powers transactions at Malaysia’s Sepang Circuit

More than 200 Festipay devices are operating at the circuit near Kuala Lumpur, with the entire technological infrastructure supported by a 12-member team of Hungarian professionals. The Hungarian-developed and operated system therefore contributes to the visitor experience and the smooth running of one of the world’s largest motorsport events.

If you missed it: Budapest is taking on a bigger role at one of the world’s biggest banks

“Our partnership launched in Bahrain in 2024 and, following its success in the Middle East and Hungary, our enhanced hybrid payment system is now proving itself in Southeast Asia as well. The combination of bank card and RFID-based payment at this level of security and reliability is a unique solution and the result of 100% Hungarian software engineering,” said Attila Solti, CEO of Festipay Zrt.

For Festipay, this race is more than just another international venue: the introduction of the system in Bahrain in 2024 was an important milestone in the company’s expansion into the Middle East. Since then, the BIC PAY system has continued to demonstrate that Hungarian-developed event technology can operate reliably at some of the world’s largest and most complex events.

Hungarian payment technology powers transactions at Malaysia’s Sepang Circuit

At the Hungaroring, during the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix and other races, the Festipay system is also used as the exclusive payment solution.

World.title: Hungary’s next competitiveness question is how fast institutions can adapt
World.content:
Hungary’s recent investment performance makes institutional adaptability more than an abstract public-sector question. In 2025, the Hungarian Investment Promotion Agency (HIPA) supported 108 investment projects representing about €7.07 billion in capital and 18,227 new jobs. Electronics accounted for more than 55 per cent of the investment volume, while automotive projects represented another €1.1 billion. HIPA also recorded 14 research-and-development investments worth nearly €570 million, its highest number and value to date. These figures show an economy competing not only for factories, but increasingly for technologically complex, high-value activity. In such an environment, the speed and quality with which public institutions adapt can become part of the investment proposition itself.

By Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi (A.S. Alhebsi)

This is especially relevant because advanced manufacturing does not operate inside one administrative box. A major industrial investment can depend simultaneously on energy capacity, transport, workforce availability, environmental permissions, digital infrastructure, cyber resilience, incentives and local development. Hungary’s automotive sector illustrates the scale of that coordination challenge: HIPA reported 27 automotive investment decisions in 2025, a record for the agency. When investment becomes more technologically intensive and supply chains become more exposed to external shocks, competitiveness depends partly on whether institutions can move information and decisions across these boundaries without creating avoidable delay.

A global survey presented at the World Governments Summit’s Ambassadors’ Retreat 2026 in Dubai provides useful international context, but it should not be read as a measurement of Hungary. The Global Ministers Survey 2026, conducted by the World Governments Summit with PwC, covered 61 ministers from around the world. Seventy-nine per cent expected the role of government to increase in the future, while 34 per cent said their governments had fully embraced change. Respondents identified funding, skills and cybersecurity among the main barriers to change. These are global findings; they do not describe Hungary specifically.

My interpretation of the distance between expanding government responsibility and the capacity of institutions to adapt is what I call the Government Readiness Gap. This is not an index or metric used by the Global Ministers Survey. It is an analytical concept: the gap that emerges when the number, speed and complexity of responsibilities placed on government grow faster than the institution’s ability to absorb new technology, coordinate across domains and move a consequential decision to the authority capable of acting on it.

Hungary offers a concrete reason to take this gap seriously. In July 2026, HIPA announced that investment-incentive decision-making had restarted after a months-long standstill, allowing negotiations on eight investment projects to move forward. The episode does not prove that Hungary has a broad readiness problem, and it should not be treated that way. It does, however, demonstrate something important for any investment-intensive economy: the administrative path behind a decision can have economic consequences. Capital may be global and factories increasingly automated, but permissions, incentives, infrastructure coordination and public decisions still move through institutions.

If you missed it: PM Magyar signals possible end to Hungary’s food margin caps

This suggests that competitiveness should be assessed not only through tax rates, labour costs, infrastructure or the volume of announced investment. A further variable is institutional response time: how quickly a government can recognise a material change, verify what it means, coordinate the relevant bodies and place the decision before the authority empowered to act. I refer to one part of this as time to authorised decision. It is not simply the speed of bureaucracy. A fast but poorly verified decision can be costly. The objective is to shorten the distance between reliable information and accountable authority without weakening scrutiny.

The comparison with the United Arab Emirates is useful here not because the two economies are identical, but because they face different versions of the same institutional challenge. The UAE has deliberately embedded digital transformation across government strategy. Its Digital Government Strategy set out a cross-government approach built around digital-by-design services, data, resilience, proactivity, digital skills and legislative readiness. The federal Digital Customer and Digital Government Service Policy also emphasises proactive services, system integration and continuity of digital services. In other words, modernisation is treated not simply as the purchase of technology but as a question of how government structures, capabilities and services operate together.

Hungary’s strength is different. Its position in European manufacturing networks, its automotive and electronics base, and the scale of recent foreign investment create strong incentives for institutional coordination around real industrial activity. The UAE’s experience is relevant because it shows one approach to making digital capability, legislative readiness and cross-government integration explicit parts of government modernisation. Hungary’s experience is relevant to the UAE in the opposite direction: it demonstrates how institutional readiness is tested when industrial investment, supply chains, technology and regional development must converge in physical projects. The comparison is therefore reciprocal rather than a claim that one model should be copied by the other.

The next stage of competitiveness will make this coordination harder. Artificial intelligence will enter administrative and industrial processes. Cyber incidents will increasingly have operational consequences. Energy systems will have to support new forms of manufacturing. Supply-chain disruptions may require rapid coordination between companies and public authorities. In such conditions, the institution that first detects a problem may not be the institution authorised to resolve its consequence.

This is why skills shortages should also be understood more broadly. Governments need technical specialists, but they also need institutional translators: people who can understand enough technology to question a recommendation, enough industry to recognise its economic consequences, and enough governance to know when a matter must move to another authority. A country can possess excellent engineers and still lose time if technical information cannot travel effectively through the decision structure.

The same applies to digitalisation. Technology can reduce processing time, improve access to information and automate routine decisions. But automation can also make institutional weakness less visible. A digital process may appear efficient until an exceptional case falls outside its assumptions. A decision-support system may produce an answer quickly while leaving unclear who can challenge it. A dashboard may show a problem instantly while the authority to respond remains several organisational steps away. Readiness begins where the normal process stops being sufficient.

For Hungary, this matters because the investment figures themselves suggest a transition toward more complex economic activity. HIPA’s 2025 results show significant electronics investment and record R&D activity alongside the country’s established automotive role. The more knowledge-intensive the investment becomes, the more investors depend on ecosystems rather than isolated incentives: skills, regulation, infrastructure, research links, data, cyber resilience and predictable administrative coordination. Institutional adaptability therefore becomes part of the environment in which investment decisions are made and expanded.

A practical government-readiness test would ask four questions. Can an institution detect a meaningful change early enough? Can verified information cross organisational boundaries without losing context? Can it reach the correct authority quickly enough to matter? And can the decision be revised when conditions change without the institution treating the original plan as something that must be defended? These questions are deliberately operational. They test whether transformation has reached the decision-making core of an institution rather than remaining at the level of strategy documents or technology procurement.

Hungary’s competitiveness debate should therefore not be reduced to whether the country can continue attracting capital. Its 2025 investment results show that it can attract major projects. A more forward-looking question is whether the institutional environment can adapt at the same speed as the technologies, industries and risks arriving with that capital. The distinction matters because investment attraction and investment retention are not identical achievements.

The global ministerial survey is useful precisely because it highlights the wider pressure: governments expect their responsibilities to expand while many are still adapting to change. The Government Readiness Gap is my proposed way of interpreting that tension, not a score assigned to Hungary or any other country. For an economy deeply connected to manufacturing and cross-border investment, closing that gap can become a competitive capability in its own right.

The countries that succeed in the next phase of economic competition may not simply be those with the most technology or the largest incentive packages. They may be those whose institutions can absorb change without losing accountability — and can move from verified information to an authorised decision before an opportunity, disruption or risk has already moved on.

Author bio: Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi (A.S. Alhebsi) is an Emirati Author and Researcher specializing in Security, Heritage, Risk Management, and Control Room Operations. ORCID: 0009-0007-1301-7927.

World.title: PM Magyar signals possible end to Hungary’s food margin caps
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Friday that the government should consider phasing out the country’s food retail margin caps, arguing that the measure is increasingly damaging farmers and small shops.

Speaking during a stop in Kisvárda as part of his nationwide tour, Magyar said the measure had originally been introduced by the previous government to slow food price increases, but had produced serious side effects across the agricultural and retail sectors.

According to the prime minister, low procurement prices are putting pressure on Hungarian producers, while large retail chains are increasingly turning to cheaper imported products in order to offset losses created by the margin restrictions.

He claimed that in Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg County alone, dozens of small shops had gone out of business as a result of the measure, MTI reported.

Small shops and farmers under pressure

Magyar said the previous government had tried to protect smaller retailers by exempting them from the margin cap, but argued that the policy ultimately strengthened larger chains, which were better able to absorb the losses.

He also criticised the effect of the measure on Hungarian agriculture, saying that artificially low procurement prices had made it harder for domestic producers to remain competitive.

Magyar said the government should now assess the future of the measure together with chambers of commerce, food retailers and other market participants.

His remarks come at a time when inflation in Hungary has fallen sharply compared with the levels seen during the previous government.

If you missed it: Danube water levels could fall way below 200-year low

Inflation has fallen sharply in 2026

Annual inflation stood at 1.7 percent in June, according to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office, while food prices were only 0.2 percent higher than a year earlier. Excluding catering services, food prices actually fell by 2.4 percent year on year.

Inflation eased further during the summer. The National Bank of Hungary reported that annual inflation fell to 1.2 percent in July and 1.3 percent in August, while food inflation also declined.

This has also strengthened the debate over whether extraordinary price-control measures are still necessary.

Central bank says removing the cap would not threaten price stability

The Hungarian National Bank has already signalled that the margin caps could be withdrawn without causing a major inflation shock.

In its June assessment, the Monetary Council said that even an immediate removal of the price margin caps would not push inflation above the central bank’s 3 percent target.

The central bank’s June Inflation Report also noted that the large international food retailers it examined were collectively loss-making in 2025, although the scale of losses had decreased compared with the previous year.

At the same time, the MNB has repeatedly stressed that the stronger forint, softer food price dynamics and weaker inflation expectations have all contributed to a more favourable inflation environment this year.

Magyar therefore argued that, with inflation now significantly lower than in previous years and several food prices already falling, the government should seriously consider gradually ending the margin cap regime.

World.title: Forint gets a boost from falling oil and a softer dollar
World.content:
The Hungarian forint strengthened against both the euro and the US dollar on Friday, supported by falling oil prices and weaker-than-expected US labour market data.

The Hungarian forint has enjoyed a stronger period since Hungary’s parliamentary election earlier this year, helped by improving investor sentiment, expectations surrounding EU funds and the government’s plans for eventual euro adoption. Friday brought another notable move, although the currency was far from stable throughout the session.

Friday brought another volatile session. The forint briefly strengthened below HUF 368 per euro and HUF 326 per dollar, before giving back part of those gains later in the day. The National Bank of Hungary’s official exchange rates for 2 October were HUF 367.87 per euro and HUF 326.94 per US dollar.

The National Bank of Hungary’s official exchange rates for 2 October were HUF 367.87 per euro and HUF 326.94 per US dollar.

Oil prices gave the forint a boost

Oil dropped by more than 3 percent during the day, with Brent crude falling back towards USD 100 per barrel after news that additional strategic fuel reserves could be released onto the market.

Lower oil prices are generally supportive for Hungary because the country is a major energy importer. A lower import bill can reduce pressure on the trade balance and ease some of the inflationary risks associated with expensive energy.

Portfolio noted that the combination of cheaper oil and changing expectations on US interest rates created a more favourable environment for the forint during Friday trading.

Weak US jobs report puts pressure on the dollar

The other major market-moving event came from the United States. The US economy added just 29,000 non-farm jobs in September, far below the roughly 90,000 expected by economists. August’s figure was also revised lower, while the unemployment rate rose to 4.2 percent.

The weaker-than-expected figures reduced expectations that the US Federal Reserve would raise interest rates again at its October meeting. The dollar weakened after the release, while stock markets moved higher.

A weaker dollar can provide support to emerging-market currencies such as the forint, particularly when global investors become more willing to take on risk.

If you missed it: Danube water levels could fall way below 200-year low

Global markets remain volatile

Friday’s move came after several difficult sessions for European currencies.

The US dollar has strengthened significantly in recent weeks, supported by high US Treasury yields and expectations that American monetary policy could remain tight for longer. The euro has also come under pressure amid fiscal and political concerns in several European countries.

At the same time, energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty continue to produce sharp movements across financial markets. For the forint, this means that favourable developments such as falling oil prices or a weaker dollar can provide short-term support, but international market sentiment remains an important source of volatility.
