From a BNPL app to a bank

BillEase – one of the better-known names in BNPL – has ridden that hype all the way into banking, with a former Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) deputy governor sitting on its board.

That would be Eduardo Bobier, who retired from the BSP in 2024 after nearly four decades at the central bank. Before leaving government, Bobier was also pulling in one of the heftiest paychecks as the central bank’s deputy governor for corporate services, earning P23.75 million in 2024 and ranking ninth among the country’s highest paid officials.

Quite the hire for a company best known, until fairly recently, for letting shoppers pay for purchases later.

BillEase acquired a majority stake in the Rural Bank of Sta. Maria in Ilocos Sur in November 2025, then formally renamed it BillEase Bank in September. Its newfound status as a rural bank gives BillEase a way to move beyond lending and into deposits, savings, and other banking services, although its in-app banking products are still being rolled out.

Atome has taken another route, putting BNPL onto a Mastercard that can be used online, in stores, or abroad. In an earlier Rappler interview, Atome Philippines country manager Chris Quiros said the card had proven particularly popular among young professionals, including gig and freelance workers and those just starting their careers, as well as consumers trying to manage monthly household budgets.

Shopee is in on it too. Its SPayLater service lets eligible users defer payment or split purchases into installments, putting BNPL a click away on the online shopping giant’s checkout page. And as BNPL has become harder to avoid, it has also become easier to trust.

BNPL feels less sketchy too

That may be another reason the product has taken off. Filipinos are not only more familiar with BNPL, they’re beginning to see it as safer too.

TransUnion found that 78% of respondents considered BNPL services safe in 2026, up six percentage points from a year earlier. It still trails traditional banks at 88% and digital banks at 84%, but it’s now viewed to be as safe as e-wallets. (READ: GCash prices Philippines’ biggest-ever IPO at P6.60 per share)

Online lending apps, meanwhile, did not get quite the same vote of confidence. Digital money lending services had the lowest perceived safety among the financial services TransUnion measured, at just 57%, while 31% of respondents described them as “risky,” the highest share among the credit products singled out for that label.

Faulhaber said fairness and transparency can make or break that trust. If consumers have problems with particular lenders, he said, that would “definitely dent” perceptions of those companies and could eventually hurt the reputation of the broader segment, although TransUnion’s survey has not yet picked up a wider deterioration in fintech sentiment.

All that said, these loan products have to be used responsibly. In other words, don’t forget the other half of the equation – actually paying later. As the credit bureau head put it, consumers shouldn’t treat available credit as “free money or an extra salary.” – Rappler.com

World.title: For advocates, CHED’s openness to lived names policy brings hope
World.content:
PRIDE. Members of the LGBTQ+ community gather at the University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City for the annual Pride March, June 28, 2025.

There is no blanket policy yet that would allow transgender and queer students to be recognized by their lived names during graduation rites

MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) has expressed openness to discussing a policy that would allow transgender and queer college students to use their lived names during graduation ceremonies, bringing hope to advocates.

Lived names are the chosen names of individuals used in daily life, different from their legal names.

“CHED actually does not see any legal impediment. CHED is, in fact, very open to a discussion regarding this,” Makati City 1st District Representative Monique Lagdameo said on September 23, during the plenary deliberations on the commission’s proposed 2027 budget in the House of Representatives.

Akbayan Representative Perci Cendaña brought the matter to the plenary after the Polytechnic University of the Philippines committed to allow its trans graduates to be recognized using their lived names during commencement exercises.

A similar policy was also implemented in other institutions such as the University of the Philippines, Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila, Philippine Normal University, De La Salle University, and Ateneo de Manila University, according to Cendaña.

However, Lagdameo, who spoke on behalf of CHED as its budget sponsor, noted that official records would still reflect the students’ names based on their birth certificates.

“I think maganda rin po itong way (this is a good way) for us to really navigate, how to literally open our minds and open our government into accepting and fully recognizing trans people and queer individuals with their lived name as well,” said Jira Samson, 22, who was not permitted to use her lived name during her graduation ceremony.

In an interview with Rappler, Samson, who recently graduated from Batangas State University, said the possible policy may benefit her “trans-siblings” who have just started their college journey.

Francheska Louise Chua, a 26-year-old medical student, said the openness to talks is a “big step forward” that could make a difference in the future.

But worries persist. “We are all scared, because as much as it is a conversation, hindi pa siya (it’s still not) undergoing implementation. So there’s still a big chance [a policy will not be issued],” she told Rappler.

“Obviously, there will be voters for yes or no, and it’s a long process…. This openness to conversations such as this is already a big step. So, as much as we are scared, we are still hopeful.”

Challenge for genuine inclusivity

Samson said university staff were sympathetic to her request to be recognized using her lived name during their graduation. But it was not granted as there was no specific CHED policy allowing for it to happen.

She noted that being recognized using one’s lived name is part of the gender-affirming and transitioning process of transgender and queer people, which must be respected.

Other than the recognition of lived names, Samson said dress code policies should be inclusive for LGBTQ+ students, and gender-responsive education must be strictly implemented.

“Ano ba naman po ‘yong i-recognize kami ng graduation, eh kung buong taon kami nakakaranas ng discrimination? Wala rin, ‘di ba?” she said. (What’s the use of being recognized by our lived name during graduation, if the whole year we experience discrimination? It would be useless, right?)

Recently, at Batangas State University, a transgender student was allegedly harassed by a security official as she was told to take off her bra in public because of dress code violations.

“It is just sad to note [that] such [a] university has not communicated this incident to CHED. But now that you have brought it to the attention of CHED, please know CHED will look into it and address the same,” Lagdameo told Cendaña during the September 23 budget deliberations.

CHED maintained it has existing memorandum orders recognizing the rights of students, as well as observing inclusivity in campuses.

Stalled legislation

Chua, who is a beauty queen, also conducts awareness campaigns about the LGBTQ+ community in Iloilo province.

But more than that, she believes the passage of a bill banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics (SOGIESC) “will really promote genuine inclusivity.”

In the 20th Congress, there are seven pending SOGIESC bills in the House, and two in the Senate.

The proposed measure has been languishing in Congress for over two decades already. (READ: Why is it taking so long to pass the SOGIESC bill?)

Ahead of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s fifth State of the Nation Address in July, his son, House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, said he would be “happy to pass it when one comes to light,” but added that consultations are needed on whether or not it should be a priority bill.

Play Video

Another pending proposal is the lived identities recognition bill, which seeks to allow transgender, intersex, and non-binary people to amend legal documents, specifically for name change and gender recognition, without going to court. – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Forgotten Island’: Filipino American stories are Filipino stories
World.content:
'Forgotten Island' is definitely an achievement worth celebrating, but Filipino storytelling does not begin nor does it end here. We have to take it upon ourselves to add to the narrative and tell the story of the Filipino as we know it.

October is Filipino American History Month.

And when award season rolls around in early 2027, I hope Filipinos back home, Filipino Americans, and others all around the world will be cheering for DreamWorks Animation’s Forgotten Island. It was a feat — and feast — for the senses. It was a fast-paced film, packed with ’90s nostalgia, provincial life, and filled to the brim with food, cultural nuance, music, and karaoke singing.

It captured everything that makes us Filipino: from our hospitality, love of family, and respect for elders to the underlying tension that comes with all that is deeply ingrained in the Filipino story.

As a Filipino American who lived in the Philippines for 10 years as a journalist — learning to speak Tagalog and improving my Cebuano to near fluency — I also noticed the Americanisms of the film, but I was not bothered by them, unlike some criticism I saw on social media. In my opinion, it did not diminish the Filipino-ness of the work.

When I used to go on Twitter, I would often see the “Filipino vs. Fil-Am” discourse, which inevitably surfaced again when this film came out, although to a lesser extent than I had seen in previous years.

But to me, nitpicking a character’s accent, scrutinizing the authenticity of folklore, or quibbling over “tayo na” vs. “tara na” misses the point entirely. (Both terms are accurate anyway, and anyone who thinks “tayo na” is wrong just needs to listen to more OPM.)

Because folklore isn’t even the most relatable part of the film to Filipinos.

The film’s true resonance lies in the parts of the story that take place outside of the mythical island of Nakali. It is Jo’s dad calling to say he isn’t taking her to America — a painful reality for millions of Filipino children left behind by migrating parents. And it is a story I sought to highlight when I was Rappler’s overseas Filipinos editor over a decade ago.

It is the immense pressure Raissa faces from her family to leave the Philippines because success so often dictates leaving home behind.

It is the overwhelming grief of leaving behind your friends and community once you board that flight, knowing that the move is likely for good.

An American colleague of mine was shocked to learn that the Philippines has entire government institutions built specifically to address overseas Filipino issues, driven by the country’s reliance on overseas remittances. Whether it intended to or not, this film may have been a first window, or conversation starter, for millions of non-Filipinos, who may not have realized there are countries like the Philippines where not being able to see your children grow up is just…life.

For me, the Filipino story here is not just one of creatures, spirits, magic. It is one of leaving, and returning — we even have a word for that: “balikbayan.” And, once you do leave, it is about never forgetting where you came from, navigating a new world that expects you to change, but never being able to fully leave behind the place and the people you came from. So you always return.

I won’t dig into the deep-seated disconnects between Filipinos in the motherland and those in the diaspora. Instead, I choose to focus on what binds us.

I don’t see the story of Filipinos in the Philippines and the story those abroad as two separate stories — they are one. A Filipino is a Filipino wherever they are — whether or not they speak fluent Filipino, and whether the last time they stepped foot home was a year ago, a decade ago, or 40 years ago. The through line of our collective story emanates from the cities and provinces, stretches out across oceans to the diaspora, and, for many born overseas like me, finds its way back again.

I understand the frustration or disappointment of viewers who may not see their exact representation as a Filipino in a single movie. But, for me, the amazing thing about living today is that we don’t have to put all our hopes for representation in one piece of work. Nor do we need Hollywood to tell or to validate our story.

While it is exciting to see our stories distributed to a massive global audience — and I will be loudly cheering for this film to win an Oscar — hopefully with all the other Filipinos. Respectfully, seeking validation from Hollywood is tired and overrated.

Yes, Forgotten Island is definitely an achievement worth celebrating, but Filipino storytelling does not begin nor does it end here.



If you want true representation, I say we have to take it upon ourselves to add to the narrative and tell the story of the Filipino as we know it. Write it. Speak it. Sing it. Paint it. Draw it. Tell it however you can — with whatever platforms you have. Neither Hollywood, nor any other big machine in the west, is the validator of our experiences as Filipinos. We are. – Rappler.com

Ryan Macasero is a reporter for the Mercury News, covering the city of San Jose, California. He is a former Rappler multimedia reporter and editor of the #BalikBayan section.

World.title: Carlos Yulo to get P4 million for golden double as medalists cash in on Asian Games success
World.content:
ALL HEART. Gold medalist Carlos Edriel Yulo of the Philippines celebrates after winning the men's vault final in the 2026 Asian Games.

Gymnastics star Carlos Yulo once again reaps the financial rewards of his brilliance after winning two of the Philippines' four gold medals in the 2026 Asian Games

MANILA, Philippines – Two years after receiving more than P100 million in incentives and rewards for his Olympic exploits, Carlos Yulo will benefit from another cash windfall after leading the Philippines’ campaign in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.

The artistic gymnastics star will get P4 million from the government following his golden runs in the men’s floor exercise and vault — the same events in which he won his two Olympic gold medals at the 2024 Paris Games.

Under Republic Act No. 10699 or the National Athletes and Coaches Benefits and Incentives Act, Yulo is entitled to P2 million for each of his two gold medals. Meanwhile, silver and bronze medalists stand to receive P1 million and P400,000, respectively.

Yulo joined an exclusive list of Filipino athletes who won multiple golds in a single Asian Games edition, becoming only the eighth member of the club.

Others who achieved the feat were swimmers Artemio Salamat (two in 1951), Jacinto Cayco (two in 1951), and Haydee Coloso (two in 1954), tennis player Raymundo Deyro (two in 1958), athletics icon Mona Sulaiman (three in 1962), bowling legend Bong Co (three in 1978 and two in 1986), and golfer Yuka Saso (two in 2018).

In ruling the Asian Games, Yulo completed his collection that also includes titles from the World Championships, Asian Championships, World Cup, and Southeast Asian Games.

Pole vaulter EJ Obiena and taekwondo jin Jeus Gabriel Derick Yape will receive P2 million each after delivering the Philippines’ two other gold medals.

Obiena stands to pocket more after breaking his own Asian Games mark by clearing 5.91 meters. Under RA 10699, athletes who surpass a Philippine record or any ranking in a measurable international sports competition are entitled to additional cash incentives, with the amount to be determined by the Philippine Sports Commission.

The only Asian to clear six meters, Obiena became only the fourth back-to-back men’s pole vault champion in the history of the continental showpiece.

Meanwhile, Yape will bag an additional P400,000 after also winning bronze in the men’s individual poomsae before striking gold in the mixed individual virtual taekwondo, an event that debuted at the Asian Games.

The victory made Yape the first-ever Filipino to capture a taekwondo gold in the quadrennial meet.

Aside from the four golds, the Philippines claimed nine silvers and 16 bronzes for a total of 29 medals — its most in six decades — as it replicated its 17th-place finish in the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China.

The incentives may ease the disappointment for athletes who fell short of gold as mixed martial artist Jean Claude Saclag, archer Amaya Amparo Cojuangco, taekwondo jins Juliana Mykhail Candelaria, Tachiana Mangin, and Kurt Barbosa, boxer Carlo Paalam, and jiu-jitsu athlete Alexandria Enriquez will earn P1 million each for their silvers.

In team events, the silver medalists in women’s 3×3 basketball — Kacey dela Rosa, Kennan Ka, Amyah Espanol, and Maria Pasilang — and women’s sepak takraw double — Jean Marie Sucalit, Abegail Sinogbuhan, and Nelly Jay Salon — will share the incentives provided under the law.

Teams with less than five members will equally split the rewards, while those part of squads with five or more participants will receive 25% of the incentives given to individual medal winners.

So Dela Rosa, Ka, Espanol, and Pasilang will get P250,000 each, while Sucalit, Sinogbuhan, and Salon will pocket P333,300.33 each.

Another big winner is weightlifter Albert Ian delos Santos, who will cash in more than P400,000 for his bronze after establishing new world junior and Asian junior records in the men’s 70kg class.

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] Mary Jane Veloso made us cry and realize why we want to be journalists
World.content:
Our reporters followed Mary Jane Veloso for 48 hours — from her release from prison to her homecoming in Nueva Ecija

September 25 was supposed to be a normal Friday work day, until President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced in an interview: he has pardoned former overseas worker Mary Jane Velasco.

I alerted my desk editors, broke the story, and triggered Rappler’s 48-hour coverage of Veloso’s release and freedom.

Hello! This is justice reporter Jairo Bolledo.

TEARS OF JOY. Mary Jane Veloso is emotional during a video call with her family before a press conference, prior to her repatriation to the Philippines, at the Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in Jakarta, Indonesia, December 17, 2024. Photo by Ajeng Dinar Ulfiana/Reuters

I broke down in tears as I was choosing a display photo for the story on Veloso’s pardon. I picked a 2024 photograph where she was crying and talking to her family via video call. It was taken on the day of her return to the Philippines.

I knew it was going to be a long weekend ahead of us. At any moment, Veloso would be released from the Correctional Institution for Women (CIW) in Mandaluyong City.

While waiting for updates in the afternoon, I wrote, shot, and edited a video explainer on Veloso’s case. In the early evening, as I headed for dinner with colleagues, a Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) official announced that Veloso would be released that night — at 8 pm.

Because all Rappler cars were out on other coverages, head of news operations Acor Arceo drove me and fellow reporter Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring to CIW. We arrived a few minutes before 8 pm.

There was a table set up inside the CIW’s holding area. The last time I was in that room was when I covered Veloso’s transfer from Indonesia to the Philippines.

At past 8:30 pm, a smiling Veloso — dressed in white shirt and gray sweatpants — entered the room. She was beaming the whole time. She was a different Veloso.

I learned about her case in 2015 as a freshman journalism student. I pictured her as a woman who was always worried and timid. She was on death row at the time.

Nine years later, in 2024, I covered her return as a reporter. I saw a happy Veloso. Then on September 25, 2026, I had the ultimate privilege of covering her release. I witnessed a truly free Mary Jane.

After a short press conference with BuCor Director General Gregorio Catapang Jr., Veloso stayed with her lawyers from the National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers and advocates from Migrante International, who had seen her case through.

I approached the groups and asked if I could get 15 minutes of Veloso’s time for a Rappler Talk interview. The groups said yes. Veloso enthusiastically accepted my offer. It was her first exclusive and sit-down interview since her pardon.

Play Video

I talked to Veloso as if we were long-time acquaintances. I held back tears while listening to her story about her life in prison, her plans for her family, and how she feels about the people who had wronged her.

WITH MARY JANE. A photo with Mary Jane Veloso after the Rappler Talk interview on September 25, 2026.



That was one of the most important interviews I had ever done in my career. It was a coverage of a lifetime.

Afterwards, I tried shaking Veloso’s hands, but she hugged me instead. She is warm. She is grateful. She still is a cheerful person after all the hurdles she had faced.

We stayed in CIW to cover her reunion with family. We followed the family until their transfer from CIW to a hotel in Manila in the early hours of September 26.

Veloso’s story is one of those that makes us realize why we do what we do. Why we chose journalism. Why we chose public service.

It’s not every day that we win in our crusade for a better world or against the atrocities. Veloso’s freedom after 16 years is a win for everyone — for herself, her family, and for all the people who have been helping her in the last 16 years.

RAPPLER TEAM FOR VELOSO. Production specialist Jon Vic Digma (most left); assistant production specialist and driver Ramil Cedeño (upper center); reporter Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring (lower center); and Jairo Bolledo (most right).

That’s why Veloso’s journey back home to Nueva Ecija was also part of the wins that must be documented.

Hi! Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring here. I report about social issues, including migration and overseas Filipino workers (OFWs).

I met Mary Jane Veloso again at the Siena College Chapel in Quezon City at 9:40 am on Saturday, September 26. She was attending Mass — her first activity as a free woman. While waiting for the Mass, I asked her how she slept after her release from the CIW.

“Hindi po ako makatulog. Ito po, namamaga ang mata ko. Pasens’ya na po, siguro masyado akong nao-overwhelm sa pamilya, sa lahat ng sumusuporta,” she said. (I cannot sleep. Look, that’s why I have puffy eyes. I’m sorry, maybe I’m too overwhelmed with my family and all those who are supporting me.)

Later, I would learn from her sister, Maritess Laurente, that Veloso gets carsick easily. It was Darling Cando, the closest sibling to Veloso, who made sure that they would bring Bonamine for her.

It was surreal for me that Veloso decided to attend Mass and hold a news conference first before traveling for hours to her home province with lack of sleep. I thought, her will and determination to give thanks to God and supporters were unmatched.

I interviewed her siblings to learn more about the family she came from. And this is what I saw: love was patient and overflowing between them.

At 3 pm, the Veloso family began their trip to Nueva Ecija. Our team went ahead of them.

HOMECOMING. The family of Mary Jane Veloso set up a simple celebration for the return of the former overseas Filipino worker in General Mamerto Natividad, Nueva Ecija, on September 26, 2026. Photo by Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring/Rappler

Upon arriving in General Mamerto Natividad town, we saw some tables and chairs set up. There were homecoming banners, small balloons, and a crowd of relatives and neighbors. She arrived — finally home — at 5:43 pm.

I knew I was there to cover. But I also remember asking myself: Why, really, am I here?

The answer came during their dinner. Veloso, happily eating her requested pinakbet and inihaw na tilapia, was surrounded by her family. The Veloso family, complete. I took a video of that moment, not as a way of intruding into their family, but to help announce that Mary Jane was home at last and will be starting life anew.

This, ultimately, is the journalism I want to keep doing: the one that puts the spotlight on ordinary families, and where they are in the policies and systems that the powerful create for them.

Like Mary Jane Veloso, many Filipinos may also be risking everything to provide for their families. And they are taken advantage of because of that vulnerability. Her documented cautionary tale must push the government to better protect our countrymen.

That’s where journalism helps. And you, too, join us in this mission when you decide to support the journalism that Rappler does.

VELOSO BACK HOME. Rappler reporter Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring recaps the coverage of Mary Jane Veloso’s trip back home to General Mamerto Natividad, Nueva Ecija, on September 26, 2026. Photo by Jon Vic Digma/Rappler

– Rappler.com

World.title: New Comic Book Explores Parallels Between George Washington and Abylai Khan in Story of Leadership
World.content:
ASTANA – The parallel lives of George Washington and Abylai Khan, two leaders who lived in the same era but on opposite sides of the world, are explored in “When Eagles Soar,” a new bilingual comic book written by Shymkent-based author Bek-Ata Daniyal and illustrated by Astana-based artist Abylay Karin.

The comic book brings together the first U.S. president and the Kazakh ruler through their experiences as military leaders and political figures who sought to unite their people during periods of major change. Their stories highlight the challenges they faced, the decisions they made and the legacies they left for their countries.

“When Eagles Soar,” which was presented on Sept. 29 at the American Centers in Astana and Shymkent, is available in English and Kazakh.

For Daniyal, the similarities between the two historical figures make the story particularly compelling.

“Both comics are historical and educational, but the second comic, ‘When Eagles Soar,’ seems the most fascinating to me because it shows how similar the lives of these two great rulers and contemporaries were. The project shows what decisions Abylai Khan and George Washington made for the benefit of their countries,” Daniyal told The Astana Times.

“When Eagles Soar” is the second installment in a comic book series marking the 250th anniversary of U.S. independence. It follows the debut e-comic, “The Long Journey to Liberty,” also created by Daniyal and Karin.

Daniyal, who holds a degree in film and television, said the decision to use comics as a storytelling format was driven by their ability to combine historical information with visual storytelling and reach younger audiences.

“Comics as a form of storytelling are not new. They are widely used in the United States, Europe, Korea, Japan and other countries through stories in pictures. Information is better perceived by young people in this format, and many adults also enjoy it. Information is conveyed not only through text but also through visual perception,” said Daniyal.

For Daniyal, the visual element is an important part of making historical narratives accessible without reducing their educational purpose. The format allows readers to follow historical events through both dialogue and imagery.

The two projects were developed through close collaboration between Daniyal and Karin. Daniyal worked on the scripts and proposed ideas for the characters and scenes, while Karin developed the visual interpretation.

“I proposed the images and wrote the script, but our artist, Abylay Karin, found wonderful visual solutions and made the comics colorful,” Daniyal said.

Daniyal said he grew up reading Marvel and DC comics and watching Western animation. His interest in American culture was strengthened through visits to his brother in the United States.

Karin, an artist from Astana, is the creator of “Alterno,” a comic sold through stores across Kazakhstan. Alongside illustration, he studies programming and is interested in game development and entertainment design.

The project was written by Ali Leilich, a former press and public affairs officer at the U.S. Embassy in Astana. The bilingual publication was developed as part of cultural and educational activities marking the 250th anniversary of U.S. independence.

“Comic books are a universal language for connecting young audiences with history. Through the remarkably parallel lives of George Washington and Abylai Khan, we hope readers in Kazakhstan see how these two men, alive at the same time in history yet from different parts of the world, wrestled with the same challenges as boys, then gaining responsibilities as young soldiers, who then became military leaders and political unifiers and true statesmen, each leading their people independence,” said Ali Lejlic.

A digital edition is available free of charge through the U.S. Embassy in Kazakhstan’s Instagram account.

World.title: Caves, DNA and Metal Trace Kazakhstan’s Ancient Past
World.content:
ASTANA — Cave sediments may help identify ancient human populations in Kazakhstan even where no skeletal remains survive, as new methods allow archaeologists to reconstruct how people lived and adapted to environmental change tens of thousands of years ago.

Researchers are turning their attention to Tuttybulaq 1 and Aqtogai, two cave sites in the Karatau range of southern Kazakhstan.

“Our work will aim to expand the existing test excavations and determine the palaeoecological setting and human adaptations to the climatic instabilities,” Abay Namen, a postdoctoral researcher at Nazarbayev University’s School of Sciences and Humanities, told The Astana Times during an archaeological symposium in Astana on Sept. 24-25.

Caves can preserve evidence that is often lost at exposed archaeological sites. Organic material is more likely to survive in enclosed caves and rock shelters, while ancient DNA can remain in sediment even when human bones are absent. This can help researchers determine which hominins – modern humans or their extinct relatives – once occupied a site.

Namen’s research combines cave excavations in southern Kazakhstan with work at open-air sites in the Almaty Region in collaboration with the National Museum of Kazakhstan and New York University. The project examines human behavior and adaptation during the last glacial cycle, approximately 115,000 to 11,700 years ago.

The research was among the topics discussed at the symposium, organized by the Margulan Institute of Archaeology and Nazarbayev University to mark the institute’s 35th anniversary. More than 150 researchers from Kazakhstan and abroad participated in the event.

Tracing Kazakhstan’s earliest inhabitants

The country has accumulated substantial Stone Age material since the early 1990s, when a major Kazakh-Russian program began investigating Paleolithic sites across Kazakhstan. Over the past 10 to 15 years, new dating methods have allowed archaeologists to establish more precise timelines for many of those discoveries.

Talgat Mamirov of the Margulan Institute of Archaeology pointed to a series of stratified Upper Paleolithic sites in southern and southeastern Kazakhstan, including Rakhat, Uzynagash and Maibulak.

“It was the study of these sites that made it possible to understand the processes of settlement of the territory of Kazakhstan by modern humans within the period of 40,000-30,000 years ago,” Mamirov told The Astana Times.

“In collaboration with researchers from other countries, particularly the Institute of Archaeology of the Russian Academy of Sciences, a new archaeological culture – the Tian Shan Aurignacian – was identified in Zhetysu for the Upper Paleolithic. Over the past 10 to 15 years, there has been a qualitative leap in identifying and interpreting this material,” he said.

Elsewhere, researchers have dated six cultural layers at Shiderty-3 in northeastern Kazakhstan, providing a reference point for comparing archaeological material from neighboring areas. Mamirov also cited Kukentau as Kazakhstan’s earliest known Neolithic burial.

Caves could now fill further gaps in that record. While researchers had studied individual cave sites before, Mamirov said research has become more systematic, with dozens of larger sites identified for further investigation.

“Caves represent a localized archaeological source for obtaining information about the life, activities and everyday existence of ancient people. There, we can obtain radiocarbon dates and conduct an entire range of interdisciplinary studies, including identifying traces of DNA and studying how deposits accumulated, fauna, spores and pollen to reconstruct the climate. Human remains can also be found there,” he explained.

The symposium brought Kazakh researchers together with archaeologists studying caves in Azerbaijan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Uzbekistan, Russia and France, including specialists with experience at Denisova Cave in Russia’s Altai region and Arago Cave in France.

The exchange could also lead to new fieldwork. Mamirov said a potential Kazakh-French archaeological mission involving the Margulan Institute and France’s National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS) could search for and study cave sites in Kazakhstan dating from the Stone Age through the Bronze Age.

New tools reveal more from old evidence

Methods beyond traditional excavation increasingly support the search for early human traces. Archaeologists now combine fieldwork with ancient DNA analysis, studies of plant and animal remains, remote sensing and digital documentation.

LiDAR, for example, uses laser pulses to map terrain and can reveal archaeological features that are difficult to detect from the ground. Three-dimensional scanning creates detailed digital models of caves and artifacts, while microscopic analysis can identify traces left by stone-tool use.

Mamirov said researchers working with international specialists have found organic residues on some stone artifacts, helping identify tools that were once parts of more complex, composite implements.

These methods are being applied well beyond the Stone Age. Data presented by Margulan Institute Director General Akan Ongaruly show that approximately 800 samples have been prepared for paleogenetic analysis, while zooarchaeological collections from 123 sites are being used to study animal use and changes in ancient economies.

The institute also produced more than 150 3D scans in 2024 and has digitized approximately 3,800 archaeological reports, creating material that can be revisited as research methods develop.

From Bronze Age metal to medieval cities

Scientific analysis is also providing new details about Kazakhstan’s Bronze Age metallurgy.

According to Ongaruly, research at Taldysai, Atasu, Myrzhyk and Akmaya has helped reconstruct how ancient communities obtained raw materials, smelted ore and processed metal. At Taldysai, near Zhezkazgan in the Ulytau Region, researchers identified production of pure and arsenical copper, while Akmaya in central Kazakhstan contains a metallurgical complex with furnaces and chimneys representing a full production cycle.

“These data allow us to compare the technological traditions of individual centers and determine their place in Eurasian metallurgy,” said Ongaruly.

“The scientific significance of these results lies in the opportunity to study economic strategies and cultural differences within specific natural environments. The next step is to align regional chronologies, conduct serial dating and compare technological data,” he said.

Evidence from later periods broadens the picture further.

According to Ongaruly, finds from Berel in the East Kazakhstan Region, Shilikti in the Abai Region and Taldy-2 in the Karagandy Region have expanded knowledge of early nomadic elites, art and burial practices. At Berel, preserved organic material has revealed techniques for working with wood, felt and leather.

Settlement archaeology provides evidence of another side of Saka life. Research at Tushai and Talgar-3 in southeastern Kazakhstan has documented sedentary life, agriculture and crafts, while finds at Chirik-Rabat in the Kyzylorda Region include evidence of barley and millet cultivation, textile production and jewelry making.

The archaeological record later expands to major medieval urban centers. Ongaruly noted that long-term research at Otyrar and Sauran in the Turkistan Region, Syganak in the Kyzylorda Region, Taraz in the Zhambyl Region and Talgar in the Almaty Region has refined knowledge of city planning, irrigation, crafts, monetary circulation and urban chronology.

Connecting 35 years of discoveries

As research produces more archaeological material and new ways to analyze it, preserving and connecting that evidence has become another priority.

Ongaruly outlined plans for a national archaeological register and compatible catalogs linking archaeological sites with field reports and collections. A national archaeological service and repository are also being considered to improve the preservation, storage and future study of archaeological material.

Another long-term initiative is the multi-volume academic publication “Archaeology of Kazakhstan.” Ongaruly said its preparation would involve reviewing archaeological sources and coordinating terminology, regional chronologies and maps.

The institute is also developing fields such as archaeogenetics, landscape archaeology, bioarchaeology, paleoanthropology and experimental and virtual archaeology, alongside training specialists in archaeobotany, archaeometallurgy, traceology, conservation and other areas.

World.title: First Przewalski’s Horse Foals Born in Kazakhstan Named Botai and Tumar
World.content:
ASTANA – The first Przewalski’s horse foals born in Kazakhstan have been named Botai and Tumar, marking a new stage in the country’s efforts to restore the endangered species to its historical habitat.

The foals were born this summer at the Alibi Reintroduction Center in the Altyn Dala State Nature Reserve in the Kostanai Region, reported the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources. Their mothers, Tessa and Umbra, arrived in Kazakhstan from Berlin’s Tierpark in 2024 as part of an international conservation programme.

The program entered a new stage in 2026 with the arrival of additional horses, while specialists continued preparing earlier arrivals for release into the wild.

The names Botai and Tumar reflect Kazakhstan’s cultural and historical heritage. Botai refers to the ancient Botai culture of northern Kazakhstan, associated with some of the earliest archaeological evidence of horse domestication. Tumar is a traditional Kazakh name meaning an amulet or protective talisman.

The birth of the foals is particularly significant for the reintroduction program because it demonstrates that the horses brought from Europe are adapting to Kazakhstan’s natural conditions and beginning to reproduce. Earlier this month, the birth of the second foal at the same center was reported after the first foal was born on Aug. 22.

Przewalski’s horse, also known as kerqulan or kertaqy in Kazakh, is considered the last surviving wild horse species. The species disappeared from the wild during the 20th century but survived through captive breeding programs.

Kazakhstan began its current reintroduction program in 2024, when the first seven horses arrived from Prague Zoo. Another seven were brought in 2025, followed by eight more in 2026. The initiative involves the Committee of Forestry and Wildlife, the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, European zoos and conservation organizations.

The animals spend an adaptation period at the reintroduction center before being released into the reserve. Specialists monitor their health, behaviour and movements, with GPS collars used for some animals after release.

The Altyn Dala reserve was selected for the program because of its extensive steppe landscape, pasture and water resources. The horses are expected to play an ecological role as large grazers, contributing to natural vegetation cycles and the wider steppe ecosystem.

The program aims to establish a sustainable population of Przewalski’s horses in Kazakhstan, with plans to bring approximately 40 animals to the country by 2029.

The birth of Botai and Tumar adds a new dimension to the project, shifting its focus from simply bringing the species back to Kazakhstan toward establishing a population capable of reproducing and eventually surviving in the wild.

World.title: Tokayev Highlights AI’s Potential to Transform Creative Industries at Astana AI Film Festival
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence in cinema and the creative industries, while stressing the importance of responsible AI development and safety. He made the remarks at the opening of the first international Astana AI Film Festival on Oct. 2.

Addressing the festival, Tokayev described it as a unique platform bringing together creative and innovative talents from around the world.

“Artificial intelligence is bringing fundamental changes to all areas of the global economy. In short, technological progress has acquired a truly global scale,” he said.

New opportunities for creators

Tokayev said the festival reflects the rapid development of Kazakhstan’s creative industries and noted that AI is lowering barriers to film production.

“Today, even small creative teams can compete successfully with major studios. Creative people and film crews no longer need to knock on the doors of production companies or look for sponsors to make films. Access to the market has become significantly easier,” he said.

He added that AI could become an important tool for creative professionals.

“Of course, artificial intelligence will not replace the spark of the Creator, but it can become an indispensable tool for everyone who has chosen creativity as their path in life,” Tokayev said.

Responsible use of AI

President Tokayev said that rapid technological development must be accompanied by common rules for safe and responsible AI use.

“We must give the highest priority to safety and develop common rules of the game for the responsible development and use of artificial intelligence to ensure a safe future for the younger generation,” he said.

More than 8,000 applications from 125 countries were submitted for the festival, including entries from Brazil, China, France, India, Japan, South Korea, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Tokayev said the festival would create opportunities for international exchange and future joint projects in the creative industries.

World.title: Beyond ChatGPT: What Could AI Mean for Kazakhstan’s Creative Industries?
World.content:
ASTANA – Artificial intelligence is increasingly shifting beyond text and image generation into art, design and immersive digital experiences. For Kazakhstan, this development presents an opportunity to adopt new technologies, but also rethink the role of creativity in the country’s emerging digital economy.

Nicola Plant, an artist, researcher and lecturer at the Creative Computing Institute (CCI) at the University of the Arts London (UAL) in the United Kingdom (UK), delivered a lecture on AI, creative computing and arts in Astana on Sept. 30. The event formed part of AI Month 2026 and AI & Digital Bridge 2026.

According to Aika Alemi, founder and director of Born Nomad, one of the main challenges for Kazakhstan and other countries in the region is the perception that art is primarily entertainment rather than a business.

“Creative computing and creative AI technologies have huge potential, and it’s still untapped,” Alemi said.

She also noted that technology and creativity increasingly operate together. Digital products, augmented reality and immersive technologies rely on creative decisions involving design, color, visual language and user experience.

“We just need to recognize art as the next frontier of making money and as the space where creativity and genuine human innovation come together,” Alemi said.

Creativity behind the technology

The growing use of AI makes this connection more visible. Generative AI can support emerging artists and designers as they experiment with new forms of visuals and digital expression. Technologies such as virtual reality, motion capture and interactive installations also create new ways for audiences to understand the art.

Creative computing brings these fields together by combining technology, coding, design and artistic practices.

For Alemi, recognizing the economic value of creativity is essential for developing the industry. She pointed to the UK’s creative industries as an example of how creativity can contribute to the wider economy when it receives recognition as an economic activity rather than just entertainment.

“Creativity is the engine and it’s the source of everything that’s happening in technology,” she mentioned.

For Kazakhstan, this approach could create new opportunities across digital media, gaming, design, film and immersive technologies. It could also create a demand for a workforce that combines technological knowledge with creative skills.

What Kazakhstan can bring to creative AI

The development of creative AI also raises questions about cultural representation in technology.

Nicola Plant said that technology has historically developed largely from Western perspectives, including major technology companies and the datasets used to train AI systems. She highlighted the importance of giving other cultures and communities a greater role in shaping digital tools.

“It’s really important for cultures around the world, including Kazakhstan and Central Asia, to have their voices heard in the way that tools are built and who they are for,” Plant said.

The issue is particularly relevant to creative AI, where training data can influence the images, stories and other content generated by AI systems. Greater participation from different cultural communities could contribute to technologies that better reflect a wider range of perspectives.

For Kazakhstan, this means participation in creative AI does not have to be limited to adopting technologies developed elsewhere. Local artists, designers, researchers and developers can contribute their cultural knowledge and perspectives to the development and use of new tools.

Building technology and questioning it

Plant also emphasized the importance of combining technological development with critical thinking.

“You have to be critiquing the technology at the same time as making it,” she said, explaining that developers should consider how technologies are built, who they influence and who they could potentially harm.

The need to balance technological progress with responsible development was also highlighted at AI&Digital Bridge 2026, where President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for responsible AI development.

This approach places creative computing at the intersection of technology, culture and human experience. It also broadens the discussion around AI development beyond creating increasingly advanced tools to questions about how those tools should be designed and used.

Kazakhstan’s efforts to build a stronger AI ecosystem have also involved engagement with major global technology companies, including NVIDIA.

As Kazakhstan continues to develop its AI ecosystem, developing creative industries will be an important part of that progress. Creativity can turn technology into new ideas and products, while also creating opportunities for filmmakers, artists and designers. At the same time, a stronger creative sector can help Kazakhstan bring its own culture and perspective into the global development of AI.

World.title: Astana as Bridge: From Financial Centre to Family Office and Private-Capital Hub
World.content:
Central Asia is entering a new phase of economic development. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are attracting rising international investment, regional capital markets are deepening, entrepreneurial wealth is accumulating, and a new generation of business owners is beginning to think seriously about succession, diversification and the preservation of family wealth.

Yet one part of the region’s financial architecture remains underdeveloped. Central Asia has no natural home for private capital and family offices. Astana has an opportunity to change that.

Through the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), Kazakhstan has already built much of the institutional architecture an internationally credible financial Centre requires: an English-law framework, an exchange in AIX, an independent court and regulator. The next step should be more ambitious — transforming Astana from a financial jurisdiction into the capital-allocation and family-wealth Centre of Central Asia.

This would not require Astana to become another Singapore, Switzerland or Dubai. Attempting to imitate those centers would probably be a mistake.

Ecosystems, not buildings

Successful financial centers are ultimately ecosystems rather than towers, tax regimes or regulatory frameworks. A wealthy family does not establish a family office because a jurisdiction offers an attractive license. It needs private banks, investment managers, lawyers, accountants, trustees, tax advisers, fund administrators, private-equity specialists and succession advisers. Most importantly, it needs other families and investors nearby. That is the network effect which distinguishes established centers, and it is why Singapore’s position rests on far more than a single regulatory initiative, and Switzerland’s on far more than its private banks.

Astana must think in the same terms. The AIFC’s dedicated family-office framework was an important move, but regulation is the beginning of a strategy rather than its conclusion. The bigger question is what grows around those family offices.

One logical next step would be an AIFC Family Wealth and Private Capital Centre whose purpose extends well beyond licensing — bringing family offices, private banks, asset managers, lawyers, trustees, private-equity and venture managers and family-governance specialists under a recognizable institutional umbrella.

Regional, not national

Astana should resist positioning itself as Kazakhstan’s family-office Centre. The far more powerful proposition is Astana as Central Asia’s international wealth-management jurisdiction, with an addressable market extending to entrepreneurs and families in Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, and potentially the Caucasus and Mongolia.

Many wealthy Central Asian families currently look to Zurich, London, Singapore or Dubai for private banking, custody and wealth structuring. There is nothing wrong with that; those centers hold expertise accumulated over generations. Astana does not need to replace them. It can connect them to Central Asia. An AIFC Singapore corridor is a tangible and realistic proposition.

A family office might be established in the AIFC while maintaining custody relationships with Swiss, Singaporean or Emirati banks and investing through international managers. The model becomes: Central Asian family → Astana family office → global financial system. Astana becomes the bridge rather than attempting to recreate the entire international financial system domestically.

Multi-family offices deserve particular attention. Not every wealthy family wants the cost and complexity of its own investment institution. A capable MFO can provide several families with investment advice, consolidated reporting, asset allocation, manager selection, governance support and succession coordination — a model well suited to a region where large private fortunes are numerous but individually below the scale that justifies a standalone office. Ten or twenty credible platforms would bring with them lawyers, auditors, administrators and investment professionals.

Where the real advantage lies

Astana is unlikely to compete with Switzerland in private banking or Singapore in global portfolio management. It does not need to. Its competitive advantage lies closer to home, in Central Asian private markets.

This is the part of the proposition no other center can replicate. Infrastructure, logistics, mining and metals processing, agriculture, energy transition and a young technology sector, across a market of some 80 million people, all require capital the region’s banks alone cannot supply. International investors seeking that exposure need local partners, local diligence and local judgement. A family office in Zurich cannot originate a Kyrgyz hydro deal or a Tashkent logistics platform; an Astana-based one can. Proximity to deal flow, not proximity to custody, is the genuine edge. So was it in Singapore and so could it be in Astana with the right strategic action plan.

Private banking should still form part of the strategy, but in a realistic form. International private banks could establish Central Asian advisory desks in Astana without full booking centers: assets custodied in Switzerland, Singapore or the UAE, while relationship managers and family-office specialists sit in Astana. Rather than competing with global custody centers, Kazakhstan integrates itself into their networks.

The academic foundation

Every serious financial center rests on an educational base, and this is the element most easily overlooked because its returns arrive a decade late. Singapore’s rise as a wealth-management hub was underwritten by sustained investment in its universities and by the deliberate importation of foreign faculty and curricula. Switzerland’s private-banking tradition is sustained by a dense network of institutes, certification bodies and executive programs that continuously replenish its talent pool. Neither position was built on regulation alone.

A joint AIFC–Nazarbayev University center for private capital and family enterprise — combining academic research, executive education and practitioner teaching — would give the jurisdiction something more durable than a licensing regime.

The AIFC’s own professional training capability should be broadened accordingly. Its existing focus on financial regulation and market infrastructure needs to be extended into family-office advisory, trust and succession law, private-markets investing, compliance, philanthropy, impact investing, digital assets and the application of artificial intelligence to portfolio and risk management.

Research deserves equal weight. Reliable data on Central Asian private wealth, family-business ownership structures and regional private-market returns barely exists, and its absence is itself a barrier to investment. An annual Central Asia Family Wealth Report, produced to academic standards, would give international allocators something to reference and would establish Astana as the authority on its own market — a role London, Zurich and Singapore each play for their regions.

Finally, a Central Asia NextGen Family Enterprise Program could bring together young members of prominent business families from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and neighboring economies for a structured curriculum in governance, investment and philanthropy. Its immediate financial impact would be hard to measure. Its long-term impact could be considerable: the relationships formed in such programs tend to determine, twenty years later, where a generation chooses to domicile its capital.

Bringing it together

Astana should also create a flagship gathering built specifically around private capital — a Central Asia Family Capital Summit of perhaps 300 to 500 principals, CIOs, private bankers, sovereign funds and entrepreneurs. Its value would come from selectivity rather than scale.

Family offices become anchor investors around which entire ecosystems form. They allocate to private equity and venture capital, invest alongside sovereign funds, finance entrepreneurs and employ professionals. Singapore can remain Asia’s portfolio-management center; Switzerland can remain synonymous with wealth preservation; Dubai can, thanks to Emirates airlines, remain a global crossroads. Astana should establish a category of its own to make the central Asian family office GREAT again.

The question is no longer how many family offices Astana can register. It is whether Astana can become the place where Central Asia’s private capital comes together.

The author is Rainer Michael Preiss, Partner and Portfolio Strategist, DAS Family Office.

World.title: Kazakhstan Commemorates 85 Years of Bakhytzhan Momyshuly’s Literary Legacy
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan marks the 85th anniversary of Bakhytzhan Momyshuly, a prominent writer and translator, whose literary work preserved the stories of prominent Kazakh figures and explored themes of memory, resilience and spiritual strength.

The son of legendary Kazakh war hero, Panfilov Guards officer, and writer Bauyrzhan Momyshuly, he spent much of his life in the shadow of a celebrated father. Yet he developed a literary voice of his own, leaving behind works that combined personal memory with the stories of people and a country undergoing profound change.

Bakhytzhan Momyshuly was Born Oct. 3, 1941, in Almaty. His childhood was marked by long periods of separation from his father, who served in the military and later taught at military academies in Russia and Cuba. His mother died when he was young.

As a child, Momyshuly underwent several operations on his hip following complications from polio. Despite these challenges, he completed secondary school and graduated from the Almaty Institute of Foreign Languages, now the Ablai Khan Kazakh University of International Relations and World Languages.

His father sent him to the family’s village in the Zhambyl Region during summer vacations so that he could learn the Kazakh language and traditions.

Momyshuly later recalled that he had once felt embarrassed when his classmates spent their summers at resorts or abroad, while he worked in the village and helped prepare hay for the winter. With time, however, he came to see his father’s decision differently.

“I later realized that my father was wise. He wanted his son to understand where he came from and who his relatives were. Only with the years did I understand that the Kazakh village became the place where I recognized my roots and absorbed a love for my homeland,” Momyshuly recalled.

From translation to literature

Literature became the defining pursuit of Momyshuly’s life. He began his career as a literary translator, bringing the works of leading Kazakh writers to Russian-speaking readers.

Over the years, he translated works by Sherkhan Murtaza, Zhaisanbek Moldagaliyev, Oralkhan Bokey, Kemel Tokayev, Kaldarbek Naimanbayev, Bek Toguspayev, Madi Aimbetov, Kakimzhan Kazybayev, Shaim Shavayev and others.

His professional path included work as a proofreader at the “Novaya Zhizn” newspaper in the Zhambyl Region, a translator at the “Znamya Truda” regional newspaper and a literary staff member at “Leninskaya Smena.” He later became an editor at the “Zhazushy” publishing house in Almaty.

Momyshuly began publishing his own fiction alongside his translation work. He published his first collection of short stories, “Good Bridges,” in 1971. It was followed by “Scorching Stones” in 1974, “Transparent Ice” in 1976, “Quiet Voices” in 1978, “I Am Still a Child” in 1982 and “Giant Children” in 1988.

Among his best-known works is “Sons of the Great Wolf,” a collection of stories about his father, Bauyrzhan Momyshuly, and other prominent figures, including Dinmukhamed Kunayev, Zeynolla Kabdolov, and Sherkhan Murtaza. His other books include “The Wolf’s Heart,” “Refraction of Light,” “The Legend of the Princes of Time,” “The Appearance of the Blue Tauyeke,” “A Bird’s Trail in the Sky” and “Voices of the Children of the Sun,” about conductor Tolepbergen Abdrashev.

His works often focused on real people and explored questions of truth, spirituality and human resilience during periods of profound change. His portrayal of people who endured hardship without losing their sense of purpose became a defining feature of Momyshuly’s literary legacy.

He was elected several times to the governing board of the Union of Writers of Kazakhstan. For his contribution to Kazakh culture and literature, he received several government medals, the Order of Kurmet and a special award from the Union of Writers of Kazakhstan.

A father’s lasting influence

Bauyrzhan Momyshuly remained an important figure throughout his son’s life. The time they spent together was brief, but Bakhytzhan later described it as an invaluable education in life and wisdom.

Recalling their conversations, Momyshuly said that as a child he was often eager to run outside and play with other children, but his father would sometimes stop him, sit him down and tell him stories and parables.

One phrase stayed with him for decades: “You are running away from me for nothing. Wherever you go, I will meet you.”

“After my father’s death, I came to understand the meaning of those words. Wherever I traveled, from Moscow and Volokolamsk to Tashkent, Bishkek or various parts of Kazakhstan, I continued to encounter people who had fought alongside my father, known him or read his books. My father continued to “meet” me through those people and through the enduring legacy of his work,” Momyshuly said.

Momyshuly died in 2012 at age 71. In 2018, a memorial plaque was installed on the facade of the Almaty house where he and his family lived from 1986 to 2012, at the intersection of Kaldayakov and Gogol streets.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Investment, Raw Materials and Transport Partnerships
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles on Kazakhstan featured in international media worldwide this week. This week’s foreign media digest covers new investment in Kazakhstan’s manufacturing sector, growing Kazakhstan-Germany cooperation on raw materials and trade routes, the country’s call for stronger multilateral cooperation, and more.

Carlsberg Kazakhstan opens $344 million beverage plant, positioning Kazakhstan as a regional manufacturing and supply hub for Central Asia

Carlsberg Kazakhstan officially opened a new $344 million beverage production facility in the Almaty Region, one of the largest recent investments in Kazakhstan’s food and beverage manufacturing sector. The plant will expand local production for Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan and strengthen Kazakhstan’s role as a regional manufacturing and supply hub for Central Asia, while advancing the strategic partnership between Carlsberg Group and PepsiCo, reported the company’s press service on Oct. 1.

The facility will manufacture under license PepsiCo beverage brands for consumers and customers in Kazakhstan and the Kyrgyz Republic. Kazakhstan will serve as the primary market, while the plant will also supply products to the Kyrgyz Republic.

The $344 million investment represents a significant inflow of foreign direct investment into Kazakhstan’s manufacturing sector and reflects the long-term confidence of Carlsberg Group and PepsiCo in the country’s economic outlook, workforce and consumer market. It also highlights the role of international partnerships in bringing capital, technology and global operating expertise into Kazakhstan. The presence of Denmark’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Lars Løkke Rasmussen, alongside representatives of Kazakhstan’s national ministries, the Akimat of Almaty Region, the diplomatic community, Carlsberg Group and PepsiCo underscored the project’s importance to commercial ties between Kazakhstan and Denmark.

Kazakhstan calls for new era of practical multilateralism as global trust comes under strain

EU Reporter published an article on Sept. 28 about Kazakhstan’s call for renewed international cooperation at the UN General Assembly, highlighting its positions on nuclear disarmament, Ukraine, Gaza, water security, AI governance and UN reform.

“Addressing the General Debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Sept. 25, Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi placed the restoration of trust at the center of his country’s foreign-policy message.

Kazakhstan, he said, remains committed to the principles of the UN Charter and sees multilateralism not as an abstract diplomatic concept but as a practical means of finding common ground and addressing shared global challenges.

The address reflected an increasingly prominent strand of Kazakhstan’s international positioning: that middle powers can play a larger role in bridging geopolitical divisions at a time when relationships between the major powers are becoming more difficult,” reads the article.

Germany and Kazakhstan: raw materials, trade routes, and new partnerships

Kazakhstan is moving into the spotlight for Germany, both economically and geopolitically. Cooperation with Central Asia is the central focus of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s visit to Berlin. For Germany, this also involves reducing dependencies regarding key raw materials, reported Euronews on Sept. 29.

“When Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met Chancellor Friedrich Merz at the Chancellery on Tuesday, the discussion went beyond traditional diplomacy. According to the Federal Government, the agenda included expanding the bilateral energy and raw materials partnership, regional cooperation in Central Asia, and international security policy,” reads the article.

We offer Germany a raw materials partnership

Kazakhstan produces 21 of the 34 raw materials deemed strategically important for Europe. Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev is proposing joint value and production chains to Berlin, Handelsblatt reported on Sept. 30.

“Trust and reliability are vital assets in politics and business. In times of international turbulence, both are becoming increasingly important. Kazakhstan and Germany have built trust over the course of more than three decades. Our strategic partnership thrives on political dialogue, the implementation of agreements, and tangible results.

For Kazakhstan, Germany is far more than just a trading partner and investor. We are united by economic interests and a clear commitment to international law. Our cooperation extends beyond the bilateral agenda: it connects Asia and Europe while strengthening economic resilience, energy security, and transport routes across the Eurasian region,” reads the article.

Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and UAE to explore new CASA railway route

Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates have agreed to jointly explore a new railway corridor linking Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan (CASA), with access to Pakistan’s seaports.

The agreement was formalized through a memorandum of understanding signed by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Transport and the UAE Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure, the Kazakh government said in a statement, reported news.az on Oct. 1.

The proposed railway route is designed to strengthen transport connectivity between Central and South Asia and provide new opportunities for international freight transit, trade and logistics.

The project is also expected to create additional prospects for investment cooperation among the participating countries, while expanding transport links between Central Asian markets and Pakistan’s seaports.

World.title: All four German political foundations halt work in Georgia; ALDE calls for EU sanctions
World.content:
German foundations close in Georgia

German Ambassador to Georgia Barbara Voss said all four German political foundations that had operated in the country for many years have been forced to close because of restrictions introduced by new legislation, including the Law on Grants.

According to the ambassador, worsening relations between Georgia and Germany have put years of cooperation at risk, including ties in education.

Against this backdrop, the European Liberal, Democrat and Reform Party (ALDE) sent a letter to EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas, calling on the European Union to respond with concrete action.

On 30 September, the Konrad Adenauer Foundation closed its office in Tbilisi. The Georgian office of the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which had worked in the country for 20 years, followed. The Heinrich Böll Foundation and Friedrich Ebert Foundation have also closed their offices.

What the German ambassador said

Barbara Voss, who replaced Peter Fischer as Germany’s ambassador to Georgia in August 2026, said that years of cooperation between the two countries had been seriously damaged.

“All four of our political foundations, which have supported Georgia and its people for decades on their path towards European integration, have been forced to suspend their work following a decision by the Georgian government. Two of the four foundations were forced to close their offices just two days ago,” the ambassador said.

Voss also highlighted Ilia State University, which has long-standing academic ties with Germany and is, according to the ambassador, one of Georgia’s most internationally recognised universities.

She said the university is now at risk of closure.

“These developments are also worsening relations between Georgia and the EU. In the coming years, I personally, as ambassador, will work to preserve what can still be preserved,” Voss said.

The diplomat said Germany would continue to meet its commitments in certain areas, including support for civil society, environmental protection and conservation of natural resources.

The German ambassador also spoke about security cooperation between the two countries. She stressed that Berlin and Tbilisi share common interests and face common challenges in this area.

“Russia is trying to destabilise Europe and divide people through disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression,” Voss said.

She said the Georgian population was well aware of the consequences of Russian military aggression. The ambassador noted that 20% of Georgia’s territory is occupied by Russia and said Moscow’s goal was not to maintain a balance of power but to establish dominance.

According to Voss, Germany continues to support Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as its right to determine its own security policy.

“In this context, we will support cooperation with the Georgian Defence Forces within the NATO framework to further strengthen their defence capabilities against potential aggression and contribute to the security of the South Caucasus and Europe,” the German ambassador said.

“Enough! The Georgian Dream regime is silencing independent voices”

“Enough is enough! The Georgian Dream regime is squeezing out independent voices and pushing Georgia further away from Europe.

After more than 20 years in the country, Friedrich-Naumann-Stiftung für die Freiheit has been forced to close its Tbilisi office because it could no longer operate independently.

ALDE Party President Svenja Hahn and European Liberal Forum President Jan-Christoph Oetjen are calling on the EU to act.

Targeted sanctions against those responsible for repression and the systematic undermining of democracy. No more looking the other way. Our joint letter to Kaja Kallas and Marta Kos,” ALDE said in a social media post.

The letter says the Friedrich Naumann Foundation for Freedom was forced to close its Tbilisi office, which had operated in the country for more than two decades, after the Georgian authorities rejected its application for foreign funding.

“The Georgian authorities made it clear that the foundation’s activities would only be permitted if they were aligned with their priorities. Under these conditions, FNF concluded that it could no longer carry out its mission as an independent political foundation,” the letter says.

The letter describes this as “another clear example of the growing restrictions on independent civil society and the wider repression of protesters, opposition figures, journalists and independent voices.”

“These developments show how far the Georgian Dream government is moving away from the standards expected of an EU candidate country and send a worrying signal to all those with European aspirations.

What is happening in Georgia matters not only to its citizens, but also to the credibility of the EU’s enlargement policy and its commitment to democracy and fundamental rights,” the letter says.

The authors again called on the EU to “respond with targeted sanctions against those responsible for the repression and systematic undermining of democracy and fundamental freedoms in Georgia”.

“The EU must ensure that those defending democracy and fundamental freedoms are not left without support,” ALDE said.

“We are not concerned about unfair sanctions” – ruling party representative

“We are not particularly concerned about their [the EU’s] incompetent and completely unfounded sanctions packages, introduced year after year or month after month,” parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtchkhalia said in response to ALDE’s call.

“We should not be surprised by such statements from ALDE or the EU’s political establishment. For years, our country has been subjected to direct and unfair attacks from them.

No package of sanctions can force us to abandon the course chosen at the request of our society. That course is peaceful development, progress and prosperity for every citizen and, above all, the peaceful reunification of our country,” Kirtchkhalia said.

News in Georgia

World.title: Now ruling party leader indefinitely; Ilham Aliyev makes new tough foreign policy statements
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev rejects criticism from Turkey

At the eighth congress of the Yeni Azerbaijan Party, held in Baku on 2 October, the party abolished the five-year term limit for its chairperson. The leader – currently Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev – will now remain in the post indefinitely.

In his speech, Aliyev placed particular emphasis on claims that Azerbaijan achieved its military victories in the Second Karabakh War and the subsequent operation entirely on its own.

The president said no outside assistance had been provided to Azerbaijan and that all weapons had been purchased through regular channels.

The remarks came amid criticism in Turkish media after Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the UN General Assembly hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech on 24 September, unlike delegations from many countries that walked out in protest over Israel’s military operation in Gaza.

The ruling party leader can now remain in office indefinitely

According to the state-run APA news agency, the party’s congress removed a provision from its statutes that limited the chairman’s term to five years.

Nizami Safarov, who presented the amendment, justified the removal of the limit by pointing to the victories achieved under Aliyev’s leadership. He called Aliyev the “leader of Azerbaijan’s unprecedented victories” and said he considered the decision in line with the country’s political and legal realities.

According to Safarov, Aliyev’s indefinite leadership “will lead the party to new successes and greater victories”.

The change removes the requirement to re-elect the chairman after a set period. However, this does not mean that elections for party chairman will never be held again or that Aliyev will not take part in future party congresses.

The change concerns the party leadership and does not affect the procedure for electing the country’s president.

Politically, the change means there is no longer a mechanism for the party chairman’s mandate to be periodically renewed.

Role of Turkey in the Second Karabakh War: Aliyev denies any outside help for Azerbaijan

“We are shaping our foreign policy, and we must continue to do so in a way that prevents anyone from interfering in our affairs. We do not need anyone’s help or anyone’s protection.

When we needed help, no one helped us. When we had one million refugees, no one reached out to us. Everything we received, we bought with our own money. This includes all the weapons we acquired, paying world market prices down to the last bullet.

I am telling you this with full responsibility, as supreme commander-in-chief and as the person who oversaw all these processes. You know how much Azerbaijan strengthened its military capabilities since 2003: we developed our own production and bought weapons abroad.

Not once were we given a discount of even one manat or one dollar. In fact, sometimes weapons were sold to us at several times the world market price. We had to turn a blind eye to this. So this is a very serious issue.” […]

“Our advantage is that, unlike some countries, we do not need to create myths. In some countries, certain leaders try to take credit for past achievements or exaggerate their own role by distorting history. We do not need that,” Aliyev said.

In another notable part of his speech, Aliyev accused some leaders of trying to take credit for past achievements and “exaggerate their own role”.

Although he did not say whom he meant, social media users and experts have suggested that he was referring to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

From a political perspective, the remarks appear to downplay any role played by Turkey or other external actors in Azerbaijan’s military success during the Second Karabakh War.

Aliyev’s remarks have a specific historical context when viewed against Turkey-Azerbaijan relations.

On 28 July 2024, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, speaking in Rize about Israel, said: “Just as we entered Karabakh, just as we entered Libya, we can do the same to them.”

The Karabakh victory was therefore used in political speeches as an example of Turkey’s regional power even before the current debate over Azerbaijan’s position at the UN.

The earlier position of Aliyev himself is also important.

On 19 February 2024, speaking in Ankara, he said Turkey had stood by Azerbaijan throughout the war, and that Erdoğan’s initial statements had deterred other powers from intervening. In the same speech, Aliyev spoke about joint military exercises and the adoption of the Turkish army model in Azerbaijan.

Turkey’s support during the war could later have become a political and moral basis for expecting solidarity from Baku on other issues, including Israel. Ankara has not officially made such demands so far.

From this perspective, Aliyev’s remarks can be seen not so much as a denial of Turkey’s support, but as a rejection of the idea that such support creates political obligations: being allies does not mean that Baku has to coordinate all its foreign policy decisions with Ankara.

Why did Azerbaijan’s position during Netanyahu’s UN speech spark debate?

On 24 September, when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the UN General Assembly, several delegations, including Turkey’s, walked out. Turkish newspaper Sözcü and other media outlets specifically pointed out that the Azerbaijani representative remained in the hall.
