World.title: Trump’s bluff is too late to save him
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets Opinion Trump’s bluff is too late to save him Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 5, 2026 — 11:58am

October 5, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Donald Trump coerced G7 countries into a release of their emergence reserves of oil and diesel in an attempt to lower prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections. Will his gambit work? It might, in the short term, with oil and diesel prices dipping after the announcement that the countries – Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States—would release up to 100 million barrels of oil and diesel over the next four months, including a “front-loaded” substantial release of diesel stocks over the next 20 days. Donald Trump’s bluff has had some impact, but it isn’t likely to last. AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta The announcement was in response to Trump threat to ban US exports of diesel. With the European Union and UK heavily reliant on imports from the US and the northern winter looming, that was a very direct threat to their economies and societies, even though Trump now says that “we were never going to do it.”



Trump, while toying with the idea of an export ban because record gasoline and diesel prices are hurting US consumers and farmers and adding to Republican fears of a wipeout at next month’s midterms, had been told by the US oil industry that a ban might produce short-term relief but could subsequently exacerbate the problem. Related Article US election With a month to go, Republicans’ midterm prospects are ‘catastrophically bad’ Their advice was that it would lead to a rapid increase in domestic inventories that would inevitably force US refiners and oil producers to cut their production of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. Trump’s bluff had some impact. After dipping below $US100 a barrel in response to the G7 announcement, however, the oil price bounced back up to more than $US102 a barrel. US gasoline and diesel prices edged down, but US gasoline prices are still 40 per cent higher than they were at this time last year and diesel is more than 70 per cent higher. The release is a palliative for the deep wounds in the world’s oil markets caused by Trump’s war in the Middle East.



Releasing 100 million barrels of oil and oil products – and it is the products, particularly diesel, that matter – over four months represents an addition to global supply over less than a million barrels a day. The G7 statement didn’t detail the split between oil and diesel releases, but the industry view seems to be that it will be roughly 50 million barrels of each. Unwinding the damage done to energy markets by the war will not happen overnight. AP Global refinery output is currently about 7 million barrels a day lower than at the same time last year. Global oil inventories are at their lowest levels for five years. Unless and until the Strait of Hormuz is fully re-opened on pre-war terms, war-damaged refineries in the Middle East are back to full production and Russia, whose refineries have been very successfully targeted by Ukraine, resumes exports of refined product, the market for refined products will be short of supply relative to demand.



While the US has claimed to have reopened the strait and says that volumes have been nearing pre-war levels, recent Iranian attacks on tankers transiting the strait – at least four and as many as seven have been targeted in the past week – have again reduced the flow of oil and its derivatives from the region. Related Article Analysis

US midterm elections America’s billionaires are turning their backs on Trump It’s also not just about flows. Before the war tanker rates to ship oil via the strait ranged from about $US30,000 a day to more than $US100,000, depending on the size of the tanker. They’re now over $US800,000 a day. Insuring a tanker used to cost about $US250,000 pre-war. Now, where it is available – a lot of insurers have stopped providing coverage – it can cost up to $US10 million for the larger ships. For those tankers avoiding the strait and taking longer routes to reach their end markets, there are additional operational costs.



All those new risks and costs are built into oil prices and will remain there unless and until there is a conclusive end to hostilities in the region and something akin to the pre-war norms for transiting the strait are in place. It would also take months, even years, for the damage to Middle Eastern refineries to be remedied. Before the war, the Saudis were the world’s second-largest producer of diesel and produced more than 3 million barrels a day of refined products, although about half of that output was devoted to its domestic market. Today its refined product volumes are less than 60 per cent of their pre-war levels. Soaring fuel prices are going to hurt Trump in the midterm elections. AP Releasing G7 stocks may provide temporary relief, but it doesn’t address that underlying shortfall of supply and, on the meantime, runs down the buffers available to deal with the potential for the future shocks that caused to reserves to be built.



Despite the release, the market for diesel could tighten further. Russia – once the world’s second-largest exporter behind the US, has banned diesel exports until at least the end of this month (more likely indefinitely) because of the damage Ukraine has inflicted on its refining infrastructure. Ukraine has vowed to intensify those attacks. China – the world’s second-largest consumer of oil and refined products behind the US – has also, again, stopped refined product exports. It was exporting about a million barrels a day before the war. More fundamentally, those refineries unaffected by the war – predominantly in the US – are operating at near capacity levels, or around 95 per cent of capacity. The refineries are experiencing massive margins and generating enormous profits, but don’t have the ability to expand production meaningfully and their inventories of refined product have been run down.



US refineries’ diesel inventories are at their lowest seasonal level since data on diesel stocks started being collected in 1982. With global demand for refined products having recovered somewhat from its nadirs after the outbreak of the war, supply isn’t capable of responding significantly. The release is a palliative for the deep wounds in the world’s oil markets caused by Trump’s war in the Middle East. The reserves release might temporarily close the gap, but it doesn’t resolve the underlying mismatch of supply and demand and creates the risk that, with depleted inventories, there’s less of a buffer to deal with a prolongation of the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine or some new threat to energy supplies. That suggests oil, gasoline and diesel prices will remain higher for longer. It is, of course, the refined product prices that matter – no-one pours crude into their tanks.



A survey of US oil and gas executives by the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas last month found that nearly half of them – 48 per cent – expected it would take more than a year for diesel prices to return to last year’s levels. Trump’s anxiety about the impact of the near-record prices for gasoline and diesel in the US is well-founded. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump’s ‘betrayal’ of America’s heartland will cost him The higher costs of gasoline and, in particular, diesel – because its fuels trucks, freight trains, ships, tractors, construction machinery and has a host of other industrial applications are starting to feed into goods prices – are feeding into the costs of end-products to customers and the inflation rate. Because of the war, US farmers are experiencing both elevated diesel and (because the Middle East has been a major fertiliser producers) fertiliser prices. The backlash against the increase in the cost of living and doing business is spreading throughout America, hence Trump’s dismal personal ratings and the prospect of big gains for the Democrats next month.



If sustained at current levels, those higher input costs will both lift the inflation rate and reduce economic activity, risking stagflation. Even if Trump’s success in “convincing” the rest of the G7 that releasing oil and diesel reserves was in their best interests, the impact so late in the political cycle is likely to be immaterial to the outcome of the elections and the impact of the war in the Middle East on domestic gasoline and diesel prices will still be there and still discolouring the second half of his term as president. World.title: Couple buys $1,825,000 Erskineville house as vendor cuts reserve price
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Couple buys $1,825,000 Erskineville house as vendor cuts reserve price Carmen Forward October 5, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An engaged couple paid $1,825,000 for an Erskineville house at auction the day before their wedding, when the vendor cut their reserve by $25,000 to sell. The three-bedroom family home at 33 Eve Street had a private courtyard, a loft level bedroom, and skylights. The property was one of 521 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 53 per cent from 307 reported results throughout the week and 87 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The volume of homes for sale was low due to the long weekend, the first weekend after the Reserve Bank’s decision to lift interest rates to 4.6 per cent.



Two parties registered, both looking to upsize and both participated. The underbidders were another young couple. Related Article Auctions Inner west art deco apartment sells for $900k to Bondi couple Bidding opened at the home’s guide of $1.7 million and several small rises increased the price to $1.75 million. Then the highest bidder, a couple to be married the next day, bid against themselves by $75,000. The vendor adjusted their $1.85 million reserve down and the home sold under the hammer for $1,825,000. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



Ray White’s Shaun Stoker said the buyers had been looking for over three months. “I’m finding [that] if buyers don’t see value, they’re not acting ... Owners have to be aligned with the buyer to get interest.” Stoker’s colleague Moira Verheijen said the couple had each purchased their first property from her separately before purchasing their first home as a couple on the eve of their wedding. “It’s very nice when you go on a journey with people over 10 years of your career, it’s … a real privilege.”



The vendors have purchased in Annandale and are upsizing. The property last traded for $1.41 million in 2020, records show. In Liverpool a three-bedroom house at 271 Memorial Avenue that was purchased in March this year for $1,505,000 sold for $1,325,000. The property had an existing lease in place and the buyer is keeping the tenants on. Four parties registered and all four were active. Bidding opened at $1.1 million and jumped to $1.2 million quickly before selling for $25,000 below its $1.35 million reserve for $1,325,000.



Selling agent Michael Sleiman from First National Real Estate Daystar said it is the, “worst market I have experienced in my 30 to 40 years of real estate.” Related Article Auctions Young couple pays $1.65 million for charming Stanmore terrace “This makes the GFC, COVID, Royal Commission, 13 rate rises look like a lovely … sunny day compared to this market.” Sleiman said the biggest impact has been the “the negative gear and capital gains changes.” He added that he “felt sorry” for his vendor and that he had even “tried many times to convince him not to sell.”



“But in the end, it was a good result for him because it means he can move on now.” In Rhodes, a two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment with sweeping city skyline views at 2306/7 Rider Boulevard sold for $1,309,000. Two registered, both interested parties were young professionals and both were active. Bidding opened at $1.18 million and rose in mostly $10,000 increments until it sold for $1000 above its $1,308,000 reserve.



The initial guided range of $1.3 million to $1.4 million was adjusted down a week prior to auction to $1,231,000 due to a $1.23 million offer received. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Moguls behind Kylie Jenner-endorsed sunglasses brand list Byron Shire mansion Selling agent Rex Sam from Vue Property Estate Agents said, “Even with this recent rate rise, the buyers that I’m working with are still looking to purchase.” Sam doesn’t think the interest rate has affected family home buyers. “Good home, good location, presented nicely. They’ll always have demand.”



The vendor is upsizing to a house. The flat last traded for $825,000 in 2013, records show. Chief economist at AMP Dr Shane Oliver said Domain’s clearance rate of 53 per cent for Sydney is a “soft outcome”. “You’ve always got to be a little bit cautious in interpreting data on the long weekends ... But even allowing for the long weekend, these are still fairly weak results in the numbers [compared to] a year ago,” he said. Oliver predicts we won’t see rate cuts until the second half of next year.

World.title: ‘More arrests are on the table’: Qantas hack gang member nabbed
World.content:
TechnologyCybersecurity ‘More arrests are on the table’: Qantas hack gang member nabbed David Swan October 5, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A suspected key player in the hacking alliance behind the Qantas data breach has been detained in Jordan and is cooperating with the FBI. Saif al-Din Khader, known online as Rey, was taken into custody by Jordanian authorities last week, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters. Qantas was hacked in June 2025, when a caller posing as IT support persuaded a worker at an offshore call centre to connect a Salesforce customer platform to a malicious data-extraction tool. Australian Financial Review. Khader is helping the FBI and police around the world track down other members of ShinyHunters, two of the sources told the news agency. ShinyHunters is the extortion gang that claimed last month to have stolen data on every FBI employee. One source said Khader was walking investigators through his electronic devices and digital correspondence. In November last year, US security journalist Brian Krebs identified Khader as one of the administrators of Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters. It is a loose alliance of mostly English-speaking hacking gangs, including ShinyHunters.



Khader told Krebs at the time he had been trying to leave the group and had been working with law enforcement since June 2025. ShinyHunters continued its attacks into this year, claiming break-ins at Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar Games and education platform Canvas. Cybersecurity researchers linked Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters to the leak of 5.7 million Qantas customers’ personal details on the dark web last October. Neither Reuters nor any law enforcement agency has alleged Khader was personally involved in the Qantas attack. The AFP and Qantas were contacted for comment. View post on X The FBI declined to comment to Reuters on any arrest abroad, but said it had already worked with partners to arrest multiple subjects and would “spare no resource in bringing each of the responsible individuals to justice”. FBI director Kash Patel went further, signalling the investigation was widening. “FBI teams are working new leads RIGHT NOW,” he posted on X on Wednesday. “More arrests are on the table.”



Patel’s post followed confirmation by Dutch police that a 24-year-old Amsterdam man had been arrested in September in an investigation into ShinyHunters. He has been identified by Krebs and others as Pepijn van der Stap, a hacker convicted in the Netherlands in 2023 over a string of data thefts and extortions. ShinyHunters has said van der Stap had no association with the group. The gang claimed on September 22 that it had hacked the FBI in retaliation for an advisory accusing it of exaggerating its access to victims’ systems. It gave the bureau a week to withdraw the advisory. Since then, its dark website has disappeared. In its most recent email to Reuters, the group said it wanted “no further escalation” with the FBI. Police have struggled to prosecute members of related groups such as Lapsus$ and Scattered Spider, Reuters has reported. Many of the hackers are young, the groups are chaotic and informal, and victims often decline to help investigators. Qantas was hacked in June 2025, when a caller posing as IT support persuaded a worker at an offshore call centre to connect a Salesforce customer platform to a malicious data-extraction tool. When Salesforce refused a ransom demand, the hackers published the data. Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind. Nine



Most records held names, email addresses and frequent flyer details. About 1.7 million also included home or business addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers and meal preferences. Qantas said passport and credit card details were not on the system. Related Article Exclusive

Cybersecurity Qantas says no to ransom. 96 per cent of Australian businesses say yes In July, Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind declined to open a formal investigation into the airline. She said the evidence did not support the likelihood that Qantas had breached privacy law. Serious or repeated breaches of the Privacy Act can attract penalties of more than $50 million, and the watchdog has left the door open. “It is still open to the commissioner to commence an investigation of Qantas with respect to these or other practices,” Kind said. Law firm Maurice Blackburn is also pursuing a proposed class action on behalf of customers whose personal information was stolen and published online. Maurice Blackburn was contacted for comment. World.title: Five years and $10,000 later: Why upgrading Melbourne apartments is proving impossible
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Five years and $10,000 later: Why upgrading Melbourne apartments is proving impossible Angelica Snowden October 5, 2026 — 11:54am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Inner-city residents Carla Campbell-Redl and Ying-Lan Dann want to electrify their 1960s apartment block. The goal – to move away from gas – sounds simple. But Campbell-Redl, who is chair of the Owners Corporation committee managing the low-rise brick building in North Melbourne she and Dann call home, say about $10,000 paid to five consultants in as many years has not yet yielded a solution. Ying-Lan Dann (left) and Carla Campbell-Redl (right) want to electrify their North Melbourne apartment block. Simon Schluter “One of our biggest frustrations is that we have not been able to get reliable technical advice to establish even an approximate cost for the complete electrification project,” Campbell-Redl says. Many owners at the Haines Street block “share the same values” and support the committee’s investigation into renewables to boost the building’s environmental credentials and save on bills, Dann says. But the hurdles are not unique to their block.



An expert review into the Owners Corporation Act found there is “strong” interest from many apartment owners across Victoria who want to install electric car chargers and replace gas stovetops with induction models, but reported many sustainable upgrades failed to proceed due to a 75 per cent threshold needed to approve changes to common property. Related Article Exclusive

Strata ‘Not a single prosecution’: Watchdog ignored thousands of strata complaints over 10 years As the city’s population races to nine million, strata-titled apartments will be a key housing option for inner-city living. Growing calls from experts, consumer advocates and some inner-city councils, are pushing for laws to clarify the powers of individuals and committees seeking to upgrade sustainability measures. Campbell-Redl says her two-bedroom unit is her “forever home”. “It’s a place I can live in the city. When I’m old, and I can’t drive, I will be able to catch the bus and tram; I’m close to all the infrastructure,” she says.



“Living in the city is a choice about using the existing infrastructure in a way that benefits people without an undue cost,” she says. Dann, who is raising her two children in her unit, doesn’t intend to leave either. She points out that “all this infrastructure already exists”, and notes there are hundreds of other apartment blocks from the same era that will likely want to make similar transitions and upgrades at some point. Carla Campbell-Redl (right) and Ying-Lan Dann (left) want to electrify their apartment block. Simon Schluter Campbell-Redl and Dann’s best current estimate is that each of the 33 units in their block would need to chip in about $24,800 to cover upgrades to the block’s infrastructure – about $818,000 in total. The infrastructure needed includes a new network cable ($300,000), a potential substation ($100,000), cable trays in common areas ($75,000), wiring into each apartment ($100,000), hot water plumbing and metering ($198,000), nine hot water units ($36,000) and electrical cabling ($9000).



The committee stressed these figures are indicative only and don’t include the cost to install solar panels or batteries. Campbell-Redl says the key point is that “we still cannot establish a reliable overall project cost”. Related Article Exclusive

City life Slow lifts, disgusting carpets, cracked windows: Residents face crumbling tower as rival strata companies battle for control “We have had difficulty obtaining the technical expertise and information needed to determine what infrastructure will be required, particularly in relation to the electricity network and any substation or network upgrades,” she says. An expert review into Victoria’s Owners Corporation Act reported that while solar uptake on Victorian homes has doubled since 2018 and now sits at over 30 per cent, it has occurred almost exclusively on detached houses. “Eligible OC projects have failed to proceed due to challenges navigating the collective decision-making requirements embedded in strata governance, despite strong interest from OCs,” the review noted.



One major impediment is the requirement of a 75 per cent special resolution to approve changes to common property, with funding being another barrier, where projects stall unless an owners corporation has money in the bank to pay for sustainability upgrades, according to the report. In its submission to the Owners Corporation Act review, the City of Melbourne said the law should define what “sustainability items” are – for example, electric-vehicle charging – to clarify what power committees and individual lot owners have to make sustainability upgrades. As Melbourne’s population races to nine million, apartments will be a key part of the housing mix. The Age City of Melbourne, the council area covering North Melbourne, has backed lowering sustainability upgrade resolutions from 75 per cent owner approval to 50 per cent owner approval. Lord Mayor Nick Reece told The Age that apartment residents and owners corporations face a “maze of costs, regulations and technical decisions when trying to move away from gas and improve their buildings”.



“Medium and high-density apartments house more than 80 per cent of Melbourne residents - yet they’re being left to navigate the transition to a more sustainable future alone,” he said. Related Article City life Eight towers, 900 apartments: Plans revealed for redeveloped Preston Market Responding to the particular challenges faced by residents in Haines Street, Consumer advocacy group Australian Apartment Advocacy director Samantha Reece says there was no support for older blocks to transition from gas to electric. She backed lowering the voting threshold to 50 per cent for sustainability items only. “If you were to lower it to 50 per cent, there would have to be a very clear communication to strata managers and also OC committees that [lowering the threshold] was only to do with sustainability measures,” she said. Reece says she supports recommendations made in the expert review, including the introduction of a strata commissioner who could administer grants to allow owners corporations to do energy audits.



Adam Promnitz, co-founder of Strata Owners Alliance, told this masthead he is reluctant to support a carve-out of particular items requiring lower voting thresholds. “The loading thresholds are for significant alterations [common property]. This would say there are certain alterations that are more worthy than others,” he said. “If you are going to reduce [the threshold] then it’s got to be for something that you can show there will be a financial gain.” The Victorian government supported all the expert panel’s recommendations to review barriers stopping the introduction of sustainability options in existing and new buildings. The first tranche of legislation to update the Owners Corporation Act has passed, focussing on lot owners in financial hardship. World.title: The Conservative Party has a bold agenda – but there’s a problem
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeUK leadership The Conservative Party has a bold agenda – but there’s a problem David Crowe October 5, 2026 — 11:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A sharp remark about British complacency highlighted the immense challenge for Kemi Badenoch, when the leader of the nation’s Conservative Party sought to outline her mission in a major speech on Sunday. Her warning in the address also underscored a grim outlook for the country. UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch. Getty Images Her message? “The money is not there.” Badenoch argued that the UK could simply not afford all the policies it would like to have and would have to cut its spending to suit the times. This is not a popular position when families are being punished by rising prices and burdened by low wages. Many voters expect the government to help them by spending more on household assistance and subsidies.



But that did not stop Badenoch from attempting some “tough love” in her address to the annual Conservative Party conference. It was risky. It was also a contrast with Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, who used his address to the annual Labour Party conference one week ago to talk about spending increases, not cuts. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Can Burnham save Britain? Finally, he reveals his plans – with one glaring omission “We are the lucky generation,” Badenoch told the event in Birmingham on Sunday. “We didn’t have to deal with World War One or World War Two. We haven’t had many of the problems that previous generations did. Advancements in medical technology or just general technology have made life pretty comfortable. “But I think that that is making us – across the West, to be honest, not just the UK – very complacent.” One example, she said, was the plan under former prime minister Keir Starmer, who was removed in June, to settle the future of the Chagos Islands in the Indian Ocean (and the Diego Garcia base the UK shares with the United States) by agreeing to pay billions of dollars to Mauritius to “lease” the territory.



The problem? “This belief that we are rich because we are rich and we are always going to be rich,” Badenoch said. “So we can spend loads of money on foreign aid and we can give away the Chagos Islands and pay £35 billion ($66 billion) for it. And we can do all sorts of foolish and silly things because the money is just there. The money is not just there. We have to make the money so we can do everything else.” Badenoch is yet to prove she can replace Burnham. She has led the Conservatives for about two years and made some small gains in the polls, but most of the attention on the right of the political spectrum goes to Nigel Farage and his anti-immigration party, Reform UK. Badenoch and the Conservative Party lag behind Nigel Farage’s Reform UK in the polls. Getty Images The Conservative leader does a good line in light mockery, however, and is trying to leap ahead of Farage when he is under scrutiny for accepting big donations from crypto investors. The latest YouGov survey showed 25 per cent of voters backed Reform, 24 per cent supported Labour and 19 per cent backed the Conservatives. Badenoch, 46, is a departure from the mostly white, male leaders of the Conservative Party. She was born in London to Nigerian parents and initially raised in Nigeria before joining her mother, a professor, in the United States.



She was educated in the UK from the age of 16, went to university to study engineering and law, and became a software engineer. Active in Conservative politics since she was 25, Badenoch married Hamish Badenoch, a banker, when she was 32. They have two daughters and a son. Related Article Analysis

Crime Why British PM named Iran as likely culprit in air base plot Her speech to the opening day of the Conservative conference came at a testing time for her and the party. Badenoch shone when she was skewering Starmer in parliament during his long slide towards resignation, but she has a harder task with Burnham. Put simply, she is now up against a much better communicator. While she projects her policies with a smile, she is anathema to the progressive side of politics. She stands for cutting welfare, cancelling net-zero climate goals, easing the regulation of businesses and developing more oil and gas deposits. On Sunday, she was especially pointed on migration. She argued that those who arrived should embrace British values so the country would maintain one shared culture. That language goes to the heart of the unease in Britain over the number of migrants, especially asylum seekers who arrive by boat in the English Channel.



“I don’t want lots of little ghettoes of separatist communities where they’re recreating the place that they came from,” she said. “That will ruin the United Kingdom. We’ve never had race-based citizenship in this country, but I do want to emphasise that British culture means something.” Badenoch had no instant solutions in her address. In fact, one of her policy ideas is to widen the eligibility for childcare assistance – a new spending, not a saving. She had no plan to stop the boats in the English Channel, nor any thorough proposal on how to restrict migration without hurting economic growth. What she had, instead, was an uncomfortable truth for the public: the country was not as rich as they thought. And she had a point. At a household level, incomes have flatlined in the UK since the global financial crisis of 2008. Median wages have fallen over the period. Universal Credit, a government program that transfers money to seven million households, is one factor that is preventing families from going backwards. About one quarter of all households now rely on this and other assistance to stay afloat. For a single young person, the baseline is £338.58 per month. It is higher for families, and there is some flexibility to work while receiving the assistance. Universal Credit cost £42.6 billion in the 2023 fiscal year and is forecast to reach £88.1 billion in 2029, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility.



Related Article Analysis

UK politics Farage says Britain is broken and only Reform can fix it. Now the pressure is on to deliver At a national level, Britain remains one of the world’s advanced economies, but its budget is stretched. Public sector net debt is about £3 trillion, according to the Office of National Statistics, and the annual budget is in the red. Debt interest payments are estimated to be £111.2 billion this year. At this rate, the country will soon spend more on the interest bill than on defence – which costs about £65.4 billion a year. Australia also has these problems. The demand for spending outweighs the commitment to saving in Canberra each year. But the pressure in Britain is greater because the budget is weaker. Badenoch is doing more than Burnham to highlight this problem. Will she come up with a solution? In her address on Sunday, she explicitly borrowed from former prime minister Margaret Thatcher, an iconic leader for the modern Conservatives, by issuing a manifesto for the next government.



The ambition is clear, but it will never be realised if Badenoch remains in third place in the polls. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: After the ICAC brought political dirty dealing to light, one operative remained elusive
World.content:
PoliticsNSWOperation Rosny After the ICAC brought political dirty dealing to light, one operative remained elusive Jessica McSweeney October 5, 2026 — 11:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For almost 10 weeks, the state’s corruption watchdog painstakingly extracted evidence from backroom political operatives – and even fugitive developer Jean Nassif from his Beirut bedroom – but there was one central figure who remained the ghost of Operation Rosny. One-time Liberal powerbroker Christian Ellis, who skilfully evaded a parliamentary inquiry by hiding in the forests south of Sydney in 2023, again managed to dodge efforts to bring him to give public evidence about his role in an alleged illegal donations scheme to the Independent Commission Against Corruption. Christian Ellis dodged public scrutiny in both the NSW Parliament and ICAC inquiries. Final exhibits tendered to the inquiry, which wrapped last week, reveal the ways the ICAC bent over backwards to secure the evidence of Ellis, who moved to the UK earlier this year and has no plans to return to Australia. The ICAC wrote to Ellis and his lawyer several times, offering to sit into the evening to allow for the time difference, offered a break every two hours and proposed that he dial in from his home so as not to disrupt family commitments, the documents reveal.



Still, that wasn’t enough to convince Ellis. The ICAC is now assessing the evidence given by his former political allies and clients before it decides if any of Ellis’s conduct amounts to corruption. The founding member of the Reformers right-wing sub-faction of the Liberal party wasn’t staying completely in the dark. As the ICAC heard, his mate and former business partner Jeremy Greenwood was in regular contact, and had even flown to meet Ellis in London in June, just weeks before the public inquiry was announced. Ellis wanted to cooperate with the public inquiry, he told Greenwood over the phone, but didn’t know how. Greenwood relayed this to the ICAC during his own questioning. “If Mr Ellis is listening, the commission waits for his response,” assistant commissioner Fabian Gleeson, SC, said.



In a letter to Ellis the next day, an ICAC investigator reiterated the arrangements they could make to facilitate his evidence. Editor's pick Investigation

Investigation Inside Operation Rosny Documents also revealed that Ellis’ lawyer, Simon Diab, had offered participation in the public inquiry only by responding to written questions. The ICAC refused. The documents also showed that the ICAC refused Diab’s application to represent Ellis at the public inquiry, although the reasons given for this refusal were redacted. Ellis gave evidence in a private hearing in 2024, although only a short excerpt was tendered to the public inquiry, and has remained silent since the public hearings began. Ellis is no stranger to life on the run.



Related Article Exclusive

Operation Rosny The 11-hour drive and profane putdown: Inside the meeting that killed a Liberal Party takeover When Liberal MP Ray Williams stood up in parliament and made extraordinary claims about alleged corruption in his own party in 2022, Ellis was hard at work for his right wing factional group the Reformers. He was waging factional warfare in Deniliquin in the federal seat of Farrer, not to unseat a rival political party, but to oust moderate Liberal Sussan Ley and instead seize the branch for the right faction. And he was having some success. “Word from the south,” fellow Reformer and once Catholic Schools NSW staffer Robert Assaf texted some factional friends. “Tobias Lehmann has just lost the presidency of Farrer FEC. Big result for the team down there. All thanks to Christian for his work on this.”



Meanwhile, the Reformers were holding events with conservative titans such as Alan Jones, and working to recruit new religious conservatives to the Liberal Party, especially in the Hills Shire. At the same time, Ellis and Greenwood were being paid large cheques from Jean Nassif’s Toplace, allegedly in partnership with Charles Perrottet in exchange for political outcomes. In 2021, Ellis attended a Liberal fundraiser, headlined by then-treasurer Dominic Perrottet and Robyn Preston, with a friend in tow – Toplace’s lawyer and one-time Labor Strathfield councillor Sharangan Maheswaran, another star witness in the ICAC inquiry. Money was also coming in from Catholic Schools NSW, via an allegedly sham contract approved by the CEO, fellow right-wing Liberal Dallas McInerney, to Ellis’s government relations firm Beckington, allegedly a way to help fund the work of the Reformers. McInerney has denied wrongdoing. Despite his powerful political connections and months of scheming to stack branches in Farrer, Ellis would fail in his mission to dump Ley, losing a vote during a November 2022 branch meeting after Ley made a secret 11-hour drive from Canberra to the regional NSW town of Finley for the vote.



Ley walked up to Ellis, looked him in the eyes and said: “You f---ed with the wrong person, you gutless prick.” Another thorn in Ellis’s side came a month later when the NSW Parliament launched an inquiry into the allegations raised in Williams’s speech, which specifically named Ellis. He was called as a witness, along with Greenwood, and Perrottet brothers Jean-Claude and Charles. Christian Ellis moved his family to Deniliquin to try and take over the seat of Farrer for the right wing faction. Alex Ellinghausen Ellis went into hiding, managing to dodge process servers hired by the parliament to track him down. His wife at one point answered the door to their rural Deniliquin home and told the agent she didn’t know her husband’s movements. “The agent noted the female person to appear nervous and evasive,” a report given to the inquiry said.



Rumours were flying around Deniliquin. Long-time Liberal branch member Shirlee Burge told the parliamentary inquiry she believed Ellis was living on a property backing onto dense forest where “people could disappear in there forever”. There had been sightings of vehicles going into the forest, she said. Burge said she believes she saw Ellis driving around wearing a black, full-face ski mask. Ellis managed to evade a statewide manhunt despite the best efforts of the parliamentary inquiry, and after the Liberal Party lost the 2023 state election, Ellis and the Reformers went quiet. In August 2023 Ellis was expelled from the party for bringing it into disrepute. While Operation Rosny never heard from Ellis in the public hearings, his connections to powerful people became clear through evidence before the ICAC. McInerney, for example, spoke at a Reformers event and agreed to sign-on Catholic Schools NSW as Beckington’s first client. He was supportive of Ellis not just professionally and politically, but also personally.



Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny From Hunters Hill to the Star and beyond: The ultimate ICAC pub crawl across Sydney Documents tendered to the ICAC show McInerney wrote a character reference for Ellis in 2019 after a drink-driving offence, praising Ellis as respectful and professional. “Without equivocation, I provide this reference in support of a fine young citizen held in high regard by many for his outstanding character,” McInerney wrote. It’s unclear if the reference was ever used in court. With Ellis refusing to cooperate with the ICAC’s public hearings, the commission will have to determine if Ellis and his friends solicited unlawful political donations, and if they engaged in corruption, without his public testimony. While Ellis’ career in Australian politics is over, he remains in the UK where the ICAC’s jurisdiction doesn’t reach. World.title: This haunting play celebrates the solidarity and strangeness of found family
World.content:
Key points THEATRE: Luke makes its world premiere at Red Stitch

MUSICAL THEATRE: Spamalot returns to Melbourne

THEATRE: Harold Pinter’s The Homecoming is performed at the Athenaeum

MUSIC: Metal band Health finishes their show with an invite to Cherry Bar

MUSIC: Kristian Bezuidenhout performs Handel and Bach with the MSO

THEATRE

Luke ★★★★

Red Stitch, until October 11 Local playwright Angus Cameron has teamed up with Red Stitch for the world premiere of Luke – a disturbing, emotionally complex three-hander that weaves a provocative play of ideas into a psychological mystery of troubling currency. Will Lonsdale, Olga Makeeva and Dion Mills in Luke Parenthesy I was bewildered by the opening sequence. Two adults race across a living room playing dress-ups. They’re engaged in some kind of private game, based on the Bolshevik assassination of the Romanovs during the Russian Revolution, but something about the scene feels off, inauthentic somehow. A clever reason for this will remain an enigma until well after we discover that the pair are high school teachers in country Victoria. It’s 2007, and Damon (Dion Mills) and Olena (Olga Makeeva) are unwinding at term’s end after a gruelling night of parent-teacher interviews. When Chris (Will Lonsdale) – the school’s 19-year-old rowing coach and a former student of Damon’s – joins them, the games continue.



Some of the playfulness is literary or historical – a relic of the ludic flamboyance essential to Damon’s pedagogic style. He’s an inspiring educator, discreetly gay, and his mentor-like relationship with Chris, who came out to Damon as a student, is tinged by affection and by a body of queer knowledge excluded by the official (read heteronormative) education system. Iain Sinclair’s direction guides three excellent performances. Parenthesy When conversation turns to a never-seen character, Luke – a year 11 student leaving the school after inappropriate attention from a member of staff – the game mutates through a series of twists, with a possible child sex abuse scenario, and its consequences, playing out over decades. Iain Sinclair’s direction guides three excellent performances. Mills’ suspect teacher has the charisma, passion, idealism, and sheer eccentricity of a gifted educator. There’s no question he leaves a mark on his students: his scenes with Lonsdale’s Chris are tender and haunted – enlivened by the irrepressible joy they both take in the learning game, as well as the shadow of barely repressed desire. Olena is the fulcrum of the play, and Makeeva is riveting as, through veiled parable and a clipped and embittered realism, the character weighs the truth of a situation in which the righteousness of her own acts is called into question.



She is a staunch counter to Chris – a young man heavily invested in his own righteousness, and solipsistic in the performance of it. Editor's pick Arts Three titans of politics, sport and media had a meeting in the 1980s. A new play imagines what was said Luke tackles such uncomfortable subjects as the erotics of education and the ethics of making art from life. It has stern things to say about the cultural amnesia afflicting Australian literature and drama, and it brings child protection concerns into contact with the reality of homophobia, knowing the ancient slur – the one that equates homosexuality with paedophilia – has never quite ceased to echo. Yet this haunting play celebrates, too, the solidarity and strangeness of found family, the clandestine solidarity and the mentorship relations that can exist between queer men finding their tribe. In this, it has an artistic genealogy that can be traced back to some of the most fearless and unsettling voices in queer Australian literature – the implied pederasty in David Malouf’s short story Under Southern Skies, say, or Frank Moorhouse’s The Everlasting Secret Family – updating the issues to a world of changing mores in which progressive rhetoric can disguise more difficult and painful human truths.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead



MUSICAL THEATRE

Spamalot ★★★★

Athenaeum Theatre, until October 11 You’d think that after 51 years a joke might stop being as funny as it once was. And yet, sitting in the dark watching two men debate how one swallow – or perhaps two, if they were holding some sort of string – might transport a coconut across countries, I found myself laughing as though it were the first time I’d heard this conversation. From left: Jesse Vasiliadis, Gareth Isaac, Stephen Curry, Ethan Jones and Noah Skape. Ben Fon Monty Python and the Holy Grail first hit cinemas in 1975, and Spamalot, “a new musical lovingly ripped off from the motion picture” takes the key plot and a handful of songs from the film, adds a whole lot more, and twists the story off into new directions as needed. The musical, itself now 20 years on from when it took Broadway by storm and took out the Tony Award for best musical, still feels vibrant and fun and silly. A spoof of the Arthurian legend, the story sees King Arthur (Stephen Curry) seeking knights to join his round table before being tasked by God (a video recording of Eric Idle) to find the Holy Grail.



While many jokes and scenes are lifted directly from the original film and other Python works, Spamalot, with book and lyrics by Idle, and music co-written by John Du Prez, is its own thing. Jaz Flowers and Ethan Jones as the Lady of the Lake and Sir Galahad. Ben Fon The songs written specifically for Spamalot hold their own against the older, more established tunes. Idle takes great delight in breaking the fourth wall in creative ways, and musical theatre itself is a key pillar of the story, with nods to everything and everyone from West Side Story to Liza Minnelli. Jaz Flowers as the Lady of the Lake steals almost every scene she’s in – her powerful command of every note makes light work of the parade of vocal challenges thrown her way. Her skill as a singer is matched only by her comedic timing. Her meta duet with Ethan Jones as Sir Galahad in The Song That Goes Like This is a particular highlight. Python humour remains evergreen because it is untethered from time. When it isn’t purely revelling in the absurd, it is taking aim at themes that sadly never grow old (inequality, bigotry, cowardice), joyfully ratcheting up the classics (fart jokes), and being gleefully persnickety when it comes to wordplay. With a talented cast who all appear to be enjoying every minute on stage, Spamalot is just the right amount of silly.

Reviewed by Elizabeth Flux



THEATRE

The Homecoming ★★★★

Athenaeum Theatre, until October 3 The lights come up to reveal two characters in a living room and it doesn’t take long for the sense that something is off-kilter to take hold. A pugnacious aged patriarch and ex-butcher named Max (Richard Piper) blathers on in an unpunctuated stream of consciousness to the uninterested Lenny (Ben Geurens) – we don’t find out the two are family until Max admonishes the louche Lenny for speaking such to his “lousy filthy father”. Richard Piper as Max in The Homecoming. Ben Fon The barely concealed hostilities are extended to the diametrically gentle Sam (David Field), Max’s chauffeur brother and the hulking wannabe boxer Joey (Eddie Orton), Lenny’s younger brother. No one and nothing are quite as they seem in Harold Pinter’s 1965 comedy of menace The Homecoming, even once you account for the virulent sexism, barely concealed hatred, and dearth of familial love between these characters. The intrigue deepens when all four of them retire to bed and the taciturn Teddy (Peter Houghton) enters the house, accompanied by his enigmatic wife Ruth (Kate Kendall). Teddy has effectively been estranged from his family for six years and now resides in America, with neither his wife nor family acquainted with each other. A series of decidedly strange interactions between all the characters leave audiences none the wiser as to what is about to unfold in this claustrophobic domestic setting.



Under the direction of Greg Carroll, a slowly creeping sense of foreboding and listlessness overtakes the play, only strengthening its grip on the audience as it unfolds. The world Pinter has ensconced these characters in exists in and of itself, ungoverned by the moral sensibilities and social mores of the now, let alone that of the 1960s when this play first premiered in London. Peter Houghton as Teddy and Kate Kendall as Ruth. Ben Fon Absurdist and fantastical despite its realist underpinnings, The Homecoming lulls its audience into an illusion of normalcy. When social contracts are broken with seemingly no repercussions, the play’s (and our) grasp on reality loosens – shining an uncomfortable spotlight on the confronting misogyny on display, calling into rebuke the meaning of the familial ties traditionally held so dear, and questioning the unspoken rules that allow society to function as it does. The famed Pinter Pause allows the requisite space for these consternations to fester. A muscular black room is the fitting backdrop for the exertion of these men’s fragile, toxic masculinities, while Amelia Carroll and Margaret Goy’s costume design is a stunning cloak of civility that masks the innermost depravations of these characters. Clad in a babydoll dress throughout, Ruth is read as childlike and guileless – a misnomer that allows her to exert the full force of her feminine wiliness. The strength of a production like The Homecoming lives and dies by its ensemble cast, and this one is uniformly excellent. Kendall is a particular highlight as the otherworldly, cosmically unflappable Ruth, simultaneously an antidote against the testosterone-soaked aggression of the men around her and the sun around which their neediness, desperation and contemptibility orbit.

Reviewed by Sonia Nair



MUSIC

Health ★★★★

Forum Melbourne, September 20 Metal always straddles the serious and the absurd. Tonight Los Angeles industrial metal band Health enters the stage to the theme song from Neon Genesis Evangelion. Health in 2026 is all machine beats and processed guitar riffs, with wan, emotive vocals. Richard Clifford Internet wags call Health’s brand of industrial metal “cum metal”. The band sells t-shirts that say “Sad Music For Horny People”. Tonight’s show is an industrial crush of guitar, drums, big feelings, and dudes swishing their long, lustrous hair, faces melted in metallic bliss. That’s the audience, by the way – I can’t really see the band, they’re swaddled in smoke and light, as it should be. At the start of their career, Health put out two acclaimed albums of dancey noise rock, heavy, colourful and dynamic. Since then they’ve distilled their sound into something more structured: the glam of industrial metal, with hints of shoegaze and gothic rock.



Have they polished the metal a bit too thin over the years? Health in 2026 is all machine beats and processed guitar riffs, with singer Jake Duzsik’s wan, emotive vocals. John Famiglietti opens the show with a pitch-perfect Aussie accent Richard Clifford But they push forward, and their fans come with them. Almost everything in tonight’s set is from their last two albums, Rat Wars and Conflict DLC, and just a few earlier tracks, notably Major Crimes and Tears (written for video games Cyberpunk 2077 and Max Payne 3), and We Are Water, from their 2009 second album Get Color. They’re at their peak when it all builds to something manic, like in Future of Hell and Shred Envy. A template emerges, in which something jagged and hard rears its head briefly, before they cut the decibels for Duzsik’s verses, which all merge into one overwrought cloud. Like all metal shows, there’s an air of generosity and camaraderie between the crowd and the band. Bassist/producer John Famiglietti opens the show with a pitch-perfect Aussie accent (“You sick c---ts, we’re gonna rip your f--kin’ dicks off!“) and ends it by inviting everyone to Cherry Bar for the afterparty, before crowdsurfing to the sound booth. His people love him.

Reviewed by Will Cox



MUSIC

Handel and Bach ★★★★

Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, September 19 Many Melbourne concertgoers will remember the stylish flair with which Australian fortepianist Kristian Bezuidenhout performed the complete Beethoven piano concertos with the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra on the cusp of COVID. Kristian Bezuidenhout at an earlier concert. Marco Borggreve Returning with some of that flair, Bezuidenhout directed the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra from the harpsichord in this program of works by Bach and Handel. Focusing particularly on rhythm and dynamics, Bezuidenhout brought crisp grandiloquence to the many French-style introductions on the program, whether to Bach’s Orchestral Suite No. 1 in C major or the Overture to Handel’s Admeto. There was also a general rhythmic buoyancy which lent itself well both to the dance-infused Bach Suite and Suites Nos. 1 and 2 from Handel’s familiar Water Music.



Carefully shaped dynamics applied to the whole orchestra made sense of the rise and fall of phrases and provided some well-judged dramatic contrasts. Related Article ★★★★★

Melbourne live reviews These are unapologetically political songs, and this artist is unapologetically herself Despite overall clarity, it was in Bezuidenhout’s arrangement of Bach’s incomplete Contrapunctus XIV from The Art of Fugue that the listener might have longed for some more granular detail in terms of articulation and pliability of tone in individual lines. Such qualities were more apparent in Handel’s Concerto grosso in D minor, Op. 3, no. 5 which followed. Fine wind and brass playing hallmarked the second half. Beginning with the Sinfonia from Bach’s Cantata No. 52 (otherwise recognisable as the opening of Brandenburg Concerto No. 4) followed by the Water Music, the horns and oboes took up Bezuidenhout’s brisk tempos with alacrity. Oboists Johannes Grosso and Ann Blackburn together with horn players Lucie Krysatis and Abbey Edlin crowned the festive mood of the Handel; their timbre setting up piquant contrasts with the strings, trumpets providing an additional regal air in the second suite. Thanks to Bezuidenhout, the MSO proved it can bring some idiomatic lightness to the glories of the baroque.

Reviewed by Tony Way The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Trump’s bluff is too late to save him
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets Opinion Trump’s bluff is too late to save him Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 5, 2026 — 11:58am

October 5, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Donald Trump coerced G7 countries into a release of their emergence reserves of oil and diesel in an attempt to lower prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections. Will his gambit work? It might, in the short term, with oil and diesel prices dipping after the announcement that the countries – Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States—would release up to 100 million barrels of oil and diesel over the next four months, including a “front-loaded” substantial release of diesel stocks over the next 20 days. Donald Trump’s bluff has had some impact, but it isn’t likely to last. AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta The announcement was in response to Trump threat to ban US exports of diesel. With the European Union and UK heavily reliant on imports from the US and the northern winter looming, that was a very direct threat to their economies and societies, even though Trump now says that “we were never going to do it.”



Trump, while toying with the idea of an export ban because record gasoline and diesel prices are hurting US consumers and farmers and adding to Republican fears of a wipeout at next month’s midterms, had been told by the US oil industry that a ban might produce short-term relief but could subsequently exacerbate the problem. Related Article US election With a month to go, Republicans’ midterm prospects are ‘catastrophically bad’ Their advice was that it would lead to a rapid increase in domestic inventories that would inevitably force US refiners and oil producers to cut their production of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. Trump’s bluff had some impact. After dipping below $US100 a barrel in response to the G7 announcement, however, the oil price bounced back up to more than $US102 a barrel. US gasoline and diesel prices edged down, but US gasoline prices are still 40 per cent higher than they were at this time last year and diesel is more than 70 per cent higher. The release is a palliative for the deep wounds in the world’s oil markets caused by Trump’s war in the Middle East.



Releasing 100 million barrels of oil and oil products – and it is the products, particularly diesel, that matter – over four months represents an addition to global supply over less than a million barrels a day. The G7 statement didn’t detail the split between oil and diesel releases, but the industry view seems to be that it will be roughly 50 million barrels of each. Unwinding the damage done to energy markets by the war will not happen overnight. AP Global refinery output is currently about 7 million barrels a day lower than at the same time last year. Global oil inventories are at their lowest levels for five years. Unless and until the Strait of Hormuz is fully re-opened on pre-war terms, war-damaged refineries in the Middle East are back to full production and Russia, whose refineries have been very successfully targeted by Ukraine, resumes exports of refined product, the market for refined products will be short of supply relative to demand.



While the US has claimed to have reopened the strait and says that volumes have been nearing pre-war levels, recent Iranian attacks on tankers transiting the strait – at least four and as many as seven have been targeted in the past week – have again reduced the flow of oil and its derivatives from the region. Related Article Analysis

US midterm elections America’s billionaires are turning their backs on Trump It’s also not just about flows. Before the war tanker rates to ship oil via the strait ranged from about $US30,000 a day to more than $US100,000, depending on the size of the tanker. They’re now over $US800,000 a day. Insuring a tanker used to cost about $US250,000 pre-war. Now, where it is available – a lot of insurers have stopped providing coverage – it can cost up to $US10 million for the larger ships. For those tankers avoiding the strait and taking longer routes to reach their end markets, there are additional operational costs.



All those new risks and costs are built into oil prices and will remain there unless and until there is a conclusive end to hostilities in the region and something akin to the pre-war norms for transiting the strait are in place. It would also take months, even years, for the damage to Middle Eastern refineries to be remedied. Before the war, the Saudis were the world’s second-largest producer of diesel and produced more than 3 million barrels a day of refined products, although about half of that output was devoted to its domestic market. Today its refined product volumes are less than 60 per cent of their pre-war levels. Soaring fuel prices are going to hurt Trump in the midterm elections. AP Releasing G7 stocks may provide temporary relief, but it doesn’t address that underlying shortfall of supply and, on the meantime, runs down the buffers available to deal with the potential for the future shocks that caused to reserves to be built.



Despite the release, the market for diesel could tighten further. Russia – once the world’s second-largest exporter behind the US, has banned diesel exports until at least the end of this month (more likely indefinitely) because of the damage Ukraine has inflicted on its refining infrastructure. Ukraine has vowed to intensify those attacks. China – the world’s second-largest consumer of oil and refined products behind the US – has also, again, stopped refined product exports. It was exporting about a million barrels a day before the war. More fundamentally, those refineries unaffected by the war – predominantly in the US – are operating at near capacity levels, or around 95 per cent of capacity. The refineries are experiencing massive margins and generating enormous profits, but don’t have the ability to expand production meaningfully and their inventories of refined product have been run down.



US refineries’ diesel inventories are at their lowest seasonal level since data on diesel stocks started being collected in 1982. With global demand for refined products having recovered somewhat from its nadirs after the outbreak of the war, supply isn’t capable of responding significantly. The release is a palliative for the deep wounds in the world’s oil markets caused by Trump’s war in the Middle East. The reserves release might temporarily close the gap, but it doesn’t resolve the underlying mismatch of supply and demand and creates the risk that, with depleted inventories, there’s less of a buffer to deal with a prolongation of the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine or some new threat to energy supplies. That suggests oil, gasoline and diesel prices will remain higher for longer. It is, of course, the refined product prices that matter – no-one pours crude into their tanks.



A survey of US oil and gas executives by the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas last month found that nearly half of them – 48 per cent – expected it would take more than a year for diesel prices to return to last year’s levels. Trump’s anxiety about the impact of the near-record prices for gasoline and diesel in the US is well-founded. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump’s ‘betrayal’ of America’s heartland will cost him The higher costs of gasoline and, in particular, diesel – because its fuels trucks, freight trains, ships, tractors, construction machinery and has a host of other industrial applications are starting to feed into goods prices – are feeding into the costs of end-products to customers and the inflation rate. Because of the war, US farmers are experiencing both elevated diesel and (because the Middle East has been a major fertiliser producers) fertiliser prices. The backlash against the increase in the cost of living and doing business is spreading throughout America, hence Trump’s dismal personal ratings and the prospect of big gains for the Democrats next month.



If sustained at current levels, those higher input costs will both lift the inflation rate and reduce economic activity, risking stagflation. Even if Trump’s success in “convincing” the rest of the G7 that releasing oil and diesel reserves was in their best interests, the impact so late in the political cycle is likely to be immaterial to the outcome of the elections and the impact of the war in the Middle East on domestic gasoline and diesel prices will still be there and still discolouring the second half of his term as president. World.title: Couple buys $1,825,000 Erskineville house as vendor cuts reserve price
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Couple buys $1,825,000 Erskineville house as vendor cuts reserve price Carmen Forward October 5, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An engaged couple paid $1,825,000 for an Erskineville house at auction the day before their wedding, when the vendor cut their reserve by $25,000 to sell. The three-bedroom family home at 33 Eve Street had a private courtyard, a loft level bedroom, and skylights. The property was one of 521 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 53 per cent from 307 reported results throughout the week and 87 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The volume of homes for sale was low due to the long weekend, the first weekend after the Reserve Bank’s decision to lift interest rates to 4.6 per cent.



Two parties registered, both looking to upsize and both participated. The underbidders were another young couple. Related Article Auctions Inner west art deco apartment sells for $900k to Bondi couple Bidding opened at the home’s guide of $1.7 million and several small rises increased the price to $1.75 million. Then the highest bidder, a couple to be married the next day, bid against themselves by $75,000. The vendor adjusted their $1.85 million reserve down and the home sold under the hammer for $1,825,000. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



Ray White’s Shaun Stoker said the buyers had been looking for over three months. “I’m finding [that] if buyers don’t see value, they’re not acting ... Owners have to be aligned with the buyer to get interest.” Stoker’s colleague Moira Verheijen said the couple had each purchased their first property from her separately before purchasing their first home as a couple on the eve of their wedding. “It’s very nice when you go on a journey with people over 10 years of your career, it’s … a real privilege.”



The vendors have purchased in Annandale and are upsizing. The property last traded for $1.41 million in 2020, records show. In Liverpool a three-bedroom house at 271 Memorial Avenue that was purchased in March this year for $1,505,000 sold for $1,325,000. The property had an existing lease in place and the buyer is keeping the tenants on. Four parties registered and all four were active. Bidding opened at $1.1 million and jumped to $1.2 million quickly before selling for $25,000 below its $1.35 million reserve for $1,325,000.



Selling agent Michael Sleiman from First National Real Estate Daystar said it is the, “worst market I have experienced in my 30 to 40 years of real estate.” Related Article Auctions Young couple pays $1.65 million for charming Stanmore terrace “This makes the GFC, COVID, Royal Commission, 13 rate rises look like a lovely … sunny day compared to this market.” Sleiman said the biggest impact has been the “the negative gear and capital gains changes.” He added that he “felt sorry” for his vendor and that he had even “tried many times to convince him not to sell.”



“But in the end, it was a good result for him because it means he can move on now.” In Rhodes, a two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment with sweeping city skyline views at 2306/7 Rider Boulevard sold for $1,309,000. Two registered, both interested parties were young professionals and both were active. Bidding opened at $1.18 million and rose in mostly $10,000 increments until it sold for $1000 above its $1,308,000 reserve.



The initial guided range of $1.3 million to $1.4 million was adjusted down a week prior to auction to $1,231,000 due to a $1.23 million offer received. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Moguls behind Kylie Jenner-endorsed sunglasses brand list Byron Shire mansion Selling agent Rex Sam from Vue Property Estate Agents said, “Even with this recent rate rise, the buyers that I’m working with are still looking to purchase.” Sam doesn’t think the interest rate has affected family home buyers. “Good home, good location, presented nicely. They’ll always have demand.”



The vendor is upsizing to a house. The flat last traded for $825,000 in 2013, records show. Chief economist at AMP Dr Shane Oliver said Domain’s clearance rate of 53 per cent for Sydney is a “soft outcome”. “You’ve always got to be a little bit cautious in interpreting data on the long weekends ... But even allowing for the long weekend, these are still fairly weak results in the numbers [compared to] a year ago,” he said. Oliver predicts we won’t see rate cuts until the second half of next year.

World.title: ‘More arrests are on the table’: Qantas hack gang member nabbed
World.content:
TechnologyCybersecurity ‘More arrests are on the table’: Qantas hack gang member nabbed David Swan October 5, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A suspected key player in the hacking alliance behind the Qantas data breach has been detained in Jordan and is cooperating with the FBI. Saif al-Din Khader, known online as Rey, was taken into custody by Jordanian authorities last week, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters. Qantas was hacked in June 2025, when a caller posing as IT support persuaded a worker at an offshore call centre to connect a Salesforce customer platform to a malicious data-extraction tool. Australian Financial Review. Khader is helping the FBI and police around the world track down other members of ShinyHunters, two of the sources told the news agency. ShinyHunters is the extortion gang that claimed last month to have stolen data on every FBI employee. One source said Khader was walking investigators through his electronic devices and digital correspondence. In November last year, US security journalist Brian Krebs identified Khader as one of the administrators of Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters. It is a loose alliance of mostly English-speaking hacking gangs, including ShinyHunters.



Khader told Krebs at the time he had been trying to leave the group and had been working with law enforcement since June 2025. ShinyHunters continued its attacks into this year, claiming break-ins at Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar Games and education platform Canvas. Cybersecurity researchers linked Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters to the leak of 5.7 million Qantas customers’ personal details on the dark web last October. Neither Reuters nor any law enforcement agency has alleged Khader was personally involved in the Qantas attack. The AFP and Qantas were contacted for comment. View post on X The FBI declined to comment to Reuters on any arrest abroad, but said it had already worked with partners to arrest multiple subjects and would “spare no resource in bringing each of the responsible individuals to justice”. FBI director Kash Patel went further, signalling the investigation was widening. “FBI teams are working new leads RIGHT NOW,” he posted on X on Wednesday. “More arrests are on the table.”



Patel’s post followed confirmation by Dutch police that a 24-year-old Amsterdam man had been arrested in September in an investigation into ShinyHunters. He has been identified by Krebs and others as Pepijn van der Stap, a hacker convicted in the Netherlands in 2023 over a string of data thefts and extortions. ShinyHunters has said van der Stap had no association with the group. The gang claimed on September 22 that it had hacked the FBI in retaliation for an advisory accusing it of exaggerating its access to victims’ systems. It gave the bureau a week to withdraw the advisory. Since then, its dark website has disappeared. In its most recent email to Reuters, the group said it wanted “no further escalation” with the FBI. Police have struggled to prosecute members of related groups such as Lapsus$ and Scattered Spider, Reuters has reported. Many of the hackers are young, the groups are chaotic and informal, and victims often decline to help investigators. Qantas was hacked in June 2025, when a caller posing as IT support persuaded a worker at an offshore call centre to connect a Salesforce customer platform to a malicious data-extraction tool. When Salesforce refused a ransom demand, the hackers published the data. Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind. Nine



Most records held names, email addresses and frequent flyer details. About 1.7 million also included home or business addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers and meal preferences. Qantas said passport and credit card details were not on the system. Related Article Exclusive

Cybersecurity Qantas says no to ransom. 96 per cent of Australian businesses say yes In July, Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind declined to open a formal investigation into the airline. She said the evidence did not support the likelihood that Qantas had breached privacy law. Serious or repeated breaches of the Privacy Act can attract penalties of more than $50 million, and the watchdog has left the door open. “It is still open to the commissioner to commence an investigation of Qantas with respect to these or other practices,” Kind said. Law firm Maurice Blackburn is also pursuing a proposed class action on behalf of customers whose personal information was stolen and published online. Maurice Blackburn was contacted for comment.
